explanation.pearls: A falling serum phosphate in the first week of refeeding is the earliest marker of refeeding syndrome and appears before any clinical change, so it is replaced actively rather than watched while feeding continues.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Eating Disorders

subtopic_detail: First line treatment for chronic insomnia disorder in a patient requesting a hypnotic
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 46 year old accountant has had trouble sleeping for eight months. He takes about 90 minutes to fall asleep, wakes at 3 am and lies awake for an hour or more, and this happens five or six nights a week. He is irritable and unproductive at work.

He has started going to bed at 8.30 pm to give himself the best chance, spends time in bed reading work emails, and naps for an hour most afternoons. He drinks two coffees before midday and no alcohol. He denies low mood, anhedonia, worry or panic, and he does not snore, has no restless sensations in his legs and his partner has seen no breathing pauses. His thyroid function and full blood count taken last week were normal. He asks directly for a script for zolpidem.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, Mallampati class 1 airway, normal mental state examination with euthymic mood and full affect
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and full blood count within normal limits; Epworth Sleepiness Scale score 6 of 24

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe zolpidem nightly for four weeks with a plan to taper it after that period
options.rationale: A benzodiazepine receptor agonist gives short term benefit only, carries risks of tolerance, falls and complex sleep behaviours, and is reserved for brief use when non drug treatment is unavailable or has failed (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia including sleep restriction and stimulus control
options.rationale: Structured behavioural therapy is the first line treatment for chronic insomnia disorder and directly targets the excessive time in bed, the daytime napping and the use of the bed for work that are perpetuating his pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Prescribe low dose amitriptyline at night and review the effect on his sleep in six weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antidepressants are sometimes used off label but the evidence in primary insomnia is weak and anticholinergic effects and daytime sedation are common (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange an overnight polysomnogram before making any decision about treatment for him
options.rationale: A sleep study is indicated when there are features of apnoea, periodic limb movements or narcolepsy, and none is present with a normal airway and an Epworth score of 6 (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Start an antidepressant at a standard dose and review his sleep and mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Insomnia is frequently the presenting feature of depression, but he has no low mood, anhedonia or other depressive features on mental state examination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia disorder is diagnosed when difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep occurs at least three nights a week for at least three months with daytime consequences, despite adequate opportunity to sleep. It is maintained less by the original trigger than by the compensatory behaviours that follow, particularly spending longer in bed, napping and using the bed for wakeful activity, which weaken the association between bed and sleep. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia targets exactly these mechanisms through sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive work on catastrophic beliefs about sleep and relaxation training, and its benefit persists after treatment ends unlike that of hypnotics. Digital and group programs make it deliverable in Australian primary care, and hypnotics are best reserved for short courses in acute situational insomnia.
key_points: Three nights a week for three months with daytime impairment defines the disorder
Excessive time in bed, napping and working in bed perpetuate the problem
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and its gains outlast treatment
Screen for depression, apnoea and restless legs before labelling insomnia primary
Hypnotics are for short term use in acute insomnia, not chronic disorder
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction therapy initially shortens time in bed to match actual sleep time with a floor of about five hours, and the transient increase in daytime sleepiness in the first fortnight is the reason patients must be warned before they drive.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing iron replacement before dopaminergic therapy in restless legs syndrome
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 39 year old woman who describes a crawling discomfort deep in both calves every evening. She says she has to get up and walk around to make it go away, that it is worst when she sits still after dinner, and that it settles completely while she is moving.

It has been present for a year and is now delaying her sleep by two hours most nights. She is a vegetarian with heavy periods. Her mood is normal, she takes no antidepressant or antipsychotic, and her renal function is normal. Neurological examination of the legs is normal with preserved reflexes, power and sensation, and there is no calf tenderness or swelling.

data_table.Examination: Normal lower limb power, tone, reflexes and sensation, no oedema or calf tenderness, no peripheral pulse deficit
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165); ferritin 22 mcg/L (15-200); transferrin saturation 14 per cent (15-45); urea, electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Start pramipexole at a low nightly dose and titrate it against her symptom response
options.rationale: A dopamine agonist is effective but risks augmentation with earlier and more intense symptoms over time, so it follows correction of iron status rather than preceding it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Begin oral iron replacement aiming for a ferritin above 75 mcg/L and reassess symptoms
options.rationale: Brain iron deficiency drives the syndrome and can exist with a ferritin that is technically within range, so replacement to a target well above the laboratory lower limit is the first intervention (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Prescribe gabapentin at night and review both her sleep and her symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: An alpha 2 delta ligand is a legitimate treatment particularly where pain is prominent, but it does not correct the iron deficiency that is the reversible driver here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies of both lower limbs before starting any specific treatment
options.rationale: Nerve conduction testing is for suspected peripheral neuropathy, which produces sensory loss or reflex change rather than a movement relieved urge with normal neurological examination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Prescribe temazepam at night for four weeks and review her sleep pattern after that time
options.rationale: A hypnotic may shorten sleep latency but leaves the sensory urge untreated and risks dependence in a chronic condition (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome is a clinical diagnosis resting on an urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensation, worse at rest, relieved by movement and worse in the evening or at night. Central nervous system iron deficiency is the best established mechanism, and peripheral ferritin correlates imperfectly with brain iron, which is why replacement is recommended when ferritin is below about 75 mcg/L or transferrin saturation is below 20 per cent even though those values are within the standard laboratory range. Secondary causes worth excluding at the same visit include pregnancy, renal failure and drugs, particularly antidepressants, antipsychotics, lithium and sedating antihistamines. Dopamine agonists remain effective but carry the risk of augmentation, in which symptoms appear earlier in the day and spread to the arms, so alpha 2 delta ligands are increasingly preferred when drug treatment is needed.
key_points: Urge to move, worse at rest, relieved by movement, worse at night is the diagnostic tetrad
Replace iron if ferritin is below 75 mcg/L or transferrin saturation below 20 per cent
Review antidepressants, antipsychotics and sedating antihistamines as contributors
Dopamine agonists cause augmentation with long term use
Alpha 2 delta ligands such as gabapentin are an alternative when drug therapy is needed
explanation.pearls: A ferritin of 22 mcg/L is reported as normal by most Australian laboratories but is well below the 75 mcg/L threshold used in restless legs syndrome, and treating to that higher target resolves symptoms in a substantial proportion without any dopaminergic drug.

subtopic_detail: Detecting and responding to disordered gambling presenting as an unexplained financial and mood crisis
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 34 year old man presents asking for a mental health care plan for stress. He has taken out a second personal loan, has been borrowing from family with vague explanations, and has stopped seeing friends. He has lost 6 kg and sleeps four hours a night.

When you ask what the money went on, he becomes evasive, then says he has been using an online sports betting app since it was advertised during the football and that he has been chasing his losses for about a year. He drinks two standard drinks a week and uses no other substances. He says he has thought that his family would be better off without him but has no plan and does not want to die.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, oriented with intact cognition, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start an antidepressant for his low mood and review both symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants have a role for comorbid depression but no established benefit for the gambling itself, and prescribing alone leaves the behaviour and the escalating debt untouched (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Arrange an urgent psychiatric admission because of the passive suicidal thoughts he described
options.rationale: Admission is warranted for intent, plan, means or an inability to stay safe, and passive thoughts without intent in an engaged patient are managed with a safety plan and rapid outpatient follow up (Source: RANZCP: Deliberate Self Harm).

options.text: Reassure him that the debt is the problem and refer him only to a financial counsellor
options.rationale: Financial counselling is a valuable component but treating the debt as the disorder ignores the behavioural condition that generated it and the suicide risk that accompanies it (Source: Gambling Help Online Australia).

options.text: Make a safety plan, refer for gambling specific psychological therapy, and discuss self exclusion
options.rationale: Disordered gambling carries a high suicide risk that must be addressed first, cognitive behavioural therapy is the treatment with the best evidence, and self exclusion from betting platforms removes access in the way that supports early abstinence (Source: Gambling Help Online Australia; RANZCP: Deliberate Self Harm).

options.text: Prescribe naltrexone at an anticraving dose and review his gambling behaviour in six weeks
options.rationale: Naltrexone has modest evidence in gambling disorder and is considered as an adjunct after psychological treatment has been organised rather than as an opening move (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is under detected in Australian primary care because patients rarely name it, presenting instead with stress, insomnia, relationship breakdown or unexplained debt. The features that identify it are preoccupation, escalating stakes, chasing losses, lying to conceal the extent of involvement and jeopardising relationships or employment, and the shift to online and in play sports betting has made concealment easier and losses faster. It carries one of the highest suicide rates of any behavioural condition, so risk assessment and a safety plan come first at the visit where it is disclosed. Treatment combines gambling specific cognitive behavioural therapy, financial counselling and practical access restriction through self exclusion registers and app blocking, with pharmacotherapy such as naltrexone considered as an adjunct.
key_points: Ask directly about gambling when debt, secrecy and social withdrawal appear together
Chasing losses and concealment are the two most useful screening features
Suicide risk is high and assessment precedes any other intervention
Cognitive behavioural therapy specific to gambling has the strongest evidence
Self exclusion and financial counselling are practical components of the plan
explanation.pearls: Australia has a national self exclusion register for online wagering that blocks a person from all licensed Australian betting services at once, and registering the patient at the consultation is often more effective than any single prescription.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing a stressor linked disorder from major depression when function is preserved
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 51 year old woman was made redundant five weeks ago after 20 years with the same employer. Since then she has felt flat and tearful, worries about money and sleeps poorly in the first half of the night. She asks whether she should start an antidepressant.

She still walks the dog daily, enjoys her book club and laughed several times during the consultation when talking about her grandchildren. Her appetite and weight are unchanged, and she describes no diurnal variation in mood, early morning waking or psychomotor slowing. She denies thoughts of self harm, and neither she nor her family has ever been treated for a mood disorder. She scores 11 on the Patient Health Questionnaire 9. She is applying for jobs and has an interview next week.

data_table.Examination: Tearful at times but reactive affect, normal speech rate, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 11 of 27; thyroid stimulating hormone and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start sertraline at an antidepressant dose and review her symptoms again in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants show little benefit over placebo for stressor linked symptoms of this severity and commit her to months of treatment for a reaction that is likely to resolve as circumstances change (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy assessment given the severity of her low mood score
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is for severe, psychotic, catatonic or treatment resistant depression, none of which is present in a woman with reactive affect and preserved function (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Prescribe temazepam for her sleep and review the situation once she has found new work
options.rationale: A hypnotic addresses one symptom, risks dependence and offers nothing for the adjustment process that is driving the presentation (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Diagnose major depressive disorder and refer for psychological therapy plus an antidepressant
options.rationale: Preserved reactivity, intact pleasure in activities, unchanged appetite and no biological features argue against a major depressive episode despite the questionnaire score (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Offer structured psychological support with a mental health care plan and review in two weeks
options.rationale: Symptoms tied to an identifiable stressor with retained reactivity and function are best managed with psychological support and active review, which also detects the minority who progress to a depressive episode (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

explanation.summary: Adjustment disorder describes emotional or behavioural symptoms arising within three months of an identifiable stressor that are out of proportion to it or impair function, and it is distinguished from major depression by preserved mood reactivity, retained capacity for pleasure and the absence of the biological features of melancholia. Symptom questionnaires such as the Patient Health Questionnaire 9 quantify distress but do not make a diagnosis, and a moderate score in the setting of a recent loss should prompt a careful history rather than an automatic prescription. The evidence for antidepressants in adjustment disorder is weak, whereas psychological support, problem solving and practical assistance address the stressor itself. Active review matters because a minority do go on to meet criteria for a depressive episode, and the transition is easily missed if the patient is discharged after a single visit.
key_points: Adjustment disorder follows an identifiable stressor within three months
Preserved reactivity and retained pleasure argue against major depression
Questionnaire scores measure severity but do not establish the diagnosis
Antidepressants have weak evidence in stressor linked presentations
Scheduled review detects the minority who progress to a depressive episode
explanation.pearls: Anhedonia that persists even in the patient's favourite activity is a far better discriminator of major depression than any questionnaire score, because a person with adjustment disorder still brightens when the subject changes.

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy decision for nicotine dependence acquired through vaping in an adolescent
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 16 year old girl attends alone and asks for help stopping vaping. She has used a disposable nicotine vape daily for 18 months, now vapes within ten minutes of waking, and gets headaches and irritability by mid morning at school if she does not use it.

She has tried to stop three times, the longest for two days. She has never smoked cigarettes. She has no psychiatric history, no low mood or suicidal thoughts, takes no medication and is not pregnant. You have assessed her as a mature minor who understands the treatment being discussed. She scores 7 on a nicotine dependence questionnaire.

data_table.Examination: Normal cardiorespiratory examination, normal mental state examination, no oral lesions
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative; no other investigations indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Offer behavioural support with nicotine replacement therapy and arrange structured follow up
options.rationale: Withdrawal within an hour of waking indicates significant dependence, and combining behavioural support with nicotine replacement is the recommended approach for a dependent adolescent (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start varenicline at the standard adult dose and review her tolerance of it in two weeks
options.rationale: Varenicline is effective in adults but is not established in people under 18, so it is not the first choice in an adolescent who has not tried replacement therapy (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Advise abrupt cessation with behavioural support alone and review her progress in four weeks
options.rationale: Behavioural support alone suits low dependence, but three failed attempts with early morning use and withdrawal symptoms indicate she needs pharmacological help as well (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation).

options.text: Recommend switching to a lower nicotine concentration vape and gradually reducing over time
options.rationale: Continued vaping maintains dependence and product nicotine labelling is unreliable, so this substitutes an unregulated device for a therapeutic one with measured dosing (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation).

options.text: Start bupropion at a cessation dose and review both her mood and her cravings in two weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is second line even in adults, lowers the seizure threshold and is not recommended for adolescents (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Adolescent nicotine dependence acquired through vaping is now a routine presentation in Australian general practice, and the products involved often deliver nicotine salts at concentrations well above those of a cigarette, producing rapid and severe dependence. Time to first use after waking is the most practical bedside measure of dependence, and use within 30 minutes indicates that behavioural support alone is unlikely to succeed. Nicotine replacement therapy is the pharmacotherapy with the best safety data in young people, and combination therapy pairing a patch for background craving with a short acting form for breakthrough urges outperforms either alone. Varenicline and bupropion are not established below the age of 18, and continuing to vape at a lower stated concentration is unreliable because labelled nicotine content frequently does not match the actual content.
key_points: Time to first use after waking is the most useful measure of nicotine dependence
Nicotine replacement therapy is the preferred pharmacotherapy in adolescents
Combination patch plus short acting replacement beats either alone
Varenicline and bupropion are not established under 18 years of age
Labelled nicotine concentration on vaping products is often inaccurate
explanation.pearls: A patient who vapes within 30 minutes of waking has dependence severe enough that behavioural support alone rarely succeeds, and that single question is more informative than the number of puffs or pods per day.

subtopic_detail: Separating persistent bereavement related distress from a depressive episode more than a year after a death
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a consultation clinic. A 62 year old woman was referred 15 months after her husband died suddenly. She thinks about him for most of the day, keeps his clothes laid out and his phone charged, and cannot bring herself to enter their bedroom. She says she feels that part of her died with him and that she has no idea who she is now.

She has stopped seeing the friends they had together because being with couples is unbearable, and she has not returned to the volunteering she loved. She eats and sleeps reasonably and her weight is unchanged. She feels intense yearning that comes in waves triggered by reminders rather than a constant flat mood, and she still laughs with her granddaughter. Her guilt centres on things she wishes she had said to him rather than on her own worthlessness, and she denies psychomotor slowing or thoughts of self harm.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect with tearfulness on discussing her husband, normal speech and psychomotor activity, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start mirtazapine at night and review her sleep, appetite and mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Mirtazapine targets the appetite and sleep disturbance of a depressive episode, and both are preserved here while the core problem is persistent yearning and identity disruption (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Refer for grief focused psychotherapy addressing avoidance and restoration of daily roles
options.rationale: Yearning and preoccupation persisting beyond 12 months with identity disruption, avoidance of reminders and role withdrawal define prolonged grief disorder, and targeted psychotherapy is the treatment with the best evidence (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders; BMJ Best Practice: Grief).

options.text: Reassure her that grief has no timetable and review her again in six months if needed
options.rationale: Normalising is right for uncomplicated grief, but symptoms persisting beyond a year with functional withdrawal identify a treatable disorder rather than an expected trajectory (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Start an antidepressant with a mood stabiliser and review her response again in six weeks
options.rationale: Combination pharmacotherapy is for treatment resistant or bipolar depression and is unjustified in a woman with no depressive episode and no history of elevated mood (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Arrange cognitive testing and neuroimaging to investigate her sense of altered identity
options.rationale: The altered sense of self here is the identity disruption characteristic of persistent grief, not a cognitive deficit, and her cognition is intact on examination (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder entered the main diagnostic classifications recently and describes intense yearning or preoccupation with a deceased person persisting for at least 12 months in adults, accompanied by features such as identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, intense loneliness and difficulty re engaging with life. It is separated from a major depressive episode by the object of the distress, since grief comes in waves triggered by reminders with preserved capacity for pleasure elsewhere, whereas depression produces pervasive low mood, guilt about the self, anhedonia across domains and biological disturbance. The distinction is practical rather than academic because antidepressants have not shown benefit for the grief symptoms themselves, whereas structured grief focused psychotherapy targeting avoidance and restoration of roles does. The two can coexist, so a depressive episode should be actively screened for and treated on its own merits if present.
key_points: The 12 month threshold in adults distinguishes prolonged grief disorder from acute grief
Identity disruption, avoidance of reminders and role withdrawal are core features
Grief comes in waves with preserved reactivity whereas depression is pervasive
Guilt in grief concerns the deceased whereas depressive guilt concerns the self
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms antidepressants for the grief symptoms
explanation.pearls: Keeping a deceased partner's possessions untouched while avoiding the room they are in is the combination of holding on and avoidance that distinguishes prolonged grief disorder, and both behaviours are direct targets of grief focused psychotherapy.

subtopic_detail: Excessive daytime sleepiness with emotionally triggered weakness misattributed to a mood disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar. A 19 year old university student is referred with two years of overwhelming daytime sleepiness that a previous doctor treated as depression, without benefit from two adequate antidepressant trials.

He falls asleep in lectures and once at the dinner table, and says a 15 minute nap leaves him refreshed for a couple of hours. When he laughs hard at a joke his knees buckle and his jaw sags for a few seconds while he stays fully aware of what is happening. On waking he sometimes cannot move for half a minute and has seen figures at the end of his bed while otherwise awake. His mood is reactive, he enjoys his sport and friends, and he denies anhedonia, guilt or suicidal thoughts. His body mass index is 23 kg/m2, he does not snore and his Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 19.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, Mallampati class 1 airway, reactive affect with no depressive cognitions
data_table.Investigations: Epworth Sleepiness Scale 19 of 24; full blood count, iron studies and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to a serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor and review his energy in six weeks
options.rationale: A third antidepressant continues to treat a depressive episode that is not present, given reactive mood, preserved enjoyment and absent depressive cognitions (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Prescribe modafinil for daytime sleepiness and review his alertness again in four weeks
options.rationale: Wake promoting therapy is a mainstay of treatment but is started after the diagnosis is confirmed, since prior stimulant exposure confounds the sleep latency testing (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Refer for polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day
options.rationale: Sleepiness with refreshing naps, emotionally triggered loss of muscle tone with retained awareness, sleep paralysis and hypnopompic hallucinations point to narcolepsy, and overnight study followed by daytime latency testing is the diagnostic pathway (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to investigate the episodes of collapse he describes
options.rationale: Electroencephalography investigates atonic seizures, whose near pair feature is impaired awareness during the attack, whereas he remains fully aware throughout (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry at home and start positive airway pressure if it is abnormal
options.rationale: Home oximetry screens for sleep disordered breathing, which is unlikely with a normal body mass index, no snoring and an unobstructed airway (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy type 1 is caused by loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurones and typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood, which is exactly when depression is also common, so misdiagnosis is frequent and the average delay to correct diagnosis runs to years. The pentad is excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations and disrupted nocturnal sleep, and cataplexy is close to specific when it involves brief bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion with fully preserved awareness. Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography to exclude another cause of sleep disruption, followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day showing a short mean sleep latency with at least two episodes of rapid eye movement sleep occurring soon after sleep onset. Antidepressants must usually be withdrawn before the study because they suppress rapid eye movement sleep and can mask the diagnostic pattern.
key_points: Refreshing short naps distinguish narcolepsy from the unrefreshing sleepiness of depression
Cataplexy is emotionally triggered brief atonia with fully preserved awareness
Diagnosis is polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day
Antidepressants suppress rapid eye movement sleep and confound the latency test
Sleep paralysis and hypnopompic hallucinations complete the clinical picture
explanation.pearls: Antidepressants and stimulants generally need to be withdrawn about two weeks before a multiple sleep latency test, because rapid eye movement suppression can convert a diagnostic study into a normal one.

subtopic_detail: Mood and behavioural change from androgen misuse presenting as a primary psychiatric disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24 year old man brought by his partner because of four months of irritability, verbal aggression and jealous accusations. He has been sleeping five hours a night, feels unusually confident and has been training at the gym twice a day.

He has gained 9 kg of muscle in that time, has acne across his back and shoulders, and his partner has noticed tender swelling under both nipples. He denies grandiose delusions and there are no hallucinations or thought disorder. He drinks little and uses no illicit stimulants, and a urine drug screen for amphetamines, cocaine and cannabis is negative. There is no personal or family history of bipolar disorder. When asked specifically what he takes for training, he says only protein powder and a testosterone booster from an overseas website.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 152/94, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Marked muscle bulk, truncal acne, bilateral tender gynaecomastia, small testes, no tremor or hyperreflexia
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative for amphetamines, cocaine and cannabis; haematocrit 0.54 (0.40-0.52); alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 40); high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.7 mmol/L (greater than 1.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start olanzapine for the irritability and arrange psychiatric review again in two weeks
options.rationale: An antipsychotic treats the surface symptom while the driving exposure continues, and it adds metabolic harm to an already adverse lipid and cardiovascular profile (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start lithium for a first manic episode and arrange monitoring of his serum concentrations
options.rationale: A first manic episode is the near diagnosis here, but the absence of any family or personal history alongside physical signs of androgen excess points to a substance induced picture (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Refer for couples counselling to address the jealousy and review his mood in six weeks
options.rationale: Relationship work may help later, but attributing the change to interpersonal conflict misses a reversible physical cause with cardiovascular and hepatic consequences (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Take a targeted history of injectable androgen use and measure testosterone and gonadotrophins
options.rationale: Rapid muscle gain, acne, gynaecomastia, small testes, hypertension, raised haematocrit and suppressed high density lipoprotein indicate exogenous androgen use, and suppressed gonadotrophins with a high testosterone confirm it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Admit him involuntarily under the mental health act for assessment of his aggression
options.rationale: Involuntary assessment requires risk that cannot be managed voluntarily, and he is engaging with the consultation without threat or intent to harm (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

explanation.summary: Androgenic anabolic steroid use is common among young men training intensively and is rarely volunteered, because products bought online are described as supplements or boosters rather than as injectable hormones. The psychiatric presentation of irritability, aggression, reduced sleep need and grandiosity closely mimics a manic or mixed episode, and the discriminating information is physical rather than psychological: rapid lean mass gain, truncal acne, gynaecomastia from peripheral aromatisation, testicular atrophy, hypertension, polycythaemia, transaminase rise and suppressed high density lipoprotein cholesterol. Biochemically the picture is a high or supraphysiological testosterone with suppressed luteinising and follicle stimulating hormone, the reverse of the pattern seen in genuine hypogonadism. Management is cessation with support for the withdrawal depression that follows, monitoring of haematocrit, lipids and liver enzymes, and endocrine follow up because recovery of the gonadal axis can take many months.
key_points: Ask specifically about injectable androgens rather than about drugs in general
Gynaecomastia, acne, small testes and rapid muscle gain are the physical clues
High testosterone with suppressed gonadotrophins confirms an exogenous source
Polycythaemia, hypertension and low high density lipoprotein drive cardiovascular risk
Withdrawal depression after cessation carries a real suicide risk and needs follow up
explanation.pearls: A haematocrit above 0.54 in an androgen user is an indication for cessation and venesection, since the resulting hyperviscosity contributes directly to the strokes and myocardial infarctions seen in this group.

subtopic_detail: Treatment choice when attention symptoms and a chronic tic disorder coexist in a school aged child
stem:
You are the paediatric psychiatry registrar. A 9 year old boy has been assessed as meeting criteria for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with impairment at school and at home documented on teacher and parent rating scales.

For the past two years he has also had bouts of eye blinking and shoulder shrugging, and for the last eight months a repeated throat clearing sound. His mother says these wax and wane, are worse when he is tired or anxious, and that he can hold them back briefly at the cost of building tension. He is teased about the throat clearing. His growth, cardiovascular examination and sleep are normal, and there is no family history of sudden cardiac death. His mother has read that stimulants cause tics and does not want him to have one.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 104/64, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Intermittent eye blinking and shoulder shrugs during interview, audible throat clearing, normal cardiovascular examination, height and weight on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Teacher and parent rating scales in the clinical range for inattention and hyperactivity; electrocardiogram not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start guanfacine and provide behavioural intervention with review of both sets of symptoms
options.rationale: An alpha 2 adrenergic agonist treats the attention symptoms and reduces tic frequency at the same time, which suits a child whose two conditions coexist and whose mother declines a stimulant (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP: ADHD).

options.text: Start risperidone to suppress the tics and defer any treatment of the attention symptoms
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do suppress tics but carry weight gain, metabolic and movement risks and are reserved for severe tics after other options, while leaving the functional impairment untreated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Provide behavioural intervention alone and review both sets of symptoms in six months
options.rationale: Behavioural therapy is a genuine component and comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics works well, but documented impairment at school and home warrants treatment of the attention symptoms too (Source: RANZCP: ADHD).

options.text: Start atomoxetine and refer for comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics as well
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a reasonable non stimulant choice that is tic neutral, but it lacks the direct tic reducing effect of an alpha 2 agonist in a child with both conditions (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start methylphenidate at a low dose and stop it immediately if any tics become worse
options.rationale: Stimulants are not contraindicated by tics and trial data show no consistent worsening, but starting one against a clear parental objection undermines the adherence the treatment depends on (Source: RANZCP: ADHD).

explanation.summary: Chronic tic disorder and Tourette syndrome coexist with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in a large proportion of affected children, and in most cases the attention symptoms cause more functional impairment than the tics themselves. The long standing teaching that stimulants cause or worsen tics has not been borne out by randomised evidence, and stimulants remain usable where tics coexist, but where a family is reluctant or the tics are themselves troubling, an alpha 2 adrenergic agonist such as guanfacine or clonidine treats both problems with a single agent. Tics characteristically wax and wane, are preceded by a premonitory urge, can be suppressed briefly at the cost of mounting tension, and worsen with fatigue and anxiety, all of which distinguishes them from stereotypies or seizures. Antipsychotics are effective tic suppressants but their metabolic and extrapyramidal burden confines them to severe or refractory cases.
key_points: Attention symptoms usually cause more impairment than the tics themselves
Alpha 2 agonists treat both attention symptoms and tics with one agent
Randomised evidence does not support stimulants causing or worsening tics
Premonitory urge with brief suppressibility identifies a tic rather than a stereotypy
Antipsychotics are reserved for severe or refractory tics
explanation.pearls: Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics teaches a competing response to the premonitory urge and matches antipsychotic efficacy for mild to moderate tics without any metabolic cost.

subtopic_detail: Dosing strategy for a serotonergic antidepressant in cyclical premenstrual mood symptoms
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 31 year old woman describes irritability, tearfulness and a sense of being out of control that starts about six days before each period and lifts within two days of bleeding starting. She has snapped at her children and nearly resigned from her job during these episodes.

She has kept a daily symptom chart for three consecutive cycles which shows a clear symptom free interval from day 4 to day 16 of each cycle. Her cycles are regular at 28 days. She has no depressive or anxiety symptoms outside the premenstrual window, no history of a depressive episode and no thyroid disease. She uses condoms for contraception and does not want to start a hormonal method.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic and reactive on the day of review, which is day 9 of her cycle, with normal mental state examination
data_table.Investigations: Three cycles of prospective daily symptom rating showing a symptom free follicular phase; thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Prescribe a serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken only from ovulation until menstruation starts
options.rationale: Luteal phase only dosing is as effective as continuous treatment in this condition because the response is rapid rather than taking weeks, and it halves total drug exposure (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Prescribe a serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken continuously every day of the cycle instead
options.rationale: Continuous dosing is equally effective and is preferred when symptoms extend outside the luteal phase or cycles are irregular, neither of which applies to her charted pattern (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Prescribe oral micronised progesterone during the luteal phase of each menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Luteal progesterone has repeatedly failed to outperform placebo in this condition and can itself provoke the mood symptoms in susceptible women (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual Syndrome).

options.text: Prescribe a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back oestrogen and progestogen
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression is effective but is a late line option because of bone loss and menopausal symptoms, used only after serotonergic and hormonal treatments have failed (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual Syndrome).

options.text: Prescribe a low dose benzodiazepine taken as required during the premenstrual week only
options.rationale: Intermittent anxiolytics blunt the irritability but carry dependence risk with repeated monthly use and are not a first line treatment (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is diagnosed on at least two cycles of prospective daily symptom ratings showing marked mood symptoms confined to the luteal phase with a symptom free follicular interval, which is what separates it from a mood or anxiety disorder that simply worsens premenstrually. Serotonergic antidepressants are first line and work quite differently here from their use in depression, producing benefit within a day or two through a neurosteroid mediated mechanism rather than over weeks. That rapid onset is what makes luteal phase only dosing possible, given from ovulation until menstruation begins, with efficacy equal to continuous treatment and roughly half the drug exposure and adverse effect burden. Continuous dosing is preferred when cycles are irregular, when symptoms spill outside the luteal phase, or when a coexisting depressive or anxiety disorder is present.
key_points: Prospective daily charting over at least two cycles is required for the diagnosis
A genuinely symptom free follicular phase separates it from premenstrual exacerbation
Serotonergic antidepressants act within days in this condition, not weeks
Luteal phase only dosing matches continuous dosing for efficacy
Ovarian suppression is a late line option because of bone and menopausal effects
explanation.pearls: Because the response is rapid rather than cumulative, discontinuation symptoms are uncommon when a serotonergic antidepressant used only in the luteal phase is stopped abruptly at the onset of menstruation each cycle.

subtopic_detail: Choosing between light therapy and pharmacotherapy in recurrent winter pattern depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a clinic in Hobart. A 29 year old woman has had four episodes of low mood, each beginning in late May and remitting by early October, with full return to normal function over summer in every year. She is now three weeks into this year's episode.

During episodes she sleeps ten hours and still feels unrefreshed, craves carbohydrate and has gained 5 kg each winter. She has never had an episode outside these months, has never been elevated, and there is no seasonal shift work or travel. She responded to sertraline two winters ago but stopped it because of sexual side effects and says she will not take it again. Her thyroid function and full blood count are normal, and her vitamin D is 58 nmol per litre.

data_table.Examination: Mildly slowed speech, reactive affect, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and full blood count within normal limits; serum 25 hydroxyvitamin D 58 nmol/L (50-150)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to recommend?

options.text: Prescribe high dose vitamin D supplementation and review her mood again in six weeks
options.rationale: Vitamin D supplementation has not shown antidepressant benefit in trials and her level is already within the reference range, so this delays effective treatment (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Start bright light therapy each morning with review of her response after two weeks
options.rationale: Morning bright light is a first line treatment for winter pattern depression with response rates comparable to antidepressants within one to two weeks, and it avoids the adverse effect that caused her to stop medication (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders; BMJ Best Practice: Seasonal Affective Disorder).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Seasonal Affective Disorder

options.text: Start lithium as a mood stabiliser given the regular recurrence of her mood episodes
options.rationale: Regular recurrence is not bipolarity, and lithium is not indicated without a history of elevated mood or of recurrent depression resistant to standard treatment (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Restart sertraline at the dose that worked before and manage the side effects as they arise
options.rationale: Re prescribing an agent the patient has explicitly declined for a tolerability reason predicts poor adherence, and an equally effective alternative without that effect is available (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Start agomelatine at night and review her sleep pattern and mood again in four weeks
options.rationale: Agomelatine has a melatonergic mechanism of theoretical appeal here but weaker evidence in this pattern, and it requires liver function monitoring that light therapy does not (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Depression with a seasonal pattern is a specifier applied to recurrent major depression when episodes begin and remit at characteristic times of year across at least two consecutive years, with seasonal episodes substantially outnumbering non seasonal ones over the lifetime. The winter pattern is distinguished by atypical features, namely hypersomnia, increased appetite with carbohydrate craving and weight gain, in contrast to the insomnia and weight loss of melancholic depression. Bright light therapy delivered in the morning is first line with efficacy comparable to antidepressants and a response typically evident within one to two weeks, and its main adverse effects are headache, eye strain and occasional switching to elevated mood in people with bipolar disorder. Latitude matters in Australia, and the condition is meaningfully more prevalent in Tasmania than in the tropical north, which is worth remembering when a patient's episodes track their move south.
key_points: The specifier requires a seasonal pattern across at least two consecutive years
Hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and weight gain define the winter pattern
Morning bright light therapy is first line and works within one to two weeks
Screen for a bipolar history because light can precipitate elevated mood
Prevalence rises with latitude and is higher in Tasmania than in northern Australia
explanation.pearls: Bright light therapy is delivered as 10000 lux for about 30 minutes within an hour of waking, and shifting the session to the evening loses most of the benefit because the phase advancing effect depends on morning timing.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Seasonal Affective Disorder

subtopic_detail: Acute assessment of volatile substance use in an adolescent and the hazard of catecholamine provocation
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 15 year old boy is brought in by ambulance after being found in a park unsteady, giggling and slurring his words. Paramedics found aerosol cans nearby and noted a chemical smell on his breath. Twenty minutes later he is drowsy but rousable and oriented.

There is a rash of small red spots around his mouth and nose and his clothing smells of solvent. His breath alcohol is zero and a urine drug screen is negative for amphetamines, opioids, benzodiazepines and cannabis. He becomes agitated when the nursing staff try to attach the monitoring leads and wants to leave. His mother has been contacted and is on her way.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112, blood pressure 124/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Perioral erythematous rash, solvent odour, dysarthria and gait ataxia, pupils 4 mm and reactive, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Breath alcohol zero; urine drug screen negative; capillary glucose 5.4 mmol/L (4.0-7.8); electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with normal QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intramuscular droperidol for the agitation and repeat the dose if he remains unsettled
options.rationale: Sedation for agitation is standard in many intoxications, but here calm handling comes first because the myocardium is sensitised and both the struggle and the drug add cardiac risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Give intravenous flumazenil to reverse the sedation and reassess his conscious state
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine sedation, and the screen is negative while the clinical picture and odour point to an inhaled hydrocarbon (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Give activated charcoal now and admit him to the short stay unit for overnight observation
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind inhaled volatile hydrocarbons and adds aspiration risk in a drowsy patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Nurse him calmly in a quiet area with cardiac monitoring and supplemental oxygen as needed
options.rationale: Inhaled hydrocarbons sensitise the myocardium to catecholamines so that fright or exertion can precipitate ventricular arrhythmia, and minimising stimulation with cardiac monitoring is the specific management (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology; Poisons Information Centre Australia).

options.text: Discharge him to his mother once he is fully alert with advice to see his own doctor
options.rationale: Discharge without a period of monitoring, a review of the electrolytes and renal function and a plan for follow up misses both the cardiac window and the chance to intervene (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia).

explanation.summary: Volatile substance use, most often of butane, propane and toluene from aerosols, lighter refills and glues, produces a rapid alcohol like intoxication that clears within an hour or two, so the diagnosis rests on the history, the solvent odour and the perioral rash rather than on a drug screen, which does not detect these agents. The critical pharmacology is that these hydrocarbons sensitise the myocardium to endogenous catecholamines, so a surge of adrenaline from a struggle, a fright or physical restraint can precipitate ventricular fibrillation, a phenomenon known as sudden sniffing death. Management is therefore deliberately low stimulus, with quiet nursing, cardiac monitoring and oxygen, and physical restraint and sympathomimetic drugs avoided wherever possible. Chronic use causes cerebellar and cognitive damage, a distal renal tubular acidosis with hypokalaemia from toluene, and bone marrow suppression from benzene, so electrolytes, renal function and a full blood count are checked and follow up arranged.
key_points: Routine urine drug screens do not detect volatile hydrocarbons
Perioral rash and solvent odour are the practical diagnostic clues
The myocardium is sensitised to catecholamines so fright or struggle can be fatal
Manage with quiet surroundings, cardiac monitoring and oxygen rather than restraint
Chronic use causes cerebellar damage, renal tubular acidosis and marrow suppression
explanation.pearls: Avoid adrenaline and other sympathomimetics in a patient who has inhaled hydrocarbons unless the patient is in arrest, because the sensitised myocardium responds to catecholamine with ventricular fibrillation.

subtopic_detail: Atypical features in a first psychotic presentation that redirect the workup away from a primary disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 21 year old woman admitted three days ago with a two week history of paranoid beliefs about her housemates, disorganised speech and severe anxiety. She has no personal or family psychiatric history and uses no substances, and a urine drug screen is negative.

Over the last 48 hours the nursing staff report she has become intermittently mute and then floridly agitated within the same hour. She has developed repetitive lip smacking and choreiform movements of both hands that were not present on admission and that persist during sleep observation. She has been febrile to 38.2 twice without a source, and her pulse has swung between 48 and 140 while lying still in bed. She has received two doses of olanzapine only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate fluctuating 48 to 140, blood pressure 96/58 to 158/94, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.2
data_table.Examination: Orofacial dyskinesia and hand chorea persisting in sleep, fluctuating conscious state, no neck stiffness, no rigidity or clonus
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 9 mg/L (less than 5); creatine kinase 210 U/L (less than 200); urine drug screen negative; computed tomography of the brain reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease olanzapine and start bromocriptine with active cooling and intravenous fluid support
options.rationale: That is the treatment for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, whose defining features are lead pipe rigidity and a markedly raised creatine kinase, neither of which is present after only two doses (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Increase the olanzapine dose and add regular lorazepam for the fluctuating agitation
options.rationale: Escalating antipsychotic treats the presentation as primary psychosis and risks marked sensitivity reactions in autoimmune encephalitis, while the movement disorder and autonomic instability go uninvestigated (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis).

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture with paired serum and cerebrospinal fluid autoantibody testing
options.rationale: Subacute psychosis with orofacial dyskinesia, fluctuating conscious state, seizures or autonomic instability in a young woman requires testing for antibodies against the N methyl D aspartate receptor, and the cerebrospinal fluid sample is more sensitive than serum alone (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy for a presumed catatonic presentation of psychosis
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is used for catatonia and is sometimes needed in this condition too, but committing to it before excluding an autoimmune cause bypasses the immunotherapy that alters the outcome (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis).

options.text: Start intravenous ceftriaxone and aciclovir empirically and repeat the computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Empirical cover for bacterial meningitis and herpes encephalitis is reasonable while awaiting the tap, but repeating a normal computed tomography scan adds nothing and does not substitute for the cerebrospinal fluid examination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Anti N methyl D aspartate receptor encephalitis characteristically begins with a prodrome of headache and fever followed by psychiatric symptoms, so a substantial proportion of patients are admitted to a psychiatric unit before the diagnosis is made. The features that should redirect the workup are a subacute onset over days to weeks in someone with no psychiatric history, a movement disorder that is typically orofacial dyskinesia and persists into sleep, a fluctuating conscious state, seizures, and autonomic instability with swings in heart rate, blood pressure and temperature. Diagnosis rests on antibody testing in cerebrospinal fluid as well as serum, since cerebrospinal fluid is considerably more sensitive and serum alone can be falsely negative, supported by magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography. Treatment is immunotherapy with corticosteroid, immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, escalating to rituximab or cyclophosphamide, together with a search for an underlying ovarian teratoma, and outcomes are markedly better the earlier treatment begins.
key_points: Subacute psychosis with no psychiatric history should prompt an organic workup
Orofacial dyskinesia persisting into sleep is close to specific for this condition
Autonomic instability and fluctuating conscious state are core supporting features
Cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing is more sensitive than serum alone
Search for an ovarian teratoma in young women once the diagnosis is made
explanation.pearls: Patients with anti N methyl D aspartate receptor encephalitis show marked sensitivity to antipsychotics, and a severe extrapyramidal or malignant syndrome type reaction after one or two ordinary doses is itself a diagnostic clue.

subtopic_detail: Cyclical mood symptoms confined to the luteal phase and the evidence needed before treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31 year old woman who describes becoming a different person for about a week each month. She is irritable to the point of shouting at her children, tearful, bloated and exhausted, and has twice taken sick leave because she could not face work.

She says the symptoms lift within a day or two of her period starting and that she feels entirely well for the following fortnight. This has happened for at least six months. She has no history of mental illness, drinks two standard drinks a week, and is not using hormonal contraception. Her thyroid function and full blood count taken last month were normal, and today, on day 8 of her cycle, her mental state examination is entirely unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination normal today with euthymic mood, no psychomotor change, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-165); ferritin 46 mcg/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily continuously and review her in four weeks
options.rationale: A serotonergic antidepressant is effective for this condition and can be given continuously or in the luteal phase only, but treatment follows confirmation rather than preceding it (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive taken continuously without a break
options.rationale: Continuous combined contraception is a reasonable second line treatment, and prescribing it now removes the cyclical pattern that the diagnosis depends on demonstrating (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).

options.text: Refer to psychiatry for assessment of possible bipolar II disorder now
options.rationale: Bipolar II requires discrete hypomanic episodes of at least four days with elevated or expansive mood and increased activity, and irritability tied to the luteal phase is not that (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).

options.text: Ask her to complete daily symptom ratings over two menstrual cycles
options.rationale: The diagnosis requires prospective daily ratings across at least two cycles showing symptoms in the final week before menses that improve within days of onset and are absent in the follicular phase, because retrospective report agrees poorly with prospective data (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders; DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Advise calcium and vitamin B6 supplements and review her in three months
options.rationale: Supplements have modest evidence for physical premenstrual symptoms, and offering them as the whole plan understates the functional impairment she describes (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is distinguished from premenstrual syndrome by the severity of the mood symptoms and the functional impairment they cause, and it is distinguished from an underlying mood disorder by the symptom free follicular phase. Around half of women who report a premenstrual pattern retrospectively do not confirm it on prospective daily ratings, and many instead have premenstrual exacerbation of an existing depressive or anxiety disorder, which needs different treatment. Two cycles of prospective ratings therefore change management in a substantial minority of cases. Once confirmed, serotonergic antidepressants work rapidly enough to be given only in the luteal phase, which distinguishes this condition from major depression where continuous treatment is required.
key_points: Prospective daily ratings across two cycles are required for the diagnosis
A symptom free follicular phase separates it from premenstrual exacerbation
Retrospective report agrees poorly with prospective data
Serotonergic antidepressants can be dosed in the luteal phase only
Continuous combined contraception is a reasonable second line option
explanation.pearls: Serotonergic antidepressants relieve premenstrual dysphoric symptoms within a day or two rather than the two to four weeks needed in major depression, which is why luteal phase only dosing from ovulation to menses is a legitimate regimen.

subtopic_detail: Body focused repetitive behaviour and the treatment that comes before medication
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19 year old university student who has been wearing a beanie indoors for three months. She tells you she pulls hair from her scalp while studying and watching television, sometimes without noticing she has started.

She describes a build up of tension beforehand and a sense of relief afterwards, and she has tried repeatedly to stop. She does not eat the hair. She denies any belief that her hair is abnormal or that she looks disfigured, and she is not checking mirrors or seeking cosmetic procedures. On examination there is an irregular patch of hair loss over the right parietal scalp containing hairs of varying lengths, with normal skin, no scaling, no scarring and no broken exclamation mark hairs.

data_table.Examination: Irregular right parietal patch of hair loss with hairs of differing lengths, normal underlying scalp skin, no scaling or scarring, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review her response after six weeks
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants are effective for obsessive compulsive disorder but have performed poorly for hair pulling in trials, and they are not the first choice here (Source: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Refer to dermatology for a scalp biopsy to clarify the pattern of loss
options.rationale: Biopsy would be needed if scarring alopecia or alopecia areata were plausible, and hairs of differing lengths in an irregular patch with normal skin already give the diagnosis (Source: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Start low dose olanzapine at night and monitor her weight monthly
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation has limited trial support in this condition and carries metabolic cost that is hard to justify before behavioural treatment has been tried (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Reassure her that the habit is common and review her again in six months
options.rationale: Repeated failed attempts to stop plus visible hair loss and social avoidance define a disorder rather than a habit, and passive review offers her nothing (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Refer for habit reversal training with a trained psychologist
options.rationale: Habit reversal training, which combines awareness training, a competing response and stimulus control, has the strongest evidence base of any treatment for hair pulling and is the recommended first step (Source: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

explanation.summary: Hair pulling disorder sits in the obsessive compulsive and related group but responds differently to treatment from obsessive compulsive disorder itself, which is the main clinical trap. Behavioural treatment outperforms medication, and awareness training matters because much of the pulling is automatic rather than deliberate. Two questions separate it from its neighbours: whether the person believes something is wrong with their appearance, which would suggest body dysmorphic disorder, and whether the hair is swallowed, which raises trichobezoar and warrants abdominal assessment. Dermatological mimics are excluded at the bedside by looking for scarring, scaling and exclamation mark hairs rather than by biopsy.
key_points: Hairs of varying length in an irregular patch with normal skin indicates pulling
Habit reversal training is the first line treatment
Serotonergic antidepressants perform less well here than in obsessive compulsive disorder
Ask about swallowing hair because of the risk of trichobezoar
Appearance related beliefs would point instead to body dysmorphic disorder
explanation.pearls: Ask every patient who pulls hair whether they swallow it, because trichophagia can produce a gastric trichobezoar with the tail extending into the small bowel and presenting years later as obstruction.

sources.label: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

subtopic_detail: Persisting bereavement reaction beyond the diagnostic time threshold
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58 year old woman 15 months after her husband died of pancreatic cancer. She tells you she thinks about him for most of the day, longs for him constantly, and still cannot bring herself to enter the room where he died or to give away his clothes.

She says she feels that part of her died with him and that she no longer knows who she is without him. She has stopped seeing the friends they had as a couple. She sleeps and eats reasonably and has not lost weight. She has no pervasive anhedonia, no feelings of worthlessness unrelated to the loss, and no suicidal ideation, although she says she would not mind if she did not wake up. She is still doing her job but has taken no interest in it.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking about her husband, reactive affect at other times, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, no plan or intent to harm herself
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her that this is normal grief and offer review in six months
options.rationale: Intense yearning with identity disruption and avoidance that persists past 12 months with functional impairment has crossed from expected grief into a diagnosable disorder (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Start mirtazapine at night to address her sleep and appetite as well
options.rationale: An antidepressant would be the choice if she met criteria for a depressive episode, and her sleep, appetite and weight are preserved with no pervasive anhedonia (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).

options.text: Refer for structured grief focused psychotherapy with a psychologist
options.rationale: Targeted grief focused psychotherapy, which pairs exposure to avoided reminders with work on restoring life goals, outperforms both antidepressants and general supportive counselling for this presentation (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders; DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Prescribe short term temazepam to help her sleep and review in a month
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not improve grief outcomes, risk dependence, and blunt the emotional processing that treatment depends on (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer her to a community bereavement support group run by volunteers
options.rationale: Peer support helps uncomplicated bereavement, but it has not been shown to resolve the avoidance and identity disruption that define the disorder (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder was added as a formal diagnosis to recognise a minority of bereaved people, around one in twenty, whose grief remains intense and disabling rather than gradually integrating. The threshold in adults is at least 12 months from the death, with persistent yearning or preoccupation plus features such as identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness and a sense that life is meaningless. It overlaps with but is distinct from major depression, where guilt, worthlessness and anhedonia are pervasive rather than focused on the deceased, and from post traumatic stress disorder. Getting the distinction right matters because the first line treatment is a specific psychotherapy rather than an antidepressant.
key_points: The adult time threshold is 12 months from the death
Yearning and preoccupation with the deceased are the core symptoms
Depression brings pervasive anhedonia and worthlessness beyond the loss
Grief focused psychotherapy is the first line treatment
Antidepressants are added when a comorbid depressive episode is present
explanation.pearls: Avoidance of reminders is the feature that most reliably distinguishes prolonged grief from ordinary bereavement, and it is also the specific target of the exposure component of grief focused therapy.

subtopic_detail: Somatic complaints confined to school mornings in early adolescence
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 12 year old boy brought by his mother because he has missed 14 of the last 20 school days with stomach aches and nausea. The symptoms begin as he is getting dressed and are severe enough that he cries and refuses to get in the car.

Once the decision is made that he can stay home he settles within an hour, and he is entirely well at weekends and through the recent school holidays. His mother has been working from home so that she can stay with him. He tells you he worries that something bad will happen to his mother while he is at school and that he cannot concentrate for thinking about it. He denies being bullied and his teachers report he is academically capable. His growth is normal and his abdomen is soft and non tender.

data_table.Examination: Soft non tender abdomen, no organomegaly, growth tracking along the 50th centile, normal general examination
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, C-reactive protein, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a graded return to school with the school and family together
options.rationale: Early graded return coordinated between clinician, family and school, with anxiety management skills alongside it, is the intervention with the best outcomes and it works better the sooner attendance resumes (Source: RANZCP Child and Adolescent Psychiatry; RCH CPG: School Refusal).

options.text: Start sertraline 25 mg daily and review his symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Medication is added when psychological treatment has not succeeded or when a severe comorbid disorder is present, not as the opening move in a treatable anxiety presentation (Source: RANZCP Child and Adolescent Psychiatry).

options.text: Refer to gastroenterology for endoscopy to investigate the abdominal pain
options.rationale: Symptoms confined to school mornings with normal growth, examination and screening tests do not fit organic disease, and further investigation reinforces the illness belief (Source: RCH CPG: School Refusal).

options.text: Support a period of home schooling until his anxiety symptoms settle
options.rationale: Withdrawal from school relieves the anxiety in the short term and reinforces avoidance, and the longer the absence the harder the eventual return (Source: RCH CPG: School Refusal).

options.text: Notify the education department of unauthorised absence from school
options.rationale: An enforcement response fits truancy, in which the young person conceals the absence and spends the day elsewhere, and this boy stays home with his parents' knowledge and is distressed (Source: RCH CPG: School Refusal).

explanation.summary: School refusal is anxiety driven non attendance with the parents' knowledge, and it is distinguished from truancy by the distress, the disclosure and the fact that the child stays at home. Somatic symptoms that appear on school mornings and vanish at weekends and holidays are the pattern that makes the diagnosis without extensive investigation. Separation anxiety, social anxiety, generalised anxiety and undetected learning difficulties or bullying all sit behind it and should be screened for. Prognosis worsens with the duration of absence, so the plan is measured in days rather than terms, and it must involve the school directly because a plan agreed only in the consulting room fails on the first morning.
key_points: Symptoms that disappear at weekends and holidays point away from organic disease
School refusal involves parental knowledge and distress, unlike truancy
Return to school is graded but starts early because prognosis worsens with time
The school must be part of the plan, not just the family
Screen for bullying, learning difficulty and parental mental illness
explanation.pearls: Every week of continued absence lowers the likelihood of successful return, so a partial attendance plan starting within days beats a complete plan that waits for a psychology appointment in six weeks.

subtopic_detail: Treating attention deficit hyperactivity disorder when a tic disorder coexists
stem:
You are the paediatrician reviewing a 9 year old boy who has had eye blinking and shoulder shrugging for two years, with intermittent throat clearing. The movements come and go in intensity, do not hurt him, and he says other children have stopped commenting on them.

His parents' concern today is different. He cannot stay in his seat, loses his belongings weekly, and his teacher reports he completes about a third of set work. Structured rating scales completed by parents and two teachers meet criteria for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, combined presentation, with impairment at home and at school. His father asks you directly whether starting a stimulant will make the movements worse, because a relative told him it would.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 100/62, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Intermittent eye blinking and shoulder shrugs suppressible on request, normal neurological examination, growth on the 60th centile for height and weight
data_table.Rating scales: Parent and two teacher scales meet criteria for combined presentation with cross setting impairment; tic severity rated mild with no functional impact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat the movements first with comprehensive behavioural intervention
options.rationale: Behavioural therapy for tics is the right first step when the tics are the impairing problem, and here they are mild and not troubling him while the attentional symptoms are disabling (Source: RANZCP Neurodevelopmental Disorders).

options.text: Start methylphenidate for the attentional symptoms and monitor his tics
options.rationale: Controlled data show stimulants do not worsen tics on average and treating the impairing condition is the priority, with tic severity tracked at each review so the family is not left guessing (Source: RANZCP Neurodevelopmental Disorders; Australian ADHD Guideline).

options.text: Start clonidine as a single agent to cover both sets of symptoms
options.rationale: Clonidine does treat both and is a reasonable choice when tics are moderate to severe, but its effect on the core attentional symptoms is substantially smaller than that of a stimulant (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline).
