options.text: Start risperidone at a low dose and review his movements in six weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are effective for severe tics but carry weight gain, metabolic and extrapyramidal risk that is unjustifiable for mild tics with no functional impact (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Defer all medication and reassess both problems again in six months
options.rationale: Deferral leaves a child completing a third of his schoolwork untreated for another half year, and untreated symptoms carry academic and self esteem costs (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline).

explanation.summary: Tic disorders and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder co-occur frequently, and the historical warning that stimulants provoke tics has not held up in controlled trials, where tic severity follows its natural waxing and waning course regardless of treatment. The practical approach is to identify which condition is causing the impairment and to treat that one. Mild tics that the child has adapted to need explanation and monitoring rather than drug treatment, since most tic disorders improve through adolescence. When tics are the impairing problem, comprehensive behavioural intervention is first line, with alpha 2 agonists or antipsychotics for more severe cases. Naming the myth explicitly and offering to track tic severity is what keeps the family engaged with treatment.
key_points: Stimulants do not worsen tics on average in controlled trials
Treat whichever condition is causing the functional impairment
Most tic disorders improve through adolescence
Behavioural intervention is first line when tics are impairing
Alpha 2 agonists treat both but are weaker for attentional symptoms
explanation.pearls: Tics naturally wax and wane over weeks, so an increase in the fortnight after a stimulant is started is far more likely to be the natural course than a drug effect, and stopping treatment on that basis costs the child an effective medication.

subtopic_detail: Behavioural addiction presenting as insomnia and anxiety in primary care
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 45 year old man who asks for something to help him sleep. He works as a plumber and says he lies awake with his heart racing.

On questioning he tells you he has been betting on sport through an app for three years. Over the past eight months the stakes have grown, he returns the next day to win back what he lost, and he has taken out a personal loan and a credit card that his wife does not know about. He has twice promised her he had stopped. He drinks four standard drinks a week, uses no other substances, and has no previous psychiatric history. He looks tired and says quietly that his family would be better off without him, although he has no plan and wants help.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Anxious and tired appearing, reactive affect, no psychotic features, no intoxication or withdrawal signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a short course of temazepam and review his sleep in two weeks
options.rationale: Sedative prescribing treats the presenting complaint while leaving the driver untouched, and it adds dependence risk in a man who has just expressed passive suicidal thoughts (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start sertraline for anxiety and arrange to see him again in one month
options.rationale: Antidepressants have no established role in gambling disorder itself, and a month is too long an interval given the risk he has disclosed today (Source: RANZCP Addiction Psychiatry).

options.text: Advise him to self exclude from betting apps and review him in one month
options.rationale: Self exclusion and app blocking are useful components of a plan and are undermined when offered alone, because they do not address the craving, the debt or the risk (Source: RANZCP Addiction Psychiatry).

options.text: Assess suicide risk today and refer to a gambling specific psychology service
options.rationale: Suicide risk in gambling disorder is high and the passive ideation he has disclosed requires assessment and a safety plan at this visit, alongside referral for the cognitive behavioural treatment that has the best evidence (Source: RANZCP Addiction Psychiatry).

options.text: Refer him to a financial counsellor to consolidate his debts and review later
options.rationale: Financial counselling is a valuable part of the plan, but debt restructuring without treatment of the disorder frequently funds further gambling (Source: RANZCP Addiction Psychiatry).

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is the one behavioural addiction recognised in the diagnostic manuals, and people almost never present with it as the stated problem, arriving instead with insomnia, anxiety, relationship breakdown or a physical complaint. The features to elicit are escalating stakes, chasing losses, concealment, failed attempts to stop and continued gambling despite consequences. Rates of suicidal ideation and attempts are markedly elevated compared with the general population, driven by debt and shame, so risk assessment belongs at the first consultation rather than at review. Cognitive behavioural therapy has the strongest evidence, delivered face to face or through national telephone and online services, with financial counselling, partner involvement and self exclusion as adjuncts. Naltrexone is a second line option for craving in selected patients.
key_points: People with gambling disorder rarely name it as the presenting problem
Chasing losses and concealment are core diagnostic features
Suicide risk is substantially elevated and is assessed at the first visit
Cognitive behavioural therapy has the best evidence for treatment
Self exclusion and financial counselling are adjuncts, not the whole plan
explanation.pearls: Two screening questions, whether he has ever felt he needed to bet more money and whether he has ever lied about how much he gambles, detect most cases and take under a minute in a consultation about insomnia.

subtopic_detail: Withdrawing long term hypnotic treatment in an older person after a fall
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 74 year old woman two weeks after she fell in her hallway at 2 am and fractured her wrist. She has been taking temazepam 20 mg every night for six years, started after her husband's death, and says she no longer knows whether it helps but is frightened of nights without it.

She takes perindopril and atorvastatin, drinks no alcohol, and lives alone. Her cognitive screening score is in the normal range and her orthostatic blood pressure drop is 8 mmHg. Her renal function and vitamin D are normal and her most recent bone density showed osteopenia. She tells you she would like to come off the tablet but has tried twice before and lasted two nights each time.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Steady tandem gait in a wrist cast, no focal neurology, cognitive screening within the normal range, postural blood pressure drop 8 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 60 mL/min/1.73m2; sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145); 25 hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (greater than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the temazepam now and provide written sleep hygiene instructions
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after six years of nightly use produces rebound insomnia, anxiety and in some cases seizures, and it is the reason her two previous attempts failed within days (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Substitute zopiclone at an equivalent nightly dose and continue it long term
options.rationale: The so called z drugs act at the same receptor complex and carry the same fall and fracture risk in older people, so the substitution changes the label rather than the hazard (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Reduce the dose by about a quarter every two to four weeks with review
options.rationale: A gradual taper negotiated with the patient, combined with behavioural treatment for insomnia, is what achieves durable cessation, and reductions of about 25 per cent at two to four weekly intervals are tolerated by most older people (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence).

options.text: Add prolonged release melatonin nightly and continue the temazepam as well
options.rationale: Melatonin is a reasonable adjunct during a taper in this age group, but adding it while leaving the hypnotic in place leaves the fracture risk exactly where it was (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer her for inpatient withdrawal management at the local drug service
options.rationale: Inpatient withdrawal is reserved for high dose dependence, a history of withdrawal seizures or unstable comorbidity, none of which apply to a single nightly therapeutic dose (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence).

explanation.summary: Long term hypnotic use in older people roughly doubles the risk of falls and hip fracture, and tolerance to the sedative effect means most patients gain little sleep benefit for that risk. Deprescribing succeeds when it is collaborative and slow, and when the reason for stopping is framed around what the patient values, in this case staying independent at home. Behavioural treatment for insomnia, particularly stimulus control and sleep restriction, works better than any drug for chronic insomnia and should run alongside the taper rather than after it. Withdrawal symptoms are anticipated and normalised so that a difficult fortnight is not read as proof that the medication was necessary.
key_points: Long term hypnotics substantially raise fall and fracture risk in older people
Taper gradually rather than stopping suddenly after years of use
Reductions of about 25 per cent every two to four weeks suit most patients
Z drugs carry the same risks and are not a safer substitute
Behavioural treatment for insomnia should run alongside the taper
explanation.pearls: Switching to an equivalent dose of diazepam is sometimes used to smooth a taper from short acting agents, but its long half life accumulates in older people and generally makes the fall risk worse rather than better.

subtopic_detail: Progressive household accumulation in later life and its differential
stem:
You are the doctor on a community aged care assessment visit to a 68 year old retired librarian, requested by her daughter after the council issued a notice about the state of the property.

Only a narrow path runs through each room, the kitchen bench and the stove cannot be used, and newspapers are stacked to shoulder height. She has bought items she does not need for years and cannot let anything go because she believes each item may be needed later, and she becomes acutely distressed and tearful when her daughter removes anything. She is embarrassed by the mess and will not let neighbours in. Her personal hygiene is good, she pays her bills on time, and she gives a detailed and coherent account of her finances. Her cognitive screening is in the normal range, and there is no disinhibition, no change in food preference, no rituals such as washing or checking, and no delusions or hallucinations.

data_table.Examination: Well kempt, coherent and detailed history, cognitive screening within the normal range, no frontal release signs, no disinhibition, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid stimulating hormone and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Obsessive compulsive disorder with predominant hoarding symptoms
options.rationale: Obsessive compulsive hoarding is driven by intrusive distressing thoughts such as contamination fears, and the accumulation is unwanted rather than accompanied by the pleasure of acquisition seen here (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia with collecting behaviour
options.rationale: The behavioural variant is defined by disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and altered eating, with executive impairment on testing, and her preserved social awareness and normal cognition argue against it (Source: RANZCP Old Age Psychiatry).

options.text: Severe self neglect syndrome associated with social isolation
options.rationale: Self neglect of this type is characterised by squalor with poor personal hygiene and an absence of shame about the state of the home, and she is well kempt and acutely embarrassed (Source: RANZCP Old Age Psychiatry).

options.text: Very late onset schizophrenia like psychosis with delusional beliefs
options.rationale: Late onset psychosis produces persecutory or partition delusions and often hallucinations, and her reason for keeping items is overvalued rather than delusional (Source: RANZCP Old Age Psychiatry).

options.text: Hoarding disorder with excessive acquisition and limited insight
options.rationale: Persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of value, distress at parting with them, excessive acquisition and living areas so congested that they cannot be used for their purpose is the defining picture, and it stands as its own diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Old Age Psychiatry).

explanation.summary: Hoarding disorder was separated from obsessive compulsive disorder because its course, family history and treatment response differ, and because most people who hoard have no other obsessive compulsive symptoms. It typically begins in adolescence and worsens each decade, so presentation in later life usually represents a long standing problem crossing a safety threshold rather than a new illness. The differential in an older person includes frontotemporal dementia, in which collecting is accompanied by disinhibition and executive failure, and squalor syndromes in which self care is lost. Safety is the immediate issue, with fire risk, falls and blocked exits, and treatment is prolonged cognitive behavioural therapy that includes home visits, since clear outs without therapy are followed by rapid re-accumulation and rupture with the family.
key_points: Hoarding disorder is a diagnosis in its own right, not a subtype of obsessive compulsive disorder
Distress at discarding and excessive acquisition are the core features
Preserved hygiene and shame argue against squalor and self neglect
Disinhibition and altered eating would point to frontotemporal dementia
Forced clear outs without therapy are followed by re-accumulation
explanation.pearls: Fire brigade data consistently show markedly increased fire deaths in hoarded dwellings, so a blocked exit or an unusable stove converts a chronic problem into an urgent one that justifies involving the family and the local council together.

subtopic_detail: Request for a cosmetic referral where the appearance concern is the disorder
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 22 year old man who asks for a referral to a plastic surgeon because his nose is crooked and, in his words, ruins his face. He had a rhinoplasty 18 months ago and says the surgeon did not fix it properly.

He tells you he checks his profile in reflective surfaces for around three hours a day, photographs his face from set angles each evening, and now leaves the house only after dark. He has stopped attending his apprenticeship two days a week and has lost contact with most of his friends. He denies low mood as his main problem, saying he would be fine if his nose were fixed. On examination there is minimal residual nasal asymmetry that is difficult to appreciate at conversational distance.

data_table.Examination: Minimal residual nasal asymmetry, no functional nasal obstruction, no septal deviation on inspection, reactive affect, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: No abnormality on routine screening bloods taken by the previous surgeon

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the underlying disorder and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention, with a serotonergic antidepressant added for more severe cases, is the treatment for this presentation, and naming the disorder respectfully is what makes the referral acceptable to him (Source: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Write the referral to a plastic surgeon and review him after the operation
options.rationale: Cosmetic surgery in this setting leaves the great majority of patients no better or worse, with the preoccupation commonly transferring to another feature (Source: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Arrange a second surgical opinion to assess the technical adequacy of the repair
options.rationale: Another opinion prolongs the search for a surgical solution and reinforces the belief that the defect is the problem rather than the preoccupation (Source: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Start low dose olanzapine because his belief about his nose is held firmly
options.rationale: Poor or absent insight is a recognised specifier of this disorder rather than evidence of psychosis, and antipsychotic monotherapy is not the established treatment (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Reassure him that his nose looks normal and review him again in three months
options.rationale: Reassurance is transiently soothing and is itself a maintaining behaviour, since seeking it becomes another compulsion that therapy has to unpick (Source: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder is a preoccupation with a perceived defect that others cannot see or regard as slight, accompanied by repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, camouflaging, comparing and reassurance seeking. It is markedly over represented in cosmetic and dermatology clinics, and the outcome after cosmetic procedures is poor, with dissatisfaction, repeat requests and transfer of the concern to a new body part. Suicidal ideation is common and should be asked about directly at every visit, because the shame that surrounds the condition means it will not be volunteered. Poor insight, present in a substantial proportion, does not change the diagnosis or the treatment, and the therapeutic task in primary care is to keep the person engaged rather than to win the argument about the nose.
key_points: Repetitive checking, camouflaging and reassurance seeking define the disorder
Cosmetic procedures rarely help and the concern often shifts to another feature
Poor insight is a specifier, not evidence of a psychotic disorder
Ask directly about suicidal ideation at each review
Cognitive behavioural therapy with a serotonergic antidepressant is the treatment
explanation.pearls: Serotonergic antidepressants for this disorder need higher doses and a longer trial of about 12 weeks than for depression, so declaring failure at four weeks on a standard antidepressant dose is the common prescribing error.

sources.label: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

subtopic_detail: Daytime sleepiness referred as depression with a symptom that redirects the diagnosis
stem:
You are the doctor in a youth mental health service seeing a 17 year old girl referred with a provisional diagnosis of depression. Her school reports that she sleeps in class most days and her marks have fallen from A grades to passes over the past year.

Her sleep diary shows a consistent bedtime of 10 pm, sleep onset within five minutes, and waking at 6:30 am, and she still falls asleep on the bus and during afternoon lessons. She naps for 20 minutes and wakes refreshed. She says she is flat about school but still enjoys her netball training and her friendships, and she has no suicidal thoughts or weight change. Her mother adds that for the past few months her knees have buckled and her jaw has gone slack for a few seconds when she laughs hard, which they had put down to clumsiness. She uses no substances and takes no medication.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, body mass index 22 kg per square metre, no goitre, reactive affect with preserved interest in activities
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, ferritin, thyroid stimulating hormone, iron studies and glucose all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review her mood in four weeks time
options.rationale: Antidepressant treatment addresses a depressive episode, and preserved enjoyment of netball and friendships with no weight or sleep disturbance does not meet that threshold (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).

options.text: Provide sleep hygiene education and a fixed schedule with review in a month
options.rationale: Sleep hygiene treats insufficient or irregular sleep, and her diary already documents more than eight hours of consolidated sleep with rapid sleep onset (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Repeat her iron studies and thyroid function and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Repeating tests that were normal weeks ago delays the diagnosis, and neither anaemia nor hypothyroidism explains episodic loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Refer for polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
options.rationale: Refreshing naps with episodic emotion triggered loss of muscle tone point to narcolepsy with cataplexy, and the overnight study followed by daytime nap testing is the investigation that establishes it (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Start modafinil for her daytime sleepiness and arrange follow up in clinic
options.rationale: Wake promoting treatment is started after the diagnosis is confirmed, because prior stimulant exposure alters the sleep study results and access to treatment depends on documented testing (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy typically begins in the teens and is misdiagnosed as depression, laziness or insufficient sleep for years, with a median delay to diagnosis measured in years rather than months. Two features separate it from a mood disorder at the bedside: naps that are short and refreshing, which contrasts with the unrefreshing sleep of depression, and cataplexy, a brief bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, usually laughter, with preserved consciousness. Families rarely volunteer cataplexy because they interpret it as clumsiness, so it must be asked about directly. Confirmation requires overnight polysomnography to exclude another cause of sleep disruption, followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day, and treatment is started only once the diagnosis is documented.
key_points: Refreshing short naps distinguish narcolepsy from depressive hypersomnia
Cataplexy is brief, bilateral, emotion triggered and preserves consciousness
Ask directly about knees buckling or jaw dropping when laughing
Polysomnography precedes the multiple sleep latency test
Do not start stimulants before the diagnostic study is done
explanation.pearls: Cataplexy is almost specific to narcolepsy type 1 and reflects loss of hypocretin producing neurons, so a history of the jaw or knees giving way during laughter is worth more diagnostically than any screening questionnaire for sleepiness.

subtopic_detail: Escalating gabapentinoid use in a patient stabilised on opioid agonist treatment
stem:
You are the doctor at an opioid treatment clinic reviewing a 34 year old man who has been stable on methadone 90 mg daily for two years, with negative urine drug screens and steady employment.

He was prescribed pregabalin for sciatica 10 months ago at 150 mg daily. He now asks you to increase it to 600 mg daily, telling you it is the only thing that quietens his anxiety and that he sometimes takes several days worth at once for the buzz. Real time prescription monitoring shows he has obtained pregabalin from three prescribers in the past two months. Two weeks ago his partner found him asleep and unrousable for several minutes on the couch after an evening of drinking. His sciatica has settled and straight leg raise is now negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, mildly slurred speech late in the consultation, negative straight leg raise, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for methadone only; liver function tests and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the pregabalin to 600 mg daily and review him again in one month
options.rationale: Escalating the dose in a person describing intoxicating use, multiple prescribers and a recent unrousable episode raises the risk of fatal respiratory depression in combination with methadone (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence; AMH).

options.text: Decline the increase, consolidate prescribing with you and plan a taper
options.rationale: Single prescriber arrangements with a staged reduction address both the misuse and the overdose risk while avoiding the seizures and severe anxiety that follow abrupt cessation, and the indication for the drug has resolved (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Stop the pregabalin today and provide a letter for the other prescribers
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of high dose gabapentinoid use precipitates a withdrawal syndrome with agitation, insomnia and seizures, and it commonly drives the person to source the drug illicitly (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Switch him to gabapentin at an equivalent dose and continue the same plan
options.rationale: Gabapentin belongs to the same class with the same misuse liability and the same additive respiratory depression with opioids, so the substitution does not reduce risk (Source: AMH).

options.text: Add diazepam at night for his anxiety and continue the current pregabalin
options.rationale: Adding a benzodiazepine to methadone and a gabapentinoid stacks three respiratory depressants, which is the combination most often found at post mortem in this population (Source: RACGP Prescribing Drugs of Dependence).

explanation.summary: Gabapentinoids were long regarded as low risk and are now recognised as drugs of misuse, particularly among people receiving opioid agonist treatment, where they are taken in large single doses for a euphoriant effect. The danger is pharmacological rather than behavioural: pregabalin and gabapentin potentiate opioid induced respiratory depression, and coroners' data show them present in a growing share of opioid related deaths. Real time prescription monitoring makes multiple prescribers visible and should be checked before any increase. Management combines a single prescriber agreement, staged supply, a gradual taper because withdrawal can include seizures, treatment of the underlying anxiety by non drug means, and take home naloxone with education for the patient and their partner.
key_points: Gabapentinoids potentiate opioid induced respiratory depression
Check real time prescription monitoring before increasing any dose
Abrupt cessation risks withdrawal seizures and illicit sourcing
Alcohol adds a third respiratory depressant to the combination
Provide take home naloxone and train the household in its use
explanation.pearls: An unrousable episode after drinking in a patient on methadone plus pregabalin is a sentinel event for fatal overdose, and it should trigger take home naloxone and a staged supply arrangement at that visit rather than at the next review.

subtopic_detail: Limits of confidentiality when a specific threat is made to an identifiable person
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 29 year old man in the community clinic. He stopped his risperidone six weeks ago and has slept poorly since.

He tells you that the man in the flat below is transmitting signals into his head through the ceiling and that he has worked out this will only stop if the neighbour is dealt with. He names the neighbour, describes his work hours, and says he bought a hunting knife last week and has it in his kitchen drawer. He is not intoxicated. He asks you to keep what he has told you between the two of you because his mother would be upset, and he declines admission and declines to restart medication.

data_table.Examination: Suspicious and guarded, persecutory delusions with a passivity phenomenon, no cognitive impairment, no intoxication, expressed intent with an identified means and a named target
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative for amphetamines and cannabis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Respect his request and document the threat carefully in the clinical record
options.rationale: Confidentiality yields where there is a serious and imminent threat to the life or safety of an identifiable person, and documentation alone leaves that person unprotected (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines; Privacy Act Australian Privacy Principles).

options.text: Telephone the neighbour yourself to warn him before taking any other step
options.rationale: Warning the person at risk may form part of a proportionate response, but doing it first leaves the patient unassessed in the community with the means still in his kitchen (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange urgent involuntary assessment and inform police of the specific threat
options.rationale: Containment and treatment of the untreated psychosis under mental health legislation is the intervention that reduces the risk, and disclosure limited to the specific threat is permitted where it is necessary to lessen a serious threat to another person's life (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines; Privacy Act Australian Privacy Principles).

options.text: Seek his written consent to disclose before contacting anyone about the threat
options.rationale: Consent should be sought where practicable, but a refusal cannot veto disclosure when the threat is serious, specific and imminent (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines).

options.text: Restart oral risperidone today and bring him back to the clinic tomorrow
options.rationale: A prescription he has already refused, with review in 24 hours, does nothing about tonight and relies on adherence from a man who stopped treatment six weeks ago (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Confidentiality is a strong but not absolute obligation, and Australian privacy law permits use or disclosure of health information where the clinician reasonably believes it is necessary to lessen or prevent a serious threat to the life, health or safety of any individual. The threshold is judged on specificity, identifiability of the target, expressed intent, available means and the person's history, and this presentation satisfies all of them. Disclosure should be proportionate, meaning the minimum information necessary to the people who need it, rather than a general release of the clinical record. Treating the untreated psychosis is the intervention that actually reduces risk, so the legal and the clinical responses run together rather than as alternatives. Documenting the reasoning, including what was disclosed and to whom and why, is part of the standard.
key_points: Privacy law permits disclosure to lessen a serious threat to life or safety
Specificity, an identifiable target, intent and means raise the threat above the threshold
Disclose the minimum information to those who need it
Treating the underlying psychosis is what reduces the risk
Record the reasoning, the recipients and the content of any disclosure
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the person has acquired a means and where it is kept, because a named target combined with a means already obtained is what converts a general threat into one that requires disclosure that day.

subtopic_detail: Which legal instrument authorises treatment of a physical illness in a patient who lacks capacity
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 78 year old man admitted with a community acquired pneumonia. He has severe depression with psychotic features and is already an involuntary patient under mental health legislation for that illness.

He is refusing intravenous antibiotics. When you assess him he tells you that his lungs rotted away years ago, that he has no blood left in his body, and that treatment is pointless because he is already dead. He cannot repeat back or weigh any of the information you give him about the infection or the consequences of not treating it, and his account does not change when the information is repeated. His oxygen saturation is 89 per cent on room air. There is no advance care directive and his daughter is available and is his nominated substitute decision maker.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 118/70, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 89 per cent on room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Nihilistic delusions, psychomotor retardation, unable to retain or weigh information about the infection, oriented to person only
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 180 mg/L (less than 5); white cell count 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate way to authorise the antibiotic treatment?

options.text: Treat under the existing involuntary order because he is already detained
options.rationale: Mental health legislation authorises treatment for the mental illness, and it does not extend to treatment of an unrelated physical illness (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines; Australian Guardianship Legislation).

options.text: Accept his refusal and document that he has declined treatment for pneumonia
options.rationale: A refusal only binds when the person has capacity for that decision, and he cannot retain or weigh the relevant information because of his delusional beliefs (Source: Australian Guardianship Legislation).

options.text: Apply to a tribunal for a guardianship order before giving any antibiotic
options.rationale: A tribunal application is the pathway when no substitute decision maker exists or there is dispute, and the delay is not justifiable when one is available and the patient is hypoxic (Source: Australian Guardianship Legislation).

options.text: Sedate him and give the antibiotics under restraint as an emergency measure
options.rationale: Restraint is a last resort for immediate danger, and reaching for it when a lawful consent pathway is available is neither necessary nor proportionate (Source: RANZCP Ethical Guidelines).

options.text: Obtain consent from his substitute decision maker after documenting incapacity
options.rationale: Treatment of a physical illness in an adult who lacks capacity is authorised by consent from the substitute decision maker, and the documented capacity assessment is what makes that consent lawful (Source: Australian Guardianship Legislation; RANZCP Ethical Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Two separate legal frameworks operate side by side in this situation and are frequently confused. Mental health legislation permits detention and treatment of the mental illness itself, while consent for treatment of a physical illness in an adult who lacks capacity comes from guardianship legislation through a substitute decision maker, an enduring guardian or a tribunal. Capacity is decision specific and time specific, so a person may lack capacity to decide about antibiotics while retaining it for other choices, and the assessment must show which of the four elements is failing: understanding, retention, weighing or communicating. Nihilistic delusions of the kind described interfere with weighing rather than with understanding, and that distinction is what should be recorded. Emergency treatment can always be given without consent when it is immediately necessary to save life, and that provision covers the interval while the substitute decision maker is contacted.
key_points: Mental health orders do not authorise treatment of unrelated physical illness
Capacity is decision specific and time specific
Record which element of capacity is impaired and why
Substitute decision makers consent for physical treatment when capacity is absent
Emergency life saving treatment may proceed while consent is being obtained
explanation.pearls: A patient detained under mental health legislation retains the ordinary right to consent to or refuse physical health care, so the order in the notes never answers the question of who consents to the antibiotic.

subtopic_detail: Formed visual hallucinations with retained insight in a patient with severe visual loss
stem:
You are the general practitioner making a home visit to an 81 year old woman with advanced age related macular degeneration whose corrected acuity is 6/60 in both eyes. For three months she has seen small figures in old fashioned clothing standing near her armchair, and repeating brick patterns across her lounge room wall, several times a day for a few minutes at a time.

She tells you she knows they cannot really be there and finds them more puzzling than frightening. She hears no voices, smells nothing unusual and holds no unusual beliefs. She sleeps well, has started no new medicines, and her daughter says her memory and conversation are unchanged.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid stimulating hormone and urinalysis within normal limits
data_table.Cognitive assessment: Mini Mental State Examination 28 out of 30, with points lost on the copying task

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence risperidone 0.5 mg at night and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are ineffective for this syndrome because the hallucinations arise from deafferented visual cortex rather than dopaminergic overactivity, and they add falls, stroke and mortality risk in an older woman (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence quetiapine 25 mg at night and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Choosing a lower potency antipsychotic does not change the fact that no drug is indicated, and sedation in an older person with poor vision compounds the risk of falls (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence donepezil 5 mg daily and arrange cognitive assessment
options.rationale: The near pair is dementia with Lewy bodies, where visual hallucinations occur with fluctuating cognition, parkinsonism and dream enactment, none of which are present in a woman whose cognition and conversation are unchanged (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain and admit
options.rationale: Urgent imaging is warranted when hallucinations accompany focal signs, headache, seizure or a fluctuating conscious state, and a three month history with normal cognition and normal bloods does not meet that bar (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Explain the condition, improve lighting and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Formed visual hallucinations with full insight, no other hallucinatory modality and no delusions in a person with severe visual loss is Charles Bonnet syndrome, and explanation plus optimising lighting and visual stimulation is the treatment (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists; Vision Australia).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Charles Bonnet syndrome describes complex visual hallucinations in people with acquired visual impairment who have intact cognition and retained insight. The mechanism is release phenomenon in visual association cortex deprived of input, analogous to musical hallucinations in acquired deafness, and the images are typically people, faces, patterns or landscapes seen in the affected visual field. It is common, affecting perhaps one in eight people with significant macular disease, and it is grossly underreported because patients fear being thought to have a mental illness. Explanation itself is therapeutic, and most cases settle over 12 to 18 months as visual loss stabilises or the brain adapts, so drug treatment is rarely required.
key_points: Retained insight and absence of other hallucinatory modalities are the defining features
It occurs with any cause of visual loss, not only macular degeneration
The equivalent phenomenon in acquired deafness is musical hallucination
Explanation and reassurance are the main treatment and relieve considerable distress
Antipsychotics are ineffective and carry substantial risk in this population
explanation.pearls: Increasing ambient lighting, blinking or shifting gaze can abort an episode within seconds, and telling the patient this specific manoeuvre gives them control and reduces distress more reliably than any drug.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Sequencing drug withdrawal before adding an antipsychotic in Parkinson disease psychosis
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 74 year old man with Parkinson disease of eight years duration in the movement disorder clinic. His wife says that for six weeks he has been seeing cats and small children in the hallway in the evenings, and that last week he began accusing her of hiding money from him.

He takes levodopa with carbidopa four times daily and ropinirole, which was added six months ago for end of dose wearing off. His conscious state is clear and steady through the day, his attention is intact and his memory and conversation are unchanged from six months ago. He has no urinary symptoms, no cough and no constipation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg lying and 112/66 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, liver function tests, thyroid stimulating hormone, urinalysis and chest radiograph all within normal limits
data_table.Cognitive assessment: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 25 out of 30, unchanged from six months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Reduce and cease ropinirole while continuing levodopa with carbidopa
options.rationale: Once delirium is excluded, the first step is to withdraw the antiparkinsonian drug most likely to be responsible, and dopamine agonists carry a far higher risk of hallucinations and delusions than levodopa while contributing less to motor benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Commence risperidone 0.5 mg at night and continue current therapy
options.rationale: Risperidone blocks striatal dopamine receptors and reliably worsens parkinsonism, and adding any antipsychotic before rationalising the antiparkinsonian regimen inverts the recommended order (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and continue current therapy
options.rationale: Olanzapine has been shown to worsen motor function in Parkinson disease without improving psychosis, and quetiapine or clozapine are the only antipsychotics used in this population once drug reduction has failed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence haloperidol 0.5 mg as required and review in one week
options.rationale: A high potency typical antipsychotic can precipitate severe rigidity and immobility in Parkinson disease and is contraindicated in this setting (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Increase the levodopa with carbidopa dose and review in one week
options.rationale: Increasing dopaminergic load worsens psychotic symptoms, and the near pair distinction is that levodopa is the drug retained for motor benefit while the agonist is the one withdrawn (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Psychosis affects up to half of people with Parkinson disease over the course of the illness and is the strongest single predictor of residential care admission. Management follows a fixed order: exclude delirium from infection, metabolic derangement or a new drug, then withdraw antiparkinsonian drugs from the least useful to the most useful, and only then add an antipsychotic. The usual withdrawal sequence is anticholinergics, then amantadine, then dopamine agonists, then catechol O methyltransferase and monoamine oxidase B inhibitors, leaving levodopa last because it carries the best ratio of motor benefit to psychiatric risk. When drug reduction fails or motor function cannot tolerate it, quetiapine is used first and clozapine has the strongest evidence, with pimavanserin unavailable in Australia.
key_points: Exclude delirium before attributing hallucinations to Parkinson disease psychosis
Withdraw dopamine agonists before reducing levodopa
Risperidone, olanzapine and haloperidol all worsen parkinsonism
Quetiapine then clozapine are the antipsychotics used if drug reduction fails
Preserved attention and a stable conscious state argue against delirium
explanation.pearls: Clozapine at doses as low as 12.5 to 50 mg at night improves Parkinson disease psychosis without worsening motor function, but it still requires the full haematological monitoring protocol, which is why quetiapine is usually tried first.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant selection where a cytochrome interaction would reduce the efficacy of cancer therapy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52 year old woman eight months into tamoxifen 20 mg daily for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer. For the past three months she has had low mood most of the day, has stopped seeing friends, wakes at four each morning and has lost interest in work she used to enjoy.

She also describes drenching hot flushes about ten times a day that disturb her sleep. She has no suicidal thoughts, no past psychiatric history and no history of mania. She takes no other regular medication and her ECG shows a corrected QT interval of 418 ms.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: Which antidepressant is the most appropriate choice?

options.text: Commence paroxetine 20 mg daily and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Paroxetine is the most potent cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor among the antidepressants and blocks conversion of tamoxifen to its active metabolite endoxifen, which has been associated with increased breast cancer mortality (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; eviQ).

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is also a strong cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor and its long half life means the interaction persists for weeks after it is stopped (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg daily and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is a strong cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor despite not being a serotonergic drug, so its different mechanism does not make it a safe alternative here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence venlafaxine 75 mg daily and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has minimal effect on cytochrome P450 2D6 and is the preferred antidepressant during tamoxifen therapy, with the additional benefit that serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors reduce vasomotor symptoms (Source: eviQ; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence duloxetine 60 mg daily and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Duloxetine is a moderate cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor, so within the same drug class venlafaxine is preferred when tamoxifen is being taken (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Tamoxifen is a prodrug that requires cytochrome P450 2D6 to be converted to endoxifen, the metabolite responsible for most of its antioestrogen effect. Drugs that inhibit this enzyme lower endoxifen concentrations substantially, and observational data link strong inhibitors to worse breast cancer outcomes, so Australian oncology guidance advises avoiding them for the whole duration of tamoxifen therapy. Depression and vasomotor symptoms are both common in this group, and a serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor addresses each, which is why venlafaxine has become the default. Where a strong inhibitor is unavoidable, switching to an aromatase inhibitor in a postmenopausal woman removes the interaction entirely because that class does not require metabolic activation.
key_points: Tamoxifen requires cytochrome P450 2D6 activation to endoxifen
Paroxetine, fluoxetine and bupropion are strong inhibitors of this enzyme
Venlafaxine and escitalopram have minimal effect on the enzyme
Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors also reduce hot flushes
Switching to an aromatase inhibitor removes the interaction in postmenopausal women
explanation.pearls: Venlafaxine 37.5 to 75 mg daily reduces hot flush frequency by around 60 per cent within four weeks, which makes it the single most useful antidepressant choice for a woman with both depression and vasomotor symptoms on tamoxifen.

subtopic_detail: Managing lithium toxicity precipitated by a newly added antihypertensive
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 58 year old man with bipolar affective disorder who has taken lithium carbonate 900 mg at night for nine years with concentrations consistently between 0.6 and 0.8 mmol/L. His wife says that for four days he has been vomiting, his hands have been shaking badly enough to spill his drink, and he has been walking as if he were drunk.

His general practitioner started a tablet for blood pressure three weeks ago. He is alert and orientated with slurred speech, a coarse tremor of both hands and a broad based unsteady gait. There is no fever, no rigidity, no clonus and no seizure activity.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 1.9 mmol/L (0.6-0.8), creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate 48 mL/min/1.73m2, sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 900 mg at night, indapamide 2.5 mg daily started three weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis and cease all regular medication
options.rationale: Haemodialysis is indicated for a concentration above 4.0 mmol/L, or above 2.5 mmol/L with seizures, a depressed conscious state or failing renal function, and none of those thresholds is met (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Cease lithium and indapamide and give intravenous sodium chloride
options.rationale: Thiazide type diuretics increase proximal tubular reabsorption of lithium and precipitate toxicity, so both drugs are stopped and volume is restored with isotonic saline to promote renal lithium excretion (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Halve the lithium dose and recheck the concentration in one week
options.rationale: Continuing any lithium in a symptomatic patient with impaired clearance allows the concentration to keep rising, and a week is far too long an interval for a toxic patient (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Give activated charcoal 50 g and observe on the ward overnight
options.rationale: Charcoal does not adsorb lithium because it is a small inorganic cation, which distinguishes it from most drug overdoses where charcoal has a role (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Continue lithium at a reduced dose and cease indapamide only
options.rationale: Removing the interacting drug alone leaves the patient exposed while renal function recovers, and the concentration will not fall quickly enough to relieve the neurological features (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Lithium is handled by the kidney like sodium, so anything that reduces effective circulating volume or increases proximal tubular sodium reabsorption raises the concentration. The classic culprits are thiazide and thiazide like diuretics, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, along with dehydration from any cause. Chronic toxicity produces predominantly neurological features at concentrations that would be tolerated in acute overdose, because tissue distribution has already occurred, so the concentration correlates poorly with severity. The persistent risk is the syndrome of irreversible lithium effectuated neurotoxicity, in which cerebellar signs persist after the concentration normalises, which is why prompt cessation and volume repletion matter more than the absolute number.
key_points: Thiazides, angiotensin blocking drugs and non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs precipitate toxicity
Chronic toxicity causes neurological features at lower concentrations than acute overdose
Isotonic saline restores volume and promotes renal lithium excretion
Activated charcoal does not bind lithium
Dialysis thresholds are above 4.0 mmol/L, or above 2.5 mmol/L with severe features
explanation.pearls: Recheck the serum lithium every six hours during treatment of chronic toxicity, because redistribution from tissue stores can produce a rebound rise after an initial fall and change the decision about dialysis.

subtopic_detail: Oral supplementation requirements when initiating a long acting injectable antipsychotic
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health team seeing a 26 year old man with schizophrenia who has been well on oral aripiprazole 15 mg daily for four months after a relapse that followed several weeks of missed tablets. He works shift work and tells you he forgets his morning dose whenever his roster changes.

He has agreed to a monthly injection of the same drug and has never received a long acting injectable before. He has no extrapyramidal signs, his weight and metabolic screen are stable, and his last relapse resolved fully on oral treatment.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests, fasting glucose, lipids and prolactin within normal limits
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 402 ms

lead_in: How should the first injection be managed?

options.text: Give the injection and cease oral aripiprazole on the same day
options.rationale: Aripiprazole monohydrate reaches therapeutic plasma concentrations slowly, so stopping the oral drug at the first injection leaves a two week window of subtherapeutic cover and relapse risk (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Give the injection and continue oral aripiprazole for three days
options.rationale: Three days of overlap is the pattern used for some other long acting injectables and is far too short for aripiprazole monohydrate, whose absorption from the depot is slow (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Give the injection and continue oral aripiprazole for fourteen days
options.rationale: The approved initiation for aripiprazole monohydrate is a first injection with 14 consecutive days of concurrent oral aripiprazole, which covers the interval before depot concentrations become therapeutic (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Give the injection and repeat a second loading dose after one week
options.rationale: A second injection one week after the first is the loading pattern used for paliperidone palmitate, and applying it to aripiprazole risks accumulation without providing early cover (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Give the injection and start oral olanzapine cover for fourteen days
options.rationale: Cover should be with the same drug already established as effective and tolerated, and introducing a second antipsychotic adds metabolic and sedative burden without benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Long acting injectable antipsychotics reduce relapse and rehospitalisation in schizophrenia and are particularly useful where adherence is the limiting factor rather than efficacy. Each product has its own initiation requirement, and confusing them is a common prescribing error: aripiprazole monohydrate needs 14 days of oral overlap, paliperidone palmitate uses a two injection deltoid loading schedule at day one and day eight with no oral cover, and risperidone microspheres need three weeks of oral cover because release does not begin for 21 days. Establishing tolerability on the oral form first is standard before any injectable is given. Site, needle length and the difference between deltoid and gluteal absorption also matter, and the patient should be told that a missed injection is managed differently from a missed tablet.
key_points: Aripiprazole monohydrate requires 14 days of concurrent oral aripiprazole
Paliperidone palmitate uses day one and day eight loading with no oral cover
Risperidone microspheres require three weeks of oral cover
Establish oral tolerability before any long acting injectable is commenced
Cover with the same drug rather than introducing a second antipsychotic
explanation.pearls: If a patient established on monthly aripiprazole monohydrate misses an injection by more than five weeks but less than six weeks, the next dose is given with seven days of oral aripiprazole cover rather than the full 14 day schedule used at initiation.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing a movement side effect from worsening psychosis in an inpatient
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 23 year old man admitted three weeks ago with a first episode of psychosis and started on olanzapine 15 mg at night. The voices that frightened him on admission have almost gone and he no longer believes his flatmates are recording him.

Over the past five days he has been pacing the corridor for hours and cannot stay seated through a meal. He tells you his legs feel like they have to keep moving and that this is worse than the voices ever were. There is no rigidity, no tremor, no fever and no diaphoresis, and the nursing staff have asked whether the dose should be increased.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 118 U/L (40-320), full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Constant shifting of weight from foot to foot when standing and rocking when seated, with normal tone and no cogwheeling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase olanzapine to 20 mg daily to target residual psychosis
options.rationale: Increasing the antipsychotic is the specific trap because the restlessness is dose related, and escalating worsens it while the psychotic symptoms are already resolving (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence benzatropine 2 mg twice daily and review in one week
options.rationale: Anticholinergics relieve drug induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia but are ineffective for this syndrome, and they add cognitive impairment, constipation and urinary retention (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence lorazepam 1 mg three times daily and review in a week
options.rationale: A benzodiazepine is a reasonable second line addition but does not address the dose related cause, and regular use in a young man with a new psychotic illness risks dependence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for the agitation
options.rationale: Valproate treats agitation arising from mood elevation rather than a movement side effect, and it would add weight gain to an antipsychotic that already causes it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Reduce the olanzapine dose and commence propranolol 10 mg daily
options.rationale: The subjective urge to move with objective restlessness and no rigidity is akathisia, managed first by reducing the antipsychotic dose and adding a lipophilic beta blocker such as propranolol (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Akathisia is among the most distressing antipsychotic adverse effects and is independently associated with suicidal thinking and with treatment refusal, so recognising it changes outcomes rather than merely comfort. Its defining feature is the subjective inner restlessness, which distinguishes it from psychomotor agitation driven by psychosis and from drug induced parkinsonism where tone is increased. The commonest error is to read the pacing as worsening illness and to increase the antipsychotic, which produces a rapid deterioration. Management is dose reduction or a switch to a lower risk agent, with propranolol as the best supported adjunct and a benzodiazepine or mirtazapine used when a beta blocker is contraindicated or ineffective.
key_points: The subjective urge to move is what defines akathisia
Normal tone and normal creatine kinase separate it from parkinsonism and malignant syndrome
Reduce the antipsychotic dose before adding any adjunct
Anticholinergics do not help akathisia
Akathisia is independently associated with suicidal ideation
explanation.pearls: Propranolol 10 to 20 mg two or three times daily usually improves akathisia within days, and its lipophilicity matters because water soluble beta blockers such as atenolol do not cross the blood brain barrier well enough to work.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Recognising a surgical emergency behind a common clozapine adverse effect
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 38 year old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia who has taken clozapine 450 mg daily for two years with a stable mental state. He tells you he has not opened his bowels for five days and that his belly has become tight and swollen.

He brought up dark green fluid twice this morning and has not been able to keep water down since. His abdomen is distended and tympanic with no guarding and no bowel sounds audible over two minutes. He takes an occasional docusate tablet that his mother buys for him and no other regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 9.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0)
data_table.Examination: Distended tympanic abdomen with no bowel sounds and an empty rectum on digital examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe macrogol daily and review the bowel chart in 48 hours
options.rationale: An osmotic laxative is the right long term prophylaxis but treating an obstructed bowel as ordinary constipation is the error that makes this complication fatal in around a quarter of reported cases (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Continue clozapine and add docusate with senna each evening
options.rationale: Continuing the causative drug allows the anticholinergic and antiserotonergic effect on gut motility to persist, and a stimulant laxative in a bowel with no peristalsis risks perforation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Reduce the clozapine dose and start a stimulant laxative today
options.rationale: Dose reduction is too slow and too partial for an acutely obstructed bowel, and imaging is required before any laxative is chosen (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Withhold clozapine and arrange an urgent abdominal radiograph
options.rationale: Absent bowel sounds with distension, vomiting and a rising lactate indicate clozapine induced gastrointestinal hypomotility progressing to ileus, which needs the drug withheld, urgent imaging and surgical involvement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Arrange an outpatient colonoscopy within the next two weeks
options.rationale: Colonoscopy investigates mucosal disease and is contraindicated in suspected obstruction because of perforation risk, whereas the problem here is motility rather than a luminal lesion (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia).

explanation.summary: Clozapine induced gastrointestinal hypomotility is more lethal than agranulocytosis yet attracts none of the mandated monitoring, because the drug has potent anticholinergic and serotonin antagonist effects that slow colonic transit by around fourfold. Constipation affects up to 60 per cent of patients and progresses in a minority to faecal impaction, ileus, ischaemia, perforation and death. Patients often do not report symptoms because of reduced interoceptive awareness and negative symptoms, so bowel habit must be asked about at every review rather than waited for. Australian practice is to start prophylactic laxatives at initiation for anyone with risk factors and to treat any patient with abdominal distension and absent bowel sounds as a surgical emergency until imaging proves otherwise.
key_points: Gastrointestinal hypomotility causes more clozapine deaths than agranulocytosis
Patients frequently under report bowel symptoms so they must be asked about routinely
Absent bowel sounds with distension is an emergency, not simple constipation
Withhold clozapine and image before choosing any laxative
Prophylactic osmotic laxatives are recommended from initiation in at risk patients
explanation.pearls: Anticholinergic drugs such as benzatropine, and opioids, multiply the risk of clozapine induced ileus, so review the whole medication chart for these before restarting clozapine once the obstruction has resolved.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant associated inappropriate antidiuresis in an older adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 79 year old woman who started sertraline 50 mg daily four weeks ago for a moderate depressive episode. Her daughter says she has become sleepy in the afternoons, is unsteady getting out of her chair, and twice this week could not remember the day.

Her mood and appetite had begun to improve before this change. Her mucous membranes are moist, her jugular venous pressure is visible 2 cm above the sternal angle and there is no peripheral oedema or postural drop. She takes no diuretic and her serum sodium was 139 mmol/L before the antidepressant was started.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 124 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg, urine sodium 62 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Additional tests: Thyroid stimulating hormone and 9 am cortisol within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue sertraline and restrict oral fluid to 1000 mL daily
options.rationale: Fluid restriction alone leaves the causative drug in place, and in an older woman with impaired thirst it is often poorly tolerated and only partially effective (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Switch to citalopram and recheck the serum sodium in one week
options.rationale: All selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors carry this risk as a class effect, so switching within the class invites recurrence, and citalopram adds QT prolongation in this age group (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence tolvaptan and continue the current antidepressant
options.rationale: A vasopressin receptor antagonist is reserved for persistent inappropriate antidiuresis with no removable cause, and using it here treats the consequence while leaving the trigger untouched (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Infuse hypertonic 3 per cent sodium chloride 100 mL over 10 minutes
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline boluses are for seizures or a substantially depressed conscious state, and using them for intermittent disorientation risks overcorrection and osmotic demyelination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Cease sertraline and restrict oral fluid with sodium recheck
options.rationale: A euvolaemic hypo osmolar hyponatraemia with concentrated urine, normal thyroid and adrenal function and a temporal link to a new serotonergic drug is drug induced inappropriate antidiuresis, treated by stopping the drug with fluid restriction and monitoring (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors cause hyponatraemia by promoting antidiuretic hormone release, and the risk is concentrated in the first four weeks of treatment and in older, female and low weight patients. The presentation is easy to misattribute because lethargy, unsteadiness and poor concentration overlap with both depression itself and normal ageing, so a sodium level before and a few weeks after starting is prudent in anyone over 65. Diagnosis requires demonstrating euvolaemia with a low serum osmolality, an inappropriately concentrated urine and a urine sodium above 30 mmol per litre, with thyroid and adrenal causes excluded. If an antidepressant remains necessary, agents with a lower reported risk such as mirtazapine or agomelatine are preferred, with the sodium rechecked two weeks after restarting.
key_points: Risk is highest in the first four weeks of an antidepressant in older patients
Symptoms overlap with depression itself, so check the sodium rather than assume
Diagnosis requires euvolaemia, low serum osmolality and concentrated urine
The risk is a class effect, so switching within the class often recurs
Mirtazapine carries a lower reported risk if an antidepressant is still needed
explanation.pearls: Check the serum sodium two weeks after starting or increasing any antidepressant in a patient over 65 years, because most drug induced hyponatraemia appears within the first month and is asymptomatic until it is severe.

subtopic_detail: Choosing first line management for behavioural symptoms where antipsychotic sensitivity is expected
stem:
You are the general practitioner asked to review a 78 year old man in residential aged care whose cognition has declined over three years. Staff describe days when he converses normally and days when he stares and cannot be roused into conversation, and he regularly tells them there are children standing in the corner of his room.

His wife says he shouts and kicks in his sleep and has fallen out of bed twice. He has a stooped posture and slow movements without a tremor. For the past two weeks he has been shouting and pushing staff away during evening personal care, and no trigger has been identified.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg lying, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, liver function tests, thyroid stimulating hormone, urinalysis and chest radiograph within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 4 mg daily and colecalciferol 1000 units daily, with no changes in six months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence risperidone 0.5 mg twice daily and review in one week
options.rationale: Fluctuating cognition, formed visual hallucinations, dream enactment and parkinsonism indicate a synucleinopathy, in which up to half of patients have severe sensitivity reactions to antipsychotics with rigidity and a sharp rise in mortality (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Implement a behaviour support plan and review pain and constipation
options.rationale: Non pharmacological measures with a systematic search for unrecognised pain, constipation and environmental triggers are first line for behavioural symptoms in dementia, and are especially important here because antipsychotics are hazardous in this subtype (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Dementia Australia).

options.text: Commence haloperidol 0.5 mg as required for episodes of agitation
options.rationale: A high potency typical antipsychotic carries the greatest risk of a severe sensitivity reaction in this group and is specifically avoided (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence olanzapine 2.5 mg each night and review again in one week
options.rationale: Olanzapine has substantial anticholinergic activity that worsens cognition and hallucinations in this subtype, and it shares the class risk of stroke and death in dementia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence diazepam 2 mg twice daily and review again in one week
options.rationale: A long acting benzodiazepine accumulates in older people and causes falls, sedation and paradoxical disinhibition, and it is not a first line treatment for behavioural symptoms in dementia (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms affect most people with dementia at some point and are the commonest reason antipsychotics are prescribed in residential care, despite an absolute increase in mortality and stroke and only modest benefit. Australian practice requires a structured search for unmet needs first, covering pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, sensory impairment, boredom and the manner in which personal care is delivered, since resistance during care is very often pain related. Recognising the dementia subtype changes the risk calculation sharply, because dementia with Lewy bodies brings severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions with rigidity, autonomic instability and death. When drug treatment does become necessary in that subtype, a cholinesterase inhibitor such as rivastigmine is preferred and quetiapine or clozapine are the only antipsychotics considered.
key_points: Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, dream enactment and parkinsonism define the subtype
Up to half of these patients have severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions
Search systematically for pain, constipation, infection and care delivery triggers
Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality in all forms of dementia
Cholinesterase inhibitors are preferred if drug treatment becomes necessary in this subtype
explanation.pearls: A time limited analgesic trial with regular paracetamol 1 g three times daily for two weeks reduces agitation in residential care residents with dementia, and is a safer first drug step than any psychotropic.

subtopic_detail: Managing an elevated mood state caused by a drug that cannot simply be stopped
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the respiratory ward about a 58 year old man on day five of prednisolone 50 mg daily for an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Nursing staff say he has not slept for two nights, talks over everyone, and telephoned his sister at three in the morning about buying a caravan to drive around the country.

He is irritable when interrupted but knows where he is, follows a three step command and can recite the months backwards. He sees and hears nothing unusual. He has no psychiatric history and no family history of mood disorder, and he is still wheezy with an oxygen requirement of 2 litres per minute.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 93 per cent on 2 litres per minute, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, liver function tests, thyroid stimulating hormone and urinalysis within normal limits, blood glucose 9.2 mmol/L (3.0-7.7 fasting)
data_table.Substance history: No alcohol for six years, no illicit substance use, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce prednisolone to the lowest effective dose and add olanzapine
options.rationale: Corticosteroid induced mood elevation is dose related, so the first move is to lower the dose as far as the airways disease allows, with a short course of an antipsychotic to control the elevated state while that happens (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence lithium and continue prednisolone at the current dose
options.rationale: Lithium takes one to two weeks to act, requires monitoring and carries interaction risks, and leaving the corticosteroid dose unchanged means the driver of the episode persists (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence sodium valproate and continue prednisolone unchanged
options.rationale: Valproate is a reasonable alternative antimanic drug but the same objection applies, since treating the episode without addressing the cause prolongs it unnecessarily (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Continue prednisolone and prescribe temazepam for the insomnia
