options.rationale: Treating the insomnia in isolation mislabels an elevated mood state as a sleep problem, and a hypnotic will not control the pressured speech, irritability or disinhibited spending (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Cease prednisolone abruptly and commence sertraline for the mood
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after several days of high dose corticosteroid risks both an airways relapse and adrenal insufficiency, and an antidepressant would worsen rather than treat an elevated mood state (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Psychiatric reactions occur in around 5 to 6 per cent of patients given high dose corticosteroids, with risk rising steeply above a prednisolone equivalent of 40 mg daily. Elevated or mixed states predominate in the first weeks, while depressive presentations are commoner with prolonged therapy, and the onset is typically within the first five days. The key clinical discrimination is from delirium, which is why preserved orientation, attention and the absence of perceptual disturbance are documented explicitly. Management balances two competing needs: the psychiatric episode responds to dose reduction, while the underlying condition may still require the drug, so the dose is minimised rather than stopped and a short course of an antipsychotic covers the interval. A past corticosteroid induced episode does not preclude future treatment but does warrant prophylaxis and closer observation.
key_points: Risk rises sharply above prednisolone 40 mg daily and onset is usually within five days
Elevated and mixed states predominate early, depressive states with prolonged use
Preserved attention and orientation separate this from delirium
Reduce the corticosteroid dose rather than stopping it abruptly
Antidepressants can worsen a corticosteroid induced elevated mood state
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine 5 to 10 mg daily typically controls corticosteroid induced mood elevation within days and can be withdrawn once the corticosteroid dose falls below a prednisolone equivalent of 20 mg daily.

subtopic_detail: Selecting pharmacotherapy where one antidepressant class is specifically contraindicated
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old woman who has been binge eating and then making herself vomit about four times a week for two years. She has been seeing a psychologist fortnightly for three months and finds the sessions useful but says the urges are still overwhelming.

For the past two months she has also had persistently low mood, poor concentration and early morning waking. Her body mass index is 22 kg per square metre and her blood pressure shows no postural drop. She has never had a seizure, takes no regular medication and asks whether a tablet could help.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22-32), magnesium 0.78 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), full blood count and liver function tests within normal limits
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 424 ms

lead_in: Which medication is the most appropriate addition?

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in current or past purging disorders because the seizure rate in that group is far higher than in the general population (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence topiramate 50 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
options.rationale: Topiramate reduces binge frequency in trials but causes weight loss and cognitive adverse effects, so it is a later line option rather than the first medication offered (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 60 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
options.rationale: Fluoxetine at 60 mg daily is the only antidepressant with established efficacy for reducing binge and purge frequency in bulimia nervosa and it also treats the comorbid depressive episode (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline

options.text: Commence mirtazapine 30 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
options.rationale: Mirtazapine has no trial evidence in bulimia nervosa and its appetite stimulating effect is likely to increase binge frequency (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline

options.text: Commence venlafaxine 75 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
options.rationale: Venlafaxine treats the depression but has no established antibulimic effect, and the distinguishing point is that the benefit of fluoxetine is specific to that drug rather than a class effect (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline

explanation.summary: Psychological therapy remains first line for bulimia nervosa, with eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy having the strongest evidence, and medication is an adjunct rather than a substitute. Fluoxetine is the exception among antidepressants in that the dose used for bulimia is higher than the antidepressant dose and the antibulimic effect appears independent of any change in mood. Physical monitoring matters alongside the psychiatric treatment because recurrent vomiting causes hypokalaemia, a metabolic alkalosis, dental erosion and parotid swelling, and hypokalaemia is the finding that most often leads to hospital admission. Medication is not started in place of therapy, and a lack of response at eight to twelve weeks prompts review of the therapy rather than escalation of the drug.
key_points: Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy is first line treatment
Fluoxetine 60 mg daily is the only antidepressant with proven antibulimic effect
Bupropion is contraindicated because of seizure risk in purging disorders
Recurrent vomiting causes hypokalaemia with a metabolic alkalosis
The antibulimic effect of fluoxetine is independent of its antidepressant effect
explanation.pearls: The antibulimic dose of fluoxetine is 60 mg daily, three times the usual starting antidepressant dose, and patients should be told to expect a reduction in binge frequency within three to four weeks of reaching that dose.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline

subtopic_detail: Serotonin toxicity precipitated by an antibiotic with monoamine oxidase inhibiting activity
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the surgical ward about a 45 year old woman who has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for three years. She was started on linezolid three days ago for a resistant enterococcal wound infection after other options were excluded on susceptibility testing.

She has become agitated and confused over the past eight hours and is drenched in sweat. She has brisk reflexes that are more pronounced in the legs than the arms, sustained clonus at both ankles, and dilated pupils. Her limbs move freely with normal tone, and her creatine kinase is not raised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 158/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 190 U/L (40-320), white cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 84 micromol/L (45-90), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), venous lactate 2.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0)
data_table.Examination: Sustained inducible ankle clonus bilaterally, hyperreflexia greater in the lower limbs, mydriasis, normal limb tone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease sertraline only and continue linezolid with close observation
options.rationale: Sertraline has a half life of about 26 hours and its metabolite persists longer, so leaving the monoamine oxidase inhibitor running allows the interaction to continue for days (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Cease both drugs and give intravenous benzodiazepine with cooling
options.rationale: Clonus and lower limb predominant hyperreflexia with normal tone and a normal creatine kinase indicate serotonin toxicity, treated by withdrawing all serotonergic drugs and giving benzodiazepines with active cooling (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence dantrolene and continue both drugs with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Dantrolene treats muscle rigidity in malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and the near pair distinction is that this woman has normal tone with clonus rather than lead pipe rigidity (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Commence bromocriptine and continue both drugs with cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists are used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which evolves over days with rigidity and a markedly raised creatine kinase rather than over hours with clonus (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Give intramuscular haloperidol for the agitation and observe closely
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do not treat serotonin toxicity, and their antidopaminergic and anticholinergic effects impair heat dissipation in a patient who is already hyperthermic (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Linezolid is a reversible non selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor as well as an oxazolidinone antibiotic, which is easily forgotten when it is prescribed by a surgical or infectious diseases team for a resistant organism. Combined with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor it can precipitate serotonin toxicity, usually within the first few days. The Hunter criteria make the diagnosis on the presence of a serotonergic agent plus spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or hypertonia with hyperthermia and clonus. The most useful bedside discriminator from neuroleptic malignant syndrome is the tempo and the tone: serotonin toxicity develops over hours with clonus and normal or increased tone that is greatest in the legs, while the malignant syndrome develops over days with generalised lead pipe rigidity and a high creatine kinase. Cyproheptadine is added when benzodiazepines and cooling are insufficient.
key_points: Linezolid is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor as well as an antibiotic
Clonus that is greatest in the lower limbs is the most specific sign
Onset over hours favours serotonin toxicity over neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Normal tone with a normal creatine kinase argues against the malignant syndrome
Benzodiazepines with cooling are first line, with cyproheptadine as an adjunct
explanation.pearls: When linezolid is unavoidable in a patient on a serotonergic antidepressant, the antidepressant should be stopped two weeks beforehand where possible, or the patient monitored daily for clonus, since the interaction typically manifests within the first four days of the antibiotic.

subtopic_detail: Cardiovascular prerequisites before initiating stimulant therapy in an adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 34 year old electrician whose specialist assessment has confirmed attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, supported by primary school reports and a collateral history from his mother. He has never been treated and wants to start medication because he is making costly errors at work.

His blood pressure has been 158/98 mmHg and 154/96 mmHg at two visits four weeks apart, and he has never taken an antihypertensive. His body mass index is 31 kg per square metre. He has no chest pain, no exertional breathlessness and no syncope, and there is no family history of sudden cardiac death before the age of 40.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 156/97 mmHg today, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, creatinine, fasting glucose and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, urine albumin to creatinine ratio 1.8 mg/mmol (less than 2.5)
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with normal axis, no left ventricular hypertrophy and a corrected QT interval of 406 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat the hypertension first and reassess before starting a stimulant
options.rationale: Australian guidance is that uncontrolled hypertension should be treated before a stimulant is commenced, because stimulants raise blood pressure by a further 2 to 5 mmHg and heart rate by up to 6 beats per minute (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Commence methylphenidate now and monitor the blood pressure each month
options.rationale: Monitoring after the fact does not remove the added cardiovascular load, and starting a stimulant into stage 2 hypertension is precisely the situation the pretreatment check is designed to catch (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Commence dexamfetamine at a low dose and monitor the blood pressure
options.rationale: Lowering the starting dose does not change the requirement to control blood pressure first, and dexamfetamine has at least as much pressor effect as methylphenidate (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence atomoxetine now and monitor the blood pressure each month
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor and raises blood pressure and heart rate to a similar degree, so it is not a way around uncontrolled hypertension (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Refer for echocardiography before commencing any stimulant medication
options.rationale: Routine echocardiography is not required before stimulant therapy and is reserved for those with cardiac symptoms, abnormal examination, an abnormal electrocardiogram or a family history of sudden cardiac death (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Stimulants remain first line pharmacological treatment for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and are effective in around 70 per cent of adults, but every Australian guideline requires a cardiovascular assessment before initiation. That assessment is a focused history for exertional symptoms and syncope, a family history for sudden cardiac death or inherited arrhythmia under 40 years of age, examination including blood pressure and heart rate, and an electrocardiogram is added when any of those are abnormal. Uncontrolled hypertension is a relative contraindication rather than an absolute one, so the correct move is to treat it and then proceed, not to abandon effective treatment. Blood pressure, heart rate, weight and sleep are then monitored at every dose change and at least six monthly thereafter.
key_points: Assess cardiovascular risk before commencing any stimulant in an adult
Uncontrolled hypertension is a relative contraindication that should be treated first
Atomoxetine also raises blood pressure and is not a workaround
Routine echocardiography is not required in the absence of red flags
Monitor blood pressure, heart rate, weight and sleep at every dose change
explanation.pearls: Stimulants raise systolic blood pressure by roughly 2 to 5 mmHg and heart rate by up to 6 beats per minute at usual doses, which is clinically trivial in a normotensive adult but meaningful when the baseline is already above 140/90 mmHg.

sources.label: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Structuring a benzodiazepine taper after failed abrupt cessation attempts
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 62 year old woman who has taken oxazepam 30 mg three times daily for six years, started for insomnia after a bereavement and continued ever since. She now wants to come off it because she feels foggy during the day and had a fall last month.

She has tried stopping twice on her own. On the first attempt she stopped over three days and had two nights of tremor, sweating and rebound insomnia before restarting. On the second she stopped abruptly and had a witnessed generalised seizure on day three. Her liver function tests and albumin are within normal limits and she drinks no alcohol.

data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, no tremor at rest, gait steady with normal tandem walking
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes and liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the oxazepam dose today and cease it completely in one week
options.rationale: A 50 per cent reduction in one step after six years of use carries a high seizure risk, and she has already demonstrated that risk on a slower schedule than this (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing Drugs of Dependence).
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing Drugs of Dependence

options.text: Continue the oxazepam and add temazepam at night for the insomnia
options.rationale: Adding a second short acting agent increases the total benzodiazepine load and the fall risk she has already experienced, without addressing the reason she came (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Substitute quetiapine 25 mg at night and cease the oxazepam today
options.rationale: Low dose quetiapine has no cross tolerance with benzodiazepines so it will not prevent withdrawal seizures, and it adds sedation, weight gain and metabolic risk in an older woman who has fallen (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Convert to an equivalent diazepam dose and reduce gradually each fortnight
options.rationale: Switching a short acting agent to an equivalent dose of a long half life benzodiazepine smooths the interdose troughs that drive withdrawal, and reductions of around 10 to 25 per cent of the current dose every one to two weeks, slowing further at the end, is the standard approach after a withdrawal seizure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease the oxazepam entirely now and cover withdrawal with as required diazepam
options.rationale: As required dosing reproduces exactly the peaks and troughs that provoked her previous withdrawal seizure, and it hands the reduction schedule to symptom severity rather than to a plan (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Long term benzodiazepine use in older adults is associated with falls, fractures, cognitive impairment and motor vehicle crashes, so deprescribing is worth pursuing even when the original indication has long passed. The taper rate matters more than the agent: reductions of a tenth to a quarter of the current dose at one to two week intervals, with the final steps made smaller and slower, succeed in most patients. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia should run alongside the taper, because untreated rebound insomnia is the commonest reason a taper is abandoned. A withdrawal seizure in the history is a marker of physiological dependence and mandates a slower schedule with closer review rather than a change of plan.
key_points: Reduce by 10 to 25 per cent of the current dose every one to two weeks, slowing near the end.
Converting a short acting agent to a long half life agent reduces interdose withdrawal.
A prior withdrawal seizure indicates dependence and warrants a slower taper.
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia should be started alongside the reduction.
Substituting a sedating antipsychotic does not prevent withdrawal because there is no cross tolerance.
explanation.pearls: Approximate equivalence is diazepam 5 mg to oxazepam 15 mg, temazepam 10 mg or alprazolam 0.5 mg, and getting this conversion wrong in either direction is the commonest cause of a taper failing in its first fortnight.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing Drugs of Dependence

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing a body focused repetitive behaviour from alopecia areata and choosing behavioural therapy over an antidepressant
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 19 year old university student who has noticed patches of hair loss on her scalp over the past year. She says it is worst during examination periods and that she often finds herself doing it while reading, without noticing until a handful comes away.

She describes a build up of tension beforehand and a sense of relief afterwards, and she is ashamed enough to have started wearing a beanie indoors. She has no intrusive thoughts about contamination, order or harm, and no rituals she feels compelled to complete in a set sequence. On examination the affected areas contain broken hairs of many different lengths with normal underlying skin, no scale, no scarring and no tapering hairs at the margins.

data_table.Examination: Two irregular patches on the right frontoparietal scalp, hairs of varying lengths within the patches, no erythema, no scale, no scarring, eyebrows and eyelashes intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, ferritin and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start topical minoxidil and review the scalp again in three months
options.rationale: Minoxidil prolongs the anagen phase in androgenetic and some inflammatory alopecias but has no effect where hairs are being physically removed, and it implies to the patient that the cause is a follicular disease (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists).

options.text: Refer for habit reversal behavioural therapy as initial treatment
options.rationale: Hairs of varying lengths within a patch of otherwise normal skin indicate mechanical breakage rather than an inflammatory alopecia, and habit reversal training with awareness training, competing response and stimulus control has the strongest evidence base as first line treatment (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review her again in six weeks
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants are first line for obsessive compulsive disorder, but trials in this body focused repetitive behaviour have been consistently negative, which is the key distinction between the two conditions despite their shared chapter (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and review her in four weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation has limited supportive data and its metabolic burden is not justified before a behavioural trial in a 19 year old with no functional collapse (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Refer to dermatology for scalp biopsy before any other treatment
options.rationale: The near pair is alopecia areata, which produces smooth patches of complete hair loss with tapering exclamation mark hairs at the margins rather than the mixed length broken hairs seen here, so the clinical picture already separates them and biopsy would delay treatment (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists).

explanation.summary: Body focused repetitive behaviours sit alongside obsessive compulsive disorder in current classification but behave very differently in treatment, which is the practical reason the distinction matters. The behaviour is usually automatic rather than driven by an intrusive thought, and patients often describe tension relief rather than anxiety reduction about a feared consequence. Habit reversal training, sometimes packaged as a comprehensive behavioural model that also addresses environmental and emotional triggers, is the first line intervention. Complications worth asking about include swallowing the hair, which can produce a gastric trichobezoar presenting years later with early satiety and epigastric fullness.
key_points: Mixed length broken hairs within a patch of normal skin indicate mechanical hair removal.
Alopecia areata gives smooth complete loss with tapering hairs at the margin.
Habit reversal training is first line; awareness training precedes the competing response.
Serotonergic antidepressant trials have been negative in this condition despite efficacy in obsessive compulsive disorder.
Ask about hair ingestion because a gastric trichobezoar can develop silently.
explanation.pearls: N acetylcysteine 1200 to 2400 mg daily has modest randomised evidence in adults over 12 weeks and is a reasonable adjunct when habit reversal alone stalls, but it has not shown benefit in children.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: First line management of gambling disorder presenting through insomnia and low mood
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old man who booked in for sleeping tablets. He has been awake most nights for two months, has lost interest in the football he used to play, and says he feels flat but denies any thoughts of self harm.

When you ask what keeps him awake, he tells you his wife found a sports betting app on his phone last week and that he has taken out a second personal loan without telling her. He has tried to stop several times and lasted at most a fortnight. He drinks two beers a week and uses no other substances. He wants help and has brought his loan statements with him.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Start naltrexone 50 mg daily and review his craving in four weeks
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists have modest evidence for craving driven gambling and are a reasonable second line addition, but they are not used ahead of the psychological and financial interventions that carry the primary evidence (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Advise a self imposed casino and betting app ban with review in three months
options.rationale: Venue exclusion is a useful component but does not touch online wagering, which is where his losses are occurring, and a three month interval abandons him during the highest risk period (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer for inpatient withdrawal management and review after discharge
options.rationale: There is no physiological withdrawal syndrome to manage in a behavioural addiction, and inpatient admission is reserved for suicide risk or a comorbid substance withdrawal, neither of which is present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Refer for gambling focused psychological therapy and financial counselling
options.rationale: Structured cognitive behavioural therapy addressing gambling related cognitions, combined with financial counselling and self exclusion, is the first line intervention, and the mood and sleep disturbance here are consequences that commonly settle as the behaviour is contained (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review his mood again in four weeks
options.rationale: Treating the low mood as a primary depressive episode misses that the symptoms are time locked to the gambling and its financial consequences, and antidepressants have not shown benefit for the gambling behaviour itself (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is the only behavioural addiction currently classified alongside substance use disorders, on the strength of shared reward pathway involvement, tolerance and relapse patterns. It rarely presents by name, appearing instead as insomnia, low mood, relationship breakdown or financial crisis, so a single screening question about gambling belongs in any assessment of new low mood in a young adult. Suicide risk is substantially elevated in this group, particularly around debt disclosure, so it is asked about directly at every visit. Online wagering has changed the epidemiology considerably, with continuous in play betting producing far shorter loss cycles than venue based gambling.
key_points: Gambling disorder commonly presents as insomnia, low mood or financial crisis rather than by name.
Cognitive behavioural therapy targeting gambling cognitions is first line.
Financial counselling and self exclusion from online platforms are part of the initial plan.
Suicide risk is elevated and is asked about directly, especially around debt disclosure.
Pharmacotherapy is second line and is not a substitute for psychological therapy.
explanation.pearls: The single question asking whether a person has ever felt the need to bet more and more money captures most cases, and a positive answer in someone presenting with insomnia should prompt a full financial and relationship assessment at that same visit.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Separating illness anxiety from somatic symptom disorder and stopping the reassurance cycle
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 41 year old man for the eleventh time in two years. His uncle died of motor neurone disease and since then he has been convinced he has the same illness.

He reports occasional twitching in his calves after running but says the twitching itself does not bother him; what keeps him up is what it means. He inspects his tongue in the mirror several times a day, films his hands to compare them week to week, and asks at every visit for another set of tests. Two nerve conduction studies and needle electromyography 14 months apart were normal, as were four neurological examinations including yours today. He works full time and has never sought a certificate, a benefit or a compensation claim.

data_table.Examination: Normal bulk and power throughout, no tongue fasciculation, reflexes symmetrical and normal, plantar responses flexor
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 96 U/L (30-150), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), nerve conduction studies and electromyography reported as normal on two occasions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat nerve conduction studies to provide definitive reassurance
options.rationale: Each normal result provides relief that decays within days and strengthens the belief that testing is what keeps him safe, which is the mechanism that maintains the disorder (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start regular reassurance appointments with weekly examination
options.rationale: Regular scheduled appointments are genuinely useful in this condition, but pairing them with repeated physical examination converts them into another reassurance ritual rather than a container for the anxiety (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Illness Anxiety Disorder).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Illness Anxiety Disorder

options.text: Refer to neurology for a third opinion and muscle biopsy review
options.rationale: Benign fasciculation after exercise with normal electromyography twice over 14 months effectively excludes a motor neurone disorder, since denervation would have declared itself well within that interval (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Illness Anxiety Disorder).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Illness Anxiety Disorder

options.text: Start quetiapine 50 mg at night and review him in six weeks
options.rationale: There is no delusional conviction here since he accepts the possibility that he is wrong, so antipsychotic treatment is aimed at a mechanism that is not operating (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting health anxiety
options.rationale: Preoccupation with having a serious illness in the near absence of somatic symptoms, with excessive checking and care seeking, is illness anxiety rather than somatic symptom disorder, and cognitive behavioural therapy that targets catastrophic misinterpretation and dismantles the checking and reassurance cycle is the treatment with the best evidence (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: The 2013 reclassification split the old hypochondriasis concept into two: patients with distressing physical symptoms plus disproportionate health concern now carry somatic symptom disorder, while those preoccupied with having an illness in the absence of significant symptoms carry illness anxiety disorder. Illness anxiety is further divided into care seeking and care avoidant types, and the care avoidant group is easily missed because they present late with genuine pathology. Neither is a diagnosis of exclusion, and both can coexist with real disease. The management principles are shared: one coordinating doctor, scheduled rather than symptom triggered appointments, an explicit agreement to limit investigations, and referral for a psychological therapy that targets the interpretation of bodily sensations.
key_points: Illness anxiety disorder requires preoccupation with having an illness with minimal or absent somatic symptoms.
Somatic symptom disorder requires distressing physical symptoms plus disproportionate thoughts or behaviours about them.
Absence of external incentive separates both from malingering and factitious disorder.
Reassurance and repeat investigation relieve anxiety briefly and reinforce it in the longer term.
Cognitive behavioural therapy has the strongest evidence, with scheduled reviews by a single coordinating doctor.
explanation.pearls: Booking fixed interval appointments that are not contingent on new symptoms is the single structural change that most reduces investigation rates, because it removes the need to produce a symptom in order to be seen.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
BMJ Best Practice: Illness Anxiety Disorder

subtopic_detail: Treating a recurrent winter pattern depressive illness with bright light therapy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 38 year old woman who moved from Cairns to Hobart four years ago for work. For the past three winters she has become flat, slept 11 hours a night and still felt unrefreshed, craved bread and biscuits and gained around 5 kg each year.

Each year she has been back to her usual self by October without treatment, and she describes those summer months as entirely normal rather than elevated, with no reduced need for sleep and no overspending. Her energy is the symptom that bothers her most; she has no thoughts of self harm. This year she has come in during May asking to prevent the pattern rather than wait it out. Her thyroid function is normal and her vitamin D is 68 nmol/L.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (50-150), haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-165), ferritin 62 mcg/L (20-200)
data_table.Examination: Reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Melatonin 2 mg at bedtime through the winter months each year
options.rationale: Evening melatonin shifts circadian phase in the wrong direction for a phase delayed winter pattern, and the evidence in this condition is far weaker than for morning light (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Lithium carbonate with three monthly concentration monitoring
options.rationale: A mood stabiliser would be considered if the summer months were hypomanic rather than euthymic, and she describes no reduced need for sleep, no overspending and no elevated mood (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Modafinil each morning through the winter months of each year
options.rationale: A wake promoting agent treats the hypersomnia symptomatically without addressing the mood episode, and it is not approved or evidenced for depressive illness in Australia (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Vitamin D 1000 units daily through the winter months each year
options.rationale: Supplementation is reasonable when the concentration is deficient, but hers is 68 nmol/L, and randomised trials of vitamin D for winter pattern depression have not shown benefit (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Seasonal Affective Disorder).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Seasonal Affective Disorder

options.text: Bright light therapy each morning through the winter months
options.rationale: Recurrent depressive episodes with a consistent winter onset and full summer remission, hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and weight gain define a seasonal pattern, and morning bright light is first line with a response rate comparable to antidepressant medication and a faster onset (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: A seasonal pattern is a specifier applied to recurrent major depressive or bipolar disorder rather than a diagnosis in its own right, and it requires at least two consecutive years of seasonally timed episodes with full remission in between and seasonal episodes outnumbering non seasonal ones over a lifetime. Prevalence rises with latitude, which in Australia means Tasmania and the southern mainland rather than the tropics, and a recent move south is a common trigger for a first presentation. The atypical features of hypersomnia, hyperphagia with carbohydrate craving and weight gain are far more common than in non seasonal depression. Light therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for seasonality, and serotonergic antidepressants all have supporting evidence, and starting preventively before the usual onset month works better than waiting for the episode.
key_points: The seasonal specifier needs two consecutive years of seasonal episodes with full inter episode remission.
Hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and weight gain are the characteristic atypical features.
Morning bright light therapy is first line and acts within one to two weeks.
Screen for a history of elevated mood, because the pattern also occurs in bipolar disorder.
Starting before the usual month of onset prevents rather than treats the episode.
explanation.pearls: The standard prescription is 10 000 lux at about 30 cm for 30 minutes within an hour of waking, and moving the session later in the day is the commonest reason a trial appears to fail.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
BMJ Best Practice: Seasonal Affective Disorder

subtopic_detail: Recognising cataplexy behind a referral for depression with hypersomnia
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 23 year old apprentice referred by his mother because she thinks he is depressed. He sleeps ten hours at night, still falls asleep in the training room most afternoons, and has been written up twice for it.

He tells you that when something really strikes him as funny his knees give way and his jaw goes slack for a few seconds, and that he stays completely aware throughout and can hear everyone around him. Twice on waking he has been unable to move for a minute or so, and he sometimes sees a figure at the end of the bed as he is dropping off. He describes his mood as fed up rather than sad, still plays five a side on weekends and enjoys it, and has no thoughts of self harm.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, normal cranial nerve and limb neurological examination, no neck circumference increase and no tonsillar hypertrophy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, ferritin, thyroid stimulating hormone and glycated haemoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise sleep hygiene measures and review him again in three months
options.rationale: Insufficient sleep syndrome is a genuine cause of daytime sleepiness in young adults, but it does not produce cataplexy, sleep paralysis or hypnagogic hallucinations, and three months is too long to wait with an occupational safety risk (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Arrange polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
options.rationale: Brief emotionally triggered bilateral loss of muscle tone with preserved awareness is cataplexy, and combined with daytime sleepiness, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations it requires overnight study to exclude other causes of disrupted sleep followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day for diagnosis (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review his mood in four weeks
options.rationale: He retains interest and pleasure in weekend sport and describes irritation rather than sadness, so the core criteria for a depressive episode are not met and the hypersomnia has a different explanation (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram and refer to the epilepsy service
options.rationale: Atonic seizures are the near pair for sudden loss of tone, but they impair awareness and are not reliably triggered by laughter, whereas he remains fully aware and can recount what was said (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Start modafinil 200 mg each morning and review him in four weeks
options.rationale: A wake promoting agent is part of eventual treatment but starting it before the sleep studies suppresses the very findings the studies depend on and leaves the cataplexy untreated (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy is typically diagnosed a decade after symptom onset, most often because excessive daytime sleepiness in an adolescent or young adult is attributed to depression, laziness or poor sleep habits. Cataplexy is the specific feature, and it is missed because patients describe it in ordinary language rather than as an attack, and because partial forms involving only the face, jaw or neck are common. Diagnosis requires polysomnography to exclude other sleep disruption, followed by a multiple sleep latency test showing a short mean latency with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods, and cerebrospinal fluid hypocretin measurement is used in difficult cases. Treatment separates the two symptom domains, with wake promoting agents for sleepiness and venlafaxine or sodium oxybate for cataplexy, alongside scheduled naps and driving advice.
key_points: Cataplexy is brief, bilateral, emotionally triggered loss of tone with fully preserved awareness.
Atonic seizure impairs awareness and is not laughter triggered; syncope has no emotional trigger and gives loss of consciousness.
Polysomnography precedes the multiple sleep latency test to exclude other causes of fragmented sleep.
Stimulants and antidepressants must be withheld before the sleep studies because they suppress the findings.
Driving and workplace safety are assessed at the first consultation, not after diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors suppress rapid eye movement sleep and can abolish both cataplexy and the sleep onset rapid eye movement periods the diagnosis depends on, so starting one before the sleep study can render the test falsely normal for up to two weeks after cessation.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Responding to complex sleep behaviour on a sedative hypnotic rather than substituting another agent
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 58 year old woman who has taken zolpidem 10 mg at night for eight months, originally prescribed after her mother died.

Her husband tells you he has twice found her standing at the kitchen bench at three in the morning making and eating toast, answering him in a flat voice and not remembering any of it in the morning. Last week she found biscuit wrappers on the bedroom floor and a half typed message on her phone sent to a work colleague at 2:40 am that she has no memory of writing. She drinks no alcohol and takes no other sedating medication. She sleeps about six hours a night and says the tablet is the only thing that gets her off to sleep.

data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, normal neurological examination, body mass index 26 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the zolpidem and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Sleep related eating, texting or driving with no recollection is a complex sleep behaviour that requires permanent cessation of the drug rather than dose reduction, and cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the first line replacement with durable benefit beyond the treatment period (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration Medicines Safety Update).
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration Medicines Safety Update

options.text: Halve the zolpidem dose and review her again in four weeks
options.rationale: Complex sleep behaviours have been reported at the lowest available doses and after a single dose, so reduction does not remove the risk and leaves her driving the next morning after an amnestic night (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration Medicines Safety Update).
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration Medicines Safety Update

options.text: Switch to temazepam 10 mg at night and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Temazepam is the near pair because it acts at the same receptor complex, and parasomnias including sleep related eating are reported with benzodiazepines as well, so substituting within the class reproduces the risk (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Add melatonin 2 mg at night and continue the current zolpidem
options.rationale: Adding a second agent while continuing the drug that caused the episodes does not address the problem, and prolonged release melatonin is at best a modest hypnotic in adults over 55 (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography before changing any treatment
options.rationale: This option sits on a diagnostic rather than a therapeutic axis, and while a sleep study is warranted if parasomnias continue after the drug stops, leaving her on it while awaiting a study accepts avoidable harm (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

explanation.summary: Complex sleep behaviours on sedative hypnotics carry an Australian boxed warning, and the instruction is unambiguous: any episode of sleep walking, sleep driving, sleep eating or other complex behaviour with amnesia is an absolute contraindication to further use of that agent. Risk rises with higher doses, concurrent alcohol or other central nervous system depressants, and shortened sleep opportunity, but episodes occur without any of these. The behaviours arise from incomplete arousal out of slow wave sleep, so patients appear awake and can perform coordinated acts while forming no memory. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, delivered face to face or through validated digital programs, outperforms hypnotics beyond the first few weeks and is the intervention that lets a patient come off the drug for good.
key_points: A single complex sleep behaviour episode contraindicates further use of that hypnotic.
Dose reduction does not eliminate the risk; episodes occur at the lowest doses.
Switching within the same receptor class reproduces the risk.
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and has effects that persist after treatment ends.
Next day driving impairment is an additional safety issue with these agents.
explanation.pearls: Australian dosing caps zolpidem at 10 mg for adults and 5 mg for women and those over 65, because women clear the drug more slowly and have higher morning plasma concentrations at the same dose.

sources.label: Therapeutic Goods Administration Medicines Safety Update

subtopic_detail: Separating consistent situational failure to speak from autism and from a language disorder
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6 year old girl referred by her school. She has not spoken a single word at school in the 18 months since she started, communicating with her teacher by nodding, pointing and handing over written notes.

At home she chatters constantly to her parents and her older brother, tells long detailed stories about her day and argues about bedtime. Her mother has recorded her at home and plays you a clip in which her speech is fluent, grammatical and age appropriate. She plays imaginative games with her cousins, takes turns, shares jokes and makes easy eye contact at home. She has no restricted interests, no repetitive movements and no insistence on routines. An audiology assessment last month was normal.

data_table.Examination: Interacts with the examiner by nodding and pointing, makes brief eye contact, no dysmorphic features, normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: Audiology assessment normal, growth and development otherwise age appropriate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for autism diagnostic assessment before any intervention
options.rationale: Autism is the near pair because both children may be silent with unfamiliar adults, but she shows reciprocal imaginative play, shared humour and comfortable eye contact at home with no restricted or repetitive behaviours, which does not fit (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start fluoxetine 10 mg daily and review her again in six weeks
options.rationale: A serotonergic antidepressant is a reasonable addition when a structured behavioural program has failed after an adequate trial, but it is not the starting point in a 6 year old (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange formal speech pathology language assessment and review
options.rationale: A language disorder would affect speech in every setting, and the home recording demonstrates fluent age appropriate grammar, so assessment would delay treatment (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Advise the school to allow written answers and review in a year
options.rationale: Accommodations that remove the need to speak reduce her distress in the short term but reinforce avoidance, which is the mechanism that maintains the condition, and a year of untreated avoidance worsens the prognosis (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Selective Mutism).

options.text: Refer for graded exposure therapy with a school based plan
options.rationale: Consistent failure to speak in a specific social setting for more than a month while speaking normally elsewhere is an anxiety disorder, and behavioural treatment using stimulus fading and graded exposure delivered jointly with the school is first line at this age (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is classified as an anxiety disorder and typically begins between the ages of three and six, becoming apparent when a child starts school. The diagnostic requirement is a consistent failure to speak in specific situations where speech is expected, lasting at least a month beyond the first month of school, with normal speech in other settings and no attributable communication disorder. It is commonly mistaken for shyness, oppositionality or autism, and the average delay to treatment exceeds two years. Treatment is behavioural, using stimulus fading in which a comfortable speaking partner is gradually joined by new people and new settings, and shaping in which non verbal communication is stepped up towards audible speech, delivered in the classroom rather than only in a clinic room.
key_points: Consistent situational failure to speak with normal speech elsewhere is the defining feature.
The minimum duration is one month, not counting the first month of school.
Fluent reciprocal language and imaginative play at home argue against autism and against a language disorder.
Stimulus fading and graded exposure delivered with the school are first line.
Accommodations that remove the need to speak reinforce avoidance.
explanation.pearls: Pressing a child to speak, or rewarding speech in front of the class, reliably worsens the condition; the effective step is to have the parent speak with the child in the empty classroom and then fade the teacher into the room while the conversation continues.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Managing anxiety based school refusal presenting as recurrent morning abdominal symptoms
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 9 year old boy brought by his mother with six weeks of stomach aches and vomiting on school mornings. He wakes at six, complains of pain, retches once or twice into the sink, and by ten o'clock at home he is playing and asking for lunch.

There are no symptoms on Saturdays or Sundays, and he was entirely well through the two week term break in July. He has been at school four days in the past three weeks. He tells you he worries that something will happen to his mother while he is out of the house, and he has been getting into his parents' bed most nights since his grandfather died in May. His weight is tracking along the 50th centile, he has no night waking with pain, no blood in the motions and no mouth ulcers.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no tenderness, no masses, no perianal disease, growth along the 50th centile for weight and height
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, C reactive protein, coeliac serology with total immunoglobulin A and faecal calprotectin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: A graded return to school plan developed with the school and parents
options.rationale: Symptoms confined to school mornings with complete resolution at weekends and in holidays, in a child with normal growth and normal inflammatory markers, indicate anxiety based school refusal, and the treatment is prompt graded reattendance with parallel work with the parents on separation and morning routines (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start fluoxetine 10 mg daily and review him again in six weeks
options.rationale: Medication is added when a structured behavioural and school based program has not succeeded, or when there is a comorbid depressive disorder, neither of which applies at this point (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Home schooling arrangement until the abdominal symptoms settle
options.rationale: Every week out of school makes return harder, and removing the feared situation entrenches the avoidance rather than allowing the anxiety to extinguish (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound and coeliac serology before any other management step
options.rationale: Coeliac serology with an adequate immunoglobulin A has already returned normal, and further imaging in a child with normal growth and weekend freedom from symptoms adds cost and legitimises the symptom as organic (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Refer to paediatric gastroenterology for further investigation
options.rationale: Inflammatory bowel disease is the near pair that a normal calprotectin, normal C reactive protein and centile stable growth make very unlikely, and none of its alarm features such as night waking with pain, rectal bleeding or mouth ulcers is present (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: School refusal is a presentation rather than a diagnosis, and the underlying condition is most often separation anxiety in primary school children and social anxiety or depression in adolescents. It is distinguished from truancy by the fact that the child stays at home with the parents' knowledge and is distressed rather than concealing the absence. Somatic symptoms are the usual presenting complaint and are genuine rather than fabricated, but their timing is diagnostic: confined to school mornings, absent at weekends and in holidays. The single strongest predictor of outcome is the duration of absence before intervention, so return to school is arranged in days to weeks rather than being deferred until the child feels ready.
key_points: Symptoms confined to school mornings and absent at weekends and in holidays point to school refusal.
Distinguish from truancy: the parents know, the child is at home, and there is distress rather than concealment.
Normal growth, normal inflammatory markers and normal calprotectin make organic disease unlikely.
Duration of absence before intervention predicts outcome, so return is arranged quickly.
Parent focused work on the morning routine and separation runs alongside the school plan.
explanation.pearls: A bereavement in the household within the preceding six months is one of the commonest precipitants of separation anxiety at this age, and asking directly about who has died or become ill often reframes a presentation that has been investigated as abdominal pain for months.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Choosing behavioural therapy ahead of antipsychotic medication for impairing tics
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing an 11 year old boy whose parents are worried about movements that started when he was eight. He blinks hard, jerks his head to the left and shrugs one shoulder, and for the past 18 months he has also cleared his throat repeatedly and made a short barking sound.

He tells you he gets a build up of feeling in his neck beforehand, like an itch he has to scratch, and that he can hold the movements in for a minute or two at the cost of the feeling getting worse until he lets go. The movements settle when he is absorbed in building models and are worst when he is tired or being watched. Between movements he is fully alert with no confusion and no loss of awareness. His handwriting has deteriorated because of the head jerks and two boys have started imitating him in the playground.

data_table.Examination: Multiple motor and vocal tics observed during the consultation, briefly suppressible on request, normal tone, power, coordination and gait
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start clonidine at night and review his tics again in six weeks
options.rationale: An alpha 2 agonist is the preferred medication when attention deficit hyperactivity disorder coexists because it treats both, but there is no attentional complaint here and it still sits behind behavioural therapy (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram before any treatment is started
options.rationale: The near pair is myoclonic seizure activity, but seizures are neither preceded by a premonitory urge nor voluntarily suppressible, and awareness is preserved throughout here (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Advise that no treatment is needed and review him in six months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting with psychoeducation is right for tics that do not interfere with function, but his handwriting has deteriorated and he is being teased, which meets the threshold for active treatment (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer for a comprehensive behavioural intervention for his tics
options.rationale: Multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic persisting beyond a year with a premonitory urge and brief voluntary suppressibility is the characteristic pattern, and behavioural therapy combining habit reversal with function based intervention is first line where it is available, with effect sizes comparable to medication and without metabolic cost (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start risperidone 0.5 mg at night and review him in four weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotic treatment reduces tic severity but carries weight gain, sedation and prolactin elevation in a growing child, so it is reserved for tics that remain impairing after a behavioural trial (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Tic disorders are classified by whether tics are motor, vocal or both and by duration, with a year of both types required for the full syndrome. Severity typically peaks between ages 10 and 12 and improves substantially through adolescence in most patients, which is why psychoeducation about the natural history is itself an intervention. Around half of children have coexisting attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and around a third have obsessive compulsive symptoms, and these comorbidities usually cause more functional impairment than the tics themselves. Treatment is driven by impairment rather than by tic count, and school liaison to stop peer imitation and allow discreet release of tics is often as valuable as anything prescribed.
key_points: The premonitory urge with brief voluntary suppressibility distinguishes tics from myoclonus, chorea and seizures.
Behavioural therapy combining habit reversal and function based intervention is first line.
Medication is added when tics remain impairing, chosen according to comorbidity.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive symptoms usually cause more impairment than the tics.
Severity peaks around ages 10 to 12 and improves through adolescence in most children.
explanation.pearls: Stimulants for coexisting attention deficit hyperactivity disorder were long avoided for fear of worsening tics, but randomised data show tic severity is unchanged or improved, so a stimulant is not contraindicated when the attentional impairment is the greater problem.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Requiring prospective symptom charting before treating a suspected premenstrual mood disorder
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29 year old woman who says that for five years she has become irritable, tearful and unable to concentrate in the week before her period, and that she once slammed a door hard enough to crack the frame.

She tells you the symptoms lift within two or three days of her period arriving and that she feels entirely herself for the fortnight after that. She has never written any of this down and is describing it from memory. She is not using hormonal contraception and does not wish to conceive in the next year. Her partner has told her the pattern is obvious to him but he has not tracked it either.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect on the day of review, which is day 8 of her cycle, no psychomotor change and no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, ferritin, thyroid stimulating hormone and beta human chorionic gonadotrophin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review her again in two cycles
options.rationale: A serotonergic antidepressant is effective once the diagnosis is confirmed, but starting it now removes the untreated baseline that the charting depends on and would treat an underlying disorder inadequately if that is what is present (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive and review her in two cycles
options.rationale: Continuous or extended cycle combined contraception is a reasonable second line option after confirmation, but it abolishes the luteal phase and with it any chance of establishing the pattern (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Measure serum progesterone and oestradiol on day 21 of the cycle
options.rationale: Luteal hormone concentrations are normal in this condition, which reflects altered central sensitivity to normal hormonal fluctuation rather than abnormal concentrations, so the test cannot confirm or exclude it (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Refer for gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist therapy trial
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression is reserved for severe confirmed disease that has failed antidepressant and hormonal treatment, and it requires add back therapy because of bone loss (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Prospective daily symptom rating across two consecutive cycles
options.rationale: The diagnosis requires prospective daily ratings over at least two symptomatic cycles because retrospective accounts are confirmed in only around half of women, the rest turning out to have a premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying mood or anxiety disorder that needs different treatment (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder requires at least five symptoms including one core affective symptom, present in the final week before menses, improving within a few days of onset of menses and minimal in the week after, confirmed by prospective ratings over two symptomatic cycles. The requirement for prospective charting is not bureaucratic: retrospective report agrees with prospective data in only about half of cases, and the alternative explanation, premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying depressive, anxiety or personality disorder, is treated quite differently. Once confirmed, serotonergic antidepressants are first line and can be given continuously or restricted to the luteal phase with similar efficacy, which is unusual among antidepressant indications and reflects a rapid mechanism distinct from the effect in major depression. Second line options include extended cycle combined contraception, and ovarian suppression with add back oestrogen is reserved for refractory disease.
key_points: Two cycles of prospective daily ratings are required before the diagnosis is made.
Retrospective report is confirmed prospectively in only about half of women.
Symptoms must be minimal in the week following menses, which is what separates the disorder from a premenstrual exacerbation.
Luteal hormone concentrations are normal and do not aid diagnosis.
Serotonergic antidepressants work continuously or in the luteal phase alone.
explanation.pearls: The antidepressant effect in this condition appears within a day or two rather than the usual two to four weeks, which is why luteal phase only dosing from ovulation to the onset of bleeding is a legitimate regimen here and nowhere else in psychiatry.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Separating a chronic subsyndromal bipolar spectrum illness from affective instability of personality
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 26 year old graphic designer referred with mood swings that have gone on since she was 22. She describes stretches of four or five days at a time when she needs only five hours sleep, works through the night on side projects and talks over people, followed by stretches of a week or so when she is flat, oversleeps and cancels plans.

She has never had a period of elevated mood lasting four full days with the impairment or the number of symptoms her previous psychiatrist described as needed for a formal episode, and she has never been admitted or psychotic. The shifts come on over a day or two and are not obviously set off by arguments or rejections. She has had the same partner for five years and the same three close friends since school, has never self harmed, and does not describe chronic emptiness or fears of abandonment. In four years she has never been free of symptoms for as long as two months.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic on the day of review, normal speech rate, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise watchful waiting with review of her mood in six months
options.rationale: Four years of continuous symptoms with occupational and social consequences is not a watchful waiting problem, and between 15 and 50 per cent of these patients progress to a full bipolar disorder (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Bipolar Disorder).

options.text: Commence a mood stabiliser with psychoeducation and mood charting
options.rationale: Two or more years of alternating subthreshold hypomanic and depressive periods with no symptom free interval beyond two months and no full episode defines a chronic bipolar spectrum illness, and management follows bipolar principles with a mood stabiliser, structured psychoeducation and prospective mood charting (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily with review again in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy in a bipolar spectrum illness risks switching and cycle acceleration, and it is the commonest reason these patients present later with a clear hypomanic episode (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer for dialectical behaviour therapy with weekly skills group
options.rationale: The near pair is the affective instability of borderline personality disorder, but there the shifts last hours rather than days, are triggered by interpersonal events, and sit alongside identity disturbance, self harm and chronic emptiness, none of which she describes (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Commence a stimulant trial after formal attention testing is done
options.rationale: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder produces continuous rather than episodic symptoms and begins in childhood, and a stimulant in an unstabilised bipolar spectrum illness can precipitate elevation (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Cyclothymic disorder is defined by at least two years in adults of numerous periods with hypomanic symptoms that never reach episode criteria alternating with depressive symptoms that never reach major episode criteria, present at least half the time and never absent for more than two months. It is chronically under recognised because no single period is dramatic enough to prompt presentation, and patients are frequently labelled as having a personality difficulty instead. The two discriminators that do most work are the duration of a mood shift, days in the bipolar spectrum against hours in borderline personality disorder, and whether shifts are interpersonally triggered. Progression to bipolar I or II is substantial, so treatment follows bipolar principles and antidepressant monotherapy is avoided.
key_points: Two years of alternating subthreshold symptoms with no symptom free interval beyond two months defines the disorder.
Mood shifts lasting days and occurring without interpersonal triggers point away from personality based instability.
Stable relationships, stable identity and absence of self harm argue against borderline personality disorder.
Antidepressant monotherapy risks switching and cycle acceleration.
A substantial minority progress to bipolar I or II disorder over time.
explanation.pearls: Ask what the person was like between the swings: a return to a stable baseline personality between episodes fits the bipolar spectrum, whereas persistent emptiness and identity instability continuing between mood shifts points to a personality disorder even when the swings themselves look similar.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Washout interval before a monoamine oxidase inhibitor after a long half life antidepressant
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an outpatient clinic reviewing a 47 year old man with a depressive illness that has not responded to two adequate trials. He completed 12 weeks of sertraline at 200 mg and then eight months of venlafaxine at 225 mg without meaningful improvement.

He was changed to fluoxetine 40 mg daily six months ago and took his last dose three days ago in anticipation of today's appointment. The consultant plans to start moclobemide. He takes no other medication, no over the counter preparations and no herbal products, and he has no cardiac or hepatic disease. His most recent electrolytes and liver function tests were within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: No clonus, no hyperreflexia, no tremor, no diaphoresis, normal tone
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, liver function tests and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for starting the new agent?

options.text: Start it after a 48 hour gap with close outpatient review
options.rationale: Outpatient monitoring cannot substitute for pharmacokinetic clearance, and serotonin toxicity can progress from tremor and clonus to hyperthermia and rigidity within hours (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Cross taper the two agents over the coming fortnight instead
options.rationale: Cross tapering is standard when switching between most antidepressants but is specifically prohibited when a monoamine oxidase inhibitor is one of the pair, because the overlap is the mechanism of toxicity (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Wait five weeks after the last fluoxetine dose before starting it
options.rationale: Fluoxetine's active metabolite norfluoxetine has an elimination half life of one to two weeks, so five or more elimination half lives take about five weeks, and this is the interval required before any monoamine oxidase inhibitor is introduced (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Wait two full weeks after the last fluoxetine dose before starting it
options.rationale: Two weeks is the correct washout after most other serotonin reuptake inhibitors, but fluoxetine is the exception because of its metabolite, and applying the general rule here is the classic error (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start it now because the agent is a reversible inhibitor
options.rationale: Reversibility and selectivity for monoamine oxidase A shorten the washout needed after stopping this agent, not the washout needed before starting it, and serotonin toxicity has been reported with this combination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors remain useful in treatment resistant and atypical depression, but the switching rules around them are the most error prone part of antidepressant prescribing. The general principle is that a washout of five elimination half lives of the parent drug and any active metabolite is required before starting one, and this is two weeks for most reuptake inhibitors but five weeks after fluoxetine. Going in the other direction, two weeks must elapse after stopping an irreversible inhibitor before another serotonergic agent starts, while only 24 hours is needed after the reversible agent moclobemide because enzyme function returns as the drug clears rather than requiring resynthesis. Dietary tyramine restriction is far less onerous with the reversible agent, but interactions with indirect sympathomimetics such as pseudoephedrine remain.
key_points: Washout before a monoamine oxidase inhibitor is five half lives of the drug and its active metabolite.
Fluoxetine requires five weeks; most other reuptake inhibitors require two.
Only 24 hours is needed after stopping moclobemide before a serotonergic agent starts.
