Cross tapering is never used when a monoamine oxidase inhibitor is one of the two drugs.
Serotonin toxicity presents with clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation and hyperthermia within hours.
explanation.pearls: Inducible clonus in the lower limbs with agitation or diaphoresis meets the Hunter criteria for serotonin toxicity and is the single most useful bedside sign, because rigidity and hyperthermia appear only once the syndrome is already severe.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing persistent detachment with intact reality testing from focal seizures and from panic
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 24 year old woman who describes episodes in which she feels as though she is watching herself from a few feet behind her own head, and the room looks flat, like a stage set.

The episodes come on over minutes and last from several hours to most of a day. Throughout them she knows the feeling is not real and can carry on a conversation, drive and work, and afterwards she can recount everything that happened. She has no lip smacking or hand fumbling, no rising sensation in her stomach, no unusual smells and no period of confusion at the end. There is no chest tightness, palpitations or breathlessness with the episodes. They began during a period of daily cannabis use two years ago and have continued unchanged since she stopped 18 months ago.

data_table.Examination: Normal cranial nerve, motor and sensory examination, orientated in time place and person, insight fully preserved
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid stimulating hormone and urine drug screen within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before treatment
options.rationale: Structural imaging is warranted where the neurological examination is abnormal or where the history suggests focal seizures, and neither applies, so it would delay treatment without changing it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the symptoms
options.rationale: Persistent detachment from self and surroundings with fully intact reality testing, lasting hours and free of autonomic or ictal features, is a dissociative disorder, and psychological therapy addressing catastrophic appraisal of the sensations and safety behaviours such as constant self monitoring is first line (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Arrange prolonged video electroencephalogram monitoring first
options.rationale: The near pair is a focal seizure arising from the temporal lobe, which can produce derealisation but lasts one to two minutes rather than hours, impairs awareness or produces automatisms, and is followed by confusion, none of which is present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Start propranolol before predictable stressors and review later
options.rationale: Beta blockade targets the autonomic surge of panic, and she has no palpitations, chest tightness or breathlessness, so the mechanism being treated is not the one operating (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start olanzapine 5 mg at night and review her again in six weeks
options.rationale: Preserved insight that the experience is not real excludes a psychotic disorder, and antipsychotic treatment has no established role and can worsen the subjective sense of detachment (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Depersonalisation and derealisation are common transient experiences, reported by up to half the population at some point, and become a disorder only when persistent or recurrent and causing distress or impairment. The defining feature is that reality testing remains intact throughout, which is what separates the condition from psychosis. Onset is frequently precipitated by cannabis, hallucinogens or severe stress, and the symptoms commonly persist long after the substance has been stopped, which patients find frightening and which often drives a fruitless neurological workup. The condition is under diagnosed with an average delay of many years, partly because the experience is hard to describe and patients fear being thought psychotic.
key_points: Intact reality testing throughout is what separates the disorder from psychosis.
Duration of hours to days separates it from focal seizures, which last one to two minutes.
Absence of an autonomic surge separates it from panic attacks.
Cannabis and hallucinogens are frequent precipitants and symptoms outlast cessation.
Psychological therapy is first line; no medication has established efficacy.
explanation.pearls: Comorbid depression or anxiety is present in most cases and treating it often reduces the dissociative symptoms substantially, so screening for and treating the comorbidity does more than any agent aimed at the detachment itself.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Separating persistent bereavement related distress from a depressive episode
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 62 year old woman referred by her general practitioner sixteen months after her husband died from bowel cancer. She says she aches for him every day, keeps his voicemail message on her phone and plays it most nights, and cannot bring herself to walk past the cafe where they used to meet.

She tells you she does not know who she is any more without him and feels that part of her died with him. She still meets her sister weekly, laughs at her grandchildren, cooks properly and has continued her volunteer shifts at the op shop. She denies feeling worthless, denies wanting to die, and her appetite and concentration are unchanged. She sleeps about five hours and wakes thinking of him.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect with tearfulness when speaking of her husband, no psychomotor retardation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder of moderate severity
options.rationale: A depressive episode requires pervasive low mood or loss of interest across contexts with features such as worthlessness or hopelessness, and her preserved enjoyment of family and volunteering with intact appetite and concentration argues against it (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Post traumatic stress disorder following the death
options.rationale: This requires intrusive re experiencing of a traumatic event with hyperarousal, whereas her avoidance is of reminders that provoke longing rather than fear and she has no flashbacks or startle response (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health

options.text: Prolonged grief disorder with identity disruption
options.rationale: Intense daily yearning with preoccupation, identity disruption, avoidance of reminders and emotional pain persisting beyond twelve months after the death, with clear functional impact, meets the criteria for this distinct diagnosis (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
options.rationale: An adjustment disorder is defined as resolving within six months of the stressor ending, so a syndrome active at sixteen months falls outside it (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

options.text: Uncomplicated bereavement within the expected range
options.rationale: Ordinary grief softens in intensity and frequency over the first year and does not carry sustained identity disruption or avoidance that constrains where a person will walk (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder was added as a distinct diagnosis because a minority of bereaved people, roughly one in ten after a natural death and more after a sudden or violent one, remain acutely grief stricken long past the point at which most begin to reorganise their lives. The adult threshold is twelve months since the death, with children and adolescents assessed at six months. The core is persistent intense yearning or preoccupation accompanied by symptoms such as identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, a sense that life is meaningless, intense loneliness and difficulty re engaging. The distinction from a depressive episode matters therapeutically, because grief focused psychotherapy outperforms antidepressant monotherapy for this presentation while antidepressants remain first line for a comorbid depressive episode. Risk factors include a sudden or violent death, the loss of a child, an unusually dependent relationship, and a lack of social support.
key_points: The adult diagnostic threshold is twelve months after the death, six months for children and adolescents.
Yearning and preoccupation are the core, not pervasive anhedonia or worthlessness.
Preserved enjoyment in other domains argues against a concurrent depressive episode.
Grief focused psychotherapy is first line, with antidepressants reserved for comorbid depression.
Sudden, violent or unexpected deaths substantially raise the risk of the disorder.
explanation.pearls: Structured grief focused cognitive behavioural therapy delivered over roughly sixteen sessions outperforms antidepressant medication alone for this diagnosis, and adding an antidepressant to that therapy improves outcomes only when a depressive episode is also present.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health

subtopic_detail: Choosing a household intervention over dose escalation after repeated early relapse
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an early psychosis service reviewing a 21 year old apprentice fourteen months after his first episode of psychosis. He has been readmitted twice in that time, each admission following a fortnight of escalating arguments at home.

His father tells you in front of him that the boy is lazy, could snap out of it if he tried, and needs watching every minute. His mother has given up her shifts to supervise him and phones him hourly when she is out. A depot antipsychotic has been given on schedule with dispensing records confirming every dose, and his plasma level last week was in the expected range. He uses no alcohol or other drugs and urine drug screening has been negative on each admission. Between admissions he has no delusions or hallucinations, sleeps normally and is looking for work.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no thought disorder, no perceptual abnormality, no extrapyramidal signs on examination
data_table.Investigations: Antipsychotic plasma concentration within expected range, urine drug screen negative, full blood count and metabolic panel within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Increase the depot antipsychotic dose at the next scheduled administration
options.rationale: Escalation targets inadequate exposure, and a documented adherence record with a plasma level in range removes that explanation while adding metabolic and movement side effects (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Add an antidepressant to cover the emotional distress before each relapse
options.rationale: There is no depressive syndrome described between episodes, and treating the young man alone leaves the household pattern that reliably precedes each admission untouched (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Refer for individual cognitive behavioural therapy for psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: Individual therapy is valuable for residual delusions or hallucinations, which he does not have between episodes, so it addresses a target that is absent here (Source: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis).
source_refs: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis

options.text: Arrange supported accommodation so that he moves out of the family home
options.rationale: Relocation may become part of a longer plan but removes his main support rather than changing how it is delivered, and it is offered after a household intervention has been tried (Source: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis).
source_refs: Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis

options.text: Offer structured family intervention with psychoeducation for the household
options.rationale: Criticism and emotional over involvement of this intensity roughly double the one year relapse rate, and a structured family program of at least ten sessions reduces relapse and readmission independently of medication (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Relapse in early psychosis is most often explained by non adherence or substance use, and both must be actively excluded rather than assumed before other causes are considered. When adherence is documented, drug screening is clean and the plasma level is adequate, the psychosocial environment becomes the leading candidate, and the household emotional climate is the best studied element of it. Criticism, hostility and emotional over involvement, measured as expressed emotion, predict relapse across cultures and are modifiable. Family intervention combines education about the illness, communication and problem solving skills, and planning for early warning signs, and Australian guidelines recommend offering it to every family in contact with a person recovering from a first episode. Its effect size on relapse prevention is comparable with that of maintenance antipsychotic therapy, and the two are additive rather than alternatives.
key_points: Exclude non adherence and substance use first when relapse recurs in early psychosis.
High criticism and emotional over involvement in the household roughly double one year relapse risk.
Structured family intervention of ten or more sessions reduces relapse independently of medication.
Dose escalation is not justified when the plasma level already sits in the expected range.
Individual therapy for psychotic symptoms targets residual symptoms, which are absent between episodes here.
explanation.pearls: Relapse risk tracks the number of hours per week the young person spends in face to face contact with a highly critical relative, which is why family intervention that changes the quality of that contact outperforms simply reducing its quantity.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia
Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis

subtopic_detail: Choosing the NSW instrument that records treatment preferences for a future episode
stem: In a NSW community clinic you see a 34-year-old teacher with bipolar disorder, well for eleven months on lithium. She has had three manic episodes, two ending in involuntary admission. Olanzapine caused such severe inner restlessness that she paced all night. She would accept another antipsychotic, and wants her sister rather than her father contacted. She reasons through each preference today.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no pressure of speech, insight into illness intact
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.72 mmol/L, thyroid and renal function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action at this consultation?

options.text: Arrange an enduring power of attorney so her sister manages her affairs
options.rationale: A power of attorney governs financial and legal affairs and authorises nobody to express her treatment preferences during an admission, so it answers a different question. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives

options.text: Explain that a future treating team will decide her treatment regardless
options.rationale: Compulsory powers are real, but a directive made with capacity is still taken into account, and a designated carer nomination genuinely changes who is informed and involved. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives

options.text: Record the olanzapine reaction in her file as an adverse drug reaction
options.rationale: Documenting akathisia is necessary but it is a clinical record, not an expression of her wishes, and it says nothing about who she wants involved. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Support an advance care directive and a designated carer nomination today
options.rationale: A window of stable capacity is exactly when these documents can be made. In NSW the pair that follows her into a future involuntary admission is a common law advance care directive, which the treating team should take into account, and a written nomination of her sister as designated carer, which gives her sister the statutory entitlement to notice and information. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives; NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives
NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers

options.text: Apply for a community treatment order now to prevent a further admission
options.rationale: A community treatment order requires current criteria and least restrictive care, and imposing one on a woman who is well and engaged would be neither lawful nor proportionate. (Source: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: community treatment orders)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: community treatment orders

explanation.summary: Recovery oriented practice treats the person's own expertise about their illness as clinical information. In NSW the instruments for capturing it are an advance care directive, which has no governing statute and operates at common law, and a written nomination of up to two designated carers, which lasts twelve months and determines who receives information and notice during a compulsory admission. Neither binds the treating team under the Mental Health Act 2007, but both change what the team reads and who it rings, and the clinical value is greatest in relapsing illnesses where the treatment decisions are predictable. Both are made while the person is well, because capacity is decision specific and fluctuates with illness.
key_points: An advance care directive in NSW is a common law document with no statutory form.
It is taken into account during compulsory treatment but does not override the Act.
A designated carer is chosen by the person, in writing, and the nomination lasts twelve months.
Powers of attorney govern finances, not mental health treatment preferences.
explanation.pearls: Akathisia is the antipsychotic adverse effect most strongly linked to treatment refusal and to suicidal thinking, so a documented severe episode is a prescribing constraint rather than a preference, and it belongs in both the adverse reaction record and the directive.

sources.label: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives
NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers
NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: community treatment orders

subtopic_detail: Repetitive theft of items of no use or value in a woman with intact cognition
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar asked to assess a 47 year old accountant referred by the court after her third shoplifting charge in two years. She earns a good income and had more than enough money in her purse on each occasion.

She describes a tightening tension that builds over an hour or two in the shop, a rush of relief at the moment she puts the item into her bag, and then hours of shame. The items were a hairbrush, a packet of batteries and a child's colouring book, none of which she needed. She has given them away or thrown them out unopened. She has never been in trouble otherwise, has held the same job for nineteen years, and says the whole thing horrifies her. Her sleep, appetite and energy are unchanged and she has had no periods of reduced need for sleep or increased spending.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic with appropriate shame, no pressure of speech, no grandiosity, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 29 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Manic episode with disinhibited and impulsive behaviour
options.rationale: Mania would bring reduced need for sleep, elevated or irritable mood and increased goal directed activity across weeks, and the behaviour would occur within an episode rather than in isolation over two years (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Antisocial personality disorder with a pattern of unlawful conduct
options.rationale: That diagnosis requires a pervasive disregard for others from adolescence with deceitfulness and absent remorse, and her intense shame and otherwise blameless history are the opposite pattern (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

options.text: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia presenting with theft
options.rationale: Frontal dementia can present with shoplifting but brings apathy, loss of empathy, disinhibition and stereotyped behaviours with occupational decline, none of which fits nineteen stable years in a demanding job with a near perfect cognitive screen (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Frontotemporal dementia).

options.text: Kleptomania with the characteristic tension and relief cycle
options.rationale: Recurrent failure to resist stealing objects not needed for use or monetary value, with mounting tension beforehand and gratification at the time, and no anger, vengeance or delusion behind it, is the defining pattern (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

options.text: Obsessive compulsive disorder with a compulsion expressed as stealing
options.rationale: The near pair shares tension and relief, but compulsions are performed to neutralise a feared outcome and are experienced as unwanted from the outset, whereas the act here is gratifying at the moment of performance (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

explanation.summary: Kleptomania is rare, affecting well under one per cent of the population, but it is heavily over represented among people charged with shoplifting who have no other criminal history and no financial motive. The diagnostic weight rests on what the objects are and what happens to them: items of no use or value, often discarded, given away or hoarded unopened, separate it from ordinary theft. It commonly coexists with depressive disorders, other impulse control disorders, substance use and eating disorders, so screening for these is part of the assessment rather than an afterthought. Treatment evidence is limited, with cognitive behavioural therapy using covert sensitisation the best supported psychological approach and naltrexone the best supported pharmacological one. A psychiatric report can materially change sentencing, but the diagnosis must never be inferred simply from the fact that a charge has been laid.
key_points: Objects taken have no use or monetary value and are often discarded or given away unopened.
Tension before and gratification at the moment of the act is the core, without anger or delusion as motive.
Shame and an otherwise blameless history separate it from antisocial personality disorder.
Comorbid mood, substance use and eating disorders are the rule rather than the exception.
Cognitive behavioural therapy with covert sensitisation and naltrexone have the best supporting evidence.
explanation.pearls: Naltrexone at 50 to 150 mg daily reduces stealing urges within weeks in placebo controlled work, and liver function is checked at baseline and then during the first months because dose related transaminase elevation is the limiting adverse effect.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Separating defiant oppositional behaviour from a conduct disorder in a school aged child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a community child health clinic seeing a 9 year old boy brought by his mother after a note from his teacher. For about ten months he has argued with every adult instruction, refused to do what he is asked, and needled his younger sister until she cries, then insisted she started it.

His mother says he is touchy, loses his temper several times a week when he is asked to stop what he is doing, and holds a grudge for days. He has never hurt another child or an animal, and nothing at home or at school has been broken, stolen or set alight. Between confrontations he is cheerful, plays well with two friends and is calm at his swimming club. He reads at his year level and his teacher reports he sits and finishes his written work without prompting.

data_table.Examination: Engages well in conversation, reciprocal eye contact and shared enjoyment, no repetitive behaviours, no motor tics
data_table.Investigations: Hearing screen and vision screen normal, developmental history unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder of the combined presentation
options.rationale: Inattention or hyperactivity would show up as unfinished work and difficulty staying seated across settings, and his teacher describes the opposite, so the defiance is not being driven by an attentional disorder (Source: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.text: Conduct disorder with aggression towards people and property
options.rationale: The near pair requires violation of the basic rights of others or major age appropriate norms through aggression, destruction, deceit or theft, and none of those categories is represented here (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

options.text: Oppositional defiant disorder of angry and vindictive pattern
options.rationale: Six months or more of angry irritable mood, argumentative defiant behaviour and vindictiveness directed at authority figures and a sibling, without aggression to people or animals and without destruction or theft, defines this diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

options.text: Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder with severe temper outbursts
options.rationale: That diagnosis needs persistently irritable or angry mood between outbursts observable by others in at least two settings, and he is cheerful between confrontations and calm at his swimming club (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

options.text: Autism spectrum disorder presenting as rigidity and demand refusal
options.rationale: Autistic demand refusal is accompanied by differences in social reciprocity, restricted interests or repetitive behaviour, and his reciprocal engagement and shared play with friends argue against it (Source: RANZCP: Autism spectrum disorder in children and adolescents).
source_refs: RANZCP: Autism spectrum disorder in children and adolescents

explanation.summary: Oppositional defiant disorder is defined by a pattern lasting at least six months across three symptom clusters, angry and irritable mood, argumentative and defiant behaviour, and vindictiveness, directed at least at one person who is not a sibling. Severity is graded by how many settings the behaviour appears in, which matters because behaviour confined to home often reflects a family interaction pattern that responds well to parenting intervention. About a quarter of children go on to meet criteria for conduct disorder, and the risk is highest where the behaviour is present in multiple settings and where callous unemotional traits are present. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is the commonest comorbidity and is the diagnosis most often missed underneath the defiance, so attentional symptoms are screened for directly rather than assumed absent. First line treatment is a structured parenting program rather than medication, and Australian programs with the strongest evidence run over eight to twelve group sessions.
key_points: Six months of angry mood, defiant behaviour and vindictiveness, without rights violations, defines the diagnosis.
Aggression to people or animals, destruction, deceit or theft moves the diagnosis to conduct disorder.
Persistent irritability between outbursts in two or more settings points to disruptive mood dysregulation disorder.
Screen actively for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, the commonest comorbidity.
First line management is a structured evidence based parenting program, not medication.
explanation.pearls: Behaviour confined to a single setting carries a much better prognosis than behaviour present at home, at school and with peers, and severity in the diagnostic criteria is graded on exactly that count of settings rather than on the intensity of any single outburst.

sources.label: RANZCP: Autism spectrum disorder in children and adolescents
Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Responding to a request for further cosmetic surgery driven by appearance preoccupation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 24 year old man referred by a plastic surgeon who declined to operate. He asks you to write a supporting letter for a second rhinoplasty.

He describes his nose as twisted and says people glance at it on the train. He checks it in reflective surfaces for around four hours a day, photographs it under different lights, and has stopped going to his warehouse shifts because of it. His first rhinoplasty two years ago left him more distressed than before. Two surgeons and his general practitioner have told him the nose looks normal, and he says he can accept that they see it differently but he knows what he sees. He has no hallucinations, no ideas of reference beyond his appearance, and no thought interference.

data_table.Examination: Nasal contour symmetrical with a well healed scar, mood reactive, no perceptual abnormality, no formal thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, full blood count and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide the supporting letter and refer him to a second plastic surgeon
options.rationale: Repeat surgery in this disorder leaves most patients unchanged or worse and commonly shifts the preoccupation to a new body part, so facilitating it is the recognised harm to avoid (Source: RANZCP: Body dysmorphic disorder position statement).
source_refs: RANZCP: Body dysmorphic disorder position statement

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy and start a serotonin reuptake inhibitor
options.rationale: Tailored cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention combined with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor, usually pushed to the upper dose range over twelve weeks, is the established treatment pairing for this disorder (Source: RANZCP: Body dysmorphic disorder position statement).
source_refs: RANZCP: Body dysmorphic disorder position statement

options.text: Commence an atypical antipsychotic given the fixity of the appearance belief
options.rationale: Poor or absent insight is recorded as a specifier rather than a separate psychotic illness, and the delusional form still responds to serotonin reuptake inhibitor treatment rather than to antipsychotic monotherapy (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

options.text: Refer for long term psychodynamic psychotherapy without medication
options.rationale: Insight oriented therapy alone has not been shown to reduce the checking and preoccupation that drive the impairment, and it delays access to a treatment pairing with trial evidence behind it (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder

options.text: Prescribe a short course of diazepam to reduce his distress before deciding
options.rationale: A benzodiazepine blunts distress briefly while reinforcing avoidance, and it risks dependence in a young man facing a treatment course measured in months (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder affects roughly two per cent of the population but is far more prevalent in cosmetic surgery and dermatology waiting rooms, where estimates run to one in ten. The diagnosis rests on preoccupation with a perceived defect that others cannot see or regard as slight, accompanied by repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, camouflaging, skin picking or reassurance seeking, and by clinically significant distress or impairment. Insight is graded from good to absent, and about a third hold their belief with delusional conviction, which does not change the treatment. Surgical or dermatological intervention is associated with no improvement in the great majority and with occasional deterioration, litigation and, rarely, violence towards the operating surgeon. Suicidality is high, with rates of attempts well above those in obsessive compulsive disorder, so risk assessment is a standing part of every review.
key_points: Preoccupation with a defect others cannot see, plus repetitive checking or camouflaging, defines the disorder.
Delusional conviction is an insight specifier, not a separate psychotic diagnosis, and treatment is unchanged.
Cosmetic procedures rarely help and frequently shift the preoccupation to another body part.
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors at the upper dose range for twelve weeks plus tailored therapy is first line.
Suicidal ideation and attempts are common and require explicit assessment at every review.
explanation.pearls: Doses used are higher and trials longer than in depression, with fluoxetine commonly taken to 60 to 80 mg daily and a full twelve to sixteen weeks allowed before the trial is called a failure.

sources.label: RANZCP: Body dysmorphic disorder position statement
BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing accumulation driven by difficulty discarding from neglect driven squalor
stem:
You are the medical registrar on a hospital in the home round visiting a 68 year old retired librarian after the fire brigade raised a welfare concern. Newspapers, books, empty jars and folded plastic bags are stacked from floor to ceiling through the hallway and both bedrooms, leaving a narrow path to a single chair and the kitchen bench.

She washes daily, her clothes are clean, there is no rotting food and no animal or human waste in the house. She explains that each item might be needed, that the jars are perfectly good, and becomes visibly distressed when you ask what would happen if a box went out with the rubbish. She has been buying newspapers she does not read for about fifteen years and the accumulation has grown steadily. She has no handwashing rituals, no checking rituals and no intrusive thoughts that she tries to neutralise.

data_table.Examination: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 out of 30, self care intact, mood reactive with no anhedonia, insight partial
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Obsessive compulsive disorder with contamination related saving
options.rationale: In that disorder saving is driven by intrusive thoughts and is experienced as unwanted and distressing in itself, whereas she attributes value to the items and has no rituals or neutralising thoughts (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

options.text: Obsessive compulsive personality disorder with rigidity about possessions
options.rationale: Miserly rigidity about money and possessions is one trait of that personality pattern, but it requires a pervasive lifelong style of perfectionism and control across work and relationships rather than a single escalating behaviour (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

options.text: Severe domestic squalor from self neglect with cognitive decline
options.rationale: The near pair is defined by filth and neglect of self and dwelling rather than by saving, and her intact grooming, clean clothes, absent waste and near normal cognitive screen separate the two (Source: RANZCP: Severe domestic squalor).

options.text: Major depressive disorder with amotivation and household neglect
options.rationale: Depressive accumulation follows a loss of motivation and energy over months, whereas her accumulation has been active and purposeful for fifteen years and her mood is reactive without anhedonia (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Hoarding disorder with excessive acquisition of unneeded items
options.rationale: Persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of value, distress at the thought of discarding, and accumulation that renders living areas unusable defines the disorder, and the excessive acquisition specifier applies to the unread newspapers (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

explanation.summary: Hoarding disorder became a separate diagnosis because its course, its poor response to standard obsessive compulsive treatment and its neurocognitive profile all differ from obsessive compulsive disorder. It typically begins in adolescence, worsens each decade, and only comes to attention in later life when the volume creates a fire, fall or public health risk. Insight is frequently poor and forced clearouts are followed by rapid re accumulation and a lasting rupture of trust, which is why coordinated intervention with the person rather than around them is the recommended approach. Cognitive behavioural therapy specifically adapted for hoarding, addressing acquisition, sorting decisions and beliefs about possessions, is the intervention with the best evidence, and serotonin reuptake inhibitors are less effective here than in obsessive compulsive disorder. Fire risk, falls, structural load on floors, blocked exits and vermin are the concrete harms that determine urgency.
key_points: Difficulty discarding with distress at discarding and unusable living space defines the disorder.
Squalor is defined by filth and neglect, not by saving, and often coexists with cognitive impairment.
Insight is commonly poor and forced clearouts are followed by rapid re accumulation.
Hoarding specific cognitive behavioural therapy outperforms standard obsessive compulsive treatment.
Blocked exits, floor loading, falls and vermin determine how urgently the situation must be addressed.
explanation.pearls: Fire deaths in hoarded dwellings are driven by blocked egress and by the fuel load rather than by ignition risk, which is why a fire brigade referral and a clear path to two exits are the first concrete goals rather than total clearance.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Pathway to gender affirming hormone treatment for a competent adolescent in Australia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in an adolescent clinic seeing a 15 year old who was recorded female at birth, attends with both parents, and asks you to start testosterone. He has consistently described himself as male since the age of nine, uses a male name at school, and says the distress about his chest and periods has worsened each year.

Both parents support him and say the request has been consistent for years. He is in year 10, attends school daily and has close friends. Breast development is complete and he has been menstruating for three years. He describes his reasoning clearly, understands that some effects of testosterone are permanent while others are not, and asks about fertility preservation without prompting. He denies self harm and has no current suicidal thoughts.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, height on the 60th centile, blood pressure within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function, renal function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a multidisciplinary gender service for assessment of readiness and competence
options.rationale: Australian standards place hormone treatment inside a multidisciplinary assessment covering diagnosis, mental health, competence, fertility counselling and family support, and referral is what actually moves this young person towards treatment (Source: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.text: Apply to the Family Court for authorisation before any hormone treatment begins
options.rationale: Court authorisation is no longer required where the adolescent is competent and the parents and treating team agree, and insisting on it now adds cost and delay that Australian case law removed (Source: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.text: Commence a gonadotrophin releasing hormone analogue to suppress further puberty
options.rationale: Puberty suppression is the intervention for an adolescent in early or mid puberty, and at completed breast development with three years of menses there is no remaining pubertal progression for it to prevent (Source: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents).
source_refs: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.text: Commence testosterone today with a written treatment agreement and monitoring
options.rationale: Prescribing before the multidisciplinary assessment skips the fertility, mental health and competence components that Australian standards place before initiation, and initiation sits with the specialist service (Source: RANZCP: Recognising and addressing the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria).
source_refs: RANZCP: Recognising and addressing the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

options.text: Advise that no medical treatment can be considered until he turns eighteen
options.rationale: There is no age of eighteen threshold in Australian practice, and deferral of this kind is associated with worsening distress rather than with a neutral wait (Source: RANZCP: Recognising and addressing the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria).
source_refs: RANZCP: Recognising and addressing the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

explanation.summary: Care for trans and gender diverse young people in Australia is organised in stages, with puberty suppression available in early puberty, gender affirming hormones considered from mid adolescence, and surgery generally deferred to adulthood. Australian law changed in 2017 so that court authorisation is not required for gender affirming hormone treatment where the adolescent is competent to consent and the parents and treating team agree, and a court application is now reserved for genuine disputes about competence or about the treatment itself. Assessment is multidisciplinary because coexisting depression, anxiety, autism and eating disorders are common and change the sequencing of care without removing the indication. Fertility counselling occurs before hormones start, since testosterone reduces fertility and oocyte preservation is easier before treatment. Ongoing monitoring covers haematocrit, liver and lipid profiles, bone health and mental state.
key_points: Court authorisation is not required when the adolescent is competent and parents and clinicians agree.
Puberty suppression applies in early to mid puberty, not once pubertal development is complete.
Assessment is multidisciplinary and covers mental health, competence, family support and fertility.
Fertility counselling and preservation options are discussed before hormones are started.
Deferring all care to adulthood is not a neutral option and is associated with worsening distress.
explanation.pearls: Testosterone raises haematocrit within the first months, so a baseline and six monthly full blood count is standard and a haematocrit above about 0.50 prompts dose reduction rather than cessation.

sources.label: RCH Melbourne: Australian standards of care and treatment guidelines for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents
RANZCP: Recognising and addressing the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

subtopic_detail: Conducting a first mental health assessment when the accompanying relative is interpreting
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 42 year old man who arrived in Australia two years ago and holds a bridging visa. He has come about eight months of daily headaches and broken sleep, and his 16 year old son has come to translate for him.

Through his son he says only that his head hurts and that he is tired. When you ask about his mood, he looks at the floor and the son answers that his father is fine and just needs tablets. Physical examination including neurological examination is normal and there are no red flag features for the headache. He shakes his head when the son asks whether anything happened before he came to Australia, but you notice his hands begin to tremble.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no papilloedema, no neck stiffness, blood pressure within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue the consultation with his son translating and explore his mood directly
options.rationale: A family member as interpreter, and a child in particular, filters what is asked and answered, exposes the young person to distressing material, and is a recognised barrier to disclosure of trauma (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health

options.text: Engage an accredited interpreter by telephone and continue the assessment today
options.rationale: An accredited interpreter, available free to practitioners through the national service, allows the son to leave the room and lets you explain confidentiality and its independence from visa status before asking about trauma (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health

options.text: Refer directly to a specialist torture and trauma service without further assessment
options.rationale: Specialist referral is likely to follow, but sending him on without a basic assessment or an explanation he can understand risks non attendance and leaves the headache unexplained (Source: Australasian Society for Traumatic Stress Studies: Working with refugees and asylum seekers).
source_refs: Australasian Society for Traumatic Stress Studies: Working with refugees and asylum seekers

options.text: Prescribe mirtazapine for the insomnia and review him again in four weeks
options.rationale: Prescribing without a diagnosis treats a symptom that is likely to be one feature of a trauma related disorder, and it confirms his son's framing that tablets are what is required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Ask him to return with a written translation of his symptoms at the next visit
options.rationale: Written translation places the burden on the patient, may not be possible if he has limited literacy in his own language, and defers an assessment that can be completed now (Source: Australasian Society for Traumatic Stress Studies: Working with refugees and asylum seekers).
source_refs: Australasian Society for Traumatic Stress Studies: Working with refugees and asylum seekers

explanation.summary: People from refugee backgrounds carry high rates of post traumatic stress disorder, depression and somatic presentations, and headache, back pain and fatigue are frequently the presenting complaint rather than psychological symptoms. Disclosure depends on conditions the clinician controls: a professional interpreter of the right language and dialect, ideally not from a small local community where confidentiality feels uncertain, and an explicit statement that the consultation is confidential and separate from any immigration process. Using a relative, and especially a child, distorts the history and imposes a burden that has its own harms. Insecure visa status is itself a potent and ongoing stressor that worsens outcomes independently of past trauma. Trauma focused therapy is effective in this population, but stabilisation of housing, income and immigration uncertainty often has to run alongside it.
key_points: Use an accredited interpreter rather than a family member, and never a child.
State explicitly that the consultation is confidential and separate from immigration processes.
Somatic complaints such as headache and fatigue are common presenting symptoms of trauma related disorders.
Insecure visa status is an ongoing stressor that independently worsens mental health outcomes.
Specialist torture and trauma services accept direct referrals but a basic assessment should precede them.
explanation.pearls: The national Translating and Interpreting Service is free for medical practitioners consulting people who hold a Medicare card, so an accredited interpreter can usually be on the telephone within minutes rather than being deferred to a later appointment.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health
Australasian Society for Traumatic Stress Studies: Working with refugees and asylum seekers

subtopic_detail: Acting on fabricated illness in a child when only one observer reports the events
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see the mother of a 3 year old girl on the paediatric ward. This is her seventh admission in fourteen months for reported episodes in which she stops breathing and goes blue.

Every episode has been witnessed by her mother alone, including two that were reported as occurring in the bathroom during previous admissions. Prolonged video electroencephalography over four days recorded no events and no epileptiform activity, and cardiac, metabolic and airway investigations have all been normal. Nursing staff document that the girl is playful and eats well, and that she has had no episodes across three nights when her mother was not on the ward. Her mother trained as an enrolled nurse, has researched the condition extensively, and has requested transfer to a fourth hospital.

data_table.Examination: Child alert, playful, growth on the 50th centile for weight and height, no bruising and no injuries
data_table.Investigations: Four day video electroencephalography with no recorded events, echocardiogram normal, metabolic screen normal, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Discharge home with a monitor and outpatient paediatric review in two weeks
options.rationale: Sending the child home returns her to the environment in which the reported events occur, and monitoring equipment tends to generate further reported alarms rather than to protect her (Source: RACP: Child at risk guidelines).

options.text: Arrange covert video surveillance of the mother in the ward cubicle
options.rationale: Covert surveillance has a limited place, requires formal legal and institutional authorisation and police involvement, and cannot be arranged by a treating team acting on its own initiative (Source: RACP: Child at risk guidelines).

options.text: Notify child protection services and convene a multidisciplinary case meeting
options.rationale: Repeated presentations reported by one observer, extensive negative investigation and absence of events when the reporter is away meet the threshold for a mandatory notification, and the statutory service rather than the ward team then leads the assessment (Source: RACP: Child at risk guidelines).

options.text: Interview the mother alone and put the inconsistencies in the history to her
options.rationale: Confronting the reporting parent before protection is in place risks flight from the hospital, escalation of the fabricated illness or an abrupt change of hospital, which is why disclosure follows rather than precedes notification (Source: RANZCP: Factitious disorder imposed on another).
source_refs: RANZCP: Factitious disorder imposed on another

options.text: Repeat the neurological workup with extended ambulatory monitoring at home
options.rationale: Further testing is the mechanism by which harm accumulates in this presentation, since each investigation carries risk and validates the reported illness without adding information (Source: RANZCP: Factitious disorder imposed on another).
source_refs: RANZCP: Factitious disorder imposed on another

explanation.summary: Fabricated or induced illness in a child is a form of child abuse, and the psychiatric diagnosis sits with the perpetrating adult while the paediatric response is driven entirely by the child's safety. The warning pattern is a persistent illness that does not fit any recognised course, symptoms and signs witnessed only by one carer, resolution when that carer is absent, extensive negative investigation, multiple institutions consulted, and a carer with medical knowledge who is comfortable in hospital settings. Doctors sustain the harm through investigation and treatment, so recognising the pattern requires reviewing the whole record across hospitals rather than the current admission alone. Notification to the statutory child protection service is mandatory for medical practitioners in every Australian state and territory and does not require certainty, only reasonable suspicion. Siblings must be considered as well, since mortality in this form of abuse is substantial and other children in the household are frequently affected.
key_points: Events witnessed by only one carer that stop when that carer is absent is the central warning pattern.
Mandatory notification requires reasonable suspicion, not proof, and applies to all Australian medical practitioners.
Do not confront the carer before protective arrangements are in place.
Further investigation perpetuates the harm and rarely adds information.
Assess siblings, who are frequently affected and are at risk of the same harm.
explanation.pearls: Assemble a chronological record across every hospital the child has attended before the case meeting: the pattern is almost never visible within a single admission and becomes unmistakable when presentations, investigations and negative results are laid out on one timeline.

sources.label: RANZCP: Factitious disorder imposed on another
RCH Melbourne: Child abuse clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: First line treatment choice for established post traumatic stress disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 29 year old paramedic nine months after a highway crash in which the driver she was treating died. She reports vivid intrusive images of the scene several times a day, wakes at three most mornings after the same dream, and has driven a forty minute detour to avoid that stretch of road every shift since.

She startles when a colleague drops equipment and has stopped attending the station debrief because the talk brings it back. Her mood lifts at home with her partner and she has not lost interest in her hobbies. She drinks two standard drinks a week, uses no other substances, and has no delusions or hallucinations. She has taken no medication and asks what will actually help.

data_table.Examination: Alert and engaged, hypervigilant to noise in the corridor, no psychomotor retardation, no anhedonia
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What treatment would you recommend first?

options.text: A single session structured psychological debriefing about the crash
options.rationale: Single session debriefing does not prevent or treat the disorder and has been associated with worse outcomes in some trials, which is why it is no longer recommended in Australian practice (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health

options.text: Trauma focused psychological therapy delivered over eight to twelve sessions
options.rationale: Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing are the recommended first line treatments, with larger effect sizes and more durable benefit than medication in adults who can access them (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health

options.text: Sertraline titrated to an effective dose with review at four weeks
options.rationale: A serotonin reuptake inhibitor is the recommended pharmacological option and moves to first line when therapy is unavailable, declined or ineffective, but it sits behind trauma focused therapy when that is accessible (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Diazepam at night for the sleep disturbance and morning waking
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not treat the disorder, impair the extinction learning on which exposure based therapy depends, and carry dependence risk in a young person facing months of treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Non directive supportive counselling with her workplace employee service
options.rationale: Supportive counselling helps with practical stressors but does not target the trauma memory or the avoidance, and it performs measurably worse than trauma focused therapy in head to head trials (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health

explanation.summary: Post traumatic stress disorder is diagnosed when intrusion, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and hyperarousal persist beyond a month after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence. Australian guidelines put trauma focused psychological therapy ahead of medication for adults, and both cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing carry the same first line recommendation. Medication is added when therapy is unavailable, declined, or has not produced adequate benefit, and when a comorbid depressive disorder needs treating in its own right. Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, with depression, alcohol use disorder and other anxiety disorders each present in a substantial minority, and identifying alcohol use matters because heavy drinking undermines exposure based work. Occupational groups repeatedly exposed to trauma, such as paramedics, police and firefighters, need the diagnosis considered explicitly rather than attributed to the job.
key_points: Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation are equal first line treatments.
Medication is second line for adults unless therapy is unavailable, declined or has failed.
Single session debriefing is not recommended and may worsen outcomes.
Benzodiazepines impair the extinction learning that exposure based therapy depends on.
Screen for depression and alcohol use disorder, which are common and alter the treatment plan.
explanation.pearls: Sertraline is the serotonin reuptake inhibitor most often started in Australia for this indication, and the trial should run eight to twelve weeks at an adequate dose before being called a failure, which is considerably longer than clinicians typically allow.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for post traumatic mental health
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Impaired control over gaming with functional collapse in a final year school student
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 17 year old brought by his father after failing three year 12 subjects. For about eighteen months he has played an online game for eight to ten hours a day, mostly overnight, and has told his parents he was studying when he was playing.

He quit the soccer team he had played in since he was eight and no longer sees the friends he played with. He has twice tried to cut back to two hours a day and lasted a few days each time. When his father took the console away last month he shouted, punched a door and did not sleep. He describes himself as absorbed and content while playing and flat and restless when he cannot. He drinks no alcohol, uses no other substances, and his weight and appetite are unchanged.

data_table.Examination: Reactive affect that brightens when discussing the game, no psychomotor retardation, no thought disorder, no self harm
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder with withdrawal and loss of interest
options.rationale: Depressive anhedonia is pervasive and would not spare the activity itself, whereas he is absorbed and content while playing and his sleep loss is a consequence of the schedule rather than early waking (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Social anxiety disorder with avoidance of peers through online activity
options.rationale: Social avoidance here followed the gaming rather than preceding it, and he played team sport socially for years without fear of scrutiny (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

options.text: Adjustment disorder in response to academic pressure in year 12
options.rationale: An adjustment disorder follows an identifiable stressor and would not explain a pattern that began eighteen months before the academic decline and that produced it (Source: DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria).

options.text: Gaming disorder with impaired control and functional deterioration
options.rationale: Impaired control over gaming, escalating priority over other interests and daily activities, continuation despite clear harm, and a duration beyond twelve months with school, sport and friendship losses meets the diagnostic pattern (Source: World Health Organization: ICD-11 gaming disorder).
source_refs: World Health Organization: ICD-11 gaming disorder

options.text: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder presenting as academic failure
options.rationale: That diagnosis requires symptoms present before the age of twelve and across settings, and he sustained schoolwork and a team commitment for years before this pattern began (Source: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Gaming disorder is recognised in the international classification as a disorder due to addictive behaviours, and it is characterised by impaired control, increasing priority given to gaming over other interests and daily activities, and continuation or escalation despite negative consequences. The behaviour must normally be evident for at least twelve months and must cause significant impairment in personal, family, educational or occupational functioning, which is what separates it from heavy but harmless play. Most adolescents who game for long hours do not have the disorder, and the diagnosis rests on functional collapse rather than on hours alone. Comorbid depression, anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder are common and need separate assessment, since treating an underlying disorder often reduces the gaming. Family based intervention and cognitive behavioural approaches that build alternative reinforcement are the mainstays, and abrupt confiscation without a replacement plan tends to produce the kind of escalation his father encountered.
key_points: Impaired control, escalating priority and continuation despite harm are the three core features.
Duration is normally at least twelve months with clear functional impairment.
Hours played alone do not make the diagnosis; loss of function does.
Screen for comorbid depression, anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
Abrupt device removal without a replacement plan commonly escalates conflict.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about failed attempts to cut down and about what happens when access is removed: two or more self initiated failed attempts plus an angry dysregulated response to enforced abstinence discriminates the disorder from heavy recreational play far better than any hours threshold.

sources.label: World Health Organization: ICD-11 gaming disorder
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Deep unconsciousness at a dance party with bradycardia and no response to an opioid antagonist
stem: A 22-year-old man is brought in 40 minutes after swallowing a capful of clear liquid at a warehouse party. He is deeply unconscious, localising to a trapezius squeeze. Intranasal naloxone 800 micrograms produced no change. A jaw thrust and lateral position keep his airway clear and he ventilates spontaneously.

data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 7, pupils 4 mm and reactive, glucose 6.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue airway positioning and close monitoring
options.rationale: Gamma hydroxybutyrate produces abrupt deep coma with bradycardia and a patent airway that reverses spontaneously over one to four hours, so meticulous airway support and monitoring avoid an unnecessary intubation. The failure to respond to naloxone with normal pupils is the finding that separates this from opioid poisoning (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Give further intravenous naloxone until he wakes
options.rationale: Escalating an opioid antagonist is futile when an adequate initial dose has produced no response and the pupils are mid sized rather than pinpoint. Higher doses are justified when partial response suggests a long acting or high potency opioid (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil and reassess
options.rationale: Flumazenil risks precipitating seizures in a patient with unknown co ingestants and possible benzodiazepine dependence, and it has no effect on this class of drug. Its narrow role is in iatrogenic oversedation with a known single agent (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and give activated charcoal
options.rationale: Charcoal binds this compound poorly, the ingestion was over half an hour ago, and instilling it into an unprotected airway risks aspiration pneumonitis. Decontamination is considered for early large ingestions of adsorbable toxins in a protected airway (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Perform rapid sequence intubation for his coma
options.rationale: A coma score alone does not mandate intubation when the airway is patent, gas exchange is adequate and rapid spontaneous recovery is expected within hours. Intubation is indicated if he vomits, desaturates, loses his gag or fails to improve as predicted (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Gamma hydroxybutyrate and its precursors are used recreationally for euphoria and have an extremely narrow margin between the recreational and the anaesthetic dose, which is why coma after a small volume of an unlabelled liquid is a common Australian emergency presentation. The characteristic picture is sudden profound coma with bradycardia, preserved respiratory drive, normal pupils and no response to naloxone, followed by abrupt agitated awakening. Because the drug is cleared rapidly, most patients recover within one to four hours and can be managed with airway positioning and monitoring, avoiding the complications of intubation. Deterioration, vomiting, or failure to wake within the expected window should prompt reassessment for co ingestion or another cause such as head injury. Regular users can develop dependence with a severe withdrawal syndrome resembling delirium tremens, which requires high dose benzodiazepines.
key_points: Profound coma with bradycardia, normal pupils and preserved ventilation suggests this class of drug
Absent response to an adequate naloxone dose argues against opioid poisoning
Recovery is typically abrupt within one to four hours
A low coma score alone does not mandate intubation when the airway is patent and gas exchange is adequate
Flumazenil is hazardous with unknown co ingestants and does not reverse this agent
explanation.pearls: Withdrawal in a dependent user begins within hours of the last dose and can require very large cumulative diazepam doses, so ask specifically about daily dosing intervals in anyone presenting with agitation and tremor after this drug.

subtopic_detail: Seizure at a music festival after a stimulant and large volumes of water with a serum sodium of 118
stem:
You are the emergency registrar called to a 19 year old woman who had a two minute generalised seizure in the department. Her friends say she took two tablets sold as ecstasy about six hours ago and has been drinking water steadily all evening because she was worried about overheating.

She vomited twice before the seizure and had complained of a severe headache. She is now drowsy but rousable and has not seized again. Her temperature is normal, her skin is dry, and there is no rigidity, clonus or trismus. She takes no regular medication and has no history of epilepsy. Her serum sodium is 118 mmol/L, her serum osmolality is 248 mOsm/kg, her urine osmolality is 620 mOsm/kg and her urine sodium is 58 mmol/L. Her creatine kinase is 210 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 620 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 58 mmol/L, creatine kinase 210 U/L (less than 200), capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Restrict her fluid intake to 800 mL daily and recheck her serum sodium in six hours time
options.rationale: Fluid restriction alone corrects sodium far too slowly for a patient who has already seized, leaving her at risk of further seizures and cerebral herniation. Restriction is the treatment for asymptomatic or chronic hyponatraemia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Give a bolus of hypertonic 3 per cent saline and reassess her symptoms and sodium afterwards
options.rationale: Severe hyponatraemia with seizures is a neurological emergency requiring a rapid small rise in serum sodium, achieved with a bolus of hypertonic saline that can be repeated until symptoms resolve. The aim is a rise of about 4 to 6 mmol/L to relieve cerebral oedema rather than full correction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Infuse two litres of 0.9 per cent sodium chloride over four hours and monitor her urine output
options.rationale: Isotonic saline given to a patient with high urine osmolality from antidiuretic hormone excess can paradoxically lower the sodium further as the salt is excreted and the water retained. It is appropriate when hyponatraemia is driven by hypovolaemia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Administer intravenous mannitol to reduce cerebral oedema and arrange urgent computed tomography
options.rationale: An osmotic diuretic loses free water and solute in an unpredictable ratio and is not the agent of choice for hyponatraemic encephalopathy. Imaging is warranted if she fails to improve or has focal signs, but it must not delay correction of the sodium (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Commence dantrolene and active cooling for presumed serotonergic hyperthermia from the tablets
options.rationale: She is normothermic with a near normal creatine kinase and no rigidity or clonus, so the hyperthermic toxidrome is not present. That syndrome is the other classic life threat with this drug and is treated with cooling, benzodiazepines and sometimes dantrolene (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Two mechanisms combine to produce dangerous hyponatraemia after methylenedioxymethamphetamine use, namely drug induced release of antidiuretic hormone and the deliberate drinking of large volumes of water to prevent overheating. Young women appear disproportionately affected. Because the fall in sodium happens over hours, the brain has no time to adapt and cerebral oedema develops at levels that would be tolerated in chronic hyponatraemia. The urine osmolality above serum osmolality with a raised urine sodium confirms inappropriate antidiuresis rather than simple water intoxication with suppressed hormone. Correction targets symptom resolution with a rise of a few millimoles per litre, and the total rise is capped over 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination, although that complication is rare in acute presentations.
key_points: The mechanism is antidiuretic hormone release plus excessive free water intake
Seizure with severe hyponatraemia is treated with hypertonic saline, not fluid restriction
Aim for a rise of about 4 to 6 mmol/L acutely and cap the 24 hour rise
Isotonic saline may worsen the sodium when antidiuretic hormone activity is high
Normothermia with a normal creatine kinase argues against the hyperthermic toxidrome
explanation.pearls: Limit correction to about 8 to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours even after an acute drop, and consider desmopressin with free water if an unexpected water diuresis threatens to overshoot that ceiling.

subtopic_detail: Third relapse of psychotic depression within months of two successful acute electroconvulsive therapy courses
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 68 year old woman in the outpatient clinic. Over eighteen months she has had two episodes of severe depression with nihilistic delusions, each of which responded fully to a course of electroconvulsive therapy after failing to improve on medication.

After the second course she was maintained on venlafaxine at a therapeutic dose with lithium augmentation, and a dispensing record confirms she has collected every prescription. Her lithium level a fortnight ago was 0.72 mmol/L and her thyroid function and renal function are normal. Over the past three weeks she has again stopped eating, is sleeping two hours a night and has begun saying her bowels have rotted away. She scores 26 on a depression rating scale. Her cognition between episodes has returned to her baseline and she lives independently with her husband.

data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, poor oral intake, nihilistic delusions concerning her abdomen, no thoughts of self harm elicited but limited engagement
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.6-0.8 maintenance), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 60 mL/min/1.73m2, full blood examination and electrolytes normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate long term treatment plan once this episode is treated?

options.text: Switch her antidepressant to a tricyclic agent and continue outpatient review every four weeks
options.rationale: She has relapsed repeatedly despite an adequately dosed antidepressant with lithium augmentation, so a further medication switch has a low probability of preventing the next episode. A switch is the logical step when relapse follows an inadequate trial or poor adherence (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Increase the lithium dose to achieve a level at the upper end of the therapeutic range for her
options.rationale: Her level already sits within the maintenance range and pushing it higher in a 68 year old raises the risk of neurotoxicity and renal injury without evidence of preventing further relapse. Dose increase is reasonable when the level is subtherapeutic (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange maintenance electroconvulsive therapy at spaced intervals alongside her current medication
options.rationale: Repeated relapse soon after a successful acute course, in a patient whose illness reliably responds to that treatment and not to medication, is the recognised indication for continuation and maintenance electroconvulsive therapy delivered at progressively spaced intervals. It reduces relapse rates compared with medication alone in this group (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on electroconvulsive therapy).
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on electroconvulsive therapy
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Refer her for cognitive behavioural therapy delivered weekly as the mainstay of relapse prevention
