options.rationale: Structured psychotherapy has a limited role as sole prevention in severe psychotic depression, where the acuity and delusional content impair engagement. It has value as an adjunct once the episode has remitted (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Add a second generation antipsychotic and reduce the frequency of her clinic reviews accordingly
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is standard within an episode of psychotic depression but has not held her well between episodes, and reducing review frequency in a patient with a relapsing severe illness is unsafe. Adding it without addressing the relapse pattern repeats what has already failed (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

explanation.summary: Electroconvulsive therapy has the highest response rate of any treatment for severe depression with psychotic features, but relapse after an acute course is common and is the main limitation of the treatment. Continuation therapy in the six months after remission and maintenance therapy beyond that are used when relapse has occurred despite adequate pharmacotherapy, when previous courses have been rapidly effective, and when the patient prefers it. Sessions are typically spaced from weekly to fortnightly and then monthly, with the interval guided by symptom re emergence. Cognitive effects are monitored formally because anterograde memory disturbance is the principal adverse effect, and the older patient with independent baseline function tolerates spaced treatments well. Consent requirements and review by a second practitioner are set out in each state and territory mental health act.
key_points: Relapse after a successful acute course despite adequate medication is the indication for continuation therapy
Intervals are spaced progressively and titrated against symptom re emergence
Response to previous courses strongly predicts response to maintenance therapy
Formal cognitive monitoring is part of every maintenance program
Antidepressant and lithium therapy usually continue alongside rather than being stopped
explanation.pearls: Lithium is continued during maintenance electroconvulsive therapy in most protocols but is often withheld on the morning of treatment, since higher levels around the time of the seizure are associated with prolonged confusion.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on electroconvulsive therapy
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Rapid weight gain fourteen weeks into olanzapine treatment that has finally controlled a first episode psychosis
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24 year old man in the early psychosis clinic. His first episode involved persecutory delusions and command hallucinations that persisted through an adequate trial of risperidone, stopped for intolerable akathisia, and then aripiprazole, stopped for lack of benefit.

He has been on olanzapine 15 mg at night for fourteen weeks and is now free of hallucinations, back at his apprenticeship and keen to stay on the medication that finally worked. His weight has risen from 74 to 83 kg over that period and his waist circumference is 104 cm. He eats takeaway most nights and has stopped playing football. He is not diabetic and has no family history of diabetes. His fasting glucose is 5.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L and high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.85 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 per minute, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Weight 83 kg, waist circumference 104 cm, fasting glucose 5.9 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), glycated haemoglobin 5.6 per cent (less than 6.0), triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L (less than 1.7), high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.85 mmol/L (greater than 1.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his metabolic changes?

options.text: Switch him to a different antipsychotic with a lower metabolic burden and taper the olanzapine
options.rationale: Switching is the first consideration when alternatives remain untried, but he has already failed both of the lower risk agents that would be candidates and has only just achieved remission. The relapse risk of another change outweighs the metabolic gain in this particular patient (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Halve the olanzapine dose so that the metabolic effect falls while some antipsychotic cover remains
options.rationale: Metabolic effects of this drug are only weakly dose related, whereas relapse risk climbs steeply below an effective dose in the first year after a first episode. Dose reduction is considered later in a sustained remission with specialist involvement (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Continue the olanzapine, add metformin and refer him to a structured diet and exercise program
options.rationale: Metformin added to an antipsychotic that cannot be changed produces a modest but real reduction in weight and improves insulin sensitivity, and it is the best supported pharmacological adjunct for this problem. Combining it with a structured lifestyle program gives a larger effect than either alone and preserves the treatment that achieved remission (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Give dietary advice at each review and repeat his metabolic screen again in twelve months time
options.rationale: Advice alone rarely reverses antipsychotic associated weight gain, and a twelve month interval is far longer than the recommended monitoring schedule in the first year of treatment. Screening intervals are measured in weeks to months early on (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Add topiramate as a weight loss agent and monitor his cognition and renal function during treatment
options.rationale: Topiramate has some evidence for antipsychotic associated weight gain but carries cognitive slowing and word finding difficulty that are particularly unwelcome in a young man returning to work. It sits behind metformin as an adjunct (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: People with schizophrenia die around fifteen to twenty years earlier than the general population, and most of that gap is cardiovascular rather than suicide, which makes metabolic care a core part of psychiatric treatment rather than an afterthought. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the greatest weight and glycaemic burden, and the largest weight gain occurs in the first three to six months of treatment. Monitoring includes weight and waist at every visit early on, with fasting glucose or glycated haemoglobin and lipids at baseline, three months and then at least annually. When the offending drug cannot be changed because it is the only agent that has worked, metformin plus a structured lifestyle intervention is the best supported response. Smoking cessation and blood pressure management complete the cardiovascular risk plan.
key_points: Weight gain on antipsychotics is fastest in the first three to six months of treatment
Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden of the available agents
Metformin is the best supported adjunct when the antipsychotic cannot be changed
Structured lifestyle programs outperform generic advice and add to the drug effect
Metabolic screening occurs at baseline, three months and at least yearly thereafter
explanation.pearls: A weight gain of more than 5 per cent of body weight within the first three months of an antipsychotic predicts substantial longer term gain, which makes that threshold the practical trigger for adding metformin rather than waiting for obesity to become established.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Starting medication in a newly diagnosed adult who drives a heavy vehicle for a living
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 29 year old woman whose assessment, including collateral from her mother and school reports, has confirmed attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with childhood onset. She has never been treated.

She drives a rigid truck for a delivery company and has had two at fault low speed collisions in the past year, both while distracted. She smoked cannabis most weekends until two years ago and has not used it since. She has no chest pain, no exertional syncope and no palpitations, and there is no family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiomyopathy. Her mood is stable and she is not pregnant and uses an implant for contraception. Her physical examination including cardiovascular examination is normal and her thyroid function is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 per minute, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular examination with no murmur, weight 68 kg, height 166 cm
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood examination and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment plan?

options.text: Order an electrocardiogram and echocardiogram before any medication because of her occupational driving
options.rationale: Routine cardiac investigation before stimulant treatment is not required in an adult with no cardiac symptoms, no abnormal examination and no family history of sudden death. Occupational driving does not by itself create that indication (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Prescribe atomoxetine as first line because her history of cannabis use makes a stimulant unsuitable
options.rationale: Remote cannabis use with two years of abstinence is not an active substance use disorder and does not displace stimulants from first line, and treating the condition itself reduces later substance use. Atomoxetine is preferred when there is current stimulant misuse or diversion risk (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Offer structured psychological therapy alone and reserve any medication for a later review point
options.rationale: Psychological and skills based approaches are valuable adjuncts but have smaller effects on core inattention than medication in adults, and she has a safety critical occupational problem now. Therapy alone is a reasonable primary choice when a patient declines medication (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Record baseline pulse, blood pressure and weight, then start a long acting stimulant with review in four weeks
options.rationale: Long acting stimulants are first line for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and require baseline cardiovascular observations and weight with regular repetition rather than routine cardiac imaging. Early review allows titration against symptom response and adverse effects before her next licence assessment (Source: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Begin an immediate release dexamfetamine preparation dosed three times daily to allow flexible timing
options.rationale: Multiple daily immediate release doses give a fluctuating effect, worse adherence and greater diversion risk than a single long acting preparation. Short acting forms are used to supplement a long acting base or where cost prevents its use (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: The Australian guideline for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder recommends medication as first line for adults with moderate to severe impairment, with long acting stimulants preferred for adherence and smoother symptom coverage. Baseline assessment consists of cardiovascular history, family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiomyopathy, examination, and measurement of pulse, blood pressure and weight, with investigations reserved for those in whom this screen raises a concern. Stimulant prescribing in Australia additionally requires authority from the relevant state or territory health department, and the requirements differ between jurisdictions. Untreated disorder is itself associated with a higher crash risk, and treatment reduces it, so occupational driving supports rather than opposes effective treatment. Patients must be counselled that driving is not permitted while impaired and that licensing authorities have their own reporting standards.
key_points: Long acting stimulants are first line for adults with significant impairment
Baseline monitoring is pulse, blood pressure and weight, plus a cardiac symptom and family history screen
Routine electrocardiography and echocardiography are not required without cardiac red flags
Remote cannabis use with sustained abstinence does not preclude stimulant treatment
Stimulant prescribing requires a state or territory authority in addition to the clinical decision
explanation.pearls: Repeat pulse, blood pressure and weight at every dose change and then at least six monthly, because a sustained rise of more than about 10 mmHg systolic or 10 beats per minute is the trigger to reduce the dose or reconsider the agent.

sources.label: Australian Evidence Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Dizziness and sensory disturbance four days after abruptly stopping a serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old woman who stopped taking venlafaxine 150 mg four days ago. She had been well for nine months after a single depressive episode and decided to stop when her repeat prescription ran out while she was away.

Since the second day she has felt light headed whenever she turns her head, has had brief sensations she describes as a zap through her scalp when she moves her eyes, and has felt nauseated and unusually irritable. Her sleep is broken by vivid dreams. She still enjoys her hobbies, has been at work every day, denies any low mood or loss of interest, and her appetite and concentration are unchanged. There are no thoughts of self harm. Her neurological examination is normal and her blood pressure shows no postural drop.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 per minute, sitting blood pressure 118/74 mmHg with no postural drop, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Normal cranial nerve, cerebellar and gait examination, no nystagmus, mood reactive with normal range of affect

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Diagnose an early relapse and increase her venlafaxine above the dose she was previously taking
options.rationale: Relapse presents with returning low mood, anhedonia and cognitive symptoms over weeks, not with dizziness and sensory zaps within days of cessation. Dose escalation would be right if depressive symptoms had genuinely returned (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine to cover the symptoms until they settle by themselves
options.rationale: Sedatives blunt the irritability and insomnia but do not address the underlying withdrawal and introduce dependence risk in a woman who needs a structured taper. Their use is confined to severe short lived distress where no other option exists (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Switch her to fluoxetine and then stop that agent after a fortnight without any further tapering
options.rationale: Substituting a long half life agent is a recognised strategy but is reserved for patients who cannot tolerate a gradual taper of the original drug. Using it first adds a second medicine and a switch related risk that a simple taper avoids (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Reassure her the symptoms will fade within a week and review her again if they have not resolved
options.rationale: Symptoms do usually resolve but she is significantly distressed now and untreated withdrawal is a common reason patients conclude they can never come off the drug. Watchful waiting suits mild symptoms in someone who is comfortable to continue (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Restart venlafaxine at her previous dose and reduce it gradually over several weeks with review
options.rationale: Reinstating the drug settles discontinuation symptoms within one to three days, which also confirms the diagnosis, and a gradual taper then allows her to stop successfully. Venlafaxine has a short half life and is one of the agents most likely to produce these symptoms on abrupt cessation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Antidepressant discontinuation symptoms appear within a few days of stopping or markedly reducing a drug taken for more than about six weeks, and are commonest with short half life agents such as venlafaxine and paroxetine. The characteristic features are flu like malaise, insomnia with vivid dreams, nausea, imbalance, sensory disturbances including electric shock sensations, and hyperarousal with irritability. Separating this from relapse is the central clinical task, and the timing, the symptom profile and the absence of core depressive features do it reliably, with a response to reinstatement within days confirming it. Prevention is a slow taper, often over four weeks or considerably longer after long term treatment, with the final steps taken most slowly. Patients should be told about this phenomenon when the drug is first prescribed so that they do not stop abruptly when a prescription lapses.
key_points: Onset within days of cessation with sensory zaps and imbalance indicates discontinuation, not relapse
Short half life agents such as venlafaxine and paroxetine carry the greatest risk
Reinstatement produces relief within one to three days and confirms the diagnosis
Taper over weeks with the smallest reductions at the lowest doses
Relapse instead presents with returning mood and cognitive symptoms over weeks
explanation.pearls: Warn every patient starting a short half life antidepressant that missing more than a day or two can produce dizziness and electric shock sensations, because unrecognised withdrawal is a frequent reason people restart the drug believing their illness has returned.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Sodium valproate maintenance in a woman of reproductive age who is not using reliable contraception
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar conducting an annual review of a 26 year old woman with bipolar affective disorder. She has had two manic episodes, the last three years ago, and has been well on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily since then.

She works full time, has a new partner of six months, and says she is not trying to conceive but is using condoms inconsistently and would continue a pregnancy if one occurred. She has never been counselled about the medication and pregnancy. Her mother took the same drug for epilepsy without problems, which she mentions as reassurance. Her mood is euthymic, she has no psychotic symptoms and her sleep is regular. Her weight is stable, her full blood examination and liver function are normal, and her serum valproate concentration is within the usual maintenance range.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features, weight stable at 64 kg
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination normal, liver function normal, serum valproate within the maintenance range, beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Counsel her on the fetal risks, arrange reliable contraception and plan a switch to another mood stabiliser
options.rationale: Valproate carries a roughly 10 per cent risk of major congenital malformation and a substantially higher rate of neurodevelopmental impairment, so it should be avoided in people who could become pregnant unless no alternative works. Because she would continue an unplanned pregnancy, reliable contraception and a planned switch while she is euthymic are both required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Continue the valproate unchanged and add high dose folic acid to reduce the risk to a future pregnancy
options.rationale: Folate supplementation does not prevent valproate associated neural tube defects or the neurodevelopmental effects, unlike its role in the general population. Recommending it as the sole measure gives false reassurance (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Continue the current dose and repeat her serum concentration and liver function every six months
options.rationale: Routine monitoring is appropriate for someone who must remain on the drug but does nothing about the reproductive risk that dominates this consultation. It would be the correct answer for a woman who cannot become pregnant (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease the valproate at today's visit and review her in the clinic in four weeks to assess her mood
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal of a mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder carries a high risk of rebound mania, particularly when stopped quickly rather than cross tapered. The change must be made while cover from an alternative agent is established (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Change her directly to lithium at a standard starting dose and defer discussion of pregnancy planning
options.rationale: Lithium is a reasonable alternative but it also carries fetal cardiac risk and demands its own preconception discussion, so deferring the conversation misses the point of the switch. Any change is made alongside contraception and planning, not instead of it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Valproate is the most teratogenic of the commonly used mood stabilisers, with major malformations in around one in ten exposed pregnancies and impaired neurodevelopment in a substantially larger proportion, including a raised rate of autism spectrum disorder. Australian regulators require that it not be used in people who can become pregnant unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated, and then only with reliable contraception and documented counselling that is repeated at least annually. The window to act is when the patient is well, because switching during an acute episode is far riskier. Alternatives in bipolar disorder include lithium, lamotrigine and several second generation antipsychotics, each with its own reproductive profile that needs its own discussion. Where valproate genuinely cannot be replaced, the plan must include contraception the patient will actually use and a documented shared decision.
key_points: Valproate causes major malformations in roughly 10 per cent of exposed pregnancies
Neurodevelopmental impairment affects a larger proportion and is not prevented by folate
Counselling and reliable contraception are mandatory whenever the drug is used in someone who could conceive
Switch while the patient is euthymic, using a cross taper rather than abrupt cessation
Every alternative agent needs its own reproductive risk discussion
explanation.pearls: Document the pregnancy prevention discussion at least annually in anyone of reproductive potential taking valproate, since regulators treat repeated documented counselling, not a single conversation at initiation, as the standard of care.

subtopic_detail: Tachycardia with a rising troponin during the third week of a clozapine titration
stem: A 27-year-old man on day nineteen of a clozapine titration, now 250 mg daily, has three days of fatigue and breathlessness on the ward stairs with a tachycardia that does not settle.

data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), C reactive protein 96 mg/L, was 4, troponin I 180 ng/L (<16)
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph clear, ejection fraction 48 per cent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue clozapine and add a beta blocker
options.rationale: Rate control masks the key monitoring sign while the myocardial injury continues, and continuing exposure to the drug is what drives the process. Beta blockade addresses benign persistent tachycardia only once myocarditis has been excluded (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease clozapine and refer urgently to cardiology
options.rationale: A rising C reactive protein with a troponin above twice the upper limit and impaired ventricular function in the fourth week of titration is clozapine induced myocarditis until proven otherwise, and cessation is the treatment. Continuing the drug risks progression to cardiogenic shock and death (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Halve the clozapine dose and repeat the troponin
options.rationale: The reaction is not dose dependent in a way that makes reduction safe, and repeating tests three days later delays a decision that must be made today. Dose reduction is appropriate for sedation, hypersalivation or postural drop, not for myocardial injury (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine monitoring guidance).

options.text: Attribute this to benign titration tachycardia
options.rationale: Benign tachycardia is common early in titration but does not raise troponin, produce a rising C reactive protein or impair ventricular function. The near pair to separate here is a drug effect on heart rate from drug induced myocardial inflammation (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine monitoring guidance).

options.text: Start antibiotics for presumed pneumonia
options.rationale: He has no cough, no focal signs and a clear chest radiograph, and a normal white cell count with eosinophilia fits a drug hypersensitivity reaction rather than bacterial infection. Antibiotics would delay withdrawal of the causative agent (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Clozapine induced myocarditis occurs in roughly one to three per cent of patients in Australian cohorts, which is higher than international reports, and almost always presents between days 14 and 28 of titration. The early features are non specific, comprising fatigue, breathlessness, fever, flu like symptoms and tachycardia, so monitoring is biochemical rather than symptom based. Australian protocols check troponin and C reactive protein at baseline and weekly through the first four weeks, with a troponin above twice the upper limit of normal or a C reactive protein above 100 mg/L defining probable myocarditis and mandating cessation. Most patients recover fully after the drug is stopped, though a minority develop cardiomyopathy. Rechallenge has been performed in specialist centres with intensive monitoring but is not undertaken routinely.
key_points: Myocarditis clusters between days 14 and 28 of clozapine titration
Weekly troponin and C reactive protein monitoring through the first four weeks detects it before collapse
A troponin above twice the upper limit or a C reactive protein above 100 mg/L mandates cessation
Eosinophilia supports a hypersensitivity mechanism and often accompanies the reaction
Benign titration tachycardia does not raise troponin or impair ventricular function
explanation.pearls: Slower titration reduces the incidence, which is why Australian protocols increase clozapine in small increments over the first fortnight rather than following faster overseas schedules.

subtopic_detail: Confusion and coarse tremor in a long term lithium user whose serum level is within the therapeutic range
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 72 year old woman brought in by her son. She has taken lithium for twenty years for bipolar affective disorder and has never had a manic relapse.

For three days she has been unsteady, has slurred her words and has been muddled about the day of the week, and this morning she could not manage her own kitchen. She had four days of vomiting and diarrhoea last week after a family gathering and has been drinking little. Her general practitioner started perindopril for hypertension five weeks ago. On examination she has a coarse irregular tremor of both hands, myoclonic jerks in her legs, and an unsteady wide gait. There is no fever, no rigidity, no clonus and no rash, and her neck is supple.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.94 mmol/L (0.6-0.8 maintenance), creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90, baseline 78), sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), estimated glomerular filtration rate 38 mL/min/1.73m2, thyroid stimulating hormone 3.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatine kinase 140 U/L (less than 200)
data_table.Examination: Coarse irregular tremor, leg myoclonus, wide based ataxic gait, no rigidity or clonus, no neck stiffness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue lithium at the usual dose because the serum concentration is not in the toxic range
options.rationale: Chronic toxicity produces marked neurological features at concentrations that look acceptable, because tissue levels exceed serum levels after years of treatment. A reassuring number is the classic trap in the long term user (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Prescribe benzatropine for the tremor and arrange outpatient review of her lithium level next week
options.rationale: An anticholinergic does not treat lithium induced tremor and worsens delirium in an older patient, and outpatient follow up leaves an unsafe woman at home. Anticholinergics treat drug induced parkinsonism, which is not the picture here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Withhold lithium, rehydrate with intravenous sodium chloride and monitor levels and renal function
options.rationale: Volume depletion with a new angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor has reduced lithium clearance and produced chronic toxicity, so cessation with isotonic rehydration to restore renal excretion is the treatment. Serial levels, electrolytes and neurological assessment then determine whether extracorporeal removal becomes necessary (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Arrange immediate haemodialysis on the basis of her neurological signs and impaired renal function
options.rationale: Dialysis is reserved for severe toxicity with markedly elevated concentrations, seizures, depressed conscious state, or failure to fall with supportive care and renal impairment. Starting with rehydration allows most chronic cases to clear without it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Treat her for neuroleptic malignant syndrome with dantrolene and supportive cooling measures
options.rationale: That syndrome features fever, lead pipe rigidity and a markedly raised creatine kinase, all absent here, and she takes no antipsychotic. Its overlap with lithium toxicity is the tremor and confusion, which is why the rigidity and creatine kinase are the discriminating findings (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity is divided into acute overdose, acute on chronic, and chronic toxicity, and it is the chronic form that catches clinicians out because neurological features dominate at concentrations barely above the therapeutic range. The drug is cleared entirely by the kidney and handled like sodium, so any state that reduces glomerular filtration or increases proximal sodium reabsorption raises the level, including dehydration, vomiting, diarrhoea, heart failure and a hot climate. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, thiazides and non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are the classic interacting medicines. Management is cessation, isotonic fluid to restore clearance, correction of the precipitant and serial monitoring, with extracorporeal removal for severe or refractory cases. A minority of patients are left with persistent cerebellar dysfunction, which is why early recognition matters.
key_points: Chronic toxicity causes marked neurological signs at near therapeutic serum concentrations
Dehydration, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, thiazides and non steroidal drugs are common precipitants
Isotonic sodium chloride restores renal clearance and is the mainstay of treatment
Dialysis is for severe toxicity, seizures, coma or failure of levels to fall
Absent rigidity with a normal creatine kinase argues against neuroleptic malignant syndrome
explanation.pearls: Recheck the lithium level and renal function within five to seven days of starting any angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor, thiazide or regular non steroidal anti inflammatory drug, since these interactions can raise concentrations by a quarter or more within a fortnight.

subtopic_detail: Frequent prolonged attacks with normal video telemetry captured during a typical event
stem:
You are the neuropsychiatry registrar reviewing a 26 year old woman referred after four admissions this year. She has three to five attacks a week in which she falls, shakes and is unresponsive for eight to twelve minutes.

During a typical attack captured on video telemetry this week, her eyes were tightly closed with resistance to opening, her head moved from side to side, the shaking waxed and waned in amplitude, and she was talking within thirty seconds of it stopping. The electroencephalogram showed normal awake rhythms throughout the event and afterwards. A venous lactate taken fifteen minutes after the attack was normal. She has taken levetiracetam and lamotrigine at therapeutic doses without any change in frequency. She discloses a history of childhood sexual abuse and has never been offered psychological treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 per minute, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Video electroencephalogram during a typical event shows normal awake rhythms with no ictal correlate, venous lactate 1.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) at 15 minutes post event, magnetic resonance imaging of brain normal, levetiracetam and lamotrigine within therapeutic ranges

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Add a third antiepileptic drug and titrate it to the maximum tolerated dose over eight weeks
options.rationale: Two adequately dosed antiepileptic drugs have failed and the recorded event had no electrographic correlate, so further antiepileptic therapy adds adverse effects without prospect of benefit. A third agent is the correct step in genuinely refractory epilepsy with recorded ictal discharges (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines).

options.text: Instruct the emergency department to give intravenous levetiracetam whenever an attack lasts over five minutes
options.rationale: Treating these events as status epilepticus exposes her to sedation, intubation and intensive care admission for a non epileptic process, which is one of the major iatrogenic harms in this condition. Parenteral loading is reserved for electrographically confirmed prolonged seizures (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Repeat ambulatory electroencephalography over a week before accepting the telemetry findings as valid
options.rationale: Video telemetry capturing a habitual attack is the diagnostic standard and an ambulatory study is less informative, so repeating testing simply delays treatment. Further recording is justified only when the captured event was not typical of her usual attacks (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Explain the diagnosis to her carefully and refer for psychological therapy while withdrawing the antiepileptics
options.rationale: A habitual event recorded without electrographic change establishes dissociative seizures, and the way the diagnosis is communicated is itself therapeutic because acceptance predicts outcome. Structured psychological therapy is the treatment with the best evidence, and antiepileptic drugs are withdrawn gradually once epilepsy has been excluded (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines).

options.text: Refer her to an epilepsy surgery program for evaluation of a possible frontal lobe seizure focus
options.rationale: Frontal lobe seizures are the classic mimic because they are brief, bizarre and may have no scalp correlate, but they last seconds to two minutes and are stereotyped rather than waxing and waning over ten minutes. Her prolonged fluctuating events with immediate recovery do not fit that pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Dissociative seizures account for a substantial minority of patients referred to epilepsy monitoring units and are frequently misdiagnosed for years, during which patients accumulate antiepileptic drugs, emergency intubations and injury. Semiological pointers include prolonged duration, waxing and waning motor activity, side to side head movement, eye closure with resistance, ictal weeping, memory for the event and rapid reorientation afterwards, while a normal post event lactate and prolactin add supportive evidence. None of these features is individually diagnostic, so video electroencephalography during a habitual attack remains the reference standard. Communication of the diagnosis is the intervention with the greatest immediate effect, and a script that affirms the attacks are real, names the condition and explains the mechanism without implying fabrication improves engagement. Cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for these seizures is the best supported treatment, with antiepileptic drugs withdrawn under supervision.
key_points: Video electroencephalography during a habitual event is the diagnostic standard
Prolonged waxing and waning attacks with eye closure and rapid recovery favour a dissociative mechanism
A normal post event lactate supports the diagnosis but is not by itself sufficient
How the diagnosis is explained strongly influences whether treatment works
Cognitive behavioural therapy is the treatment of choice and antiepileptics are withdrawn gradually
explanation.pearls: Venous lactate rises within minutes of a generalised tonic clonic seizure and typically exceeds 2.5 mmol/L when measured in the first 30 minutes, so a normal value taken promptly after a prolonged convulsive event argues strongly against an epileptic mechanism.

subtopic_detail: Detailed recurrent visual hallucinations with fluctuating attention and mild parkinsonism in an older man
stem: A 76-year-old man has twelve months of forgetfulness. His daughter describes days when he converses normally and days when he stares blankly for hours. Several times a week he sees small children in the lounge room and describes their clothing. For years he has shouted and thrashed during sleep.

data_table.Examination: Mild bradykinesia and rigidity, no tremor; mini mental state examination 23 of 30

lead_in: How should his hallucinations be managed?

options.text: Prescribe regular haloperidol at a low dose
options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics carry the highest risk of severe sensitivity reactions in this condition, with irreversible parkinsonism, autonomic instability and death reported after single doses. Haloperidol retains a role in hyperactive delirium from another cause, not here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start low dose risperidone titrated to effect
options.rationale: Risperidone has substantial dopamine blockade and produces the same sensitivity reaction, and it also carries the increased mortality seen with antipsychotics in dementia. It is the agent with the most evidence for aggression in Alzheimer disease, which is a different clinical problem (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence olanzapine at night for sleep too
options.rationale: Sedating him overnight does not treat the underlying disorder and risks the same sensitivity reaction alongside falls and further cognitive decline. Sleep disturbance in this condition is better managed by treating the sleep behaviour disorder specifically (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Use quetiapine as the safest antipsychotic here
options.rationale: Quetiapine is the least antidopaminergic option and is sometimes used when psychosis is dangerous and untreatable otherwise, but evidence for benefit is weak and it still carries the mortality signal. It is a fallback after a cholinesterase inhibitor has failed, not a first choice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Modify the home environment and start rivastigmine
options.rationale: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder identify Lewy body dementia, in which cholinesterase inhibitors reduce hallucinations and improve attention. Antipsychotics are avoided because up to half of patients have a severe sensitivity reaction that can be fatal (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is defined by dementia plus core features of fluctuating cognition with variation in attention and alertness, recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, and spontaneous parkinsonism. It is commonly mistaken for Alzheimer disease with behavioural symptoms or for delirium, and the consequence of that error is prescription of an antipsychotic. Severe sensitivity reactions occur in a large minority and include worsening parkinsonism, impaired consciousness, autonomic instability and a syndrome resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with substantially increased mortality. Cholinesterase inhibitors are unusually effective in this dementia, improving hallucinations, apathy and attention. Sleep behaviour disorder is managed with environmental safety measures and melatonin or clonazepam, and orthostatic hypotension needs non pharmacological measures before drugs are added.
key_points: Fluctuating cognition, formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and sleep behaviour disorder define the syndrome
Antipsychotic sensitivity affects up to half of patients and can be fatal
Cholinesterase inhibitors reduce hallucinations and improve attention in this dementia specifically
Rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder often precedes cognitive symptoms by years
Quetiapine is a reluctant fallback only when psychosis is dangerous and other measures fail
explanation.pearls: Ask every patient with new visual hallucinations whether they act out their dreams, since rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder can precede the cognitive syndrome by a decade and is the single most useful pointer away from Alzheimer disease.

subtopic_detail: Agitation and racing thoughts emerging five weeks after an antidepressant was added for bipolar depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 31 year old woman with bipolar II disorder, diagnosed after two clear hypomanic episodes and multiple depressive episodes. Her general practitioner started sertraline five weeks ago for a depressive episode and increased it a fortnight ago. She takes no mood stabiliser.

She says her mood is as low as ever and she cries daily, but she now cannot sit still, her thoughts race so fast she cannot hold a conversation, and she has slept three hours a night for a week without feeling tired. She is irritable with her family and has spent two evenings cleaning the house until dawn. She denies grandiosity, has no psychotic symptoms and has no thoughts of self harm. She uses no alcohol or other drugs, and her thyroid function and full blood examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Restless with psychomotor agitation, pressured speech at times, mood described as low with an irritable and reactive affect, no psychotic features, insight retained
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood examination and electrolytes within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her treatment?

options.text: Cease the sertraline and start quetiapine, with close review of her mood and sleep
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder can precipitate a mixed state, recognisable here as depressive mood with agitation, racing thoughts and reduced sleep need, and withdrawal of the antidepressant is the first move. Quetiapine has the strongest evidence of the agents effective across bipolar depression and mixed features (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose further because her depressive symptoms have not yet responded
options.rationale: Escalating an antidepressant that has produced activation worsens the mixed state and increases the risk of a full manic switch. Dose escalation is appropriate for a partial response in unipolar depression without activation (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Add lamotrigine and continue the sertraline while the lamotrigine is slowly titrated upwards
options.rationale: Lamotrigine has a role in preventing bipolar depression but requires weeks of slow titration for rash risk and does nothing for the acute mixed presentation, and continuing the antidepressant maintains the driver. It is a maintenance rather than an acute option (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Add lithium at a standard dose while maintaining her current antidepressant treatment unchanged
options.rationale: Lithium is a sound long term choice for her illness but leaving the antidepressant in place allows the activation to continue while the level is titrated over weeks. Adding a mood stabiliser without removing the precipitant treats around the problem (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Prescribe a hypnotic for her insomnia and reassess her symptoms in the clinic in four weeks
options.rationale: Reduced need for sleep in a mixed state is a symptom of the mood disturbance rather than primary insomnia, and a four week interval is unsafe given the risk of escalation. Hypnotics may be used briefly alongside definitive treatment, not instead of it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Mixed features occur when depressive and manic symptoms are present at the same time, and they are common in bipolar II disorder, frequently precipitated or worsened by antidepressant monotherapy. The clue is that the patient describes persistent low mood while displaying agitation, racing thoughts, irritability and reduced sleep need, and the reduced need for sleep rather than an inability to sleep is the key distinction from depressive insomnia. Mixed states carry a higher suicide risk than pure depression and often respond poorly to antidepressants, so guidelines advise stopping the antidepressant and using an agent with evidence across both poles. Quetiapine, olanzapine and some other second generation agents are used acutely, with lithium and lamotrigine playing larger roles in maintenance. Frequent review is required until sleep and agitation settle.
key_points: Depressive mood with agitation, racing thoughts and reduced sleep need indicates a mixed state
Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder can precipitate mixed or manic states
Reduced need for sleep, rather than inability to sleep, marks the manic component
Mixed states carry a higher suicide risk than pure depressive episodes
Lamotrigine and lithium are maintenance agents and are too slow for the acute mixed picture
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the patient feels tired the next morning after a short night, because feeling refreshed on three hours of sleep points to a manic component and changes the treatment away from antidepressants entirely.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Four months of memory complaints with prominent distress and early morning waking after a bereavement
stem:
You are the geriatrician assessing a 72 year old retired accountant referred with memory loss. His wife died five months ago and his daughter dates the change to the weeks that followed.

He reports his memory in detail and with obvious distress, saying he is a burden and that his mind has gone. During cognitive testing he answers do not know to most questions without attempting them, yet later recalls the name of the ward clerk and the route he took to the clinic. He wakes at four each morning and has lost 6 kg without dieting. He has stopped attending bowls and no longer reads. His gait, tone and reflexes are normal, there are no hallucinations, and his mini mental state examination is 25 out of 30 with variable effort across items.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 per minute, blood pressure 134/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, restricted affect, no focal neurological signs, normal gait and tone
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, magnetic resonance imaging of brain shows mild generalised atrophy appropriate for age with no hippocampal predominance

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start donepezil now and repeat cognitive testing again in six months to assess his trajectory
options.rationale: A cholinesterase inhibitor treats established Alzheimer disease and would neither address his mood syndrome nor clarify the diagnosis. Starting it first risks anchoring on dementia and leaving a treatable depression untreated (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines).

options.text: Treat the depressive episode and repeat formal cognitive assessment once his mood has responded
options.rationale: A subacute onset dated to a bereavement, prominent self reproach, early morning waking, weight loss and do not know responses with preserved incidental recall point to cognitive impairment driven by depression, which improves with treatment of the mood disorder. Reassessing cognition after response is essential because a substantial proportion of these patients later develop a true dementia and need ongoing follow up (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines).

options.text: Refer him for fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography to define the pattern of hypometabolism
options.rationale: Functional imaging is reserved for atypical or diagnostically uncertain dementia after treatable causes have been addressed, and depression itself alters metabolic patterns. Using it now would produce a result that is difficult to interpret (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines).

options.text: Attribute his presentation to normal grief and arrange bereavement counselling with review in three months
options.rationale: Grief does not typically produce pervasive worthlessness, marked weight loss, psychomotor retardation and functional collapse, which mark a depressive episode requiring treatment. Counselling alone would leave a treatable and potentially dangerous illness unaddressed (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Commence a low dose antipsychotic to address his belief that he is a burden on his family
options.rationale: A sense of being a burden is a depressive cognition rather than a delusion in the absence of fixed unshakeable false beliefs, and antipsychotics increase mortality in older people with cognitive impairment. Antipsychotic augmentation is considered only for psychotic depression (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Depression in older people frequently presents with cognitive impairment, and distinguishing it from an early dementia is one of the recurring diagnostic problems of old age medicine. Features favouring a mood driven picture include a relatively short and datable history, a patient who complains vigorously about memory rather than minimising it, do not know responses with preserved recall when off guard, prominent self reproach and biological symptoms such as early morning waking and weight loss. Neurodegenerative disease more often produces a gradual course, confabulation or minimisation, impaired recognition memory and a hippocampal predominant pattern on imaging. Effective antidepressant treatment usually improves the cognitive performance substantially, though not always to a normal level. Longitudinal follow up remains essential because a large minority of these patients convert to dementia within a few years, so the two conditions are best thought of as overlapping rather than mutually exclusive.
key_points: Datable subacute onset with prominent complaint of memory loss favours a mood driven picture
Do not know responses with preserved incidental recall are characteristic
Early morning waking, weight loss and self reproach support a depressive episode
Treat the depression first, then repeat formal cognitive assessment
A substantial minority later develop dementia, so follow up is required regardless of response
explanation.pearls: Repeat formal cognitive testing about three months after a full antidepressant response, since performance that fails to improve at that point substantially raises the probability of an underlying neurodegenerative process.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Involuntary lip and tongue movements emerging in the fourth year of antipsychotic treatment in a woman also taking an anticholinergic
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 62 year old woman with schizophrenia in a community clinic. She has taken risperidone 4 mg daily for four years, and benzatropine 2 mg daily was added in the first month for stiffness and a tremor which settled and has not returned.

Her daughter has noticed over the past four months that her mother is constantly chewing on nothing and that her tongue pushes against the inside of her cheek. On examination there are repetitive lip smacking and tongue rolling movements with occasional finger movements, which stop briefly when you ask her to open her mouth and hold still and which her daughter says are absent while she is asleep. She has no rigidity, her arm swing is symmetrical, and she sits comfortably without shifting or pacing. Her psychotic symptoms have been in remission for three years and she is distressed that people stare at her at the shops.

data_table.Examination: Repetitive lip smacking and tongue rolling with choreiform finger movements, briefly suppressible on request, no cogwheel rigidity, symmetrical arm swing, no truncal restlessness
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 4 mg orally daily for four years, benzatropine 2 mg orally daily for four years
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests, thyroid function and calcium all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Increase the benzatropine dose to control the abnormal facial movements
options.rationale: Anticholinergics relieve drug induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia but reliably aggravate this movement pattern, so increasing the dose makes the presenting problem worse. The absence of rigidity and the preserved arm swing show there is no parkinsonism left for it to treat (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Add propranolol 10 mg three times daily and review her again in two weeks
options.rationale: Propranolol treats the inner restlessness of akathisia, which is a subjective urge to move relieved by moving, and this woman sits still without pacing or shifting. Treating the wrong movement disorder also leaves the anticholinergic contribution untouched (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Increase the risperidone dose to suppress the movements more completely
options.rationale: More dopamine blockade does mask these movements for weeks to months, which is exactly why it is a trap: the underlying receptor supersensitivity worsens and the movements return in a more entrenched form. Dose increases are the classic way a reversible problem is made permanent (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Order a brain MRI and refer to neurology before changing any medication
options.rationale: Structural imaging is warranted when the movements are asymmetrical, progressive, accompanied by cognitive decline or arise without dopamine blocking exposure, none of which applies after four years of an antipsychotic with normal metabolic and thyroid screening. Waiting for imaging also prolongs the exposure that is driving the movements (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease the benzatropine and arrange review of her antipsychotic regimen
options.rationale: Withdrawing the anticholinergic removes a well documented aggravating factor and often produces measurable improvement within weeks, and it is the one change with no psychiatric downside because her parkinsonism resolved years ago. Reviewing the antipsychotic addresses the cause, with a lower dose or a switch to an agent with weaker striatal blockade considered against her three years of remission (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Tardive dyskinesia arises after months to years of dopamine receptor blockade and typically involves the oro bucco lingual region, with choreoathetoid limb and trunk movements in more extensive cases. It is distinguished from akathisia by the absence of a subjective urge to move and from drug induced parkinsonism by the absence of rigidity and bradykinesia, and it characteristically disappears in sleep and can be briefly suppressed voluntarily. Risk rises with age, female sex, longer exposure, diabetes and a history of acute extrapyramidal reactions, and anticholinergic co prescription both worsens established dyskinesia and offers no prophylaxis. Management is exposure reduction where the psychiatric state allows, withdrawal of anticholinergics, and consideration of a vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitor or clozapine in persistent cases. Movements can worsen transiently on dose reduction before improving, which is worth warning the patient about so the change is not abandoned early.
key_points: Suppressible oro bucco lingual movements absent in sleep after prolonged exposure indicate tardive dyskinesia
Anticholinergics worsen tardive dyskinesia and do not prevent it
Raising the antipsychotic dose masks the movements short term and worsens them long term
Absence of rigidity and of subjective restlessness excludes parkinsonism and akathisia
Routine screening with a structured movement scale should occur at least every six to twelve months
explanation.pearls: Movements often flare for four to twelve weeks after the offending antipsychotic is reduced, which is withdrawal emergent dyskinesia rather than treatment failure, so warn the patient in advance and hold the new dose rather than reversing the reduction.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Two years of escalating rule breaking and aggression in a fourteen year old who describes it flatly and shows no remorse
stem: A 14-year-old boy is referred after a second school suspension. Over two years he has had repeated fights, twice forced entry into a neighbour's shed, stayed out overnight, and last month deliberately injured a neighbour's cat. He describes this flatly and shows no remorse. No abuse or neglect is identified.

data_table.Examination: Flat, unconcerned affect; mood, sleep and appetite normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; cognitive testing in the average range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start risperidone to reduce his aggression
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have modest short term effects on aggression in this population and carry weight gain, metabolic disturbance and sedation, so they are reserved for severe aggression that persists despite psychosocial treatment or that occurs with intellectual disability. Prescribing first also signals to the family that the problem is medical rather than relational (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents).
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

options.text: Refer the family for a structured parenting program
options.rationale: Structured family based interventions such as parent management training, functional family therapy and multisystemic therapy have the strongest evidence in conduct disorder and are first line, working through consistent limits, monitoring and reinforcement of prosocial behaviour across home and school. Family based treatment remains first line even where limited prosocial emotions are present, although response rates are lower and treatment needs to be longer and reward focused rather than punishment focused (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents).
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

options.text: Refer him for weekly insight oriented psychotherapy
options.rationale: Individual insight oriented work has not been shown to change externalising behaviour in adolescents and depends on a motivation to change that he does not express. Group based interventions with other antisocial adolescents can also worsen outcomes through peer reinforcement (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents).
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

options.text: Start fluoxetine and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants are indicated when a depressive or anxiety disorder coexists, which is common in this group but is not present here given his unchanged sleep, appetite and mood and his absence of distress. Treating an absent disorder delays the intervention that works (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents).
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

options.text: Refer him to a residential wilderness program
options.rationale: Boot camp and wilderness style programs have consistently failed to reduce reoffending and several have increased it, most likely through aggregating antisocial peers away from the family system where the behaviour is maintained. It differs from the correct option in removing the young person from the setting the treatment needs to change (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents).
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

explanation.summary: Conduct disorder is a repetitive and persistent pattern of behaviour violating the rights of others or major age appropriate norms, grouped into aggression to people and animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious rule violations. DSM-5 added a specifier for limited prosocial emotions, requiring at least two of lack of remorse or guilt, callous lack of empathy, unconcern about performance, and shallow or deficient affect, present over at least twelve months across settings. That specifier identifies a group with a more severe and persistent course and a poorer response to punishment based approaches, which is why treatment emphasises reward for prosocial behaviour rather than escalating sanctions. Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, particularly attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, substance use, learning difficulties, depression and trauma related disorders, and each identified comorbidity is treated in its own right. Early onset before age ten carries a worse prognosis than adolescent onset, and outcomes are substantially better when the family system engages with treatment.
key_points: Conduct disorder involves aggression, destruction, deceitfulness and serious rule violation
The limited prosocial emotions specifier marks a more severe and persistent subtype
Family based psychosocial interventions are first line at any severity
Medication is reserved for comorbid disorders or severe persisting aggression
Group and residential programs that aggregate antisocial peers can worsen outcomes
explanation.pearls: Screen specifically for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, since it coexists in roughly a third to a half of children with conduct disorder and treating it reduces both impulsive aggression and the rate of subsequent offending, which no conduct focused intervention achieves on its own.

sources.label: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

subtopic_detail: Repeated hair pulling with visible scalp loss in a woman who describes tension before and relief afterwards, without any intrusive thought
stem: A 23-year-old student has pulled hair from her scalp since she was fifteen. She pulls in the evening while watching television, with a build up of tension that eases as each hair comes out. She denies any intrusive thought or fear preceding it. She has tried repeatedly to stop and now avoids swimming.

data_table.Examination: Broken hairs of varying lengths within the patch, no scaling or scarring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start fluoxetine and titrate over six weeks
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are effective in obsessive compulsive disorder but have repeatedly failed to outperform placebo for hair pulling in randomised trials, which is one of the reasons this condition is classified separately. Medication is added for comorbidity or for treatment resistance rather than used first (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer for a scalp biopsy before any treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy is warranted when the diagnosis is uncertain, and here the broken hairs of differing lengths within a patch with normal, non scarred, non inflamed skin, together with the described behaviour, make it clear. Alopecia areata by contrast produces smooth complete loss with exclamation mark hairs (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Advise her to keep her hands busy instead
options.rationale: Substituting an activity is one element of the structured treatment but delivered as brief advice without awareness training, stimulus control and a specific competing response it performs no better than no treatment. Three months of unstructured self management also risks further hair loss and demoralisation (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer for habit reversal training with a therapist
options.rationale: Habit reversal training, combining awareness training, a competing physically incompatible response and stimulus control, has the strongest evidence for this disorder and is first line in Australian practice. Her account of automatic pulling that begins without her noticing is precisely what the awareness component targets (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Start low dose risperidone for the behaviour
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is a later option in refractory cases and brings metabolic and extrapyramidal risk to a young woman who has had no first line treatment. The behaviour is a body focused repetitive behaviour rather than a compulsion driven by an obsession, which is why the antipsychotic evidence from obsessive compulsive disorder does not transfer (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Trichotillomania sits within the obsessive compulsive and related disorders in DSM-5 and requires recurrent hair pulling causing hair loss, repeated attempts to stop, and clinically significant distress or impairment. It differs from obsessive compulsive disorder in that there is no intrusive obsession driving the behaviour, and the pulling is preceded by tension and followed by relief or gratification, which places it among the body focused repetitive behaviours alongside excoriation disorder and nail biting. Pulling is often automatic rather than focused, occurring during sedentary activities without the person noticing they have begun, and this distinction shapes the behavioural treatment. Habit reversal training is first line, with N acetylcysteine having some supportive randomised evidence in adults, while serotonin reuptake inhibitors have performed poorly. Trichophagia should always be asked about, since swallowing the pulled hair can produce a gastric trichobezoar with obstruction, and dermatological differentials include alopecia areata, tinea capitis and traction alopecia.
key_points: Tension before and relief afterwards without any preceding obsession defines the behaviour
Hairs of differing lengths within a non scarred patch distinguish it from alopecia areata
Habit reversal training is first line treatment
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors have not outperformed placebo in this condition
Ask about hair eating because of the risk of gastric bezoar
explanation.pearls: Ask directly whether she swallows any of the hair, because trichophagia occurs in around 10 to 20 per cent and a gastric trichobezoar can present years later with obstruction, and the question is almost never volunteered without being asked.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Constant pacing ten days into antipsychotic treatment in a young man whose psychotic symptoms are simultaneously improving
stem: A 24-year-old man admitted ten days ago with first episode psychosis had aripiprazole increased from 10 to 20 mg four days ago. Since yesterday he paces continuously and cannot sit for meals, with restlessness in his legs eased only by walking. His psychotic symptoms have improved.

data_table.Examination: Normal tone, temperature 36.9 degrees C, creatine kinase 118 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reduce the aripiprazole and add propranolol 10 mg three times daily
options.rationale: A subjective inner restlessness localised to the legs and relieved by movement, appearing days after a dose increase, is akathisia, and the primary treatment is to reduce the causative dose because the effect is dose related. Propranolol is the best supported adjunct in Australian practice while the dose change takes effect (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Add benzatropine 1 mg twice daily for the extrapyramidal effect
options.rationale: Anticholinergics work for acute dystonia and drug induced parkinsonism, both of which require rigidity, bradykinesia or sustained muscle spasm that this man does not have. Trials in akathisia specifically have shown no benefit over placebo, which is what separates it from the other extrapyramidal syndromes (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Increase the aripiprazole, as this is psychotic agitation
options.rationale: Reading this as psychotic agitation and escalating the dose is the error that turns a treatable side effect into a crisis, and it is contradicted by his account of quieter voices and resolved persecutory beliefs. Untreated akathisia is a recognised contributor to suicidal acts during admission (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Add diazepam 5 mg twice daily and change nothing else
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do relieve akathisia and are a reasonable second line adjunct, but using one while holding the causative dose treats the symptom and leaves the cause running. Dose reduction is the intervention that resolves the problem rather than covering it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cease the aripiprazole and give intramuscular haloperidol
options.rationale: A high potency typical antipsychotic carries a higher akathisia rate than the drug he is already taking, so this would intensify precisely the symptom being treated. Abrupt cessation also throws away a regimen that is working on his psychosis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Akathisia appears in roughly a fifth to a quarter of patients starting or escalating an antipsychotic and is most often mistaken for worsening psychotic agitation or for anxiety. The defining feature is subjective: an inner restlessness, usually referred to the legs, that is temporarily relieved by moving, which separates it from the objective slowness of parkinsonism and from the suppressible oro lingual movements of tardive dyskinesia. It matters because it is genuinely distressing and has been linked to treatment non adherence, aggression and suicide during admission. Management is dose reduction or a switch to a lower risk agent first, with propranolol as the best supported adjunct and a benzodiazepine as an alternative, while anticholinergics have consistently failed to show benefit. Objective rating with a structured akathisia scale at each dose change catches it earlier than waiting for the patient to volunteer it.
key_points: Akathisia is defined by subjective inner restlessness relieved by movement
It appears within days to weeks of starting or increasing an antipsychotic
Dose reduction or a switch is first line, with propranolol as the preferred adjunct
Anticholinergics are ineffective in akathisia despite working for other extrapyramidal effects
Normal tone, temperature and creatine kinase exclude neuroleptic malignant syndrome
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient directly whether the restlessness is inside them or only in how they look, because a patient who paces but denies any inner urge to move is far more likely to have psychomotor agitation, and only the inner urge responds to propranolol.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Amenorrhoea and milk discharge in the second year of antipsychotic treatment with a prolactin level in the range that overlaps drug effect and tumour
stem: A 27-year-old woman has taken risperidone 3 mg daily for fourteen months after a single episode of psychosis. Her periods stopped eight months ago and for three months she has had bilateral milky nipple discharge.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral milky discharge; normal visual fields; no headache
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1780 and 1850 mIU/L on two mornings (less than 500); pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add cabergoline 0.5 mg weekly and continue risperidone
options.rationale: A dopamine agonist opposes the very receptor blockade that is treating her illness and carries a real risk of precipitating psychotic relapse, so it is reserved for cases where the antipsychotic genuinely cannot be changed. Removing the cause is both safer and more effective than adding a second drug to counteract it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Order an MRI of the pituitary before any change
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when prolactin exceeds roughly 4000 mIU/L, when there are headaches or visual field defects, or when the level fails to fall after the causative drug is changed, none of which applies to a level under 2000 mIU/L with normal fields on a known prolactin raising drug. Imaging first also delays the intervention that would both diagnose and treat (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia).

options.text: Switch her to aripiprazole and repeat the prolactin
options.rationale: Risperidone raises prolactin more than any other second generation agent because it blocks tuberoinfundibular dopamine receptors while barely crossing back out of that circulation, and aripiprazole is a partial agonist that lowers prolactin, often to normal within four to eight weeks. Repeating the level after the switch is what distinguishes drug effect from a coincidental adenoma, so the change is both treatment and diagnostic test (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Add a combined oral contraceptive pill to restore periods
options.rationale: Replacing oestrogen protects bone density and gives withdrawal bleeds but leaves the prolactin elevated, the galactorrhoea untreated and any underlying lesion unexamined. It is a reasonable adjunct only once the cause has been established and the antipsychotic cannot be altered (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia).

options.text: Stop all antipsychotic treatment and monitor the prolactin
options.rationale: Ceasing treatment entirely at fourteen months after a first episode carries a relapse risk of the order of 60 to 80 per cent within two years, which is a far greater harm than the endocrine side effect being treated. Switching agents achieves the same fall in prolactin while maintaining cover (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic induced hyperprolactinaemia is common, under asked about and clinically consequential, producing amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, infertility and accelerated bone loss through hypogonadism. Risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride and the typical antipsychotics are the strongest offenders, while aripiprazole, quetiapine and clozapine are prolactin sparing.
