options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants add anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension and cognitive impairment, compounding rather than relieving her falls and memory concerns. Sedating antidepressants are considered only when a coexisting mood disorder justifies them. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Hypnotic agents acting at the benzodiazepine receptor, including the non-benzodiazepine z-drugs, are recommended only for short term use of two to four weeks because tolerance to the hypnotic effect develops quickly while the adverse effects persist. In older adults these agents roughly double the risk of falls and hip fracture and contribute to daytime sedation, cognitive impairment and motor vehicle accidents, and long term use is a recognised deprescribing priority. Withdrawal must be gradual, typically reducing by around a quarter of the dose every one to two weeks with slower steps at lower doses, because abrupt cessation causes rebound insomnia that patients interpret as proof they still need the drug. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the first line treatment for chronic insomnia and outperforms medication in the long term, with sleep restriction and stimulus control the components that carry most of the effect. Success depends on framing the taper collaboratively, since patients who feel the medicine is being removed against their wishes rarely complete it.
key_points: These agents are indicated for two to four weeks only; tolerance develops while harms persist
In older adults they approximately double the risk of falls and hip fracture
Abrupt cessation causes rebound insomnia that drives relapse and reinforces perceived need
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and outperforms medication long term
Substituting another hypnotic maintains dependence rather than resolving it
explanation.pearls: Taper by roughly 25 per cent of the dose every one to two weeks, slowing further below half the starting dose, and warn the patient in advance that two to three nights of worse sleep after each reduction is expected withdrawal rather than proof the drug is still needed.

subtopic_detail: Abdominal symptoms in a patient established on clozapine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 38 year old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia who has taken clozapine 450 mg daily for three years with good symptom control. He tells you he has not opened his bowels for nine days and has vomited twice today.

His abdomen is distended and tympanic with sluggish bowel sounds and generalised discomfort but no guarding. He mentions he stopped taking his laxative several months ago because he disliked the taste. He has no fever, no cough and no urinary symptoms. His last full blood count two weeks ago showed a neutrophil count within the normal range, and he has had no missed doses.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 5.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C-reactive protein 22 mg/L (less than 5), lactate 1.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.0), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Withhold clozapine and arrange urgent full blood count to exclude neutropenia
options.rationale: His neutrophil count is normal and haematological monitoring is up to date, so agranulocytosis does not explain abdominal distension and vomiting. Withholding clozapine for more than 48 hours also forces a slow retitration with risk of psychotic relapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange urgent echocardiography and troponin testing to assess for myocarditis
options.rationale: Clozapine induced myocarditis occurs characteristically within the first four to eight weeks of treatment and presents with tachycardia, fever and chest symptoms rather than nine days of constipation with distension. It remains an important complication but the timing and presentation do not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe a stimulant laxative and reassess his bowel function in 48 hours on the ward
options.rationale: Oral laxatives alone are inadequate once obstruction is suspected, and stimulant agents can precipitate perforation in a distended atonic bowel. Laxatives are the mainstay of prevention and of treating uncomplicated constipation, not of suspected ileus. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe an antiemetic and increase his oral fluid intake with a review the following morning
options.rationale: Symptomatic treatment delays recognition of a condition with a case fatality far exceeding that of agranulocytosis, and many antiemetics further slow gut transit. Antiemetics are appropriate once obstruction has been excluded. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Arrange urgent abdominal imaging and surgical review for suspected bowel obstruction
options.rationale: Nine days without bowel action, vomiting and a distended tympanic abdomen in a patient on clozapine indicates gastrointestinal hypomotility progressing towards ileus, which carries a mortality substantially higher than agranulocytosis and demands urgent imaging and surgical assessment. Recognising it requires actively asking about bowels, since patients rarely volunteer the symptom. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Clozapine remains the only agent with established efficacy in treatment resistant schizophrenia, and its monitoring program is built around agranulocytosis, yet gastrointestinal hypomotility is both more common and more lethal. The drug has potent anticholinergic and antiserotonergic effects on the gut, slowing colonic transit in the majority of patients and producing a spectrum that runs from constipation through faecal impaction to paralytic ileus, toxic megacolon, ischaemia and perforation. Case fatality once ileus develops is high, and deaths substantially outnumber those from agranulocytosis. Patients frequently do not report the symptom, partly through negative symptoms and reduced interoceptive awareness, so bowel function must be asked about at every review rather than waiting for a complaint. Prophylactic laxatives are recommended for all patients on clozapine, and constipating co-prescriptions such as anticholinergics and opioids should be avoided or minimised.
key_points: Gastrointestinal hypomotility causes more clozapine deaths than agranulocytosis
Patients under-report bowel symptoms, so ask directly at every review
Myocarditis typically occurs in the first four to eight weeks, not after years of stable therapy
Prophylactic laxatives are recommended for all patients taking clozapine
Suspected ileus needs imaging and surgical review, not further oral laxatives
explanation.pearls: Avoid adding anticholinergic agents such as benzatropine to a patient on clozapine, since the combined gut slowing is a recognised precipitant of ileus, and prescribe a regular osmotic laxative from initiation rather than waiting for constipation to be reported.

subtopic_detail: Acute behavioural and mood change after commencing high dose corticosteroid
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to review a 54 year old woman on the respiratory ward. She was admitted six days ago with a severe asthma exacerbation and started on prednisolone 50 mg daily. Over the past three days she has slept only two to three hours nightly, talks rapidly and has been ordering expensive items online.

Nursing staff report she is irritable when interrupted and has been telling other patients she has been chosen to reform the hospital. She has no personal or family history of mood disorder and has never had a similar episode. She takes salbutamol and a preventer inhaler, and is on no antibiotics. She is fully oriented with no fluctuation in attention and no visual hallucinations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 136/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), calcium corrected 2.36 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence lithium and arrange level monitoring for a first presentation of bipolar disorder
options.rationale: A mood stabiliser committing her to long term therapy and monitoring is not justified when a clear pharmacological precipitant is present and the syndrome typically resolves with dose reduction. Lithium would be considered if manic episodes recurred independent of steroid exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Discuss reducing the corticosteroid dose with the treating team and start an antipsychotic
options.rationale: The temporal link to high dose corticosteroid with no prior mood history identifies a substance induced mood disturbance, so the priority is to reduce the causative exposure as far as her asthma safely allows while a short course of an antipsychotic controls the acute symptoms. Most cases resolve within days to weeks of dose reduction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease the corticosteroid abruptly today and observe her mental state over the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after six days of high dose therapy risks both loss of asthma control and adrenal insufficiency if her exposure is longer than documented. The correct approach is the fastest safe reduction negotiated with the respiratory team, not immediate withdrawal. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence an antidepressant given the disturbed sleep and marked change in her behaviour
options.rationale: Her presentation is elevated and expansive rather than depressed, and an antidepressant would risk worsening the elevated mood state. Antidepressants have a place in the depressive form of steroid induced mood disturbance, which is actually more common overall. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Treat as hyperactive delirium with regular haloperidol and full delirium precautions
options.rationale: Delirium requires disturbed attention and awareness with a fluctuating course, and she is fully oriented with stable attention and no perceptual disturbance. The near-pair distinction rests on attention and fluctuation, which are the defining features of delirium and are absent here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Corticosteroid induced neuropsychiatric effects are common, dose dependent and frequently misattributed to a primary psychiatric disorder, particularly when a patient has no prior history. Risk rises steeply above the equivalent of 40 mg of prednisolone daily, and symptoms typically emerge within the first two weeks of treatment. The presentations span elevated mood, irritability and psychosis at higher doses, depression which is more common with prolonged therapy, and cognitive disturbance, with a prior psychiatric history a much weaker predictor than is often assumed. Management centres on reducing the corticosteroid to the lowest dose that controls the underlying disease, in negotiation with the treating team rather than unilaterally, since abrupt cessation risks both disease flare and adrenal insufficiency. Symptomatic treatment uses an antipsychotic for elevated or psychotic presentations and an antidepressant for depressive ones, and most episodes resolve within days to weeks of dose reduction.
key_points: Risk rises steeply above the equivalent of 40 mg of prednisolone daily
Symptoms usually appear within the first two weeks of treatment
Elevated and psychotic presentations predominate acutely; depression predominates with prolonged use
Delirium is excluded by preserved attention and the absence of a fluctuating course
Reduce the dose in negotiation with the treating team rather than stopping abruptly
explanation.pearls: Document the reaction prominently, because recurrence on re-exposure is common and a patient who has had steroid induced mania may warrant prophylactic antipsychotic cover if a future high dose course is unavoidable.

subtopic_detail: Weighing antipsychotic risk against harm in dementia related agitation
stem:
You are the visiting medical officer at a residential aged care facility asked to review an 84 year old man with moderate Alzheimer disease. Over three weeks he has become increasingly agitated in the late afternoon, calling out and pushing staff away during personal care, and last week he struck a carer.

Staff have tried moving him to a quieter area without benefit. He has been checked for constipation, urinary retention and infection, all of which were absent, and a hearing aid battery was replaced two weeks ago. His pain is difficult to assess but he has severe knee osteoarthritis and is on no regular analgesia. He is not distressed at other times of day, his attention is stable and there is no acute cognitive fluctuation.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function and C-reactive protein within normal limits; midstream urine culture shows no growth; no new medicines in the past three months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence regular risperidone at a low dose with review of benefit at 12 weeks
options.rationale: An antipsychotic may eventually be justified but not before untreated pain has been addressed, and a 12 week review is far too long given the stroke and mortality risk. Where an antipsychotic is used, review is recommended at around four to 12 weeks with an explicit plan to withdraw. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence regular scheduled paracetamol and reassess the behaviour after two weeks
options.rationale: Untreated pain is among the commonest reversible drivers of agitation in dementia, personal care and movement are exactly when osteoarthritic pain is provoked, and he receives no analgesia despite severe knee disease. A trial of regular simple analgesia is low risk and has good evidence for reducing agitation before any antipsychotic is considered. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a benzodiazepine at night to reduce his arousal and improve his sleep pattern
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines increase falls, confusion and paradoxical agitation in this population and do not address the daytime trigger. They are reserved for short term use in acute severe distress where other measures have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor to improve cognition and thereby reduce his agitation
options.rationale: These agents produce modest cognitive benefit but have little effect on established agitation and take months to show any change. They are indicated for cognitive symptoms rather than as a behavioural intervention. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence an antidepressant given that late day distress may indicate an underlying depression
options.rationale: Depression is worth considering in dementia but his distress is confined to personal care and movement rather than being pervasive, which points to a pain trigger. An antidepressant trial would be reasonable if there were persistent low mood, tearfulness or withdrawal across the day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia are best approached as communication of an unmet need rather than as a target for sedation, and a structured search for precipitants precedes any medication decision. The standard sequence examines physical causes including pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, sensory impairment and medication effects, then environmental and interpersonal triggers such as noise, overstimulation, unfamiliar carers and the manner in which personal care is delivered. Pain is the most frequently missed contributor because people with moderate to severe dementia cannot report it reliably, and observational pain scales or an empirical trial of regular simple analgesia are the practical responses. Antipsychotics carry a clear increase in stroke and all cause mortality in older people with dementia, so they are reserved for severe distress or risk after non-pharmacological measures have failed, used at the lowest effective dose with informed consent from the substitute decision maker and a defined plan for withdrawal. Australian aged care regulation requires documented justification and review of any psychotropic used for behaviour.
key_points: Treat behaviour as an unmet need and search systematically for precipitants first
Pain is the most commonly missed driver because self report is unreliable in dementia
Agitation confined to personal care and movement points strongly to a pain trigger
Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality risk and require consent and a withdrawal plan
Benzodiazepines worsen falls and confusion and can cause paradoxical agitation
explanation.pearls: A trial of regular scheduled paracetamol, rather than as required dosing, is the single highest yield intervention for agitation in moderate dementia, and benefit should be assessed over about two weeks before escalating to any psychotropic.

subtopic_detail: Persistent sleepiness and low mood in a rotating shift worker
stem:
A 29 year old process operator attends your practice reporting eight months of exhaustion, difficulty concentrating and irritability. He works a rotating roster of four night shifts, then four days off, then four day shifts, and has done so since starting the job.

He says he sleeps only three to four hours after night shifts because of daylight and household noise, and sleeps well for eight hours on his days off, waking refreshed. He enjoys his weekends with friends and denies anhedonia, guilt, hopelessness and suicidal thoughts, and says he feels normal by his third day off. He drinks four cups of coffee during each night shift. He does not snore and his partner has noticed no pauses in his breathing.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, thyroid function and HbA1c all within normal limits; body mass index 24 kg/m2; sleep diary confirms 3 to 4 hours of daytime sleep on night shift blocks and 8 hours on days off

lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?

options.text: Shift work disorder from misalignment between his roster and his circadian rhythm
options.rationale: Sleepiness and mood symptoms that track his roster and resolve completely on days off, with normal restorative sleep when he can follow his own rhythm, define a circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder rather than a primary psychiatric or medical illness. The complete recovery within days off is the finding that separates it from a depressive episode. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

options.text: Major depressive disorder presenting predominantly with fatigue and poor concentration
options.rationale: A depressive episode requires persistently low mood or anhedonia for most of the day nearly every day, and his symptoms remit entirely on days off with preserved enjoyment and no guilt or hopelessness. Fatigue alone is insufficient for the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnoea causing fragmented sleep and consequent daytime impairment
options.rationale: He has no snoring, no witnessed apnoeas and a normal body mass index, and his sleep on days off is restorative, which argues against a breathing related disorder. Sleep study referral would be indicated if any of those features were present. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

options.text: Chronic insomnia disorder maintained by conditioned arousal and poor sleep habits
options.rationale: Chronic insomnia requires difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep despite adequate opportunity, and his problem is inadequate opportunity because he is trying to sleep in daylight against his circadian drive. He sleeps normally when the opportunity aligns with his rhythm. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

options.text: Caffeine use disorder producing rebound fatigue and irritability between shift blocks
options.rationale: His intake is substantial and worth addressing, particularly its timing late in a night shift, but caffeine does not account for eight months of sleepiness that resolves entirely on days off. Withdrawal symptoms would be expected on days off when intake falls, which is when he feels best. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

explanation.summary: Shift work disorder is a circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder in which the work schedule conflicts with the endogenous circadian drive, producing insomnia during the designated sleep period, excessive sleepiness during work, and consequent mood and cognitive symptoms. Around one in five to one in three shift workers meet criteria, and the diagnosis is frequently mislabelled as depression because fatigue, irritability and poor concentration dominate the presentation. The discriminating feature is that symptoms track the roster and resolve when the worker can sleep according to their own rhythm, whereas a depressive episode persists across days off with anhedonia and negative cognitions. A sleep diary over two weeks is the key diagnostic tool and also exposes the inadequate sleep opportunity that patients often normalise. Management combines sleep hygiene adapted to shift work, strategic light exposure and avoidance, planned napping, careful caffeine timing and forward rotating rosters, with the occupational stakes real because drowsy driving after night shift is a major cause of vehicle crashes.
key_points: Symptoms that resolve completely on days off point to circadian misalignment, not depression
A two week sleep diary is the central diagnostic tool
Chronic insomnia requires adequate sleep opportunity, which shift workers often lack
Forward rotating rosters are better tolerated than backward rotating ones
Drowsy driving after night shift is a major occupational safety risk
explanation.pearls: Advise wearing dark sunglasses on the drive home after a night shift and blocking daylight in the bedroom, since morning light exposure resets the circadian clock in the wrong direction and undoes the day sleep he is trying to obtain.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift Work and Sleep

subtopic_detail: New low mood in the menopausal transition with vasomotor symptoms
stem:
A 49 year old woman attends your clinic with five months of low mood, poor concentration and loss of interest in activities she previously enjoyed. Her periods have become irregular over the past year, with two gaps of more than 60 days.

She has 10 to 12 hot flushes daily and wakes drenched most nights, which she says is the worst part. She has never had a depressive episode before and has no history of postnatal depression or premenstrual mood change. She denies suicidal thoughts, has no alcohol or drug use, and thyroid function and full blood count are within normal limits. She has no personal or family history of breast cancer, no migraine with aura and no history of venous thromboembolism.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 68 micrograms/L (30-300), HbA1c within normal limits; body mass index 26 kg/m2

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor as first line treatment for the mood symptoms
options.rationale: Antidepressants are first line for a major depressive episode but treat the vasomotor symptoms less effectively than hormonal therapy, and here the flushes and night sweats are driving the sleep disruption that sustains the mood disturbance. They become the preferred choice when hormone therapy is contraindicated or declined. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

options.text: Measure follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol to confirm the menopausal transition first
options.rationale: Hormone levels fluctuate widely during the transition and are not recommended for diagnosis in a woman over 45 with typical symptoms and menstrual change. Testing would delay treatment without changing the management decision. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

options.text: Commence menopausal hormone therapy and review both mood and vasomotor symptoms at six weeks
options.rationale: Where new depressive symptoms arise in the perimenopause alongside prominent vasomotor symptoms and no prior mood history, hormone therapy improves both the flushes and the mood and is the appropriate first recommendation in a woman with no contraindications. Reviewing at six weeks allows an antidepressant to be added if mood does not follow the vasomotor response. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy alone and review her mood symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: Psychological therapy is a valuable component and helps the distress associated with flushes, but used alone it leaves the nightly vasomotor sleep disruption untreated. It is a reasonable primary choice when a woman declines or cannot take pharmacological treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Recommend a phytoestrogen supplement and lifestyle modification with review in three months
options.rationale: Complementary preparations have inconsistent evidence and do not reliably control moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms or depressive symptoms, so three months of waiting has a substantial opportunity cost. They may suit women with mild symptoms who prefer non-prescription options. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

explanation.summary: The menopausal transition carries a genuinely increased risk of depressive symptoms and of a first depressive episode, with the vulnerability concentrated in the perimenopause rather than after the final menstrual period, and it is greatest in women with a history of premenstrual mood change, postnatal depression or previous depression. Distinguishing a depressive episode arising in this context from one occurring independently matters because the treatment differs: where prominent vasomotor symptoms are disrupting sleep and driving the mood change, hormone therapy improves both, whereas an established major depressive episode with prior history is treated with standard antidepressant and psychological therapy. Diagnosis of the transition itself is clinical in women over 45, and hormone measurement is explicitly not recommended because levels fluctuate unpredictably. Hormone therapy also requires assessment of contraindications including hormone sensitive cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding, active liver disease and prior venous thromboembolism, and transdermal preparations carry lower thrombotic risk than oral ones. Where mood does not improve as flushes settle, an antidepressant is added rather than substituted.
key_points: Perimenopause carries greater depressive risk than the postmenopausal years
Prior premenstrual, postnatal or major depression identifies the highest risk group
Hormone measurement is not recommended for diagnosis in women over 45 with typical symptoms
Hormone therapy treats both vasomotor symptoms and associated mood disturbance
Add an antidepressant if mood fails to improve once vasomotor symptoms are controlled
explanation.pearls: Transdermal oestrogen avoids first pass hepatic metabolism and does not carry the increased venous thromboembolism risk seen with oral preparations, making it the preferred route in women with raised body mass index or other thrombotic risk factors.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: Menopause and Mood

subtopic_detail: recurrent hair pulling with visible patchy loss and mounting tension before pulling in an adolescent
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old girl brought by her mother after the school nurse noticed patchy hair loss. The girl acknowledges, once her mother steps out, that she pulls hair from her scalp while doing homework and watching television.

She describes a build-up of tension before pulling and relief afterwards, followed by shame. She has tried to stop several times and has not managed more than a few days. She does not swallow the hair and has no abdominal pain. On examination there are irregular patches of thinned hair over the right frontoparietal scalp with hairs of varying lengths and no scaling, no scarring, no erythema and no broken hairs elsewhere. She denies low mood, has friends, is doing well academically, and there is no self harm, no restrictive eating and no substance use. Thyroid function and iron studies requested by the nurse are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Irregular patches of thinned scalp hair with hairs of varying length, no scaling, scarring or erythema, eyebrows and eyelashes intact
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and iron studies within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, engaged, no suicidal ideation, no restrictive eating, no substance use

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start N-acetylcysteine at a standard adult dose and review the pulling in twelve weeks
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine has shown benefit for hair pulling in some adult trials and is sometimes used as an adjunct, but the adolescent evidence is weak and it has not displaced behavioural therapy as first line. Offering a supplement first also implies that the behaviour cannot be modified directly, which is the opposite of the message that helps. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Begin self monitoring of pulling episodes and refer for habit reversal training now
options.rationale: Habit reversal training, in which awareness training, a competing physical response and stimulus control are taught together, is the first line treatment for hair pulling disorder at every age and outperforms medication. Starting a record of when and where pulling happens gives the therapist the pattern to work with and begins the awareness training component immediately. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review the response after six weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are effective for obsessive compulsive disorder itself but have not shown consistent benefit for hair pulling, which is a body focused repetitive behaviour rather than a compulsion driven by an obsession. Medication is considered when behavioural therapy has failed or when a comorbid disorder such as depression is present, and she has neither. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Prescribe topical minoxidil solution to the affected scalp and review the regrowth in three months
options.rationale: Topical minoxidil treats androgenetic hair loss, which produces diffuse thinning rather than irregular patches with hairs of different lengths. Regrowth here depends on stopping the pulling, and prescribing a topical agent implies that the scalp rather than the behaviour is the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology, Hair disorders)

options.text: Arrange a scalp biopsy to distinguish scarring from non-scarring causes of the hair loss
options.rationale: Biopsy is useful when the cause of patchy alopecia is uncertain, particularly to identify scarring processes, but here the girl has described the mechanism directly and the scalp shows no scarring or inflammation. Investigating further risks conveying disbelief at the moment she has disclosed something difficult. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology, Hair disorders)

explanation.summary: Hair pulling disorder is classified among the obsessive compulsive and related disorders and is characterised by recurrent pulling with repeated attempts to stop, often preceded by tension and followed by relief. The examination findings of irregular patches containing hairs of varying lengths, with a normal non-scarred scalp, distinguish it from alopecia areata and from fungal infection. First line treatment is habit reversal training, a behavioural package of awareness training, a competing response and stimulus control, which outperforms medication in this condition. Asking specifically about swallowing hair matters because trichobezoar can cause obstruction, and screening for depression and anxiety is routine since comorbidity is common.
key_points: Hairs of varying length in irregular patches with a normal scalp point to pulling rather than alopecia areata
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms serotonin reuptake inhibitors
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are reserved for comorbid disorders or failed behavioural therapy
Ask about swallowing hair, since trichobezoar can cause gastrointestinal obstruction
explanation.pearls: Ask two questions when you see patchy hair loss with intact scalp skin: does the tension build before and ease after, and does she swallow the hair? A yes to the first makes habit reversal training the treatment, and a yes to the second makes an abdominal examination for a trichobezoar urgent.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: deliberate under-dosing of insulin for weight control with recurrent ketoacidosis and normal body weight
stem: A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes since age nine is admitted with her fourth episode of diabetic ketoacidosis in eight months. She skips her long acting insulin because she gains weight when her glucose is controlled, and checks her body repeatedly in the mirror.

data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 11.8 per cent, risen from 7.4
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21.5 kg/m2, weight stable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Refer for joint eating disorder and diabetes care
options.rationale: Insulin restriction for weight control is an eating disorder expressed through diabetes, so treatment has to be delivered jointly by a service able to address body image and by the diabetes team able to reintroduce insulin at a pace that limits the fluid shift, oedema and neuropathic pain that rapid normalisation causes. Addressing either side alone reproduces the pattern of escalating glycated haemoglobin and repeated admissions. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Increase her long acting insulin with clinic review
options.rationale: Adjusting the prescription treats the number rather than the reason the insulin is not being taken, and prescribing more of a drug she is deliberately omitting predictably fails. Dose optimisation becomes useful once the eating disorder is being treated alongside it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Start sertraline and review her mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Depressive symptoms are common alongside this presentation and may need treatment, but an antidepressant alone does not alter insulin restriction, which is the behaviour causing life threatening episodes. Mood treatment sits within the joint plan rather than replacing it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Apply mental health legislation for involuntary care
options.rationale: Compulsory treatment is reserved for patients who lack capacity or pose an imminent risk that cannot be managed voluntarily, and she is engaging, disclosing and willing to talk. Beginning with legislation would damage the therapeutic relationship that her long term recovery depends on. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Discharge with diabetes educator follow up and a sick day plan
options.rationale: Sick day education addresses ketoacidosis triggered by intercurrent illness, whereas hers is triggered by deliberate omission, so the plan targets the wrong mechanism. Education alone has already failed across three previous admissions. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

explanation.summary: Deliberate insulin restriction for weight control is a disordered eating behaviour unique to type 1 diabetes and is easily missed because body weight is normal and the classic purging signs are absent. The clues are a rising glycated haemoglobin, repeated admissions with ketoacidosis, clinic non-attendance, and body checking with weight-related reasoning about insulin. It carries a substantially increased risk of retinopathy, nephropathy and early death, which makes it more dangerous than the numbers alone suggest. Effective management is joint: an eating disorder service for the body image and behavioural work, and the diabetes team to restart insulin gradually, since rapid normalisation of glucose can cause oedema, worsening retinopathy and neuropathic pain that reinforces avoidance.
key_points: Normal body weight does not exclude an eating disorder in type 1 diabetes
Rising glycated haemoglobin with repeated ketoacidosis and clinic avoidance is the pattern to recognise
Ask directly about omitting insulin to control weight, since it is rarely volunteered
Reintroduce insulin gradually within a joint eating disorder and diabetes plan
explanation.pearls: Ask every young person with type 1 diabetes and recurrent ketoacidosis whether they ever take less insulin than prescribed to influence their weight. A yes reframes the admission from poor adherence to an eating disorder, and the treatment becomes joint eating disorder and diabetes care with deliberately gradual insulin reintroduction.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders
InsideOut Institute: Eating disorders and diabetes

subtopic_detail: request to assess whether a man with early dementia can validly instruct a solicitor to change his will
stem: A solicitor asks whether a 79-year-old man with mild Alzheimer disease can change his will to favour the daughter who cares for him. He knows what a will does, names his three children and his approximate assets, gives a coherent reason, and accepts the others may be upset. No coercion is evident.

data_table.Cognition: Mini-Mental State Examination 23 out of 30 six months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the solicitor?

options.text: Advise that dementia itself invalidates his will
options.rationale: Capacity is decision specific and is not abolished by a diagnosis, and many people with mild dementia retain the ability to make a will. Treating the diagnosis as decisive would deny him a legal right he still holds. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent

options.text: Report that he shows the abilities required
options.rationale: The test is whether he understands the nature of the act, appreciates the extent of his property, recalls those who might expect to benefit, and is free of a disorder of mind that distorts the disposal, all of which he demonstrates in this interview. Recording his own words against each element is what makes the opinion useful if the will is later contested. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent

options.text: Recommend that his caring daughter decide instead
options.rationale: A substitute decision maker can never make a will on another person's behalf, and appointing the principal beneficiary to any decision making role here would create a clear conflict of interest. Substitute decision making applies to health, accommodation and financial decisions, not testamentary ones. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent

options.text: Suggest repeat cognitive testing before any opinion
options.rationale: Screening scores describe cognitive performance but do not determine capacity for a specific decision, and no cut-off on a brief test establishes or excludes testamentary capacity. Deferring for a number risks him losing the ability to make the will while waiting. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent

options.text: Decline because capacity is for the courts alone
options.rationale: A court makes the final legal determination, usually long after the person has died, but it does so largely on the strength of contemporaneous clinical assessment. Declining to assess removes the very evidence that protects his wishes from later challenge. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent

explanation.summary: Testamentary capacity is assessed against four established elements: understanding the nature and effect of making a will, knowing the extent of the property being disposed of, comprehending and appreciating the claims of those who might expect to benefit, and being free from any disorder of mind that perverts the disposal. It is decision specific and time specific, so neither a dementia diagnosis nor a screening score determines it. A man who explains his assets, names all potential beneficiaries, gives a coherent and non-delusional reason for favouring one, and anticipates the reaction of the others satisfies the test despite mild impairment. The clinician's task is to document the reasoning verbatim against each element and to comment on voluntariness, since undue influence is a separate ground for challenge.
key_points: Capacity is decision specific and is not abolished by a diagnosis or a screening score
The four elements concern the nature of the act, the property, the potential claimants and freedom from distorting disorder
A substitute decision maker cannot make a will for another person
Contemporaneous documentation in the person's own words is what withstands later challenge
explanation.pearls: Document the person's own words against each of the four testamentary elements rather than recording a cognitive score: a Mini-Mental State Examination result neither confers nor removes capacity, and it is the verbatim account of assets, beneficiaries and reasons that a court relies on years later.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on capacity and consent
Australian Law Reform Commission: Equality, capacity and disability

subtopic_detail: intense dread of giving birth in a first pregnancy with avoidance of antenatal care and no prior birth trauma
stem:
You are the psychiatrist in a perinatal clinic. A 28-year-old woman at 22 weeks in her first pregnancy is referred by her midwife because she has missed three appointments and becomes distressed whenever labour is mentioned.

She describes intrusive images of dying in childbirth, nightmares about being torn, and panic with palpitations and sweating when she passes the birth suite. She has been avoiding antenatal classes and the hospital tour, and says she has considered not attending for the birth at all. She wanted this pregnancy and is looking forward to the baby. She has no history of sexual assault, no previous birth, no previous trauma and no history of depression or an anxiety disorder, and she is not misusing substances. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 11 with a zero response on the self harm item, and she sleeps poorly only on nights when she has been thinking about labour.

data_table.Symptoms: Intrusive images of dying in childbirth, nightmares, panic on approaching the birth suite, avoidance of classes and appointments
data_table.Screening: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 11 with zero on the self harm item
data_table.History: First pregnancy, no prior trauma or assault, no previous psychiatric history, wanted pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe diazepam to be taken before antenatal visits and again during early labour
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines relieve anticipatory anxiety briefly but reinforce avoidance, and regular use late in pregnancy risks neonatal sedation and withdrawal. Using them as the plan would prevent the graded exposure that actually reduces the fear. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline

options.text: Advise that she request a planned caesarean section so that labour can be avoided altogether
options.rationale: Mode of birth is a decision for the woman with her obstetric team and caesarean birth is a legitimate outcome of that discussion, but recommending it now as the treatment for her fear removes the opportunity to reduce it. Women whose fear is addressed psychologically often choose vaginal birth and report better experiences either way. (Source: RANZCOG: Caesarean section on maternal request)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Caesarean section on maternal request

options.text: Offer structured psychological therapy for childbirth fear with a birth planning session
options.rationale: Severe fear of childbirth responds to a brief structured psychological intervention that combines cognitive work on catastrophic beliefs with graded exposure to the hospital environment, delivered alongside a midwife-led session that produces a written birth plan. This addresses the avoidance that is currently putting her antenatal care at risk while leaving her choice about mode of birth open. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline

options.text: Start sertraline given the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score and review in six weeks
options.rationale: A score of 11 is below the usual threshold prompting further assessment and her elevated items reflect anxiety about a specific situation rather than pervasive depression, with preserved interest in the pregnancy and the baby. An antidepressant may become appropriate if a depressive or generalised anxiety disorder emerges, but it is not the first response to a focal phobia. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline

options.text: Reassure her that anxiety about a first birth is normal and arrange midwife review at 34 weeks
options.rationale: Ordinary apprehension does not cause someone to miss three appointments, avoid all preparation and consider not presenting for the birth, so normalising it misses a disorder that is already affecting care. Waiting until 34 weeks leaves little time for a therapy that needs several sessions. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Severe fear of childbirth is distinguished from ordinary apprehension by avoidance that damages care: missed appointments, refusal of preparation, and contemplation of not attending for the birth. It occurs both in women with no obstetric history and in those with previous traumatic birth, and it predicts requests for caesarean birth, longer labour and postnatal traumatic stress symptoms. Treatment is psychological and relatively brief, combining cognitive work on catastrophic beliefs with graded exposure, and is most effective when paired with a midwifery session that produces a concrete written birth plan including pain relief preferences and a plan for regaining control. Mode of birth remains the woman's decision and is discussed after the fear has been treated, not instead of treating it.
key_points: Avoidance that disrupts antenatal care separates a phobic disorder from normal apprehension
Brief cognitive and exposure based therapy is first line, ideally started well before term
Pair psychological treatment with a midwife-led session that produces a written birth plan
Antidepressants and benzodiazepines are not the primary treatment for a focal childbirth phobia
explanation.pearls: Missed antenatal appointments are the sign that turns fear of childbirth into a treatable disorder rather than normal nerves. Refer for brief cognitive and exposure based therapy by the mid second trimester and pair it with a midwifery birth planning session, so there is time for several sessions before term.

sources.label: RANZCP: Perinatal mental health clinical practice guideline
RANZCOG: Caesarean section on maternal request
COPE: Australian perinatal mental health guideline

subtopic_detail: vivid formed visual hallucinations with full insight in an older adult with advanced macular degeneration
stem:
You are the doctor at a residential aged care facility. Staff ask you to review an 84-year-old woman who has been describing children in period costume standing at the end of her bed and patterned brickwork spreading across the wall.

She tells you calmly that she knows they are not really there, that they appear most in the late afternoon and last several minutes, and that she finds them curious rather than frightening. She has advanced age related macular degeneration with vision of 6/60 in both eyes after a recent further decline. She hears nothing unusual, has no delusions and no persecutory ideas, and she is oriented to place and person and gives a clear account of her day. There is no fluctuating attention, no tremor, no rigidity, no falls, no recent change in medication and no urinary symptoms, and her observations and screening bloods are unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: No tremor or rigidity, no postural instability, attention sustained through the interview, oriented to place and person
data_table.Vision: Visual acuity 6/60 bilaterally with advanced age related macular degeneration and recent further decline
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, renal function, calcium, thyroid function and urinalysis all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start risperidone 0.25 mg at night and review the frequency of the hallucinations in two weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do not reliably abolish these hallucinations and expose an older woman to falls, stroke and increased mortality for a symptom she is not distressed by. Their use would also be difficult to justify given she retains full insight. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the brain to exclude an occipital infarct or tumour
options.rationale: Structural imaging is indicated when hallucinations accompany focal neurological signs, headache, seizures or an abrupt change in conscious state, and none are present. Scanning an older person with a classical syndrome yields incidental findings more often than answers. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

options.text: Treat for delirium with a septic screen, medication review and regular orientation by staff
options.rationale: Delirium is the correct first thought for new hallucinations in an older person, but it requires disturbed attention and a fluctuating course, and her attention is sustained and her account coherent. The negative screening investigations and absence of new medications complete the case against it. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Explain the visual origin of the images, review her vision, and monitor with staff education
options.rationale: Formed visual hallucinations with retained insight and no other psychotic or cognitive features in someone with severe visual loss are generated by the deafferented visual cortex, and explanation itself is the main treatment because the distress comes mostly from fearing madness. Optimising remaining vision, improving lighting and environmental stimulation, and teaching staff to recognise the syndrome prevent unnecessary antipsychotic prescribing. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor for probable dementia with Lewy bodies and monitor closely
options.rationale: Dementia with Lewy bodies is the alternative cause of formed visual hallucinations in this age group, but it requires cognitive impairment and is supported by fluctuating attention, parkinsonism, falls or dream enactment, all of which are absent. Her cognition is intact and her insight is preserved, which is not the pattern of that disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

explanation.summary: Complex formed visual hallucinations occurring in a person with significant visual loss, with full insight and no other psychotic symptoms or cognitive decline, constitute Charles Bonnet syndrome. The mechanism is release activity in visual cortex deprived of input, and the images are characteristically vivid, detailed and often of people, faces, patterns or scenes. The main clinical task is recognition, because patients frequently conceal the symptom for fear of being thought mentally ill, and explanation alone relieves much of the distress. Management is conservative: optimise remaining vision, improve lighting and daytime stimulation, educate carers, and avoid antipsychotics, which carry substantial risk in older people and have little effect on these hallucinations.
key_points: Preserved insight with no other psychotic features distinguishes this from a psychotic disorder
Sustained attention and coherent account argue against delirium
Absent parkinsonism, fluctuation and cognitive decline argue against dementia with Lewy bodies
Explanation, vision optimisation and carer education replace antipsychotic prescribing
explanation.pearls: Ask any patient with severe visual loss whether they ever see things they know are not there, because most never volunteer it for fear of being thought mad. Vivid formed images with full insight and no cognitive decline is Charles Bonnet syndrome, and naming it to the patient and the aged care staff is more effective than any antipsychotic.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard
Vision Australia: Charles Bonnet syndrome information

subtopic_detail: depressive episodes recurring each winter with hypersomnia and carbohydrate craving that remit fully in spring
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who moved from Darwin to Hobart four years ago. Each year since, from late May, she has become flat, sleeps 10 to 11 hours and still feels unrefreshed, craves bread and sweet foods, gains about 5 kg, and withdraws from her netball team.

By early October she is back to her usual self, energetic and social, with the weight coming off without effort, and she stays well right through summer. This has now happened four winters in a row and has never happened at any other time of year. She works indoors in an office with no window. She denies elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or overspending at any time, and there is no alcohol or other substance misuse. Her thyroid function, full blood count, iron studies and vitamin D are all within normal limits, and she is currently five weeks into this year's episode with no suicidal ideation.

data_table.Symptom pattern: Four consecutive winters of low mood with hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and 5 kg weight gain, full remission each spring
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, full blood count, iron studies and vitamin D within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: Low mood with reactivity preserved, no suicidal ideation, no history of elevated mood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment for this episode?

options.text: Start lithium as a mood stabiliser given the regular recurrence of her mood episodes
options.rationale: Lithium is used for bipolar disorder and as augmentation in resistant depression, and its use here would require a history of elevated mood, which she clearly denies. Regularity of recurrence alone does not make a mood disorder bipolar. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Prescribe high dose oral vitamin D through winter and review her mood in eight weeks
options.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency is worth correcting when present, particularly in southern Australian winters, but her level is already normal and supplementation has not been shown to treat this pattern of depression. Choosing it would leave the episode untreated for another two months. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Begin bright light therapy each morning with structured behavioural activation alongside it
options.rationale: Daily morning exposure to a bright light source is an established first line treatment for depression with a seasonal pattern, with response usually apparent within one to two weeks, and it suits someone who works indoors without daylight. Pairing it with scheduled activity and re-engagement with her sport targets the withdrawal that maintains the episode. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy because the episodes have recurred for four consecutive years
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is reserved for severe depression with high risk features such as food refusal, psychosis or persistent suicidality, or for failure of multiple adequate treatments. A recurrent but moderate and fully remitting illness does not meet that threshold. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Advise watchful waiting until October, since her episodes have always resolved spontaneously
options.rationale: Predictable remission does not make four months of impairment each year acceptable, and untreated episodes carry occupational, social and suicide risk. The predictability is better used to plan treatment before the next episode starts. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

explanation.summary: A seasonal pattern is specified when depressive episodes occur at a characteristic time of year with full remission at another, across at least two consecutive years and with seasonal episodes substantially outnumbering non-seasonal ones. The atypical features of hypersomnia, increased appetite with carbohydrate craving and weight gain are typical of the winter pattern, and the presentation is more common at higher latitudes, which in Australia means Tasmania and southern Victoria. Bright light therapy given in the morning is first line, generally producing a response within one to two weeks, and is often combined with behavioural activation. Antidepressants and psychological therapy remain effective options, and because the timing is predictable, treatment can be started before the expected onset in subsequent years.
key_points: Diagnosis requires the seasonal relationship across at least two consecutive years with full remission between
Hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and weight gain are the characteristic atypical features
Morning bright light therapy is first line, with response usually within one to two weeks
Predictable timing allows preventive treatment started before the expected onset next year
explanation.pearls: Once a seasonal pattern is established over two or more years, use the predictability: start morning bright light therapy in the fortnight before the usual onset next autumn rather than waiting five weeks into the episode, which is when most patients present.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: patient request for a psychedelic assisted treatment after reading about its regulatory approval
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 46-year-old man with a 14 month depressive episode. He asks to be started on psilocybin assisted therapy, having read that it is now legally available in Australia for treatment resistant depression, and says he does not want to try another tablet.

His current episode has been treated with sertraline titrated to 200 mg daily for 10 weeks with partial response, then a switch to venlafaxine 225 mg daily for 9 weeks with no further improvement. He has had 12 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy. He has never had psychosis or mania, has no family history of bipolar disorder, drinks two standard drinks a week, and takes no other medication. He remains able to work part time and denies suicidal ideation. He asks you directly whether you can prescribe it for him at this appointment or whether he should buy it privately from an overseas supplier.

data_table.Treatment history: Sertraline 200 mg daily for 10 weeks with partial response, venlafaxine 225 mg daily for 9 weeks with no improvement, 12 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy
data_table.Risk: No suicidal ideation, no psychosis or mania, no family history of bipolar disorder
data_table.Substance use: Two standard drinks per week, no other substances

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to his request?

options.text: Prescribe psilocybin yourself today, since it is now approved for this indication in Australia
options.rationale: Access is restricted to psychiatrists who hold specific authorisation for this purpose and who deliver it within an approved protocol including preparation, supervised dosing and integration sessions. Prescribing outside that framework would breach the conditions under which access exists. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Access to psilocybin and MDMA)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Access to psilocybin and MDMA

options.text: Tell him that the treatment is unavailable in Australia and that overseas purchase is his only route
options.rationale: This is factually wrong, since a regulated pathway exists through authorised psychiatrists, and it would push a vulnerable patient toward an unregulated supply with no screening, no supervision and legal risk. Telling a patient something is unavailable when it is not damages trust as well as safety. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Access to psilocybin and MDMA)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Access to psilocybin and MDMA

options.text: Agree to supervise a session if he obtains the substance himself and brings it to the clinic
options.rationale: Supervising the use of an unregulated substance of unknown identity and purity provides none of the safeguards of an authorised program and exposes both patient and practitioner to serious risk. Willingness to supervise does not make an unlawful supply safe. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on therapeutic use of psychedelic substances)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on therapeutic use of psychedelic substances

options.text: Explain the authorised prescriber pathway and offer an evidence based next step meanwhile
options.rationale: The honest answer is that access exists but only through psychiatrists holding specific authorisation and within a structured protocol, and that referral to such a service takes time and involves cost and careful screening. Meanwhile he has not yet had augmentation, a third agent, or a trial of an established interventional treatment, so offering one of those keeps his depression treated while the referral proceeds. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on therapeutic use of psychedelic substances)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on therapeutic use of psychedelic substances

options.text: Decline the discussion and restate that only a third antidepressant trial is acceptable now
options.rationale: Refusing to engage with a reasonable question about an approved treatment leaves him to seek information elsewhere and makes unsupervised use more likely. Recommending another antidepressant is defensible, but it should follow the conversation rather than replace it. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on therapeutic use of psychedelic substances)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on therapeutic use of psychedelic substances

explanation.summary: Since mid 2023 psilocybin may be prescribed in Australia for treatment resistant depression, and MDMA for post traumatic stress disorder, but only by psychiatrists who hold authorised prescriber approval and who deliver the substance within a protocol of preparation, supervised dosing and integration. General prescribing, compounding at home and self sourced material all fall outside this framework. Screening excludes people with a personal or family history of psychosis or bipolar disorder because of the risk of precipitating a psychotic or manic episode, and serotonergic antidepressants usually need to be tapered before dosing. The appropriate clinical response is to explain the pathway accurately, refer if the patient wishes to pursue it, and in the meantime continue evidence based treatment, which for this man has not yet included augmentation or an interventional option.
key_points: Access is restricted to authorised prescribers working within an approved protocol
Screening excludes personal or family history of psychosis or bipolar disorder
Existing serotonergic antidepressants generally require tapering before dosing
Continue established treatment while any referral for this pathway is pursued
explanation.pearls: Answer the access question accurately rather than shutting it down: psilocybin for treatment resistant depression is lawful in Australia only through an authorised prescriber delivering preparation, supervised dosing and integration, and saying so while offering augmentation or an interventional option in the interim is what keeps a patient away from an overseas supplier.

subtopic_detail: loss of control over online gaming with withdrawal from school and sport over twelve months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old boy brought by his father, who is worried about the amount of time he spends gaming. Over the past 12 months his gaming has risen to eight or nine hours daily, mostly between 7 pm and 3 am.

He has quit the soccer team, stopped seeing friends in person, and his school attendance has fallen to about half the timetable, with grades dropping from mostly B to mostly D. He becomes verbally aggressive when the internet is switched off and has repeatedly promised to cut down and failed within days. He denies low mood when he is gaming but says everything else feels pointless, and he has no suicidal ideation on direct questioning. He eats irregularly, has lost 3 kg, is not using alcohol or other substances, and there is no history of trauma or bullying that either he or his father can identify.

data_table.Pattern: Eight to nine hours daily gaming mostly overnight for twelve months, repeated failed attempts to reduce, irritability when access is removed
data_table.Function: School attendance halved with falling grades, sport and in-person friendships abandoned, 3 kg weight loss
data_table.Mental state: No suicidal ideation, no substance use, denies low mood while gaming

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Assess for depression and other comorbidity, then refer for family based psychological therapy
options.rationale: Problem gaming of this severity is usually accompanied by depression, anxiety or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and treating a missed comorbidity changes the outcome more than addressing screen time alone. The intervention with the best support involves the family, since parents control access and the treatment plan has to include sleep, school re-engagement and graded reduction rather than abrupt confiscation. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents

options.text: Advise the father to remove the console and the router permanently from the house tonight
options.rationale: Sudden total removal commonly escalates aggression and can precipitate absconding or self harm in an adolescent whose only social contact is online. Graded reduction negotiated with the young person is both safer and more durable. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents

options.text: Start an antidepressant now, since withdrawal from activities indicates a depressive episode
options.rationale: Loss of interest in previously valued activities does suggest depression, but here it may be a consequence of the gaming pattern and the reversed sleep cycle rather than an independent disorder. Assessment should establish which is present before a medicine is started. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents

options.text: Reassure the father that heavy gaming is normal at this age and recommend a screen time contract
options.rationale: Many adolescents game heavily without harm, which is exactly why the diagnostic threshold rests on impaired control plus functional damage, and halved school attendance with abandoned sport and friendships crosses it. A contract alone has already failed in the repeated attempts to cut down. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents

options.text: Refer him to a residential drug and alcohol rehabilitation program for behavioural addiction
options.rationale: Residential programs are designed around substance withdrawal and are not the established pathway for this problem, and removing him from school and family would worsen the functional losses. Outpatient psychological work with the family is the appropriate level of care. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents

explanation.summary: Gaming disorder is defined by impaired control over gaming, increasing priority given to it over other interests and daily activities, and continuation despite negative consequences, with the pattern persisting for about 12 months and causing significant functional impairment. The threshold is functional harm rather than hours played, which is why halved school attendance, abandoned sport and lost in-person friendships matter more than the raw figure. Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, so assessment for depression, anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder comes first, along with sleep, since reversed sleep cycles both worsen and are worsened by overnight gaming. Management is psychological and family based, working toward graded reduction, restored sleep and school re-engagement, since abrupt total removal of access commonly escalates conflict without producing durable change.
key_points: Functional impairment, not hours played, defines the disorder
Screen for depression, anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder before attributing everything to gaming
Family based psychological therapy with graded reduction is the mainstay
Abrupt total removal of access commonly escalates aggression and risk
explanation.pearls: Ask what the gaming has cost rather than how many hours it takes: school attendance, sport and face to face friendships are the ledger that distinguishes a disorder from an ordinary adolescent hobby, and the first move is screening for depression and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder before any screen time plan.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on screen time and gaming in children and adolescents
RCH CPG: Adolescent mental health assessment

subtopic_detail: belief that a spouse has been replaced by an identical impostor in a man with fluctuating cognition
stem: A 76-year-old man has insisted for three months that his wife is an identical looking substitute, twice asking her to leave at night. His attention fluctuates from day to day, he has seen small animals for over a year, and he acts out dreams. He is slower and stooped with a mild left resting tremor.

data_table.Investigations: Screening bloods normal, no anticholinergic medication

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the misidentification?

options.text: Start haloperidol 0.5 mg nightly for the belief
options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics can provoke severe sensitivity reactions in this condition, with marked rigidity, immobility, autonomic instability and increased mortality, and haloperidol is the agent most associated with it. This is the single most dangerous choice in an older person with this constellation. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

options.text: Admit urgently for a delirium screen and fluids
options.rationale: Fluctuating attention genuinely raises delirium, and it would be the priority if this had developed over days with an identifiable precipitant, but the course here spans a year with a stable medication list and normal screening tests. Admitting him would remove the familiar environment that currently keeps him settled. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Advise his wife to show him wedding photographs
options.rationale: Direct confrontation of a fixed misidentification typically increases agitation and can escalate to aggression, and it places the person he does not recognise at the centre of the dispute. Practical strategies such as approaching from the front, announcing herself by voice, and stepping away and re-entering are more effective. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

options.text: Begin a cholinesterase inhibitor with a carer safety plan
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are the preferred first line for psychotic and cognitive symptoms in this disorder, with better evidence and far less risk than antipsychotics, and they often reduce hallucinations and misidentification over weeks. Coupling this with carer strategies for approach and reorientation, and an explicit plan for what his wife does if he asks her to leave at night, manages the risk while the medication takes effect. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people

options.text: Commence levodopa for the parkinsonian features
options.rationale: Dopaminergic therapy may be needed for disabling motor symptoms but characteristically worsens hallucinations and delusions in this condition, so it is the wrong lever when psychosis is the presenting problem. If it becomes necessary, it is introduced cautiously at the lowest effective dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Parkinson disease)

explanation.summary: The belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an identical impostor is a delusional misidentification syndrome, and in an older person it most often occurs within dementia with Lewy bodies. The supporting features here are the full core set: fluctuating cognition and attention, recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, dream enactment behaviour, and spontaneous parkinsonism. Antipsychotics carry a serious sensitivity risk in this disorder, with rigidity, immobility, autonomic instability and increased mortality, and typical agents are the most hazardous. Cholinesterase inhibitors are therefore first line for the neuropsychiatric symptoms, combined with carer strategies and an explicit safety plan, with quetiapine at low dose reserved for severe distress or risk that does not respond.
key_points: Misidentification of a spouse in an older person points to a neurodegenerative rather than primary psychotic cause
Fluctuation, visual hallucinations, dream enactment and parkinsonism form the core diagnostic cluster
Antipsychotic sensitivity in this disorder can be severe and is worst with typical agents
Cholinesterase inhibitors plus carer strategies are first line for the psychotic symptoms
explanation.pearls: Before prescribing any antipsychotic to an older person with new delusions, ask the partner whether he acts out his dreams and whether his alertness varies from day to day. Dream enactment with fluctuation and visual hallucinations signals antipsychotic sensitivity, and a cholinesterase inhibitor with carer strategies replaces the prescription you were about to write.
