sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on antipsychotic use in older people
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

subtopic_detail: colleague smelling of alcohol before a ward round after repeated concerns raised by nursing staff
stem: Your consultant smells strongly of alcohol before the morning ward round, has a tremor and slurs words. He is due to lead a round on 18 inpatients, three detained with leave pending. No other consultant is on the ward.

data_table.Corroboration: Two nurses report the same twice last week
data_table.Response to approach: Denies drinking, irritable, declines to step back

lead_in: What should you do?

options.text: Say nothing now and raise it privately after the round
options.rationale: Waiting until after the round allows an impaired practitioner to make detention and leave decisions for 18 patients, which is exactly the harm the reporting framework exists to prevent. A conversation after the fact cannot undo decisions already made. (Source: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

options.text: Escalate to the on call senior to cover the round, then notify
options.rationale: The immediate patient safety step is to ensure the round is conducted by someone fit to practise, which means escalating now to the medical administrator or on call senior rather than negotiating with the colleague. Practising while intoxicated by alcohol meets the threshold for notifiable conduct, so a notification follows, and the two obligations run in parallel rather than as alternatives. (Source: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

options.text: Ask the nurses to document and file an incident report
options.rationale: Documentation matters, but an incident report filed at the end of the week does not remove an impaired doctor from patient care this morning. Delegating the response to nursing staff also shifts a responsibility that is personally yours once you hold a reasonable belief. (Source: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

options.text: Lead the round yourself and keep it between you
options.rationale: Covering for a colleague protects today's patients but conceals a pattern that has already been observed twice by others and leaves him untreated and still rostered. Informal accommodation of impairment is the commonest way these situations continue for years. (Source: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

options.text: Arrange a blood alcohol level and act on the result
options.rationale: You have no authority to require testing of a colleague, and the obligation to act is triggered by a reasonable belief formed on observation rather than by laboratory proof. Insisting on a test would delay the response while the round proceeds. (Source: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications)
source_refs: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications

explanation.summary: Registered health practitioners in Australia have a mandatory obligation to notify when they form a reasonable belief that another practitioner has practised while intoxicated by alcohol or drugs, engaged in sexual misconduct, placed the public at substantial risk through an impairment, or departed significantly from accepted standards. A reasonable belief rests on direct observation and corroborating information rather than proof, so no test result is required before acting. Two obligations operate at once: securing immediate patient safety by escalating so that someone fit to practise covers the clinical work, and making the notification. Treating practitioners have modified obligations in most jurisdictions, which is designed to encourage doctors to seek help for their own health, and support services for practitioners with substance use problems exist alongside the regulatory pathway.
key_points: Practising while intoxicated by alcohol is notifiable conduct, not a matter for private accommodation
A reasonable belief formed on observation is the trigger; laboratory confirmation is not required
Secure immediate patient safety by escalating for cover, then notify; the steps run in parallel
Practitioner health services support the colleague alongside the regulatory process
explanation.pearls: Two things happen at once when a colleague is impaired at work: someone fit to practise must take over the clinical load right now, and the notification follows. Waiting for a blood alcohol level or for the end of the round converts a reasonable belief into a delayed one while patients are still being seen.

sources.label: Ahpra and the Medical Board of Australia: Guidelines for mandatory notifications
Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice, a code of conduct

subtopic_detail: early script requests and a negative urine screen in a young adult prescribed stimulant medication
stem:
You are the psychiatrist reviewing a 23-year-old man diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder 18 months ago and prescribed dexamfetamine. He has requested early replacement scripts three times in five months, citing a lost bottle, a spilled bottle and a bag stolen at a music festival.

He reports that the medication works well and that he has no side effects. His flatmate telephoned the clinic last month to ask whether the tablets could be bought. A urine drug screen collected at the last visit, two days after he said he had taken his morning dose, detected no amphetamine. His weight is stable, his blood pressure is normal, and he is in his third year of an engineering degree with passing grades. He appears well, is not agitated, and there are no signs of intoxication or withdrawal, no injection marks and no reported alcohol or other substance use.

data_table.Prescribing history: Three early replacement script requests in five months with differing explanations
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative for amphetamine two days after a reported dose, weight stable
data_table.Collateral: Flatmate telephoned the clinic asking whether the tablets could be purchased

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Issue the replacement script and arrange a pharmacy owed-medication record for future losses
options.rationale: Continuing to replace without addressing the negative screen ignores evidence that the medication is not reaching the patient, and an administrative record does not alter diversion. Prescribing on the same pattern is what allows it to continue. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

options.text: Report him to police for suspected supply and cease all prescribing without further discussion
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation without discussion abandons a patient who may have a genuine disorder and severs the relationship in which the problem can actually be addressed. Suspicion of diversion is managed clinically and through the prescription monitoring system, not by an unsupported criminal allegation. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

options.text: Double the dose, on the basis that the negative screen indicates inadequate absorption of the drug
options.rationale: A negative screen two days after a reported dose points to the medication not being taken rather than to a pharmacokinetic problem, and dexamfetamine is reliably detectable in urine for one to three days after ingestion. Increasing the supply would place more of a diverted drug in circulation. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

options.text: Check the real time prescription monitoring system, discuss the findings openly, and revise the plan
options.rationale: The monitoring system shows whether other prescribers and pharmacies are involved and converts suspicion into fact before any decision is made, and the conversation that follows is what preserves the therapeutic relationship. Where the findings support diversion, the plan moves toward staged supply, more frequent review, or a switch to a non-stimulant agent. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

options.text: Switch immediately to atomoxetine without discussing the screen result or the script requests
options.rationale: A non-stimulant agent is a reasonable destination and removes the diversion risk, but changing treatment without naming the reason denies the patient the chance to explain and leaves the underlying situation unexamined. The conversation has to precede the switch. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

explanation.summary: Repeated early script requests with varying explanations, a third party asking to buy the medication, and a urine screen negative for the prescribed stimulant together suggest diversion rather than a dosing problem. Real time prescription monitoring, available across Australian jurisdictions, establishes whether other prescribers or pharmacies are supplying the same drug and turns a suspicion into documented fact before any decision is made. The clinical response is to discuss the findings openly, since a defensible plan requires the patient's account, and then to revise prescribing toward staged or weekly dispensing, more frequent review, or a non-stimulant agent such as atomoxetine or guanfacine. Abrupt cessation without discussion and continued unexamined prescribing are both failures, in opposite directions.
key_points: A urine screen negative for the prescribed stimulant is strong evidence the drug is not being taken
Real time prescription monitoring establishes multiple prescriber or pharmacy involvement
Discuss the findings with the patient before changing or ceasing treatment
Staged supply, closer review, or a non-stimulant agent are the usual revisions to the plan
explanation.pearls: A urine drug screen that is negative for the very stimulant you prescribed, taken within two days of a reported dose, is the finding that should stop the next script: check real time prescription monitoring first, then have the conversation, then move to staged supply or a non-stimulant agent.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic, Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

subtopic_detail: severe irritability and despair confined to the week before menstruation with complete resolution by day three
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33-year-old woman who describes becoming, in her words, a different person for about six days before each period. She is irritable to the point of shouting at her children, feels hopeless, cannot concentrate at work, and has cancelled social plans repeatedly.

By the third day of bleeding she feels entirely well again and stays well for the rest of the month. She has kept a daily symptom chart for three consecutive cycles at her previous doctor's suggestion, and it shows the symptoms confined to the luteal phase with symptom free scores from day three through to day 18 in every cycle. Her thyroid function and full blood count are normal. She has never had a depressive episode outside this pattern, drinks alcohol rarely, does not use contraception and does not plan a pregnancy this year, and there is no suicidal ideation now or during the symptomatic phase.

data_table.Symptom chart: Three consecutive cycles charted with symptoms confined to the six days before menstruation and complete resolution by day three of bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits
data_table.History: No depressive episodes outside the luteal phase, no suicidal ideation, no pregnancy planned this year

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe calcium and vitamin B6 supplementation and review the charts after three cycles
options.rationale: Calcium supplementation has modest evidence for milder premenstrual symptoms and vitamin B6 is widely used, so both are reasonable adjuncts for mild cases. Neither matches the effect size of the first line pharmacological option in a woman whose symptoms are severe enough to disrupt work and parenting. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Refer for a gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist with added back hormonal therapy
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression is highly effective and is used when first and second line treatments fail, but it induces a menopausal state requiring add-back therapy and bone monitoring. It is a specialist option reserved for refractory disease, not a starting point. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: Start a serotonergic antidepressant given either continuously or in the luteal phase only
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first line for this disorder and are unusual in working within a day or two rather than over weeks, which is what makes luteal phase dosing from ovulation until menstruation a genuine alternative to continuous treatment. The choice between the two schedules is made with the woman, weighing cycle predictability and tolerability against the simplicity of taking it every day. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Begin lithium at a low dose, treating this as a rapid cycling presentation of a bipolar disorder
options.rationale: Rapid cycling requires four or more mood episodes in a year meeting full criteria for depressive, manic or hypomanic episodes, and she has no elevated mood at any point. Symptoms tied to the luteal phase and resolving with menstruation are not mood episodes in that sense. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Advise aerobic exercise and sleep hygiene alone, with review only if the symptoms worsen further
options.rationale: Exercise and sleep measures help and should be part of the plan, but offered alone they are inadequate for symptoms that are already causing her to shout at her children and cancel commitments each month. Withholding effective treatment until things worsen is not a defensible threshold. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is diagnosed from prospective daily symptom ratings across at least two cycles showing affective and physical symptoms confined to the final week before menstruation, improving within a few days of onset of bleeding and absent in the week after. Retrospective recall is unreliable, which is why the charting requirement is part of the diagnosis rather than an optional extra. Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first line and act within a day or two in this condition, so they can be taken continuously or only from ovulation until menstruation begins, with similar efficacy. Combined hormonal contraception taken continuously is an alternative, particularly when contraception is also wanted, and ovarian suppression with add-back therapy is reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: Prospective daily charting over at least two cycles is required for the diagnosis
Symptoms must resolve within days of menstruation starting and be absent mid cycle
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors work within days here, allowing luteal phase only dosing
Ovarian suppression with add-back therapy is reserved for refractory disease
explanation.pearls: The rapid onset of benefit is what makes this disorder different from depression: a serotonin reuptake inhibitor works within a day or two, so it can be taken only from ovulation until bleeding starts, which many women prefer to daily dosing for a problem confined to one week in four.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic, Premenstrual dysphoric disorder

subtopic_detail: escalating self directed dose increases of a gabapentinoid with euphoria and early script exhaustion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old man who was prescribed pregabalin 150 mg twice daily for neuropathic pain after a work injury nine months ago. He asks for an early script for the third month running.

He tells you that he has been taking up to 1200 mg a day because the usual dose stopped helping, and that at the higher doses he feels relaxed and euphoric for a few hours. He has bought extra capsules from a friend twice. He drinks four to six standard drinks on most evenings, which he says helps the effect last. He is not injecting anything, has no opioid prescription, and denies stimulant use. His original pain has largely settled and his back examination today is normal, with no new neurological signs. He says he feels sweaty and anxious if he goes a day without taking any.

data_table.Medication use: Prescribed 300 mg daily, taking up to 1200 mg daily, purchasing additional capsules, early script requests three months running
data_table.Other substance use: Four to six standard drinks most evenings, no opioids, no injecting drug use
data_table.Examination: Back examination normal with no new neurological signs, original neuropathic pain largely resolved

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Plan a structured taper with staged dispensing, and address the alcohol use at the same time
options.rationale: He has developed tolerance, dose escalation, craving and autonomic symptoms on missed doses, so abrupt cessation risks a withdrawal syndrome while unchanged prescribing sustains the problem, leaving a gradual planned reduction as the safe route. Staged dispensing limits the quantity on hand, and the concurrent alcohol use must be addressed because the combination markedly increases the risk of respiratory depression and fatal overdose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse

options.text: Stop the pregabalin immediately today and provide a letter explaining the decision to him
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal from high dose gabapentinoids can produce agitation, insomnia, sweating, tachycardia and occasionally seizures, particularly alongside heavy alcohol use. Sudden cessation also predictably drives purchase from unregulated sources. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse

options.text: Increase the prescribed dose to 600 mg twice daily so that he stops buying from other sources
options.rationale: Prescribing to match a self escalated dose legitimises tolerance driven escalation and raises the overdose risk, especially with nightly alcohol. Supply from other sources typically continues rather than stopping. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse

options.text: Switch him to a slow release opioid to manage the pain and avoid a withdrawal reaction
options.rationale: His pain has largely resolved and there is no indication for an opioid, which would add a second dependence-forming drug and compound the respiratory depression risk already created by alcohol. Substituting one problematic agent for a more dangerous one is not harm reduction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic, Chronic non-cancer pain)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic, Chronic non-cancer pain

options.text: Refer to a pain clinic and continue the current prescription unchanged until he is seen there
options.rationale: Multidisciplinary pain input is valuable, but waiting lists run to months and the prescribing problem is active now, with purchasing from a friend and daily heavy alcohol use. Continuing unchanged defers the decision that this consultation exists to make. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse

explanation.summary: Pregabalin misuse has risen substantially in Australia and is characterised by self directed dose escalation, euphoria at supratherapeutic doses, sourcing from outside the prescription, and withdrawal symptoms on missed doses. The risk is greatest in combination with alcohol, opioids or benzodiazepines, since the combination is strongly associated with fatal respiratory depression, and pregabalin now features frequently in Australian overdose deaths. Abrupt cessation risks a withdrawal syndrome that can include seizures, so management is a planned taper with staged dispensing, review of the original indication, and concurrent treatment of the alcohol use. Real time prescription monitoring supports the plan by identifying additional prescribers.
key_points: Dose escalation, euphoria and sourcing outside the prescription define gabapentinoid misuse
Combination with alcohol or opioids drives the fatal respiratory depression risk
Abrupt cessation can precipitate withdrawal including seizures, so taper rather than stop
Staged dispensing and prescription monitoring support the taper plan
explanation.pearls: Ask what the patient drinks in the evening before deciding what to do about a gabapentinoid script: pregabalin with nightly alcohol is the combination that turns up in Australian overdose deaths, and the plan is a structured taper with staged dispensing plus treatment of the alcohol, never an abrupt stop.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine, Pregabalin misuse
Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic, Chronic non-cancer pain

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in a patient stabilised on clozapine
stem: A 47-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 400 mg nightly for five years; his level was 480 microg/L (target 350-600). He has smoked 25 cigarettes daily for 30 years and wants to quit.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy plan?

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg nightly titrated to 75 mg, with clozapine continued unchanged
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is second-line for smoking cessation and is not first-line in Australia. Adding a sedating tricyclic to clozapine adds anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension risk, and QT prolongation, none of which are needed given first-line agents are available. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg twice daily for twelve weeks, with clozapine continued unchanged
options.rationale: Bupropion lowers seizure threshold, an already relevant risk on clozapine (which reduces seizure threshold in a dose-dependent way), and is a poor first-line choice in this specific patient. Failing to anticipate the CYP1A2 de-induction effect on clozapine levels risks toxicity. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: clozapine)

options.text: Varenicline for twelve weeks, monitoring clozapine levels and reducing clozapine 25 percent at quit date
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective monotherapy for smoking cessation. Tobacco smoke induces CYP1A2 and increases clozapine clearance; cessation causes clozapine levels to rise by roughly 50%, risking toxicity, so a dose reduction of about 25% at the quit date with plasma level monitoring is standard. Varenicline itself is not contraindicated in stable schizophrenia. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: clozapine)

options.text: Combination nicotine replacement with patch and lozenges, with clozapine unchanged
options.rationale: Combination NRT is a reasonable second-line, but it does not remove the need to anticipate rising clozapine levels once he actually stops smoking (nicotine itself does not induce CYP1A2 - the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in smoke do). Failing to reduce clozapine at quit day risks toxicity. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: clozapine)

options.text: Abrupt cessation with peer support only, avoiding all cessation pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation without pharmacotherapy has the lowest quit rate at 12 months. Refusing pharmacotherapy in patients with severe mental illness is contrary to the RACGP smoking cessation guideline. Clozapine is not itself a contraindication to any Australian first-line smoking cessation drug. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: Smoking rates among people with schizophrenia are two to three times the general population and drive much of the mortality gap. First-line smoking cessation pharmacotherapies in Australia are varenicline (most effective monotherapy), combination NRT (patch plus fast-acting), and bupropion. Bupropion is avoided when seizure risk is heightened, including on clozapine. Varenicline was previously flagged for neuropsychiatric concerns; the EAGLES trial found no increased risk in stable severe mental illness, and it is now used routinely in this group. Critically, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke induce CYP1A2, the primary metaboliser of clozapine and olanzapine; smoking cessation de-induces CYP1A2 over 1-4 weeks, raising clozapine levels by around 50% and risking toxicity (sedation, hypersalivation, seizures, myocarditis). A pre-emptive 25% clozapine dose reduction at the quit date with plasma level monitoring is standard.
key_points: Varenicline is first-line monotherapy; EAGLES trial supports safety in stable severe mental illness.
Bupropion lowers seizure threshold; a poor choice alongside clozapine.
Tobacco smoke (not nicotine) induces CYP1A2; smoking cessation raises clozapine levels ~50%.
Reduce clozapine dose by about 25% at quit date and monitor plasma levels.
Combination NRT (patch plus lozenge/gum) is more effective than either alone.
explanation.pearls: When a smoker on clozapine stops smoking, expect the plasma level to rise about 50% over one to four weeks - drop the clozapine dose by around 25% on quit day and repeat the level at two and four weeks.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnosis and stimulant initiation in the context of anxiety and driving
stem: A 28-year-old software developer has lifelong inattention, disorganisation and lateness, worse since starting full-time work. School reports from age 8 document the same. He has moderate generalised anxiety disorder (GAD-7 12) predating the worsening.

data_table.Assessment: DIVA-5 meets combined presentation; electrocardiogram QTc 410 ms; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment plan?

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg daily, avoiding stimulants because of his anxiety and driving
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is second-line unless stimulants are contraindicated. Anxiety and long-distance driving are not stimulant contraindications; treated ADHD improves rather than worsens driving safety and stimulant-related anxiety worsening is often manageable with dose titration. (Source: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based)
source_refs: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based

options.text: Immediate release methylphenidate 5 mg twice daily, with cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Australian ADHD guidelines recommend a stimulant as first-line for adult ADHD without a contraindication (uncontrolled hypertension, arrhythmia, active substance use disorder). Methylphenidate at low dose with fortnightly titration allows monitoring of anxiety, cardiovascular and sleep effects. Concurrent CBT addresses the GAD without a benzodiazepine. (Source: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based)
source_refs: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg twice daily, deferring ADHD treatment until the anxiety settles
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not first-line for GAD, carry dependence and cognitive impairment risks, and worsen inattention. Deferring ADHD treatment indefinitely while adding a benzodiazepine is harmful. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: anxiety disorders)

options.text: Bupropion extended release 150 mg daily, titrated to 300 mg daily
options.rationale: Bupropion has some off-label evidence in adult ADHD but is not a first-line agent under Australian guidance and its noradrenergic activity typically worsens anxiety rather than treating it. (Source: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based)
source_refs: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based

options.text: Three-month trial of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy before any pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: MBCT alone has weaker evidence than pharmacotherapy for moderate adult ADHD. Deferring pharmacotherapy for three months when both ADHD and moderate GAD are functionally impairing is not aligned with Australian evidence-based guidance. (Source: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based)
source_refs: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based

explanation.summary: The Australian ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline (AADPA, 2022) endorses stimulants (methylphenidate or dexamfetamine/lisdexamfetamine) as first-line pharmacotherapy for adult ADHD without contraindication. Common contraindications are uncontrolled cardiovascular disease, established arrhythmia, active psychotic illness and current substance use disorder. Comorbid anxiety is common and is not itself a contraindication; stimulant treatment can improve or worsen anxiety and needs monitoring during titration. Non-stimulant options (atomoxetine, guanfacine XR) are second line for stimulant failure or intolerance. CBT for comorbid GAD or depression is added rather than substituted. Treated ADHD reduces motor vehicle crash risk; the driving risk in adults with untreated ADHD is roughly double the general population.
key_points: Stimulants (methylphenidate, dexamfetamine, lisdexamfetamine) are first-line for adult ADHD.
Comorbid anxiety is not a stimulant contraindication; monitor during titration.
Treated ADHD improves rather than worsens driving safety.
Atomoxetine and guanfacine XR are second-line, especially with active substance use or contraindication.
Screen for cardiovascular risk (BP, personal or family arrhythmia/sudden death) before starting.
explanation.pearls: In adult ADHD with comorbid GAD, start immediate release methylphenidate at 5 mg twice daily and titrate every 1-2 weeks; add CBT for the anxiety - benzodiazepines and non-stimulants are second line.

sources.label: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based

subtopic_detail: Catatonia recognition and lorazepam challenge in a mixed presentation
stem: A 38-year-old woman on olanzapine 20 mg nightly for schizoaffective disorder was found mute and immobile two days ago. She does not speak or follow commands. An arm raised above her head stays there a minute, with grimacing and echolalia.

data_table.Investigations: Brain imaging, cerebrospinal fluid and electrolytes normal; creatine kinase 220 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase olanzapine to 30 mg nightly, adding haloperidol 5 mg as needed
options.rationale: Adding a further antipsychotic to a catatonic patient can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome, especially in the setting of an already elevated creatine kinase. First-line treatment of catatonia is benzodiazepine, not more antipsychotic. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guideline)

options.text: Amantadine 100 mg twice daily as first line pharmacological therapy
options.rationale: Amantadine and memantine are third-line adjuncts for catatonia after benzodiazepine failure and ECT decision. Using it as first line is contrary to Australian and international guidance. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guideline)

options.text: Emergency electroconvulsive therapy without a benzodiazepine trial
options.rationale: ECT is second-line for uncomplicated catatonia after a lorazepam trial and first-line only for malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis). Standard practice is to trial a benzodiazepine first; ECT is appropriate if the patient fails 24-72 hours of adequate lorazepam. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guideline)

options.text: Lorazepam 2 mg intramuscularly, reassessed at 30 minutes, then 6 to 24 mg daily
options.rationale: A positive lorazepam challenge (>=50% reduction in catatonic signs within an hour) is diagnostic and therapeutic. Standard care is subsequent lorazepam 6-24 mg daily in divided doses, with ECT reserved for malignant features or lorazepam failure at 72 hours. Antipsychotic dose adjustment is usually deferred until catatonia has cleared. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guideline)

options.text: Intravenous midazolam 5 mg as the challenge, repeated every 30 minutes
options.rationale: Midazolam onset is faster but its short half-life makes it unsuitable for both diagnostic and therapeutic use in catatonia. The lorazepam challenge is the standardised test, and lorazepam is the therapeutic agent. Escalating midazolam risks respiratory depression without diagnostic clarity. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guideline)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is under-recognised in general medical and psychiatric wards and is commonly triggered by mood or psychotic disorders (about 50%), general medical disease (autoimmune encephalitis, systemic lupus, sepsis, metabolic derangement) and medication effects. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale screens 14 signs (three positive features are enough to justify a challenge). The diagnostic and therapeutic gold standard is a lorazepam challenge (usually 2 mg IM or IV, reassessed at 30-60 minutes); a 50% or greater reduction in signs supports the diagnosis and is followed by 6-24 mg per day of lorazepam in divided doses. ECT is second-line for uncomplicated catatonia and first-line for malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis). Antipsychotic escalation risks precipitating NMS and is generally avoided until catatonia has cleared.
key_points: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: 3 or more of 14 screening signs supports diagnosis.
First-line treatment is lorazepam challenge, then 6-24 mg/day in divided doses.
Malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis) is an ECT-first indication.
Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and are usually deferred until clearance.
Amantadine and memantine are third-line adjuncts.
explanation.pearls: A lorazepam challenge of 2 mg IM producing at least 50% reduction in Bush-Francis signs within an hour is both diagnostic and therapeutic - escalate to 6-24 mg/day in divided doses before considering ECT.

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome differentiation
stem: A 42-year-old woman has 8 hours of tremor, agitation and confusion. She takes sertraline 200 mg daily, started tranylcypromine 9 days ago and took tramadol 50 mg 12 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 178/98 mmHg, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Sustained ankle clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds, tone increased not rigid
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 380 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Phenytoin 20 mg/kg with whole body ice pack cooling to 37 degrees C
options.rationale: There is no witnessed seizure and no epileptiform discharge; the clonus is myoclonic and reflex-driven, not epileptic. Whole-body ice pack cooling can trigger dangerous shivering; targeted cooling with active surface cooling and benzodiazepine sedation is the standard approach. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: serotonin toxicity)

options.text: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg eight-hourly with dantrolene, continuing sertraline
options.rationale: Bromocriptine and dantrolene are treatments for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not serotonin syndrome. The clinical features (clonus, hyperreflexia, dilated pupils, non-rigid hypertonia) point to serotonin syndrome. Continuing the offending serotonergic drug would worsen the clinical picture. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: serotonin toxicity)

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg, with sertraline held 24 hours only
options.rationale: Antipsychotics may worsen thermodysregulation and add anticholinergic burden. Restarting sertraline within 24 hours re-exposes the patient to the offending combination. Cessation of all serotonergic drugs and specific supportive treatment is required. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: serotonin toxicity)

options.text: Stop serotonergic drugs, give fluids and benzodiazepines, then cyproheptadine 12 mg
options.rationale: The lower-limb-dominant clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, moist skin and hyperactive bowel sounds distinguish this from NMS (lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, diaphoresis but no clonus, normal pupils). MAOI + SSRI + tramadol is a classic serotonin syndrome trigger. Treatment is drug cessation, benzodiazepine sedation, active cooling, and cyproheptadine as a serotonin 5HT2A antagonist. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: serotonin toxicity)

options.text: Oral olanzapine 20 mg and transfer to a psychiatric unit overnight
options.rationale: This is a medical emergency and requires management in an appropriately monitored medical environment, not on a psychiatric ward. Antipsychotics do not treat serotonin syndrome and olanzapine adds antihistaminergic and metabolic burden that will not help. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: serotonin toxicity)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome (serotonin toxicity) develops within hours of a serotonergic combination or dose increase. Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria pivot on spontaneous or inducible clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, and hyperactive bowel sounds - typically with mydriasis. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days after antipsychotic exposure, features lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, altered mental state, autonomic instability, very high creatine kinase (often over 1000) and normal pupils. Management of serotonin syndrome is cessation of the trigger, IV fluids, benzodiazepine sedation, active surface cooling and, for moderate-to-severe cases, cyproheptadine 12 mg loading then 2 mg every two hours. Dantrolene and bromocriptine are the NMS-directed agents and are not used in serotonin toxicity.
key_points: Serotonin syndrome: clonus (esp. lower limb), hyperreflexia, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds, moist skin.
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, mental state change, autonomic instability, CK often > 1000.
MAOI + SSRI, SSRI + tramadol/linezolid, SSRI + triptan are classic serotonin syndrome triggers.
Treatment: stop trigger, fluids, benzodiazepines, active cooling; cyproheptadine for moderate/severe.
Bromocriptine and dantrolene treat NMS, NOT serotonin syndrome.
explanation.pearls: Sustained ankle clonus with mydriasis and hyperactive bowel sounds within hours of an MAOI-SSRI or SSRI-tramadol overlap is serotonin syndrome - give benzodiazepines, cool actively, and load cyproheptadine 12 mg then 2 mg every 2 hours.

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal with high seizure risk and CIWA-vs-fixed regimen choice
stem: A 54-year-old man drinks 40 standard drinks daily, last drink 30 hours ago. He has had a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure. Symptom-triggered dosing failed at a detoxification two years ago, progressing to delirium tremens.

data_table.Investigations: Sodium 133 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.1)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Symptom-triggered diazepam on the ward, electrolyte replacement and haloperidol
options.rationale: Prior symptom-triggered dosing failed for this patient and produced delirium tremens. With active seizure history plus current severe withdrawal, RANZCP guidance recommends a fixed-schedule diazepam loading regimen (or combination with symptom-triggered top-ups) in a high-observation environment. Haloperidol lowers seizure threshold and should be avoided as first-line. (Source: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline

options.text: Phenytoin 20 mg/kg, fluid restriction and as needed oral oxazepam 30 mg
options.rationale: Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures; benzodiazepines are the effective prophylaxis. Fluid restriction is inappropriate as the hyponatraemia is dilutional and may worsen with fluid restriction; correcting hypovolaemia and electrolytes safely is more appropriate. Oxazepam does not accumulate and is preferred in hepatic failure, but is under-dosing for a severe presentation. (Source: eTG Complete Addiction: alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Fixed diazepam 20 mg orally two-hourly until CIWA-Ar below 10, in high dependency
options.rationale: Prior seizures during withdrawal plus current severe withdrawal (CIWA 22) plus recent seizure today classify this as very high risk. RANZCP endorses fixed diazepam loading (20 mg every two hours until CIWA <10 or sedation) in a HDU setting. Magnesium replacement below 0.7 mmol/L is standard because low magnesium prolongs withdrawal and worsens QT. Parenteral thiamine at 300 mg three times daily prevents Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg, then 10 mg daily through withdrawal
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do not treat the underlying GABA-A receptor down-regulation of alcohol withdrawal and can lower seizure threshold. They are reserved for persistent psychotic symptoms after adequate benzodiazepine loading. Olanzapine does not substitute for a benzodiazepine load. (Source: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline

options.text: Acamprosate and naltrexone now, with hourly CIWA-Ar on the ward
options.rationale: Acamprosate and naltrexone are relapse prevention agents started after withdrawal is complete, not during acute withdrawal. Naltrexone specifically requires opioid abstinence and precipitates withdrawal if opioids present. Neither treats seizures or delirium tremens. (Source: eTG Complete Addiction: alcohol withdrawal)

explanation.summary: Acute alcohol withdrawal ranges from mild autonomic symptoms to delirium tremens (fever, autonomic instability, confusion, hallucinations, mortality up to 5% untreated). Prior withdrawal seizures and prior delirium tremens predict recurrence and drive management toward fixed-schedule benzodiazepine loading in a monitored setting. Diazepam has a long half-life and provides smoother taper; oxazepam is preferred in hepatic failure. Magnesium below 0.7 mmol/L is replaced because it prolongs withdrawal, increases seizure risk, and worsens QT prolongation. High-dose parenteral thiamine (300 mg three times daily for 3-5 days) prevents Wernicke encephalopathy - given IV or IM before any glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke. Antipsychotics are second-line, reserved for persistent psychosis after adequate sedation.
key_points: Fixed-schedule diazepam loading is preferred over symptom-triggered dosing when prior seizure or DT history.
Diazepam preferred for long half-life; oxazepam in hepatic failure.
Replace magnesium below 0.7 mmol/L to reduce seizure risk and prevent QT prolongation.
Parenteral thiamine 300 mg TDS for 3-5 days before any glucose to prevent Wernicke.
Naltrexone and acamprosate are relapse prevention agents started after withdrawal, not during.
explanation.pearls: Fixed diazepam load 20 mg every two hours until CIWA < 10 or sedation is the standard for severe alcohol withdrawal with a prior seizure history - magnesium replacement below 0.7 mmol/L and parenteral thiamine 300 mg TDS for 3-5 days round out the safe protocol.

sources.label: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Gamma-hydroxybutyrate withdrawal with autonomic instability and delirium
stem: A ventilated 26-year-old man is agitated, diaphoretic and confused over 12 hours. His partner discloses 14 months of 1,4-butanediol use every 2 hours, last dose 22 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 195/108 mmHg, temperature 39.1 degrees C
data_table.Sedation: Diazepam 30 mg plus lorazepam 4 mg intravenously, transient effect only
data_table.Investigations: CT brain and septic screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Propofol and dexmedetomidine infusions with no further benzodiazepine
options.rationale: Dexmedetomidine and propofol control autonomic and agitation symptoms but do not treat the underlying GABA receptor deficit and permit breakthrough seizures and cardiovascular instability on weaning. They are adjuncts to, not substitutes for, GABAergic loading. (Source: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline

options.text: Stop benzodiazepines and give haloperidol 10 mg with olanzapine 10 mg
options.rationale: Antipsychotic monotherapy in GHB withdrawal without an underlying benzodiazepine backbone is dangerous - it lowers seizure threshold, worsens hyperthermia, and does not treat the GABAergic receptor down-regulation that is driving symptoms. Benzodiazepines remain part of the regimen, with barbiturate or GHB replacement added. (Source: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline

options.text: High dose midazolam infusion plus phenobarbital loading 5 mg/kg
options.rationale: GHB and its prodrug 1,4-butanediol act largely through GABA-B receptors, so benzodiazepine monotherapy is frequently insufficient - the ceiling reported in case series is often above 200 mg diazepam-equivalent per day. Phenobarbital acts at GABA-A independently of the benzodiazepine site and augments control; sodium oxybate substitution under specialist supervision provides a pharmaceutical taper. Ongoing intensive care and cooling are required. (Source: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg, repeated to reverse accumulated benzodiazepines
options.rationale: Flumazenil in a benzodiazepine-tolerant patient precipitates seizures and worsens withdrawal. It has no role in managing withdrawal, and the current problem is inadequate GABAergic coverage, not benzodiazepine excess. (Source: eTG Complete Toxicology: benzodiazepine toxicity)

options.text: Baclofen 20 mg via nasogastric tube eight-hourly as sole treatment
options.rationale: Baclofen has a role in GHB withdrawal as an adjunct given its GABA-B agonism, but baclofen monotherapy is inadequate for severe autonomic instability. It is used in combination with titrated benzodiazepine and barbiturate loading, and toxicity itself can produce delirium and coma. (Source: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline

explanation.summary: GHB and its prodrug 1,4-butanediol produce dose-dependent GABA-B receptor activation with a secondary GABA-A effect. Regular around-the-clock dosing over months down-regulates both pathways, so withdrawal can begin within hours of cessation and progress to a life-threatening syndrome that includes severe autonomic instability, delirium, psychosis, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and seizures. Because the primary receptor target differs from alcohol and benzodiazepines, benzodiazepine monotherapy is often inadequate and case series report requirements above 200 mg diazepam-equivalent per day. NSW Health and the RACP addiction medicine consensus support intensive care admission for severe cases, high-dose benzodiazepine infusion plus phenobarbital loading (to a level of 25-40 mg/L), and pharmaceutical GHB (sodium oxybate) substitution under specialist supervision. Baclofen and dexmedetomidine are adjuncts.
key_points: GHB/1,4-BD act primarily at GABA-B; benzodiazepine monotherapy is often inadequate.
Onset within hours of cessation; severe cases progress within 24 hours.
Phenobarbital loading is standard adjunct (target 25-40 mg/L) via GABA-A independent of benzodiazepine site.
Sodium oxybate substitution under addiction medicine supervision provides a pharmaceutical taper.
Baclofen and dexmedetomidine are adjuncts, not monotherapy.
explanation.pearls: Around-the-clock GHB or 1,4-BD dependence needs intensive care admission with high-dose benzodiazepine plus phenobarbital loading to a level of 25-40 mg/L, not benzodiazepine monotherapy - benzodiazepines act at GABA-A and GHB's dominant target is GABA-B.

sources.label: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline

subtopic_detail: Second-generation antipsychotic metabolic monitoring
stem:
You are the community mental health registrar seeing a 28 year old man who was commenced on olanzapine 15 mg nightly six months ago after a first-episode psychosis. He has been adherent, has had no relapse, and is enrolled in an early psychosis service. He now describes low energy, snoring witnessed by his partner, and a 9 kg weight gain since commencement.

His pre-treatment weight was 78 kg (BMI 24); his weight today is 87 kg (BMI 27). His fasting bloods this week show glucose 6.4 mmol/L, total cholesterol 6.1 mmol/L with LDL 4.0 mmol/L and triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L, and HbA1c 44 mmol/mol.

He describes his mental state as stable with residual mild negative symptoms; he lives with his partner and has re-started a plumbing apprenticeship.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: BMI 27, waist circumference 102 cm, no thyroid enlargement
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), HbA1c 44 mmol/mol (<42 non-diabetic), total cholesterol 6.1 mmol/L, LDL 4.0 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L, ALT 42 U/L, TSH 1.6 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged, refer to a community dietitian, and set a review appointment for six months time
options.rationale: Watchful waiting alone does not address progressive metabolic risk in the highest-risk agent (olanzapine and clozapine c. (Source: RANZCP guidelines; eTG: Psychotropic)

options.text: Discuss switching to aripiprazole or a lower-metabolic-risk antipsychotic and start metformin plus lifestyle program
options.rationale: Olanzapine carries the highest metabolic risk of the second-generation antipsychotics. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

options.text: Add a low dose of an atypical antipsychotic like risperidone to allow olanzapine dose reduction over three months
options.rationale: Antipsychotic polypharmacy is not evidence-based for adjusting metabolic tolerability; risperidone still contributes to. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

options.text: Prescribe a moderate-intensity statin now to treat dyslipidaemia and continue olanzapine at the current dose
options.rationale: A statin addresses one component but leaves the underlying drug driver of weight gain, prediabetes and dyslipidaemia in. (Source: NHFA CVD prevention)

options.text: Cease olanzapine abruptly and monitor for return of psychotic symptoms with weekly community mental health review
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of antipsychotic after first-episode psychosis risks relapse; a cross-titration to a lower-risk agent m. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics differ substantially in metabolic risk (clozapine and olanzapine highest; quetiapine and risperidone intermediate; aripiprazole, ziprasidone and lu.
key_points: Olanzapine and clozapine are the highest-metabolic-risk antipsychotics.
Metabolic monitoring at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, then annually.
Metformin reduces antipsychotic-induced weight gain by around 3 kg.
explanation.pearls: Weight gain over 7% of baseline on olanzapine triggers active intervention: metformin, structured lifestyle, or switch to aripiprazole - not watchful waiting.

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal seizure prophylaxis in general medical ward
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 44 year old man to the general medical ward after presenting to the emergency department with 12 hours of coarse tremor, sweating, nausea and one episode of vomiting. He is a mechanic with a long-standing pattern of drinking eight standard drinks daily; his last drink was 18 hours ago when he 'decided to stop' after his wife left. He has had two previous withdrawal seizures during unmedicated abstinence attempts but has never had delirium tremens.

He is agitated but oriented. His current Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol - revised score is 18. Vital signs are stable. Bedside blood glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. He denies suicidal ideation and does not report visual or auditory hallucinations.

He has no known liver disease, no benzodiazepine dependence, and no chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.1 degC
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor bilaterally, diaphoretic, oriented, no asterixis, no jaundice, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.8 mmol/L, ALT 58 U/L, GGT 145 U/L, INR 1.1, platelets 168 x10^9/L, thiamine yet to be given

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Give oral thiamine 100 mg daily and observe without benzodiazepine because he is oriented at the moment
options.rationale: A CIWA-Ar of 18 is moderate to severe withdrawal with prior seizures; withholding benzodiazepines risks seizure and prog. (Source: eTG: Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Give oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg every 6 hours on a fixed schedule for 5 days regardless of symptom pattern
options.rationale: Symptom-triggered dosing outperforms fixed-schedule dosing in reducing total benzodiazepine load and length of stay. (Source: eTG: Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Commence oral diazepam 20 mg every 2 hours titrated to CIWA-Ar plus parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV first dose
options.rationale: Symptom-triggered benzodiazepine loading (diazepam 20 mg oral every 2 hours until CIWA-Ar <10) is the Australian standar. (Source: eTG: Alcohol withdrawal; RACP alcohol guidelines)

options.text: Commence phenytoin 15 mg/kg intravenous load and lorazepam 1 mg intramuscularly as seizure prophylaxis today
options.rationale: Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures because the pathophysiology is GABA receptor rebound, not the mec. (Source: eTG: Alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Start clonidine 150 microgram three times daily to control autonomic features without any benzodiazepine
options.rationale: Alpha-2 agonists mask autonomic features but do not prevent seizures or delirium; they should not replace benzodiazepine. (Source: eTG: Alcohol withdrawal)

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal severity is scored with CIWA-Ar; a score of 15 or more is moderate to severe and needs inpatient management with benzodiazepine loading.
key_points: CIWA-Ar over 15 is moderate to severe withdrawal - inpatient benzodiazepine loading.
Diazepam 20 mg oral every 2 hours titrated until CIWA-Ar <10 (Australian standard).
Parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV three times daily for 3-5 days BEFORE any glucose.
explanation.pearls: In Australian alcohol withdrawal protocols, diazepam 20 mg oral loading every 2 hours titrated to CIWA-Ar is the seizure-preventing regimen; thiamine 300 mg IV.

subtopic_detail: Lithium initiation pre-treatment workup
stem:
You are the community mental health registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman with bipolar I disorder recovering from her third manic episode. She has been managed with olanzapine and lorazepam during admission and is now stable on olanzapine 10 mg nightly. She wants to change to a longer-term mood stabiliser and is not pregnant, not planning pregnancy in the next 12 months, and uses a copper intrauterine device. She has no diagnosed cardiac or thyroid disease.

She is otherwise well with no NSAID or ACE inhibitor use. She works as an accountant with regular access to routine bloods. Her BMI is 24 and her blood pressure is 118/72.

After discussion of options, she prefers lithium given the family history of bipolar disorder that responded well to lithium.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Examination: BMI 24, no goitre, no oedema, cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 within normal limits, creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR >90 mL/min, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L, urine hCG negative

lead_in: Which of the following investigations is the single most important to complete before commencing lithium?

options.text: Baseline 12-lead electrocardiogram to exclude conduction abnormalities before starting lithium therapy
options.rationale: An ECG is recommended before lithium initiation for patients over 40 or with cardiac risk factors, but it is not the hig. (Source: eTG: Psychotropic)

options.text: Baseline liver function tests including ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin before commencement
options.rationale: Lithium is renally cleared and not hepatically metabolised; LFTs are not part of the routine pre-lithium workup. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Fasting glucose plus lipid profile including total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides before commencement
options.rationale: These are relevant to second-generation antipsychotics rather than lithium; they are not part of the lithium pre-treatme. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Pregnancy test plus baseline UEC, thyroid function and calcium documenting adherence to reliable contraception
options.rationale: Lithium is teratogenic (Ebstein anomaly with first-trimester exposure; historical risk about 1 in 1000, higher than base. (Source: eTG: Psychotropic; AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Anti-thyroid antibodies including anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin to identify latent autoimmune thyroid disease
options.rationale: Anti-thyroid antibodies are not part of the routine pre-lithium screen; baseline TSH is. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

explanation.summary: Pre-lithium workup includes urea, electrolytes, creatinine and eGFR, thyroid function (TSH and free T4), corrected calcium, pregnancy test in women of reproductive age, and baselin.
key_points: Baseline pre-lithium: UEC, TSH, calcium, pregnancy test, ECG if over 40 or cardiac history.
Lithium is teratogenic - Ebstein anomaly in first trimester; reliable contraception required.
Monitor lithium level, renal function, TSH and calcium every 6 months.
explanation.pearls: Before starting lithium in a woman of reproductive age, confirm negative pregnancy test and reliable contraception; Ebstein anomaly risk is around 1 in 1000 wit.

subtopic_detail: Catatonia in acute psychiatric setting
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the acute psychiatric inpatient unit to review a 24 year old man with schizoaffective disorder who has become progressively unwell over 24 hours. He was admitted a week ago for a psychotic relapse and started on risperidone 3 mg twice daily. Over the last day he has stopped eating and speaking and is now mute, staring past the interviewer.

On examination he holds his right arm in a raised position when you gently lift it, maintaining the posture for over a minute after you withdraw your hand. He resists passive movement with equal counter-force ('gegenhalten') and grimaces intermittently. There is no tremor and no lead-pipe rigidity.

His observations show mild tachycardia; he is afebrile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.0 degC
data_table.Examination: Waxy flexibility, gegenhalten, mutism, staring, negativism (turning away from food), Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score 16
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 220 U/L (<200), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), calcium and magnesium within normal limits, urine drug screen negative, blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Continue risperidone, add haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly, and reassess response within the next hour
options.rationale: Escalating antipsychotic dosing in catatonia risks neuroleptic malignant syndrome (which shares the catatonia phenotype. (Source: RANZCP acute behavioural disturbance)

options.text: Refer immediately for electroconvulsive therapy without a lorazepam trial or diagnostic challenge
options.rationale: ECT is definitive for benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia or malignant catatonia; lorazepam trial precedes ECT because m. (Source: RANZCP ECT guideline)

options.text: Start dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg intravenously for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome with rigidity
options.rationale: NMS is on the differential but this patient is afebrile with mild tachycardia and CK 220; the phenotype (waxy flexibilit. (Source: RANZCP acute behavioural disturbance)

options.text: Trial olanzapine 10 mg intramuscularly and escalate second-generation antipsychotic sedation dosing
options.rationale: Second-generation antipsychotic sedation does not treat catatonia and can worsen it, potentially precipitating NMS in an. (Source: RANZCP acute behavioural disturbance)

options.text: Give a test dose of lorazepam 1 to 2 mg intramuscularly and reassess response over 10 to 15 minutes
options.rationale: A lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IM or IV) is diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia; around 60-80% of catatonia responds. (Source: RANZCP acute behavioural disturbance; StatPearls Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia presents with mutism, staring, waxy flexibility, gegenhalten, negativism, posturing, echolalia or echopraxia, and can arise in mood disorders, psychotic disorders, and me.
key_points: Catatonia: mutism, waxy flexibility, gegenhalten, negativism, posturing, echo phenomena.
Lorazepam 1-2 mg is diagnostic and therapeutic within 15 minutes.
Malignant catatonia has fever and autonomic dysregulation; overlaps with NMS.
explanation.pearls: A single intramuscular test dose of lorazepam 1 to 2 mg both diagnoses catatonia and treats it in about 70% of cases within 15 minutes; refractory cases proceed.

subtopic_detail: Valproate in women of reproductive age
stem:
You are the community mental health registrar seeing a 26 year old woman with bipolar I disorder who has had two hospital admissions for mania. She has failed adequate trials of lithium and olanzapine (poor efficacy and metabolic weight gain respectively). Her psychiatrist is considering valproate as the next mood stabiliser. She is sexually active with her male partner, uses condoms only, and has not made pregnancy plans.

She has no personal history of neural tube defects and no family history of open spina bifida. Baseline liver function and platelet count are normal. She has been counselled that condom-only use has around a 15% typical-use annual failure rate.

She would prefer to try valproate but wants to explore what safety framework applies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: BMI 26, no goitre, no oedema, cardiovascular examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: ALT 22 U/L, platelets 268 x10^9/L, INR 1.0, urine hCG negative

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Establish highly effective LARC contraception plus signed annual acknowledgement, then commence valproate
options.rationale: The valproate pregnancy prevention framework requires documented highly effective contraception (LARC preferred, or two. (Source: TGA valproate advisory; RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Start sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily immediately, with a plan to review contraception at three months
options.rationale: Australian and international guidance (TGA and MHRA valproate pregnancy prevention program) require documented highly. (Source: TGA valproate advisory; RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Add carbamazepine as a mood stabiliser instead of valproate, since carbamazepine is safer in early pregnancy
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also teratogenic (neural tube defects, craniofacial abnormalities) and induces oestrogen metabolism, re. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Recommend lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrated up over six weeks with no additional contraceptive advice given
options.rationale: Lamotrigine has a more favourable teratogenic profile but is a poor choice for acute mania prevention; it is more effect. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Continue current management with olanzapine indefinitely because valproate is contraindicated in her situation
options.rationale: Valproate is not absolutely contraindicated in women of reproductive age in Australia; it can be used inside the pregnan. (Source: TGA valproate advisory)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is teratogenic with a 30-40% risk of congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental impairment (major malformations 10%, IQ reduction of about 8 points, autism sp.
key_points: Valproate: 30-40% congenital malformation and neurodevelopmental risk in pregnancy.
Pregnancy prevention program with LARC or dual method contraception before initiation.
Annual specialist re-consent with signed acknowledgement.
explanation.pearls: In Australia valproate is only started in a woman of reproductive age with a levonorgestrel-IUD or implant in situ (or dual method), signed annual re-consent, a.

subtopic_detail: SSRI discontinuation vs depression relapse
stem:
You are the general practitioner registrar seeing a 38 year old woman five days after she stopped her paroxetine 20 mg daily. She had been on paroxetine for 14 months for a moderate major depressive episode that fully remitted after six weeks; she stopped the medication herself on advice from a friend who felt she had 'been on it long enough'. Her last dose was five days ago.

Since then she describes new brief lightning-like sensations down her arms and legs on turning her head ('electric shocks'), vivid dreams, mild nausea, dizziness on standing, and a low-grade flu-like sensation. Her partner reports she is a bit irritable but not tearful or withdrawn. She is sleeping.

Her mood examination reveals a normal-range mood, appropriate reactivity, no anhedonia, no suicidal ideation, and no hopelessness.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg (no significant postural drop), respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, normal affective range, no psychomotor slowing, no anhedonia, no suicidality, no hopelessness

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Diagnose major depressive relapse and increase the paroxetine dose to 30 mg daily with review in two weeks
options.rationale: There is no depressive relapse: mood is euthymic, no anhedonia, no suicidal ideation, and symptoms are physical rather t. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Restart paroxetine 20 mg daily and plan a slow taper over 8 to 12 weeks with a fluoxetine bridge if needed
options.rationale: The symptom cluster (electric shock sensations, vivid dreams, dizziness, flu-like, irritability - the FINISH mnemonic) p. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; RCPsych stopping antidepressants)

options.text: Prescribe a benzodiazepine short-term for the anxiety-like symptoms and reassess response in two weeks time
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines mask discontinuation symptoms without treating the underlying serotonergic rebound; they add dependence. (Source: eTG: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add lithium as an augmentation agent for treatment-resistant depression despite prior full remission on paroxetine
options.rationale: There is no evidence of treatment-resistant depression; the depression fully remitted on paroxetine. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline)

options.text: Advise ongoing abstinence and predict resolution within 5 days regardless of severity or symptom duration
options.rationale: Ongoing abstinence with severe discontinuation symptoms is unnecessarily punishing, and paroxetine's short half-life oft. (Source: RCPsych stopping antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Antidepressant discontinuation syndrome affects up to 20-30% of people stopping SSRIs, most commonly with short-half-life agents (paroxetine, venlafaxine).
key_points: FINISH mnemonic: flu-like, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory, hyperarousal.
Paroxetine, venlafaxine, duloxetine have highest discontinuation burden.
Distinguish from depressive relapse: mood is euthymic in discontinuation.
explanation.pearls: Electric-shock sensations plus a euthymic mood after stopping paroxetine is discontinuation syndrome, not relapse; restart and slow-taper over 8-12 weeks.

subtopic_detail: Acute mania first line pharmacotherapy
stem: A 24-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has four days of reduced sleep, pressured speech and grandiose plans. He self-ceased quetiapine 300 mg nightly six weeks ago and has never taken lithium.

data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, liver and thyroid function normal; electrocardiogram normal; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg orally four-hourly as the sole pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines have a role for adjunctive sedation and sleep in acute mania but do not treat the underlying mood episode; monotherapy leaves the manic process unopposed. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021)
source_refs: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg daily titrated to 100 mg over two weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder can precipitate or worsen mania and is not indicated for acute mania; it is contraindicated in this presentation. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021)
source_refs: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021

options.text: Lithium carbonate 500 mg at night, targeting a level of 0.8 to 1.0
options.rationale: RANZCP mood disorder guideline lists lithium and second generation antipsychotics as first line for acute mania; lithium has the strongest evidence for both acute mania and long term prophylaxis, and normal renal and thyroid function make it safe to initiate. Target level for acute mania is 0.8-1.0 mmol/L. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021; eTG: Bipolar disorder)
source_refs: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021

options.text: Lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrated to 200 mg over six weeks
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is effective for bipolar depression maintenance but not for acute mania and has a slow titration required to reduce SJS risk; it does not treat the acute episode. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021)
source_refs: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily as monotherapy with review at two weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy is contraindicated in acute mania and can precipitate rapid cycling; SSRIs are not first line for a manic presentation. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021)
source_refs: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021

explanation.summary: Acute mania is treated with either lithium or a second generation antipsychotic as first line under RANZCP guidance. Lithium has the strongest evidence for acute and prophylactic treatment and is appropriate in a young man with normal renal and thyroid function who has not previously trialled it. Target acute mania level is 0.8-1.0 mmol/L with careful hydration counselling and avoidance of NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides. Combination lithium plus antipsychotic is used for severe or partial response. Antidepressant monotherapy is contraindicated in mania.
key_points: First line acute mania: lithium OR second generation antipsychotic
Lithium acute mania target level 0.8-1.0 mmol/L
Antidepressant monotherapy contraindicated in bipolar disorder
Lamotrigine used for bipolar depression maintenance, not acute mania
explanation.pearls: Lithium takes 5-7 days to reach steady state and effect is not immediate; short term benzodiazepines are often given alongside for behavioural control while lithium reaches therapeutic level.

sources.label: RANZCP mood disorders clinical practice guideline 2021

subtopic_detail: OCD SSRI titration
stem: A 28-year-old woman with obsessive compulsive disorder washes her hands four to six hours daily, with cracked painful skin. She has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for six weeks, up-titrated from 50 mg, with weekly exposure and response prevention for two months. Urge intensity is mildly less but washing is unchanged, with no side effects.

data_table.Examination: Excoriated hands, no tremor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Titrate sertraline up to 200 mg daily
options.rationale: OCD typically requires higher SSRI doses than depression and a longer trial (10-12 weeks); RANZCP and NICE recommend titrating to the maximum tolerated licensed dose (sertraline 200 mg) before declaring treatment failure. Sertraline 100 mg is a mid dose in OCD terms. (Source: RANZCP OCD guidance; NICE OCD guideline CG31)

options.text: Add risperidone 1 mg daily as an adjunct
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is reserved for OCD that has failed maximal tolerated SSRI trial at 10-12 weeks, particularly for tic-related or partial response OCD; adding it now bypasses full SSRI titration. (Source: RANZCP OCD guidance)

options.text: Switch to a benzodiazepine for the anxiety
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not indicated in OCD, are habit forming with tolerance, and do not address the underlying obsessive process; SSRIs and ERP remain first line. (Source: RANZCP OCD guidance)

options.text: Switch to venlafaxine 75 mg daily
options.rationale: SNRIs like venlafaxine have weaker evidence than SSRIs in OCD and would not be preferred without completing a maximal SSRI trial first; switching now abandons a treatment that has been shown effective. (Source: RANZCP OCD guidance)

options.text: Refer for transcranial magnetic stimulation
options.rationale: rTMS is a treatment option for treatment resistant OCD after failure of maximal SSRI trials and ERP, not a first step at six weeks on 100 mg sertraline. (Source: RANZCP OCD guidance)

explanation.summary: OCD responds to SSRIs at higher doses and needs a longer trial than depression. RANZCP recommends titrating to the maximum tolerated licensed dose (sertraline 200 mg, fluoxetine 80 mg, paroxetine 60 mg, escitalopram 40 mg) and waiting 10-12 weeks before declaring treatment failure. Exposure and response prevention is combined with SSRI first line. Antipsychotic augmentation (risperidone or aripiprazole) or switching to clomipramine is second line after maximal SSRI trial. rTMS and deep brain stimulation are options in refractory cases.
key_points: OCD needs higher SSRI doses and longer trials than depression
Sertraline goes to 200 mg, fluoxetine to 80 mg, escitalopram to 40 mg for OCD
Combine SSRI with exposure and response prevention
Antipsychotic augmentation only after maximal SSRI trial fails
explanation.pearls: Escitalopram 40 mg for OCD exceeds the TGA general 20 mg maximum but is an accepted higher licensed dose for OCD specifically - documenting the OCD indication in the notes matters when the pharmacy queries.

subtopic_detail: Clozapine agranulocytosis monitoring
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 35 year old man on clozapine for treatment resistant schizophrenia. He has been stable for three years with much reduced positive symptoms after trials of risperidone and olanzapine did not achieve remission. He attends his monthly clozapine clinic today for his four weekly review and blood collection.

His full blood count today returns with a neutrophil count of 1.3 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), down from 2.6 four weeks ago. His platelets and haemoglobin are within normal limits. He is clinically well without fever, sore throat or infective symptoms. He has been fully adherent with medication and denies smoking cessation, new medications, or substance use.

He lives independently, is engaged in supported employment and reports his best psychosocial functioning in a decade. He is very keen to remain on clozapine and asks what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, no oral thrush, no pharyngeal erythema, chest clear, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 1.3 x10^9/L (was 2.6), white cells 4.2 x10^9/L (4-11), haemoglobin 145 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, CRP <5 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose and repeat the full blood count twice weekly until stable
options.rationale: Under AU Clopine and Clozaril monitoring protocols this result is classified as amber (neutrophils 1.0-1.5 x10^9/L in non-benign neutropenia populations) - clozapine is continued with twice weekly FBC until stable or a red zone (under 1.0) is reached, at which point clozapine is ceased and haematology involved. (Source: Clopine Connect monitoring protocol; TGA clozapine risk management plan)
