Cannabis, ketamine, panic and sleep deprivation are the common precipitants
Symptom monitoring and catastrophic appraisal maintain the disorder
Cognitive behavioural therapy with psychoeducation is first line
Antipsychotics are unhelpful and may worsen the detachment
explanation.pearls: Cannabis withdrawal symptoms peak at two to six days and are essentially gone by four weeks, so any perceptual or mood symptom still present beyond a month after cessation should be reclassified as a primary disorder rather than attributed to withdrawal and watched.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Short day sleep and racing thoughts four weeks into a run of night shifts in an emergency nurse
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old emergency department nurse who is four weeks into a block of night shifts. She sleeps about four hours during the day, lies awake feeling wired at four in the morning on shift, snaps at her partner, and has been buying things online at three in the morning that she does not need.

She says her thoughts feel fast and jumbled, but when asked she describes herself as worn out rather than energised and says what she wants most is more sleep. There is no history of elevated mood, no grandiosity, no increase in goal directed activity and no reduction in her perceived need for sleep. On her five days off at the end of the previous block she slept eight hours a night and everything settled within two days. Her bedroom faces east and has thin curtains, and her neighbour is renovating.

data_table.Examination: Tired in appearance, normal rate and rhythm of speech, affect reactive, no flight of ideas, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start lithium and arrange a serum concentration measurement after five days
options.rationale: A mood stabiliser assumes a bipolar diagnosis, and the cardinal feature of hypomania is a reduced need for sleep with preserved or increased energy, whereas she is exhausted and wants more sleep. Committing a patient to lithium on shift related symptoms carries lifelong monitoring and renal and thyroid consequences. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Start quetiapine 100 mg before her day sleep and review her mood in two weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antipsychotics are sometimes used off label as hypnotics, but the metabolic and next day sedation burden is unacceptable in someone who drives home after a night shift, and it treats the symptom rather than the circadian misalignment causing it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Advise a fixed sleep schedule with timed light exposure and a dark bedroom
options.rationale: Insomnia and impaired alertness tied to a shift schedule, resolving within two days of returning to a normal routine, is a circadian rhythm problem rather than a mood disorder, and the treatment is behavioural: an anchored sleep period, bright light during the first part of the shift, dark glasses on the drive home and a blacked out quiet bedroom. Fixing the light and noise exposure addresses both the short day sleep and the irritability that follows it. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift work and sleep)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift work and sleep

options.text: Start temazepam 10 mg before her day sleep and review her sleep in two weeks
options.rationale: A hypnotic may lengthen day sleep a little but does not realign the circadian clock, and tolerance plus residual sedation are real risks in a worker whose job involves drug calculations and who then drives. It is reserved for short term use after the behavioural measures have been put in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer urgently to the mental health service for assessment of elevated mood
options.rationale: Urgent referral would be right if there were sustained elevated or irritable mood with reduced need for sleep persisting away from the trigger, and the crucial history here is that everything remitted within forty eight hours on her days off. Impulsive overnight spending during sleep deprivation is not by itself evidence of hypomania. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Shift work disorder is insomnia or excessive sleepiness occurring in relation to a work schedule that overlaps the usual sleep period, and it affects roughly a fifth to a third of rotating and night shift workers. It mimics hypomania closely because sleep deprivation produces irritability, racing thoughts, impulsive spending and emotional lability, and it mimics depression because of the fatigue and withdrawal that follow. The discriminator is the relationship to the roster: circadian symptoms track the schedule and remit within a few days of returning to normal sleep, while a genuine mood episode persists independently. Management is behavioural and environmental first, with an anchored sleep period, bright light early in the shift, light avoidance on the journey home, a blacked out and quiet bedroom, and strategic napping before the shift. Melatonin taken before the day sleep and short term hypnotics are second line, and modafinil is reserved for persisting sleepiness under specialist supervision.
key_points: Reduced need for sleep with high energy defines hypomania; wanting more sleep argues against it
Remission within days of returning to a normal roster points to a circadian cause
Anchored sleep, timed bright light and a dark quiet bedroom are first line
Sedating antipsychotics and hypnotics do not realign the circadian clock
Sleep deprivation alone can produce irritability, fast thoughts and impulsive spending
explanation.pearls: Wearing dark glasses on the drive home after a night shift is one of the highest yield single interventions available, because morning daylight on the retina is the strongest signal shifting the circadian clock in the wrong direction, and blocking it typically lengthens subsequent day sleep by around an hour.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Shift work and sleep
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Blocked hallways and inability to discard possessions after a fire service safety notice
stem:
You are the general practitioner visiting a 71 year old widow at home after the fire service attended a smoke complaint and issued a safety notice. Newspapers, containers and clothing are stacked chest high through the house, with a single narrow path between rooms, the kitchen bench and stove are not usable, and she sleeps in an armchair.

She agrees that the fire risk is real and says she is ashamed of the state of the house, but becomes visibly distressed when you pick up an empty ice cream container, explaining that she may need it. She has no beliefs that the items are alive or contaminated and no voices. Her daughter cleared the lounge room two years ago while she was in hospital; the room refilled within four months and they did not speak for a year afterwards. She manages her own banking and medications without error.

data_table.Examination: Well kempt and well nourished, no squalor and no animals, Mini-Mental State Examination 28 out of 30, no delusions elicited, distress on handling of possessions
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), vitamin B12 420 pmol/L (150-700), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a forced clean out with the council and review her at home in three months
options.rationale: Forced clearance reliably produces rapid re-accumulation and severe distress, and her own history demonstrates exactly that pattern with the loss of the relationship that went with it. It is reserved for imminent danger that cannot be managed any other way, and even then it is done alongside treatment rather than instead of it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer for hoarding specific cognitive behavioural therapy with a case manager
options.rationale: Difficulty discarding driven by a perceived need to save, with accumulation that renders living areas unusable, responds to a disorder specific cognitive behavioural approach targeting decision making, beliefs about possessions and graded sorting practice, coordinated with housing and fire safety services. Working with her rather than around her is what prevents the re-accumulation that followed the previous clearance. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start fluvoxamine 100 mg daily and review her living conditions in three months
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors help the obsessive compulsive disorder that sometimes sits alongside this condition, but response rates for the saving and difficulty discarding themselves are modest and lower than for obsessive compulsive disorder proper. Medication is an adjunct, not the initial plan. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange neuropsychological testing and brain imaging to look for cognitive decline
options.rationale: New accumulation with self neglect in an older person does warrant a cognitive assessment, and frontal syndromes can present this way, but she scores 28 out of 30, manages her banking and medications accurately and retains full insight into the risk. The behaviour here is driven by distress on discarding rather than by an inability to organise. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Apply for a guardianship order to allow decisions about her accommodation
options.rationale: Substitute decision making requires impaired decision making capacity, and she understands the risk, retains information and manages complex tasks independently, so the threshold is not met. Poor judgement in the eyes of others is not the same as absent capacity. (Source: Australian Guardianship and Administration Council)

explanation.summary: Hoarding disorder became a diagnosis in its own right in 2013 and is defined by persistent difficulty discarding possessions because of a perceived need to save them, with distress on discarding and accumulation that compromises the use of living areas. Prevalence rises steeply with age and reaches several per cent in people over 70, and the main risks are fire, falls, structural collapse, infestation and eviction. Insight varies, and its presence does not predict ability to act, which is why exhortation and clearance both fail. Effective treatment is a structured cognitive behavioural program adapted for this disorder, delivered over many months and often in the home, combined with practical coordination between the general practitioner, housing, council, fire services and family. Comorbid depression, anxiety and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder are common and worth screening for because they impede engagement.
key_points: Difficulty discarding due to a perceived need to save, with unusable living areas, defines it
Forced clearance produces rapid re-accumulation and ruptured relationships
Disorder specific cognitive behavioural therapy with multi-agency coordination is first line
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are adjunctive with modest effect on the hoarding itself
Capacity is preserved in most cases, so guardianship is rarely appropriate
explanation.pearls: Fire is the lethal risk to quantify for the family: hoarded dwellings account for a disproportionate share of fatal residential fires because the fuel load blocks egress and defeats firefighter entry, which is why a working smoke alarm and a cleared exit path are negotiated at the first visit, ahead of any sorting work.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Aerosol propellant inhalation in a fifteen year old with a rash around the mouth and falling grades
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15 year old boy brought in by his mother, who found a dozen empty deodorant cans under his bed. Over three months his grades have dropped from good to failing and he has stopped going to football.

She describes him coming home some afternoons unsteady on his feet with slurred speech that clears within about an hour, and she has noticed a chemical smell on his clothes. He is guarded but eventually says he does it with two friends behind the shops because it is free and quick. There are no injection marks and no tremor. He denies alcohol and cannabis and his breath alcohol reading today is zero.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Erythematous cracked skin around the mouth and nostrils, conjunctival injection, no needle marks, gait normal today, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), alanine aminotransferase 28 units/L (5-35), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start naltrexone 50 mg daily and refer him to a youth drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Naltrexone blocks opioid receptors and has a role in alcohol and opioid use disorders, neither of which is in play here, and there is no pharmacotherapy with established efficacy for volatile substance use. Prescribing it also implies a mechanism that does not apply. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Arrange an urgent blood lead concentration and start chelation if the level is raised
options.rationale: Lead toxicity is the specific concern with leaded petrol sniffing, which produces encephalopathy, tremor and ataxia, and chelation is then genuinely indicated. Aerosol propellants are butane and related hydrocarbons and contain no lead, so the test does not fit the substance described. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Start nicotine replacement and refer him to a youth drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Nicotine replacement treats nicotine dependence, and nothing in the history points to smoking or vaping as the problem to solve. Offering it risks the adolescent concluding that the clinician has not understood what he disclosed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Notify child protection services and arrange an involuntary admission today
options.rationale: Statutory notification is required where there is a reasonable belief of abuse or neglect, and an engaged parent seeking help is the opposite of that picture; involuntary admission requires a mental illness meeting the criteria of the mental health legislation, which volatile substance use alone does not satisfy. Both responses tend to end the therapeutic relationship at the moment it is most useful. (Source: National Health and Medical Research Council: Volatile substance use guidance)
source_refs: National Health and Medical Research Council: Volatile substance use guidance

options.text: Refer him to a youth drug and alcohol service and involve his parents in the plan
options.rationale: There is no effective pharmacotherapy for this pattern of use, so management is psychosocial: engagement with a youth specific service, family involvement, attention to the school disengagement that both causes and results from the use, and harm reduction advice about the cardiac risk. Treating the peer and school context is what shifts the behaviour. (Source: National Health and Medical Research Council: Volatile substance use guidance)
source_refs: National Health and Medical Research Council: Volatile substance use guidance

explanation.summary: Volatile substance use is concentrated in early adolescence because the products are cheap, legal and everywhere, and it is under-detected because standard urine drug screens do not include hydrocarbons, so a negative screen never excludes it. The examination clue is the rash around the mouth and nose from repeated contact with propellant, along with a chemical odour on clothing and short lived intoxication that clears within an hour. Chronic use causes cognitive impairment, cerebellar damage, renal tubular acidosis with toluene, and bone marrow suppression with benzene containing products. The acute killer is sudden sniffing death, in which myocardial sensitisation to catecholamines produces ventricular fibrillation during a surge of adrenaline, classically when the user is startled or chased. Management is entirely psychosocial: a youth specific alcohol and other drug service, family engagement, re-engagement with school and harm reduction advice, because no medication has been shown to help.
key_points: Standard urine drug screens do not detect hydrocarbons, so a negative result excludes nothing
Rash around the mouth and nose with a chemical odour is the physical sign
Intoxication is brief, typically resolving within an hour of last use
No pharmacotherapy is effective; management is psychosocial and family based
Toluene causes renal tubular acidosis and chronic use causes cerebellar damage
explanation.pearls: Advise the family never to chase or startle him while he is intoxicated: sudden sniffing death occurs when a catecholamine surge triggers ventricular fibrillation in a myocardium sensitised by the hydrocarbon, and it can occur on a first exposure, which is why the safest response to finding him mid-use is a calm approach rather than confrontation.

sources.label: National Health and Medical Research Council: Volatile substance use guidance

subtopic_detail: Night time fall at home in a 70 year old taking temazepam every night for eight years
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 70 year old woman who fell getting up to the toilet two nights ago. She grazed her elbow, there was no fracture and she did not lose consciousness.

She has taken temazepam 20 mg every night for eight years, started during the months after her husband died, and she also takes amlodipine. She tells you the tablet does not really work any more but that she lies awake for hours if she misses it, and she has come in today mainly to make sure the script does not run out. She lives alone, still drives during the day and does her own shopping. She remembers the fall clearly and describes feeling groggy and slow on her feet rather than dizzy or faint.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No postural drop on lying and standing measurement, normal gait and tandem walk, no cerebellar or peripheral neurological signs, visual acuity corrected to 6/9 bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with normal intervals, vitamin B12 380 pmol/L (150-700), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her medication?

options.text: Switch her to zopiclone at an equivalent dose and review her sleep in four weeks
options.rationale: The so called non-benzodiazepine hypnotics act at the same receptor complex and carry the same falls, fracture and motor vehicle crash risk in older people, so this swaps the label rather than the hazard. It also resets tolerance expectations and restarts the dependence clock. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Stop the temazepam now and start melatonin, reviewing her sleep in four weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after eight years of nightly use risks rebound insomnia, severe anxiety and, occasionally, withdrawal seizures, and it guarantees she will resume the tablet. Prolonged release melatonin is a reasonable adjunct in this age group but not a substitute for a planned taper. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue the current dose and reassess her falls risk again in twelve months
options.rationale: Continuing is the path of least resistance and is what usually happens, but the fall has already occurred, she describes grogginess rather than presyncope, and the postural blood pressure and cardiac assessment are normal, so the sedative is the modifiable contributor sitting in front of you. A year is far too long given the fracture risk. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Reduce the temazepam by a quarter of the dose every two weeks with sleep advice
options.rationale: A gradual reduction negotiated with the patient, paired with behavioural sleep measures, is the approach that achieves lasting cessation in long term users, and a step of about a quarter of the dose every one to two weeks is tolerable while allowing slowing near the end. Her normal cardiac and postural findings make the sedative the target worth changing. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Convert her to diazepam and reduce that gradually over the next three months
options.rationale: Conversion to a long half-life agent is a recognised technique for short acting benzodiazepines, but it is specifically cautioned against in older people and in hepatic impairment because diazepam and its active metabolites accumulate and worsen the very sedation and falls risk being treated. The difference from the correct answer is not the taper but the drug it is run on. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Long term nightly benzodiazepine use in older adults produces tolerance to the hypnotic effect within weeks while the impairment of balance, reaction time and memory persists indefinitely, which is why patients commonly report that the tablet no longer works but that they cannot stop. The associated harms are falls and hip fracture, motor vehicle crashes and accelerated cognitive impairment, and the risk is dose related but present at low doses. Deprescribing succeeds when it is negotiated rather than imposed, tapered gradually over weeks to months, and supported by behavioural treatment for the insomnia underneath, since the original sleep problem usually remains. Rates of success in general practice rise substantially when the conversation is framed around the falls or the memory rather than around dependence. Withdrawal seizures are rare but real after abrupt cessation of high dose or very long term use, which is the safety reason a taper is not optional.
key_points: Tolerance to the hypnotic effect develops but the balance and memory impairment does not
Gradual dose reduction of about a quarter every one to two weeks is well tolerated
Substituting a non-benzodiazepine hypnotic carries the same risk profile
Diazepam conversion is cautioned against in older people because of accumulation
Behavioural treatment of the underlying insomnia must run alongside the taper
explanation.pearls: Frame the taper around driving and hip fracture rather than dependence: benzodiazepine use in older adults roughly doubles the risk of a motor vehicle crash and of hip fracture, and the fracture risk is highest in the first two weeks after a dose increase or a new prescription, which is also the argument against switching her to another hypnotic.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

subtopic_detail: Cyclical irritability confined to the ten days before menses with a symptom free follicular phase
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29 year old primary school teacher who describes two years of irritability, tearfulness, breast tenderness and bloating that begin about ten days before each period and settle within two days of the bleeding starting.

She has received two formal complaints at work about how she spoke to colleagues, both in the week before a period, and she is frightened of losing her job. A prospective daily symptom record kept over three cycles shows a rating of zero on most days between the end of bleeding and mid cycle, with scores rising steeply from day eighteen. She has migraine with visual aura about twice a month. She uses condoms for contraception and has no intrauterine device in place. She has no thoughts of self harm.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic and pleasant at this mid follicular visit, affect full range, no psychomotor change, body mass index 24 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155), ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30-300)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg taken from day fourteen of the cycle until menstruation starts
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants are the most effective treatment for severe cyclical premenstrual symptoms, and unlike their use in depression the benefit appears within a day or two, which is what makes dosing restricted to the luteal phase as effective as continuous dosing while halving total exposure. The prospectively confirmed symptom free follicular phase is what establishes the diagnosis and justifies intermittent dosing. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Premenstrual disorders)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Premenstrual disorders

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive containing drospirenone taken continuously
options.rationale: Continuous combined hormonal contraception is a legitimate option for this condition and drospirenone containing formulations have the best evidence, but migraine with aura is an absolute contraindication to any combined preparation because of the stroke risk. The distinction from the correct answer is entirely her headache history rather than the efficacy of the drug. (Source: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare medical eligibility criteria)
source_refs: Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare medical eligibility criteria

options.text: Micronised progesterone 200 mg nightly during the second half of the cycle
options.rationale: Luteal phase progesterone and progestogens have been tested repeatedly in this condition and do not outperform placebo, and in some women progestogens reproduce the symptoms. The persistence of this prescribing rests on the mistaken idea that the disorder reflects progesterone deficiency. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Premenstrual disorders)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Premenstrual disorders

options.text: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with oestrogen and progestogen add back
options.rationale: Medical ovarian suppression is highly effective and is used as a diagnostic and therapeutic step, but it is third line because of bone density loss and vasomotor effects, and add back therapy is required. Starting here skips two safer tiers of treatment. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Premenstrual disorders)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Premenstrual disorders

options.text: Evening primrose oil 1000 mg twice daily through the second half of the cycle
options.rationale: Trials of evening primrose oil show benefit for cyclical breast tenderness only, with no effect on the mood and irritability symptoms that are causing her occupational problem. Offering it as the treatment for a disorder threatening her employment understates the severity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is distinguished from ordinary premenstrual symptoms by severity and functional impairment, and from a mood disorder with premenstrual worsening by the presence of a genuinely symptom free interval after menstruation. That distinction cannot be made retrospectively, which is why two cycles of prospective daily ratings are required before treatment is committed to. The underlying mechanism appears to be abnormal central sensitivity to normal luteal phase changes in progesterone metabolites rather than any abnormality of circulating hormone concentrations, which explains why measuring hormones is unhelpful and why supplementing progesterone fails. Treatment options in order are serotonergic antidepressants continuously or in the luteal phase, continuous combined hormonal contraception, and ovarian suppression, with cognitive behavioural therapy effective in parallel. Bilateral oophorectomy with hysterectomy is definitive but is reserved for women who have responded to a trial of ovarian suppression and have completed their family.
key_points: A prospectively documented symptom free follicular phase is required for the diagnosis
Serotonergic antidepressants work within days here, allowing luteal phase only dosing
Circulating hormone concentrations are normal and do not need measuring
Luteal phase progesterone does not outperform placebo
Migraine with aura rules out any combined hormonal contraceptive option
explanation.pearls: The rapid onset of benefit is the diagnostic giveaway as well as the dosing rationale: if a woman with cyclical symptoms reports that a serotonergic antidepressant helped within forty eight hours rather than over the two to four weeks expected in depression, that response pattern supports the premenstrual diagnosis rather than an underlying depressive episode.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Premenstrual disorders
Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare medical eligibility criteria

subtopic_detail: Agitation with racing thoughts and three hours of sleep three weeks after starting an antidepressant
stem: A 27-year-old woman is reviewed three weeks after starting escitalopram 10 mg daily for depression. She now sleeps three hours a night, feels revved up and miserable, with racing thoughts and new self-harm thoughts. She denies elation. At 22 she had a fortnight of sleeping little and painting all night. Her mother takes lithium.

data_table.Examination: Restless, pressured speech, dysphoric affect
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and urine drug screen normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the escitalopram to 20 mg daily
options.rationale: Dose escalation is the standard response to partial improvement at three weeks, and it is the trap here: the activation, reduced sleep and racing thoughts have appeared since the drug was started, so increasing it intensifies the very state causing the risk. Escalation would be right if she were simply not yet responding, with unchanged sleep and no activation. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Add diazepam 5 mg twice daily for agitation
options.rationale: A benzodiazepine is a reasonable short term adjunct for agitation and insomnia in this state, but adding it while leaving the antidepressant running treats the symptom and not the driver, and sedation can mask the deterioration you need to be able to see. It has a role alongside the correct answer, not instead of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add zolpidem at night and review her sleep
options.rationale: Treating the three hours of sleep as primary insomnia misreads a mood state in which the sleep change is a symptom rather than the problem, and zolpidem in particular can produce disinhibition and complex sleep behaviours in agitated patients. The sleep will correct when the underlying state does. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop the escitalopram and start quetiapine
options.rationale: Depressed mood occurring together with pressured speech, racing thoughts, psychomotor activation and markedly reduced sleep is a mixed state, and the previous fortnight of reduced sleep with increased activity plus the family history of lithium use place her on the bipolar spectrum. Antidepressant monotherapy is withdrawn and an agent effective in bipolar depression substituted, urgently, because mixed states carry the highest suicide risk of any mood presentation. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Switch to mirtazapine 30 mg at night
options.rationale: Switching between antidepressant classes is the right move for a non-responder with insomnia, but any antidepressant given without a mood stabilising agent can sustain or worsen a mixed state, so changing the molecule does not change the mechanism of harm. A two week review is also too long for someone with new self harm thoughts. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Mixed features are depressive and manic symptoms occurring at the same time, and they are missed constantly because clinicians look for elevated mood and find none, while the patient reports feeling worse and is assumed to need more antidepressant. The features to hunt for are psychomotor agitation, racing or crowded thoughts, pressured speech, irritability and a reduction in sleep in someone who still describes their mood as low. Atypical depressive features such as hypersomnia, increased appetite, weight gain and leaden paralysis, an early age of onset, a family history of bipolar disorder and a past episode of reduced sleep with increased activity all raise the prior probability of bipolarity before any drug is given. Antidepressant monotherapy in this setting can precipitate or prolong the mixed state, and mixed states carry a higher suicide rate than either pure pole, which is why the response is urgent rather than watchful. Management is withdrawal of the antidepressant with introduction of a mood stabilising agent, short term sedation if needed, and specialist involvement within days.
key_points: Low mood with agitation, racing thoughts and reduced sleep defines a mixed state
Absence of elevated mood does not exclude it and is the usual reason it is missed
Hypersomnia, weight gain and leaden paralysis flag possible bipolarity before treatment
Antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate or sustain the mixed state
Mixed states carry the highest suicide risk of any mood presentation
explanation.pearls: Ask every patient with depression about a past period of several days with reduced need for sleep and increased goal directed activity before writing the first antidepressant script, because a positive answer plus a first degree relative with bipolar disorder shifts the treatment from an antidepressant to a mood stabilising agent and is the single cheapest way to avoid this presentation.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Punching and shouting in the second half of the night in a veteran assumed to have trauma nightmares
stem: A 64-year-old veteran has shouted, kicked and punched in his sleep for eighteen months, bruising his wife last month. Episodes occur in the early hours; he wakes immediately lucid describing dreams of fighting an intruder, none involving his service. He has two years of constipation and cannot smell whether food has turned.

data_table.Examination: Reduced right arm swing, no resting tremor
data_table.History: Post-traumatic stress disorder treated ten years ago, checklist non-clinical

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start prazosin at night for the nightmares
options.rationale: Prazosin reduces trauma related nightmares in post-traumatic stress disorder, and that is the diagnosis being assumed here, but his checklist is in the non-clinical range and the dream content has nothing to do with his service. Treating the wrong condition also delays recognition of what the episodes actually predict. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for polysomnography and make the bedroom safe
options.rationale: Dream enactment in the second half of the night with immediate full alertness on waking and accurate dream recall is the pattern of rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, and the diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating loss of the normal muscle atonia during that sleep stage. Immediate safety measures matter because injury to the bed partner is the presenting harm. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Parasomnias)

options.text: Restart trauma focused psychological therapy
options.rationale: Recurrence of post-traumatic stress disorder would bring daytime re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal alongside the nightmares, and he has none of these. The dream content that he recalls is also unrelated to his deployments, which is the specific feature separating this from a trauma nightmare. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start quetiapine at night for the behaviour
options.rationale: Sedating him does not restore muscle atonia, and dopamine blocking agents are specifically hazardous in this group because many of these patients are in the prodrome of a synuclein disease and can develop severe sensitivity to antipsychotics. This is the option most likely to cause harm. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Parasomnias)

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to exclude seizures
options.rationale: Nocturnal frontal lobe seizures are the differential worth naming, and they produce brief stereotyped hyperkinetic episodes clustering many times a night with postictal confusion rather than a single coherent enacted dream with instant lucidity. A routine interictal recording would also be normal in both conditions. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Parasomnias)

explanation.summary: Rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder is the loss of the normal paralysis of that sleep stage, so the patient physically acts out dream content, typically defensive or violent, in the second half of the night when that sleep predominates. It is separated from non-rapid eye movement parasomnias such as sleep terrors by the timing, by immediate full orientation on waking and by detailed dream recall, and from trauma nightmares by dream content unrelated to the trauma and by the absence of daytime post-traumatic symptoms. Its importance is prognostic: the great majority of people with the idiopathic form eventually develop Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or multiple system atrophy, often more than a decade later, and subtle constipation, loss of smell and reduced arm swing are the early markers of that process. Management begins with making the bedroom safe, removing bedside furniture, padding the floor and considering separate beds, and melatonin is generally preferred to clonazepam as first line drug treatment in older people because of falls and sedation. How much of the prognosis to disclose is a genuine ethical question that is best negotiated with the patient rather than dumped or withheld.
key_points: Second half of the night, instant lucidity and matching dream recall define the disorder
Polysomnography confirms it by showing absent muscle atonia in rapid eye movement sleep
Constipation, loss of smell and reduced arm swing mark an evolving synuclein disease
Bedroom safety measures come before any drug treatment
Dopamine blocking drugs risk severe sensitivity reactions in this group
explanation.pearls: Melatonin at doses of 2 to 10 mg at night is preferred over clonazepam 0.5 mg in this population, because clonazepam worsens the falls, daytime sedation and obstructive sleep apnoea that older patients already carry, while the injury risk being treated is to the bed partner as much as to the patient.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: New online gambling debt and uncharacteristic sexual behaviour in a man treated for restless legs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58 year old plumber who attends with his wife. She has discovered sixty thousand dollars of debt accumulated through online sports betting over the past eight months, on accounts he opened without telling her.

He has never gambled before, not even on a work sweepstake, and he is tearful and ashamed in the room. She adds that he has been shopping compulsively online and that his sexual demands have changed in a way she finds distressing. He says he has tried to stop several times and cannot. He denies feeling elated or unusually confident, says he sleeps his usual seven hours and needs them, and has taken no new substances. His pramipexole for restless legs was increased six months ago because the symptoms had spread to his arms, and he also takes atorvastatin.

data_table.Examination: Dysphoric and tearful, normal rate of speech, no flight of ideas, no grandiosity, no psychotic features, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 29 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), ferritin 58 micrograms/L (30-300), liver function and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer him to a gambling counselling service and continue his current treatment
options.rationale: Counselling is part of the answer but leaving the drug unchanged leaves the cause in place, and psychological treatment alone performs poorly while dopaminergic stimulation continues. This would be correct if the behaviour predated the prescription. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start naltrexone daily and refer him to a gambling counselling service
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists have modest evidence in primary gambling disorder and are worth considering there, but adding a second drug to manage the adverse effect of a first one, while that first drug continues, is the wrong order of operations. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start sodium valproate and refer him to a gambling counselling service
options.rationale: A mood stabiliser presumes a manic or hypomanic episode, and he has normal sleep, no elevated mood, no grandiosity and preserved insight with genuine distress about the behaviour, none of which fits mania. The behaviour is also confined to reward seeking rather than being part of a global change in drive. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Stop the pramipexole abruptly tonight and refer him to a gambling counselling service
options.rationale: Ceasing the drug is right but doing it abruptly risks dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome, an unpleasant and sometimes prolonged state of anxiety, panic, pain, sweating and drug craving that does not respond to other dopaminergic agents. The difference from the correct answer is the rate, not the direction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Withdraw the pramipexole slowly and refer him to a gambling counselling service
options.rationale: New onset gambling, compulsive shopping and hypersexuality beginning after a dose increase of a dopamine agonist is a recognised and dose related adverse effect mediated by stimulation of mesolimbic receptors, and the behaviour usually resolves when the drug is withdrawn. A gradual reduction avoids the withdrawal syndrome, and the restless legs are then reassessed with iron studies and an alternative agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Impulse control disorders complicate dopamine agonist treatment in a substantial minority of patients, with reported rates of around one in six in Parkinson disease and appreciable rates when the same drugs are used at lower doses for restless legs syndrome. The four classic behaviours are pathological gambling, compulsive shopping, hypersexuality and binge eating, and they are dose related, more common in younger men with a personal or family history of substance use, and driven by stimulation of receptors in the mesolimbic reward pathway. Patients almost never volunteer them, both from shame and because they do not connect the behaviour to a tablet prescribed for their legs, so the question has to be asked directly and repeatedly, and the warning has to be given to the patient and to a partner when the drug is started. The behaviour usually remits on withdrawal but the withdrawal itself must be gradual because abrupt cessation causes a distinct agonist withdrawal syndrome. In restless legs specifically, dopamine agonists also cause augmentation, in which symptoms start earlier in the day and spread to the arms, which is why alpha 2 delta ligands such as gabapentin have displaced them as first line treatment.
key_points: Gambling, shopping, hypersexuality and binge eating are the four classic behaviours
The effect is dose related and occurs at restless legs doses, not only Parkinson doses
Patients rarely volunteer it, so it must be asked about directly at each review
Withdrawal must be gradual to avoid dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome
Behaviour usually remits once the agonist is withdrawn
explanation.pearls: Symptoms of restless legs that start earlier in the day and spread from the legs to the arms, as his did before the dose was increased, are augmentation rather than disease progression, and increasing the agonist in response is the error that both worsens augmentation and raises the impulse control risk; the correct response is to check ferritin, aiming above 75 micrograms/L, and to move to an alpha 2 delta ligand.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Silence at school with loud fluent speech at home in a six year old in her second year of schooling
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 year old girl whose teacher has told her parents she may need an autism assessment. In fourteen months at school she has never spoken a word to a teacher or to another child, communicating by nodding, pointing and writing.

At home she talks constantly, argues with her older brother, invents elaborate games with her cousins and does impressions of her teacher that make the family laugh. Her mother reports that she chats in the car right up to the school gate and then stops. In the consulting room she sits close to her mother, makes eye contact with you, smiles at a joke, and freezes and looks at the floor when you ask her a direct question. She reached all her language milestones on time and has no repetitive behaviours, no restricted interests and no sensory aversions. Her father describes himself as having been painfully shy as a boy.

data_table.Examination: Reciprocal eye contact and shared smiling with her mother and with the examiner, imaginative play observed with the toys, freezing and averted gaze on direct questioning, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Audiology assessment normal bilaterally, speech pathology screen of receptive language age appropriate, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for a formal autism spectrum assessment and review her after the report
options.rationale: This is the referral the school has asked for and it is the wrong one: autism requires persistent deficits in social communication across contexts, and she shows reciprocal eye contact, shared enjoyment, imaginative play and fluent conversational speech at home and in the room. The situational nature of the silence is what separates the two. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer for a speech pathology assessment of expressive language delay
options.rationale: An expressive language disorder would affect speech in every setting including the home, and her speech there is fluent, complex and age appropriate, with normal milestones and a normal receptive screen. Speech pathology may still join the school program, but not to assess a delay that is not present. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne clinical practice guideline

options.text: Refer for a behavioural program using graded speaking exposure at school
options.rationale: Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where speaking is expected, despite speaking normally elsewhere, for more than a month beyond the first year of school, is an anxiety disorder, and the treatment is a graded behavioural program run with the school that moves from non-verbal responses through whispering to single words with one adult and then widens the circle. Starting behavioural treatment early matters because the silence becomes self reinforcing across school years. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start fluoxetine and review her speaking at school in eight weeks
options.rationale: A serotonin reuptake inhibitor has evidence in this condition but is reserved for children who do not respond to an adequate behavioural program or whose impairment is severe, because the behavioural approach works in most children without drug exposure at this age. Starting here reverses the order. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Advise the school to avoid asking her direct questions for a term
options.rationale: Removing the pressure to speak feels kind and is a reasonable first step within a structured program, but as the whole plan it is avoidance, and accommodation without graded exposure predicts persistence into later school years. The distinction from the correct answer is that exposure is reduced temporarily in order to be rebuilt, not abandoned. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is classified with the anxiety disorders and affects roughly one child in one hundred and forty, with onset typically before the age of five and a delay to diagnosis often measured in years. It is regularly misread as autism, as shyness, as oppositional behaviour or as a language disorder, and the discriminating question is always whether the child speaks normally in any setting: fluent conversational speech at home with reciprocal social engagement excludes both autism and an expressive language disorder. Comorbid social anxiety disorder is present in most cases and a family history of anxiety is common. Treatment is behavioural, using stimulus fading and graded exposure delivered in the school with the teacher as a co-therapist, and typically progresses from non-verbal responses to whispered single words with one trusted adult before widening to peers and the classroom. Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are added for children who do not respond or whose impairment is severe, and outcomes are substantially better when treatment begins in the first years of school.
key_points: Speech is normal in at least one setting, which rules out a language disorder
Reciprocal social engagement and imaginative play argue strongly against autism
Duration must exceed one month and must not be limited to the first month of school
Graded exposure with the school is first line and works in most young children
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are reserved for non-response or severe impairment
explanation.pearls: The most useful single question to a parent is whether the child speaks freely to anyone at all, because a child who converses fluently at home has by definition preserved language and social reciprocity, and the answer redirects the referral from a twelve month autism assessment waiting list to a behavioural program that can start next week.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Abrupt onset of complex tic like movements over two days in a seventeen year old with no childhood history
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar assessing a 17 year old student whose movements began over two days six weeks ago and have escalated since. She flings both arms outwards, slaps her own sternum, and shouts obscene phrases in an accent that is not her own.

Her mother says the phrases are word for word the ones used by a creator she watches for several hours each night on a video sharing platform. The movements are continuous through the consultation, worsen markedly when the medical students enter, and stop entirely for around a minute when you ask her to copy a two handed tapping rhythm. She reports no warning sensation before a movement and says she cannot hold them back even briefly. She had no tics as a child, and an anxiety disorder was diagnosed a year ago.

data_table.Examination: Complex bilateral flinging movements with self striking, entrainment of the movements to an imposed tapping rhythm, no stereotyped simple motor tics, normal tone power and reflexes, no chorea
data_table.Investigations: Copper studies and caeruloplasmin within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start aripiprazole and review the frequency of the movements in four weeks
options.rationale: Dopamine blocking agents are first line for tics of Tourette syndrome, and that is the diagnosis being assumed, but the features here run against it: onset in adolescence over two days, complex movements from the outset, absent premonitory urge, no capacity for suppression and entrainment on distraction. Treating with an antipsychotic exposes her to weight gain and akathisia for no expected benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Explain the positive diagnosis and refer for tailored psychological therapy
options.rationale: Abrupt onset, absence of a premonitory urge, inability to suppress, entrainment to an imposed rhythm, worsening under observation and phrases copied from media exposure are positive signs of a functional movement disorder rather than diagnostic exclusions. Explaining the mechanism as a genuine disorder of movement control that is reversible, rather than describing what she does not have, is itself the first and most effective step of treatment. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start clonidine and review the frequency of the movements in four weeks
options.rationale: Clonidine is used for tics with comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and has a gentler adverse effect profile than antipsychotics, but it shares the same wrong premise as the other drug option and adds sedation and postural hypotension in a young woman who drives. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and review her with the result
options.rationale: Imaging is appropriate when the examination is abnormal in other domains or the movements are unilateral or fixed, and hers are not, with normal tone, power, reflexes and no chorea. Investigating to exclude rather than diagnosing positively prolongs uncertainty, and a normal scan rarely reassures a patient who has been told the cause is unknown. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer for botulinum toxin injection to the most affected muscle groups
options.rationale: Botulinum toxin is used for focal dystonia and for a small number of severe, localised and injurious tics, whereas her movements are generalised, variable and change from consultation to consultation. Injecting a shifting pattern of muscles cannot work and reinforces a structural explanation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Functional tic like behaviours rose sharply among adolescent girls from 2020 and are now a common presentation to paediatric and neurology clinics, frequently in patients with heavy exposure to social media content featuring tics. They are distinguished from Tourette syndrome by abrupt onset after childhood rather than gradual onset between five and seven years, complex rather than simple movements from the beginning, absence of the premonitory urge that patients with tics describe vividly, absence of any suppressibility, a rostrocaudal pattern that does not fit the usual face to limb progression, and entrainment or distractibility on examination. Coprolalia is common in the functional group and rare in Tourette syndrome, which inverts the usual assumption. Treatment is a clear positive explanation, reduction of the reinforcing exposure, and a tailored psychological therapy addressing the frequently comorbid anxiety, with dopamine blocking drugs specifically unhelpful. Outcomes are good when the diagnosis is delivered confidently and early, and poor when the patient is investigated repeatedly and left without an explanation.
key_points: Abrupt adolescent onset with complex movements argues against Tourette syndrome
Absent premonitory urge and absent suppressibility are key positive discriminators
Entrainment to an imposed rhythm is a positive functional sign, not an exclusion
Coprolalia is common in functional presentations and rare in Tourette syndrome
Antipsychotics and botulinum toxin are ineffective and reinforce the wrong model
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether there is a build up of tension or an itch like sensation relieved by performing the movement: that premonitory urge is reported by over ninety per cent of adolescents with Tourette syndrome and almost never in functional tic like behaviours, and a single clear negative answer is worth more than a magnetic resonance scan.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Nightmares and hypervigilance in a man on a bridging visa awaiting a protection decision with no income
stem:
You are the general practitioner at a community health service seeing a 34 year old man who arrived by boat six years ago and has been on a bridging visa for three years. A professional interpreter attends in person at his request.

He describes nightmares most nights, waking sweating, intrusive daytime memories of being beaten in custody in his home country, startling at doors closing, and avoiding the news. He has no work rights at present, is sleeping on a friend's couch after being asked to leave his room, and has not seen his wife and daughter for six years. His protection application is awaiting a decision and he says he cannot think past it. He denies thoughts of suicide, has no psychotic symptoms and asks you for sleeping tablets so that he can rest.

data_table.Examination: Guarded and watchful, startles when the door closes, well oriented, no psychotic features, healed scarring over both shins
data_table.Investigations: Vitamin D 38 nmol/L (50-150), haemoglobin 141 g/L (130-175), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.3 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start diazepam at night and review his sleep in two weeks with the interpreter
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are specifically discouraged in post-traumatic stress disorder because they do not improve core symptoms, impair the extinction learning on which trauma focused therapy depends, and carry dependence risk in a population with high rates of chronic distress. Meeting the request as made would feel responsive and would set treatment back. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder

options.text: Begin trauma focused exposure therapy at weekly sessions without further delay
options.rationale: Trauma focused therapy is the first line treatment for this disorder and will be the centre of his care, but it works on the premise that the danger is in the past, and he faces an unresolved removal decision, housing loss and separation from his family. Starting exposure work before those are stabilised commonly leads to dropout and deterioration. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder

options.text: Start mirtazapine at night and review his sleep in two weeks with the interpreter
options.rationale: Antidepressants are a reasonable second line option for this disorder when psychological treatment is unavailable or declined, but prescribing alone as the response to a presentation dominated by homelessness, destitution and an unresolved visa leaves the drivers of the distress untouched. Medication may still be added once the social situation is addressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Defer any mental health treatment until his visa application has been decided
options.rationale: Waiting for legal resolution can mean waiting years and abandons him during the period of greatest risk, and stabilisation work, sleep interventions and practical support are all deliverable now. The correct answer sequences treatment rather than withholding it. (Source: Victorian Foundation for Survivors of Torture)
source_refs: Victorian Foundation for Survivors of Torture

options.text: Refer to a specialist torture and trauma service and address housing and income
options.rationale: Survivors of torture with ongoing insecurity are treated in phases, beginning with safety, stabilisation and the practical determinants that sustain the hyperarousal, delivered by a service with interpreters and expertise in the medico-legal context, before trauma processing work begins. Housing, income support and assistance with the visa process are clinical interventions in this population rather than social extras. (Source: Victorian Foundation for Survivors of Torture)
source_refs: Victorian Foundation for Survivors of Torture

explanation.summary: Rates of post-traumatic stress disorder and depression in people seeking asylum in Australia are several times those of the general population, and the strongest predictors of ongoing symptoms are not the severity of past torture but the current post-migration living difficulties: visa insecurity, family separation, lack of work rights, and unstable housing. That finding is what drives the phased treatment model, in which safety, stabilisation, sleep, pain and the practical determinants are addressed first, and trauma focused processing follows once the environment is stable enough to support it. Specialist torture and trauma services exist in every state and territory and provide counselling, complex case work, medico-legal reports and interpreter services at no cost. Benzodiazepines are avoided, and where medication is needed a serotonergic antidepressant is preferred. A professional interpreter is used rather than a family member or bilingual friend, both for accuracy and because disclosure of torture and sexual violence is inhibited when the interpreter belongs to the patient's community.
key_points: Post-migration living difficulties predict symptom persistence more strongly than past trauma
Phased treatment puts safety and stabilisation before trauma processing
Specialist torture and trauma services are free and available in every state
Benzodiazepines impair extinction learning and are avoided in this disorder
Use a professional interpreter rather than a family member or community friend
explanation.pearls: Ask about the visa stage explicitly at every visit: the weeks around a refusal or a tribunal hearing carry a sharp rise in self harm in this population, and knowing the date of a pending decision lets you schedule a review for that week rather than discovering the deterioration afterwards.

sources.label: Victorian Foundation for Survivors of Torture
Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder

subtopic_detail: A written advance care directive naming a preferred antipsychotic during a NSW involuntary admission
stem: A 38-year-old carpenter with bipolar disorder is an involuntary patient in NSW. He has not slept for four nights, speaks continuously, spent most of his savings and refuses food, fluids and medication. Eight months ago, while well, he signed an advance care directive declining olanzapine after gaining 18 kg, accepting aripiprazole, and naming his sister as designated carer. Aripiprazole is suitable and available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 bpm, BP 142/84 mmHg, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 146 mmol/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L, creatine kinase 380 units/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Treat with the agent he named and notify his designated carer now
options.rationale: The directive is not binding on treatment given under the Mental Health Act 2007, but it should be taken into account, and here there is nothing to weigh against it: the named agent is clinically appropriate and on the ward. His sister is entitled to be told he has been detained, within 24 hours, and not contacting her is one of the commonest after hours omissions. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives; NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives
NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers

options.text: Treat with olanzapine, since his directive is not binding while unwell
options.rationale: It is true that a NSW directive cannot override treatment under the Act, but that is not permission to ignore it, and 18 kg of weight gain is a substantive reason recorded while he had capacity. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives

options.text: Apply to the Tribunal for a ruling before giving any antipsychotic medication
options.rationale: The Tribunal holds mental health inquiries and reviews orders; it does not authorise routine medication choices, and his sodium, pulse and creatine kinase make days of delay dangerous. (Source: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: involuntary patient orders)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Withhold all antipsychotic medication because he is currently refusing treatment
options.rationale: Current refusal is why he is an involuntary patient. Four nights without sleep, hypernatraemia and a rising creatine kinase carry risks of delirium, rhabdomyolysis and collapse. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Treat with olanzapine and record your reasons for departing from it
options.rationale: Documenting reasoning is right in principle, but this option is procedurally tidy and substantively wrong: there is no reason to depart when the named agent is appropriate and available. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives

explanation.summary: A NSW advance care directive is not the Victorian advance statement of preferences. There is no NSW statute on directives, no statutory duty to give written reasons for departing from one, and no nominated support person. What exists is a common law document that should be taken into account during treatment under the Mental Health Act 2007, and the designated carer, who has statutory entitlements to notice and information, including notice that the person has been detained, within 24 hours. Where the preferred agent is clinically appropriate and available there is nothing to weigh against it, and honouring a preference recorded while well costs nothing and improves engagement after discharge. Weight gain on olanzapine is not a trivial objection: it is the commonest reason patients stop antipsychotics.
key_points: A NSW directive is considered, not binding, during compulsory treatment.
A designated carer must be told of detention within 24 hours.
The carer is informed and involved but does not consent to treatment.
A clinically appropriate, available preferred drug leaves no reason to depart.
explanation.pearls: Check the sodium and creatine kinase in acute mania before anything else: several days without sleeping, eating or drinking produces dehydration, hypernatraemia and a rising creatine kinase from sustained motor activity, and it is those physical consequences that make delay dangerous.

sources.label: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives
NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: A fifth emergency presentation this year with superficial forearm cuts after a relationship ended
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 24 year old woman who arrived at eleven at night with parallel superficial cuts to the left forearm made with a craft knife after her partner ended their relationship. None require suturing and there is no tendon or nerve involvement.

This is her fifth presentation in twelve months. She has been attending a dialectical behaviour therapy program for five months and her next skills group is in three days; her therapist's crisis plan is scanned into the record and names an after hours number and two agreed strategies. She is not intoxicated and her observations are normal. Over the ninety minutes since arrival she has become notably calmer, has eaten a sandwich and now says she does not want to die and has no plan. She asks to be admitted so that she will be safe. Her two previous admissions were both complicated by escalating self injury on the ward.

data_table.Examination: Six superficial parallel forearm lacerations with no deep structure involvement, settled and coherent, no depressive psychomotor change, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Breath alcohol zero, paracetamol not detected, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit her overnight to the short stay unit and review her with the team tomorrow
options.rationale: A short stay admission looks like a compromise but still removes her from the environment in which the skills are meant to be used, and it teaches that distress at eleven at night is resolved by a bed. It is appropriate when intoxication, a medical issue or genuine uncertainty about intent needs a few hours to settle. (Source: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Admit her to the psychiatric unit for a period of safety and daily review there
options.rationale: Inpatient admission for this presentation is associated with escalating self injury, regression and prolonged stays, which is precisely the pattern her own two previous admissions followed. It is reserved for a comorbid depressive or psychotic episode or a sustained and serious suicidal crisis that cannot be managed in the community. (Source: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Follow her existing crisis plan and arrange therapist contact within two days
options.rationale: Self injury in this disorder is usually an attempt to regulate unbearable affect rather than an attempt to die, and her distress has already settled with time, food and containment, so the intervention that helps is validating the distress, treating the wounds, and reactivating the plan her own therapist wrote with her. Bringing forward contact with the existing team maintains continuity, which is the single factor most associated with reduced self harm over time. (Source: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

options.text: Give a dose of quetiapine and review her again in the department in two hours
options.rationale: Sedation has a limited role for severe acute distress that does not settle, but she has already settled without it, and drug treatment is not recommended as routine management of this disorder or of its crises. Repeated as-needed sedation in the department establishes a pattern that is hard to unwind. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Discharge her with advice to attend her next scheduled session in three days
options.rationale: Discharge is right and admission is wrong, but sending her out with no contact arranged for three days abandons the highest risk window, which is the days immediately following an episode of self harm. The difference from the correct answer is the active bridging contact rather than the destination. (Source: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder)
source_refs: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder carries a lifetime suicide rate of around one in twenty five, so the risk is real, but the evidence consistently shows that inpatient admission after an episode of non-suicidal self injury does not reduce that risk and frequently worsens short term behaviour through regression and reinforcement. Australian guidance therefore favours brief, structured, validating emergency contact with rapid return to the existing community treatment, and explicitly discourages both admission and routine drug treatment. The clinician's task is to distinguish the habitual pattern of affect regulating self injury from a superimposed depressive episode, a psychotic episode or a genuine suicidal crisis, since those do change the disposition. Attitudes matter measurably here: pejorative framing in the notes and in handover predicts worse engagement and more presentations. The strongest protective factor available in the emergency department is continuity, which means talking to the team that already knows her rather than starting a parallel plan.
key_points: Self injury in this disorder usually regulates affect rather than expressing intent to die
Admission after self injury does not reduce suicide risk and often escalates behaviour
Drug treatment is not recommended as routine management of the disorder or its crises
Reactivating the existing crisis plan and team preserves continuity
Look actively for a comorbid depressive or psychotic episode, which changes the plan
explanation.pearls: The days immediately after an episode of self harm carry the highest short term suicide risk of any point in the illness, so whatever the disposition, arrange an actual contact within forty eight hours rather than relying on an already scheduled appointment, and make it a named person rather than a service number.

sources.label: National Health and Medical Research Council: Clinical practice guideline for the management of borderline personality disorder
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Low mood and worthlessness in a woman with metastatic cancer whose prognosis is measured in weeks
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 61 year old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer on the palliative care ward. The treating team estimates her prognosis at four to eight weeks and has asked about depression.

She describes three weeks of low mood present every day and all day, and says nothing lifts it, including a visit from her grandchildren which she previously looked forward to and which she found she could not enjoy at all. She says she has always been the strong one in the family and is now nothing, and that everyone would be better off if it were over. Her attention is intact, she recalls the ward routine accurately and her mental state has not fluctuated across two assessments on different days. Her pain is well controlled on a stable opioid dose and her calcium and sodium are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Cachectic, alert and fully oriented, months of the year backwards completed without error, no asterixis, affect uniformly flat with no reactivity
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (less than 20), haemoglobin 102 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
