options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review her mood in four weeks
options.rationale: A serotonin reuptake inhibitor is the standard choice for a depressive episode, but the four to six weeks it needs to work is most or all of her remaining life. Time to benefit, rather than efficacy, is what disqualifies it here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Start mirtazapine 15 mg at night and review her mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is attractive in this setting because it also helps nausea, appetite and sleep, and it is a good choice when the prognosis is months. Its effect on mood still takes two to four weeks, which is the specific reason it loses to a faster acting agent when the prognosis is weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy and review her mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Psychological therapy retains a place in palliative care, but structured cognitive behavioural therapy requires a course of sessions and a level of energy and concentration she is unlikely to sustain. Dignity focused and meaning centred brief therapies are the ones adapted for this timeframe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Start methylphenidate in the morning and review her mood in three days
options.rationale: Pervasive anhedonia that persists through a visit she would normally enjoy, with worthlessness that is not proportionate to her illness, marks a depressive episode rather than sadness or demoralisation, and with a prognosis of weeks the treatment chosen must act within days. Psychostimulants improve mood, energy and opioid related sedation within two to three days, which is why they are recommended in this specific situation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Start olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and review her mood in three days
options.rationale: Low dose olanzapine is used in palliative care for nausea and for hypoactive delirium, and delirium is the differential worth taking seriously in a cachectic inpatient, but her attention is intact, she has no fluctuation across two assessments and there is no asterixis or metabolic abnormality. Treating the wrong syndrome costs her the weeks she has. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Depression is present in roughly one in six patients with advanced cancer and is under-treated because the somatic criteria that usually support the diagnosis, such as fatigue, anorexia and weight loss, are all produced by the disease itself. The cognitive and affective criteria carry the diagnostic weight instead: pervasive anhedonia that does not lift for anything, worthlessness or guilt out of proportion to circumstances, hopelessness that extends beyond the prognosis, and a wish to die that is not simply a wish for the dying to be over. Demoralisation, with loss of meaning and purpose but preserved capacity for pleasure, and hypoactive delirium, with inattention and fluctuation, are the two conditions most often mistaken for it and both require different treatment. When the prognosis is months, standard antidepressants are used, and mirtazapine is often favoured for its effect on nausea, appetite and sleep. When the prognosis is weeks, psychostimulants are recommended because they act within days, and they also counteract opioid induced sedation.
key_points: Somatic criteria are unreliable in advanced cancer; use the cognitive and affective ones
Pervasive anhedonia that does not lift for anything is the most useful single sign
Demoralisation preserves the capacity for pleasure; hypoactive delirium has inattention
Prognosis of months favours a standard antidepressant such as mirtazapine
Prognosis of weeks favours a psychostimulant because benefit appears within days
explanation.pearls: The single most discriminating question in this population is whether anything at all still gives pleasure, even briefly: preserved reactivity to a grandchild or a favourite piece of music points to demoralisation or sadness, while a complete and unbroken loss of that capacity in someone with intact attention points to a depressive episode worth treating within days.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Deciding disposition after a first impulsive ingestion when a screening instrument returns a low category
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 22 year old apprentice electrician who swallowed fourteen paracetamol tablets in one go six hours ago, twenty minutes after his partner ended their relationship. He told his flatmate within the hour and they drove him in.

His timed paracetamol concentration sits below the treatment line and his liver enzymes and coagulation profile are normal, so the toxicology registrar has cleared him medically and no antidote is required. He says he did it without thinking, is embarrassed, does not want to die now and has no plan. He has never presented before, takes no medication, does not drink or use drugs, and his two flatmates are in the waiting room and have offered to stay with him. The department's structured screening instrument has returned a score in its lowest category, and the consultant asks you to discharge him on that basis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and engaged, no psychomotor change, affect reactive, no psychotic features, no self inflicted wounds
data_table.Investigations: Timed paracetamol concentration below the nomogram treatment line, alanine aminotransferase 24 units/L (5-35), international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8-1.2), electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge him with the low risk score documented and advice to see his own doctor
options.rationale: Using a categorical score to authorise discharge is the specific practice that Australian guidance advises against, because these instruments have low positive and negative predictive value at the individual level and most people who go on to die by suicide were categorised as low or moderate risk. Documenting the score gives the appearance of assessment without the content of one. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm

options.text: Admit him to the psychiatric unit because any overdose indicates a high level of risk
options.rationale: Treating every ingestion as requiring admission is the mirror image error and exposes a young man with a first impulsive act, no ongoing intent and present social support to the iatrogenic harms of an admission. Admission is driven by mental state, ongoing intent and the absence of support, none of which apply here. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm

options.text: Repeat the screening instrument in two hours and decide disposition on that score
options.rationale: Repeating an instrument that was never designed to predict individual outcomes does not improve its predictive performance, and the change in score over two hours reflects how settled he feels rather than what he needs. The problem is the use being made of the tool, not the timing of its administration. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm

options.text: Discharge him with a referral letter to a private psychologist and no further follow up
options.rationale: A referral letter transfers responsibility without establishing contact, and uptake of an unassisted referral after self harm is poor, with most patients never attending. The first weeks after an act of self harm are when the repetition risk is concentrated, so the arrangement has to be active rather than nominal. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm

options.text: Complete a collaborative safety plan with means restriction and follow up in a week
options.rationale: Disposition after self harm is decided by a needs based assessment and a plan built with the patient, not by a risk category, and the interventions with actual evidence of benefit are a written safety plan naming warning signs, coping strategies and people to contact, restriction of access to means, and an arranged contact within days. Involving the flatmates in the means restriction turns the available support into something concrete. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm

explanation.summary: Categorical suicide risk stratification into low, medium and high has been progressively abandoned in Australian practice because its predictive performance at the individual level is close to chance, and because the majority of people who die by suicide were rated below the highest category at their last contact. What replaces it is a needs based formulation that describes the person's current state, the drivers of the act, what has changed since, what supports exist, and what modifiable factors can be acted on now. Safety planning, in which the patient and clinician jointly write down warning signs, internal coping strategies, people and places that provide distraction, contacts for help and steps to make the environment safer, is one of the few interventions with randomised evidence of reduced repetition. Means restriction is the other, and for paracetamol that means limiting quantities kept at home, since impulsive ingestion of what is in the cupboard is the dominant pattern. The period immediately after discharge from an emergency department following self harm carries a markedly elevated risk, which is why arranged contact within days, rather than an unassisted referral, is the standard.
key_points: Categorical risk stratification does not predict individual outcomes and should not set disposition
A needs based formulation and a jointly written safety plan replace it
Means restriction has randomised evidence of benefit and applies to household paracetamol
Arrange an active contact within days rather than sending an unassisted referral
Admission is driven by mental state, ongoing intent and absent support, not by the act itself
explanation.pearls: Paracetamol deserves specific means restriction counselling in Australia because ingestion is usually impulsive and uses whatever is in the house: reducing the quantity stored at home is the single most effective environmental intervention, and the same conversation should cover securing any firearms and limiting stored medication for everyone in the household.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm
Australian Institute of Health and Welfare: Suicide and self-harm monitoring

subtopic_detail: Choosing a mood stabiliser for a young woman when the current agent carries teratogenic risk
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24 year old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been well for eighteen months on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, started during an inpatient admission for mania two years ago.

She has a new partner, uses no contraception, and tells you she would like to start a family within the next year or two. She has had one manic episode and two depressive episodes, has never self harmed, and has had no episodes since valproate was started. Her full blood count, liver function and weight are stable, and she takes no other medication. She asks whether she can simply stop the valproate when she decides to try to conceive.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood, normal speech and thought form, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, body mass index 26 kg/m2, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the valproate dose now and continue at that level, on the basis that the risk is dose dependent
options.rationale: The risk is indeed dose related but remains substantially above background at any effective dose, so dose reduction trades relapse risk for a residual teratogenic risk. It does not resolve the problem and leaves her on the drug. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy

options.text: Continue valproate with high dose folate, and stop the valproate as soon as a pregnancy test becomes positive
options.rationale: Neural tube closure is complete by day 28 after conception, so stopping at a positive test is nearly always too late, and folate does not mitigate the malformation risk of this drug. This plan describes the exposure pattern the pregnancy prevention requirements exist to stop. (Source: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy)
source_refs: Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy

options.text: Continue valproate with a long acting reversible contraceptive, and revisit the medication when she actively conceives
options.rationale: Reliable contraception is necessary while she remains on the drug, but deferring the switch means it must occur under time pressure, and a rushed change risks relapse in early pregnancy. Planned switching while well is the whole purpose of the pre pregnancy conversation. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Stop valproate now without a replacement, and monitor her mood monthly given eighteen months of stability
options.rationale: Withdrawal of a mood stabiliser in bipolar I disorder carries a high relapse rate within the first year, and a manic relapse in pregnancy or the postpartum period is itself dangerous. Stability on treatment is not evidence that treatment is unnecessary. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Plan a cross taper from valproate to an alternative mood stabiliser now, with reliable contraception during the change
options.rationale: Valproate carries a roughly 10 percent risk of major congenital malformation and impairs neurodevelopment in around a third of exposed children, and the damage occurs in the first weeks before most pregnancies are recognised. Switching in a planned way while she is well and protected is far safer than stopping abruptly at a positive test. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is the most teratogenic of the commonly used psychotropic drugs, with a major malformation rate of around 10 percent and neurodevelopmental impairment including reduced verbal intelligence and an increased rate of autism spectrum disorder in roughly a third of exposed children. Australian regulatory advice is that it should not be used in women or girls of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated, and then only with a documented discussion and effective contraception. The practical failure is timing: organogenesis is largely complete before a woman knows she is pregnant, so a plan that depends on stopping at a positive test does not work. In a woman who is well and planning a family, the safer sequence is a planned cross taper under contraceptive cover to an agent with better pregnancy data, such as lamotrigine for a predominantly depressive course or an atypical antipsychotic such as quetiapine, with lithium considered where its benefit outweighs a small cardiac risk.
key_points: Valproate causes major malformation in around 10 percent of exposed pregnancies
Neurodevelopmental harm affects roughly a third of exposed children
Stopping at a positive pregnancy test is too late for neural tube closure
Switch in a planned way while well and under contraceptive cover
Do not stop a mood stabiliser without a replacement in bipolar I disorder
explanation.pearls: Document the pregnancy prevention discussion and the contraceptive method at every review for any woman of childbearing potential taking valproate, since the Australian requirement is a recorded annual discussion, and the absence of that documentation is what turns a foreseeable harm into an indefensible one.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline
Therapeutic Goods Administration: Valproate and pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Fever and tachycardia in the third week of titration with a normal neutrophil count
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on an inpatient unit reviewing a 27 year old man who is on day 19 of clozapine titration for treatment resistant schizophrenia, now taking 250 mg daily.

Over the past two days he has felt feverish and tired, with a temperature of 38.3 degrees Celsius, pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and SpO2 97 percent on room air. He has no cough, no dysuria, no diarrhoea and no rash, and his chest is clear. His neutrophil count is 4.8 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 96 mg/L, and troponin is elevated at six times the upper reference limit. An electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with no ST elevation. His psychotic symptoms have improved substantially on this dose.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no murmur, no rash, no focal infective source, mild ankle oedema
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 4.8 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), troponin six times the upper reference limit, electrocardiogram showing sinus tachycardia, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the clozapine at a reduced dose and repeat the troponin and C reactive protein in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Myocarditis from this drug is a hypersensitivity phenomenon rather than a dose dependent toxicity, so dose reduction does not remove the stimulus. Forty eight hours of continued exposure is how a reversible myocarditis becomes a cardiomyopathy. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

options.text: Cease the clozapine immediately and start filgrastim, treating this as a haematological adverse reaction
options.rationale: His neutrophil count is entirely normal, so there is no agranulocytosis to treat, and filgrastim carries its own risks. The fixation on the blood count is the trap, because monitoring on this drug is so strongly associated with neutrophils. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

options.text: Cease the clozapine immediately and arrange urgent echocardiography with cardiology review
options.rationale: Fever, tachycardia, a raised C reactive protein and a rising troponin in the second to fourth week of titration describe clozapine induced myocarditis, which is the commonest cause of early death on this drug. The drug is stopped at once because continuing it during myocarditis can be fatal. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

options.text: Continue the clozapine and treat with intravenous antibiotics for a presumed occult bacterial infection
options.rationale: There is no infective source and the troponin rise is not explained by sepsis, so treating for infection alone leaves an inflamed myocardium exposed to the causative drug. Cultures should still be taken, but the drug cannot continue while this is the leading diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

options.text: Continue the clozapine and prescribe regular paracetamol, treating this as the benign fever seen during titration
options.rationale: A benign transient fever does occur during titration, but it is not accompanied by a troponin rise, and using that label here discards the one result that distinguishes the two. The troponin is the discriminating investigation. (Source: RANZCP: Clozapine treatment guidance)

explanation.summary: Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with established efficacy in treatment resistant schizophrenia, but it carries a distinctive set of serious adverse effects and the monitoring culture around it is dominated by neutrophil counts. Myocarditis is the complication most likely to be missed, typically occurring between days 14 and 28 of treatment, and Australian units generally monitor troponin and C reactive protein weekly through the first month for this reason. The presentation is non specific, with fever, tachycardia, fatigue, breathlessness or flu like symptoms, which is why isolated fever during titration is so often attributed to the known benign transient fever. A troponin above twice the upper reference limit, or a C reactive protein above 100 mg/L, prompts immediate cessation and echocardiography. Rechallenge after confirmed myocarditis is possible in specialist centres but requires cardiology involvement and very slow titration.
key_points: Myocarditis typically appears between days 14 and 28 of treatment
Weekly troponin and C reactive protein through the first month detect it
Symptoms are non specific and overlap with benign titration fever
Cease the drug immediately and arrange echocardiography
A normal neutrophil count does not exclude a serious adverse reaction
explanation.pearls: Ask about any new fever or breathlessness at every review in the first six weeks and check the troponin rather than relying on the patient volunteering symptoms, because sedation and negative symptoms both blunt reporting and the early presentation can be no more than tiredness and a resting pulse that has risen by 20 beats per minute.

subtopic_detail: Selecting cessation pharmacotherapy for a heavy smoker with stable treated depression
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 47 year old man who wants to stop smoking. He has smoked 25 cigarettes daily for thirty years and lights his first cigarette within five minutes of waking.

He has recurrent major depressive disorder, well controlled on sertraline 100 mg daily for three years, with no episode in that time and no suicidal ideation ever. He has tried nicotine patches alone twice and relapsed within a fortnight both times. He has no seizure history, no eating disorder, drinks four standard drinks weekly, and his renal function is normal. He asks which medication gives him the best chance and whether any of them are risky given his depression.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychomotor change, chest clear, no signs of chronic lung disease
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy would you first recommend?

options.text: Behavioural support alone through a telephone quit service, with pharmacotherapy reserved for a later attempt
options.rationale: Counselling roughly doubles quit rates but combining it with pharmacotherapy is substantially better still, and withholding medication from a heavily dependent smoker is not justified by his psychiatric history. Support and medication are complementary. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Varenicline started a week before his quit date, with behavioural support and review at two and four weeks
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for cessation, and the large randomised safety trial found no excess of neuropsychiatric events in people with stable treated psychiatric illness. Heavy dependence with failed patch monotherapy makes the most effective option the right first recommendation. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Nicotine patch monotherapy at the highest available strength, with behavioural support and review at two weeks
options.rationale: This is the approach that has already failed him twice, and repeating it with a higher dose does not address the reason it failed. Escalating within a strategy that has not worked wastes another quit attempt. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Combination nicotine replacement using a patch with an oral form, with behavioural support and review at two weeks
options.rationale: Combination replacement clearly outperforms the patch alone and is a legitimate option, but head to head evidence still favours varenicline in heavily dependent smokers. It is the alternative if he declines the more effective agent. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Bupropion started a week before his quit date, with behavioural support and review at two and four weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is effective but less so than varenicline, and it lowers the seizure threshold and interacts with serotonergic agents. It is a reasonable second line where varenicline is not tolerated. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: Smoking remains the leading preventable cause of death in Australia and people with mental illness smoke at two to three times the rate of the general population, yet are offered cessation treatment less often, partly because of longstanding concern about neuropsychiatric harm from varenicline. The large randomised trial comparing varenicline, bupropion, nicotine patch and placebo in people with and without psychiatric disorders found no significant excess of moderate or severe neuropsychiatric events attributable to either active drug, and Australian and international regulators subsequently removed the boxed warning. Varenicline is the most effective single agent, followed by combination nicotine replacement and bupropion, and all are more effective when combined with behavioural support. Time to first cigarette within thirty minutes of waking indicates high dependence and predicts a greater need for pharmacotherapy. Stopping smoking also raises the plasma levels of several psychotropic drugs, which matters for clozapine and olanzapine in particular.
key_points: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for cessation
Stable treated psychiatric illness is not a contraindication to varenicline
Time to first cigarette within thirty minutes indicates high dependence
Combination nicotine replacement beats patch monotherapy
Pharmacotherapy plus behavioural support outperforms either alone
explanation.pearls: Remember that tobacco smoke induces cytochrome P450 1A2, so stopping smoking raises clozapine and olanzapine levels by up to half within a week or two, and a patient stabilised on clozapine who quits without a dose review can become toxic with sedation, hypersalivation and seizures.

subtopic_detail: Slowly declining kidney function after more than a decade of maintenance treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 58 year old man with bipolar I disorder who has taken lithium for fourteen years with excellent mood stability and no admissions in that time.

His estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 78 to 52 mL/min/1.73m2 over the past five years, with the most recent two readings three months apart both at 52 and 54. His twelve hour post dose lithium level is 0.78 mmol/L, urine albumin to creatinine ratio is normal, his blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, and renal ultrasound shows normal sized kidneys with no obstruction. He passes large volumes of dilute urine and drinks accordingly. He takes no non steroidal anti inflammatory medication and no diuretic, and he is euthymic with no current symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no tremor, no ataxia, normal reflexes, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 52 mL/min/1.73m2 (down from 78 over five years), twelve hour lithium level 0.78 mmol/L (0.6-0.8), urine albumin to creatinine ratio normal, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, corrected calcium 2.52 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), renal ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop lithium immediately and substitute sodium valproate, given the fall in kidney function over five years
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal carries a substantial risk of rebound mania within weeks, and this degree of impairment does not demand emergency cessation. Any change should be gradual and planned rather than driven by a single trajectory. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Continue lithium at a lower target level with nephrology review, and discuss the long term options with him
options.rationale: Progression to end stage disease is uncommon and slow, while stopping lithium after fourteen years of stability carries a high risk of relapse and of refractoriness if it is later restarted. Shared decision making with nephrology input, aiming at the lowest effective level, is the recommended approach at this stage. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Add a thiazide diuretic for the polyuria and continue lithium at the current dose and target level
options.rationale: Thiazides reduce lithium clearance and raise the level, which is the opposite of what is needed here, and the polyuria of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is treated with amiloride if treatment is required at all. This choice risks toxicity on top of impairment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Change the dosing to twice daily at the same total dose, and repeat kidney function in twelve months
options.rationale: Divided dosing produces a higher trough exposure and is associated with more renal effect than once daily dosing, so this moves in the wrong direction. Single evening dosing is generally preferred for that reason. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue lithium unchanged and repeat kidney function annually, since he remains well and the level is in range
options.rationale: A fall of 26 mL/min/1.73m2 over five years is a meaningful trajectory rather than expected ageing, so continuing without adjustment or specialist input misses the window in which the rate of decline can be modified. Monitoring needs to become more frequent, not less. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Lithium remains the most effective long term treatment in bipolar disorder and the only one with good evidence for reducing suicide, so decisions about renal effects are genuinely a balance rather than a simple stop or continue. Chronic tubulointerstitial nephropathy develops slowly over decades and appears as a gradual decline in filtration with preserved urinary protein and normal sized kidneys, often alongside nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from impaired collecting duct responsiveness. Progression to end stage kidney disease occurs in well under 1 percent of treated patients. Risk is increased by episodes of toxicity, by dehydration, by concurrent non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and thiazides, and by divided rather than single daily dosing. Management of a declining filtration rate is joint review with nephrology, minimising the effective level, avoiding nephrotoxic combinations, and an explicit conversation about the relapse risk of stopping, since psychiatric relapse also carries mortality.
key_points: Decline is slow and end stage disease occurs in well under 1 percent
Preserved urinary protein with normal sized kidneys is the typical picture
Single daily dosing is preferred over divided dosing
Thiazides, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and anti inflammatories raise levels
Abrupt cessation risks rebound mania and later refractoriness
explanation.pearls: Check the corrected calcium as well as thyroid function at every annual review, because lithium causes hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia in up to a quarter of long term users, and the resulting fatigue, low mood and cognitive slowing are routinely misread as a depressive relapse and treated with an antidepressant.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy choice for adult attention difficulties when stimulant diversion is a live concern
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 29 year old man referred with lifelong inattention, disorganisation and restlessness, with clear evidence of impairment from primary school onwards confirmed by school reports and by his mother.

He has used methamphetamine intermittently for three years, most recently four weeks ago, and drinks six standard drinks on two nights a week. He has no psychotic symptoms and no mood disorder. He lives in a shared house where another resident has previously taken his prescribed medication without asking. His blood pressure is 128/80 mmHg, pulse 78 beats per minute, and his electrocardiogram and physical examination are normal. He is engaged with a drug and alcohol service and wants treatment for his attention difficulties.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Restless but cooperative, normal speech, no psychotic features, no tremor, normal cardiovascular examination
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, urine drug screen negative today, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: Which pharmacological approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Sertraline titrated over several weeks, with continued engagement in the drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors do not treat inattention or hyperactivity and he has no depressive or anxiety disorder to justify one. Prescribing it would treat a diagnosis he does not have. (Source: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults

options.text: Atomoxetine titrated over several weeks, with continued engagement in the drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: A non stimulant avoids both the misuse potential and the diversion risk created by his housing situation, and it has no street value while remaining effective for core symptoms. Australian guidance favours a non stimulant when substance use is recent or the storage environment is insecure. (Source: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults

options.text: No pharmacotherapy until he has been abstinent for twelve months, with continued engagement in the service
options.rationale: Withholding treatment for a year worsens the impairment that drives much of the substance use, and treating attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is associated with reduced rather than increased substance use. Abstinence is not a prerequisite for non stimulant treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults

options.text: Modafinil taken each morning, with continued engagement in the drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Modafinil is not approved for this indication in Australia and the adult evidence is weak, so it is not a substitute for an agent with an established effect. Choosing it would leave his core symptoms inadequately treated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Immediate release dexamfetamine three times daily, with continued engagement in the drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Short acting stimulants carry the highest misuse and diversion potential of the available options and would be the least suitable choice in a house where medication has already been taken. Multiple daily doses also worsen adherence. (Source: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults)
source_refs: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults

explanation.summary: Diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults requires symptoms present before the age of twelve with impairment in more than one setting, and corroborating evidence such as school reports or an informant history is central because retrospective self report alone is unreliable. Coexisting substance use is common, and untreated symptoms are themselves a risk factor for it, so treatment is not withheld until abstinence is achieved. Stimulants remain first line for most adults and are more effective than non stimulants, but the choice shifts when misuse or diversion is a genuine concern: lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug requiring enzymatic conversion and has lower misuse potential than immediate release preparations, while atomoxetine and guanfacine have essentially none. Housing where medication cannot be secured is a practical reason to choose a non stimulant. Cardiovascular assessment with blood pressure, pulse and a personal and family cardiac history precedes any stimulant, and prescribing in Australia is subject to state based authority requirements.
key_points: Childhood onset with corroborating evidence is required for the diagnosis
Treatment is not withheld until substance use abstinence is achieved
Lisdexamfetamine has lower misuse potential than immediate release stimulants
Atomoxetine and guanfacine have no misuse or diversion potential
Assess cardiovascular history and blood pressure before any stimulant
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically where the medication will be stored and who else has access, because diversion in shared housing is far more common than personal misuse, and that single practical question changes the prescription more often than the substance use history itself does.

sources.label: RANZCP: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults

subtopic_detail: Parenteral sedation choice when verbal and oral measures have already failed in the department
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a 34 year old man brought in by ambulance after threatening staff at a bus station. He is pacing, shouting, striking the walls and cannot be engaged in conversation.

De escalation has been attempted for twenty minutes by two experienced nurses and he has refused oral olanzapine wafers. Security is present and physical restraint is in place. His pulse is 126 beats per minute and blood pressure 148/90 mmHg taken during a brief window of cooperation, and his temperature measured tympanically is 37.1 degrees Celsius. He is known to the service with schizophrenia and has not taken his depot for three months. A capillary glucose is 6.2 mmol/L, and no intravenous access has been achieved. There is no history of cardiac disease and no electrocardiogram is available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 not obtainable, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Agitated and pacing, shouting, striking walls, not engageable, no obvious injury, pupils equal
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 6.2 mmol/L, no intravenous access, no electrocardiogram available, no previous electrocardiogram on file

lead_in: What is the most appropriate parenteral sedation?

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine with intramuscular lorazepam together, with continuous monitoring after the doses are given
options.rationale: Combining parenteral olanzapine with a parenteral benzodiazepine is specifically cautioned against because of reports of cardiorespiratory depression and death. If both are used they must be separated in time. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol with promethazine together, with continuous monitoring after the doses are given
options.rationale: This combination is used in some settings but causes more dystonia and prolonged sedation than droperidol, and promethazine adds anticholinergic burden without improving speed of onset. It is not the Australian first choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Withhold parenteral sedation until an electrocardiogram can be obtained, continuing physical restraint meanwhile
options.rationale: Prolonged physical restraint carries its own risks of rhabdomyolysis, positional asphyxia and staff and patient injury, and an electrocardiogram cannot be obtained in a struggling patient anyway. Sedation is what makes the assessment possible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Intramuscular midazolam as a single dose, with continuous monitoring and a repeat dose if needed after fifteen minutes
options.rationale: Midazolam works quickly but causes more respiratory depression and over sedation than droperidol, and it is a second line agent or an adjunct rather than the preferred single agent. Airway complications in a restrained patient are the main hazard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Intramuscular droperidol as a single dose, with continuous monitoring and a repeat dose if needed after fifteen minutes
options.rationale: Droperidol given intramuscularly is the Australian first line for acute behavioural disturbance, achieving sedation faster and more reliably than benzodiazepine monotherapy with less respiratory depression. Large Australian emergency studies found no clinically significant arrhythmia at these doses, so the absence of an electrocardiogram does not preclude its use. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance is managed in a graded way, beginning with environmental measures and verbal de escalation, moving to offered oral medication, and using parenteral sedation only when those have failed and there is risk to the patient or others. Australian emergency practice favours intramuscular droperidol as the single most effective first line agent, supported by randomised work from Australian emergency departments showing faster and more reliable sedation than midazolam with fewer airway events. Concern about corrected QT prolongation led to restricted use for many years, but subsequent prospective Australian data found no clinically significant arrhythmia at the doses used for sedation, and routine electrocardiography is not required before giving it in an emergency. Whichever agent is used, monitoring afterwards is mandatory and includes level of consciousness, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure and temperature, with a search for medical causes of the disturbance including hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, head injury, intoxication and withdrawal.
key_points: De escalation and offered oral medication precede parenteral sedation
Intramuscular droperidol is the Australian first line parenteral agent
Routine electrocardiography is not required before emergency sedation
Avoid giving parenteral olanzapine with a parenteral benzodiazepine
Monitor consciousness, respiration, saturation and temperature afterwards
explanation.pearls: Check a capillary glucose in every acutely disturbed patient before attributing the presentation to their psychiatric diagnosis, because hypoglycaemia, hypoxia and head injury all present as agitation and are the medical causes most often missed when a person is known to the mental health service.

subtopic_detail: Weight gain and impaired glucose handling one year into second generation antipsychotic treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26 year old woman one year after her first episode of psychosis, treated with olanzapine 15 mg daily. She has had no psychotic symptoms for eight months and has returned to part time study.

Her weight has risen from 62 kg to 78 kg over the year, her waist circumference is 96 cm, and her fasting glucose is 6.5 mmol/L on two occasions with a glycated haemoglobin of 44 mmol/mol. Fasting triglycerides are 2.6 mmol/L and high density lipoprotein cholesterol is 0.9 mmol/L. Her blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg and her prolactin is normal. She has engaged with a dietitian and an exercise program for four months without weight loss, and she is clear that she does not want to risk another episode of psychosis.

data_table.Examination: Weight 78 kg, waist circumference 96 cm, body mass index 29 kg/m2, no acanthosis nigricans, euthymic with no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.5 mmol/L (3.5-5.5) on two occasions, glycated haemoglobin 44 mmol/mol, fasting triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L (less than 1.7), high density lipoprotein cholesterol 0.9 mmol/L (greater than 1.2), prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue olanzapine and start a statin for the lipid abnormality, with review of glucose in six months
options.rationale: Treating one downstream abnormality while the cause continues leaves the weight gain and glucose intolerance unaddressed, and a woman of childbearing potential on a statin needs contraceptive counselling as well. Lipid treatment may still be needed later but is not the first step. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged and intensify the dietitian and exercise program with monthly weight review
options.rationale: Lifestyle intervention has already run for four months without effect, and it is substantially less effective while the drug driving the weight gain continues. Repeating a failed strategy allows the metabolic abnormalities to progress to diabetes. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Discuss switching to an antipsychotic with a lower metabolic risk, with close monitoring for relapse during the change
options.rationale: She has impaired fasting glucose and dyslipidaemia attributable to the agent with the highest metabolic liability, and lifestyle measures have already had a fair trial. Switching to an agent such as aripiprazole improves the metabolic profile while maintaining antipsychotic cover if the change is made gradually. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Halve the olanzapine dose and continue at that level, with review of weight and glucose in three months
options.rationale: Weight gain from this agent is only weakly dose related, so halving the dose gives little metabolic benefit while meaningfully raising the relapse risk in the first two years after a first episode. It combines the disadvantages of both options. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Cease the antipsychotic entirely given eight months of remission, with monthly review for early relapse symptoms
options.rationale: Relapse rates after stopping treatment within two years of a first episode approach 80 percent, and each relapse is associated with poorer functional recovery. The metabolic problem is a reason to change the drug, not to stop treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: People with schizophrenia die fifteen to twenty years earlier than the general population, and most of that gap is cardiovascular rather than from suicide, so metabolic monitoring is a core part of psychiatric care rather than an afterthought. Second generation antipsychotics differ markedly in metabolic liability: clozapine and olanzapine carry the highest risk, quetiapine and risperidone are intermediate, and aripiprazole, lurasidone and ziprasidone are lowest. Australian guidance is to measure weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose and lipids at baseline, at six and twelve weeks, and then at least annually. When abnormalities appear, the options are lifestyle intervention, switching to a lower risk agent, or adding metformin, which has reasonable evidence for attenuating antipsychotic associated weight gain. Switching must be done gradually with cross tapering and close relapse monitoring, and metformin is a reasonable alternative when the current agent is the only one that has controlled the illness, as is often the case with clozapine.
key_points: Cardiovascular disease, not suicide, drives most of the mortality gap
Clozapine and olanzapine carry the highest metabolic risk
Monitor weight, waist, blood pressure, glucose and lipids at baseline, 6 and 12 weeks, then annually
Options are lifestyle change, switching agent, or adding metformin
Stopping antipsychotic treatment within two years of a first episode risks relapse in most patients
explanation.pearls: Add metformin rather than switching when the current agent is clozapine or is the only drug that has ever controlled the illness, starting at 500 mg daily and titrating, since it produces a modest but real reduction in weight and improves insulin sensitivity without risking the relapse that a cross taper can precipitate.

sources.label: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Broad ventricular complexes after a large ingestion of an older antidepressant
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a 41 year old woman brought in ninety minutes after taking an estimated forty amitriptyline tablets with alcohol, found by her partner with an empty bottle.

She is drowsy but rousable with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 12, her pupils are dilated, her skin is dry and flushed and her bladder is palpable. Her pulse is 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air and temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 132 milliseconds and a prominent R wave in lead aVR. Her venous blood gas shows pH 7.31 and bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, her potassium is 3.6 mmol/L and her capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 12, dilated pupils, dry flushed skin, palpable bladder, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram showing QRS 132 milliseconds with a prominent R wave in aVR, venous pH 7.31, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-32), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L, paracetamol level not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Oral activated charcoal given via nasogastric tube, repeated hourly while her conscious state is monitored
options.rationale: Charcoal is considered within an hour or two of a large ingestion but requires a protected airway in a drowsy patient, and it does not treat the cardiotoxicity already present. Decontamination never takes precedence over reversing the conduction abnormality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil given as a slow bolus, repeated until her conscious state and respiratory pattern improve
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, which she has not taken, and it lowers the seizure threshold in mixed overdose, which is dangerous when the ingested drug is already proconvulsant. It has no role here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Intravenous physostigmine given as a slow bolus, repeated to reverse the anticholinergic features she is showing
options.rationale: Physostigmine can precipitate asystole and seizures in tricyclic poisoning specifically, and it does nothing for the sodium channel blockade that is the lethal mechanism. The anticholinergic signs are a marker of the ingestion rather than the target of treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Intravenous amiodarone given as a loading infusion, repeated if the broad complexes persist on the monitor
options.rationale: Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics and amiodarone all block sodium channels themselves and worsen the toxicity that is causing the broad complexes. They are contraindicated in this poisoning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate given as a bolus, repeated until the QRS narrows and the blood pressure improves
options.rationale: A QRS above 100 milliseconds indicates sodium channel blockade and predicts seizures and ventricular arrhythmia, and hypertonic bicarbonate reverses it through both the sodium load and alkalinisation. It is given on the electrocardiographic finding rather than waiting for an arrhythmia to appear. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning remains one of the most lethal common overdoses because these drugs block fast sodium channels in the myocardium, in addition to their anticholinergic, antihistaminergic and alpha blocking effects. The electrocardiogram is both the diagnostic and the prognostic tool: a QRS duration above 100 milliseconds predicts seizures, above 160 milliseconds predicts ventricular arrhythmia, and a terminal R wave in lead aVR above 3 mm reflects the same conduction delay. Treatment is hypertonic sodium bicarbonate given in boluses titrated to narrowing of the QRS and to an arterial pH of about 7.50 to 7.55, supplemented by hyperventilation if the patient is intubated. Seizures are treated with benzodiazepines, hypotension with fluid and then noradrenaline, and antiarrhythmics that block sodium channels are contraindicated. Lipid emulsion and extracorporeal support are salvage options in refractory cardiac arrest.
key_points: QRS above 100 milliseconds indicates sodium channel blockade
Give hypertonic bicarbonate titrated to QRS narrowing, not to an arrhythmia
A terminal R wave in lead aVR is the same sign in another form
Amiodarone and class Ia and Ic agents are contraindicated
Use benzodiazepines for seizures and noradrenaline for refractory hypotension
explanation.pearls: Repeat the electrocardiogram every fifteen to thirty minutes during the first hours rather than relying on the presenting trace, because absorption continues and anticholinergic effects slow gastric emptying, so a patient who arrives with a normal QRS can deteriorate abruptly several hours after ingestion.

subtopic_detail: Lower limb clonus and agitation days after a second serotonergic agent is added for pain
stem: A 52 year old man two days after laparotomy takes sertraline 150 mg daily and started tramadol for pain. Over twelve hours he has become agitated and sweaty with diarrhoea. He has never taken an antipsychotic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 152/92 mmHg, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Spontaneous ankle clonus, hyperreflexia in the legs, dilated pupils
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 640 units/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the tramadol only, give an antipyretic and observe
options.rationale: Stopping the precipitant is correct but leaving the other serotonergic drug in place may not resolve the toxicity, and antipyretics do not work because the hyperthermia comes from muscle activity rather than a raised hypothalamic set point. Twelve hours of observation risks progression to rigidity and rhabdomyolysis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Cease both drugs, cool actively and give bromocriptine
options.rationale: That syndrome develops over days rather than hours, produces lead pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, and requires exposure to a dopamine antagonist which he has never had. Bromocriptine is the wrong mechanism for this presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Cease both drugs, give benzodiazepines and cooling, then cyproheptadine
options.rationale: Lower limb predominant hyperreflexia with spontaneous and ocular clonus developing over hours after a second serotonergic drug is serotonin toxicity, and removal of both agents with benzodiazepine sedation is the treatment. Cyproheptadine is a serotonin antagonist reserved for moderate cases that do not settle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Continue both drugs and give antibiotics for presumed sepsis
options.rationale: Sepsis does not cause clonus, ocular clonus or a lower limb reflex gradient, and his wound is clean with a barely raised white cell count. Cultures are reasonable but continuing both serotonergic drugs allows the toxicity to progress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Cease both drugs, give benzodiazepines and cooling, then dantrolene
options.rationale: Dantrolene treats the sustained muscle contraction of malignant hyperthermia and is used in severe neuroleptic malignant syndrome, neither of which produces clonus or hyperreflexia. It does not address serotonin receptor overstimulation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

explanation.summary: Serotonin toxicity is a predictable consequence of excessive serotonergic activity rather than an idiosyncratic reaction, and it arises most often when two agents acting by different mechanisms are combined. Tramadol is a frequent Australian culprit because it is a serotonin reuptake inhibitor as well as an opioid and is commonly added to the medication of a patient already taking an antidepressant. The Hunter criteria formalise the diagnosis: in the presence of a serotonergic agent, spontaneous clonus alone is sufficient, as is inducible or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or tremor with hyperreflexia, or hyperthermia with hypertonia. Onset is within hours, and the lower limbs are affected more than the upper limbs. This gradient and the presence of clonus distinguish it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which follows dopamine antagonist exposure, develops over days, and produces generalised lead pipe rigidity with depressed reflexes. Treatment is withdrawal of the serotonergic agents, benzodiazepines, active cooling and supportive care, with cyproheptadine for moderate cases and paralysis with intubation for severe hyperthermia.
key_points: Clonus and hyperreflexia greater in the legs than the arms is the signature
Onset is within hours of adding or increasing a serotonergic agent
Tramadol is a common precipitant because it inhibits serotonin reuptake
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome gives rigidity with hyporeflexia over days
Treat with withdrawal, benzodiazepines and cooling; cyproheptadine if persistent
explanation.pearls: A temperature above 41 degrees Celsius in serotonin toxicity is an indication for immediate paralysis, intubation and active cooling rather than further pharmacological treatment, because the heat is generated by muscular hyperactivity and rhabdomyolysis with disseminated intravascular coagulation follows quickly once that threshold is crossed.

subtopic_detail: Duration criterion separating prolonged grief disorder from expected bereavement in an adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old woman whose husband died of pancreatic cancer 19 months ago. She describes intense daily yearning for him, spends hours each day looking at his photographs and has kept his study exactly as he left it because moving anything feels like a betrayal.

She has stopped seeing the friends they shared because being with couples is unbearable, and says she does not know who she is without him. She sleeps reasonably, eats normally and has maintained her weight. She has no guilt beyond missing him, no anhedonia in activities unrelated to him, no psychomotor slowing and no thoughts of self harm. She has never had a psychiatric illness.

data_table.Examination: Well groomed, tearful when discussing her husband, reactive affect at other times, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her that this is a normal reaction to loss and review her again in six months
options.rationale: Grief that remains this intense and disabling beyond 12 months has crossed from an expected adaptation into a recognised disorder with its own treatment. Normalising it withholds an effective therapy and implies that continued suffering is simply to be endured. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Refer for a structured grief focused psychological therapy delivered over several months
options.rationale: Her symptoms have persisted beyond 12 months with identity disruption, avoidance of reminders and intense daily yearning causing functional impairment, which meets the threshold for prolonged grief disorder. Grief focused psychotherapy has the strongest evidence base for this condition and outperforms antidepressant monotherapy. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Suggest a community bereavement support group as the sole intervention for the next year
options.rationale: Peer support groups help many bereaved people and are a valuable adjunct, but they are not designed to treat a diagnosed disorder and have not shown efficacy for persistent grief of this severity. Offering only a group leaves the disorder untreated for another year. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine to help her tolerate the distressing memories
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines suppress the emotional processing that grief work depends on and carry dependence risk with prolonged use in this age group. Evidence suggests early benzodiazepine use after bereavement does not reduce and may prolong grief symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence an antidepressant at standard dose and review the response in four weeks
options.rationale: She lacks the pervasive anhedonia, guilt, worthlessness and neurovegetative features that would indicate a depressive episode, and antidepressants have not been shown to reduce core grief symptoms. Medication has a place when major depression coexists, which it does not here. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder entered formal diagnostic classification to describe a minority of bereaved people whose grief does not attenuate and remains disabling long after the loss. The adult duration criterion is at least 12 months from the death, with the core features being persistent intense yearning or preoccupation with the deceased alongside identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, a sense of meaninglessness and difficulty re-engaging with life. The distinction from major depression matters because the sadness in grief is focused on the lost person and comes in waves triggered by reminders, while depressive mood is pervasive and accompanied by global worthlessness and anhedonia. Treatment is psychological first, with grief focused cognitive behavioural approaches producing the largest effects, and medication reserved for comorbid depression or anxiety.
key_points: The adult duration criterion for prolonged grief disorder is at least 12 months after the death
Core features are intense yearning or preoccupation with identity disruption and avoidance
Grief sadness is focused on the deceased and comes in waves; depressive mood is pervasive
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms antidepressants for core grief symptoms
Treat comorbid major depression or post traumatic stress disorder on their own merits
explanation.pearls: The duration criterion is 12 months in adults but only 6 months in children and adolescents, so a bereaved teenager with disabling grief at 8 months meets the diagnosis while an adult with the same picture at the same interval does not yet.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Scheduled analgesic trial for agitation in advanced dementia with no verbal pain report
stem:
You are the general practitioner attending a residential aged care facility to review an 84-year-old woman with advanced Alzheimer disease who has become resistive and strikes out during personal care, particularly when staff transfer her or dress her upper body. Her speech is limited to occasional single words.

Staff report the behaviour has built over three weeks and occurs mainly during morning cares rather than at any particular time of day. She has severe knee osteoarthritis and fell onto her right shoulder six weeks ago, after which a radiograph showed no fracture. She takes no regular analgesia. Urinalysis, full blood count, electrolytes, calcium and a chest radiograph performed this week are all unremarkable, and there has been no medication change.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 132/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Grimaces and pulls away on passive right shoulder abduction, crepitus in both knees, abdomen soft, no urinary retention on bladder scan, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative, full blood count, electrolytes, corrected calcium and C-reactive protein within normal limits, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence low dose risperidone and review the behaviour after several weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are considered only after reversible causes and non-pharmacological approaches have failed, and they raise the risk of stroke and death in older people with dementia. Starting one before treating obvious untreated pain exposes her to that risk for a problem that has a safer remedy. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement

options.text: Commence a low dose antidepressant for presumed depression underlying the behaviour change
options.rationale: Depression can present as agitation in dementia and citalopram has some evidence in this setting, but the behaviour here is tightly bound to physical handling rather than pervasive across the day. The pattern points to a nociceptive trigger rather than a mood disturbance. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder before making any treatment change
options.rationale: A rotator cuff tear is plausible and imaging might confirm it, but scanning a woman with advanced dementia requires her to lie still for a prolonged period and rarely changes management at this stage. An empirical analgesic trial tests the same hypothesis without the burden. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Arrange an as-required oral benzodiazepine for staff to give before morning personal cares
options.rationale: Pre-medicating with a benzodiazepine sedates her through a painful experience rather than removing the pain, and increases falls, confusion and aspiration risk. As-required sedation before care is a form of chemical restraint when a treatable cause has not been addressed. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement

options.text: Commence regular scheduled paracetamol and reassess the behaviour after several weeks
options.rationale: Untreated pain is among the commonest reversible drivers of behavioural change in advanced dementia, and a person who cannot report it communicates through resistance during the movements that hurt. A stepwise trial of regular rather than as-required simple analgesia has been shown in randomised trials to reduce agitation substantially. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia are best understood as communication rather than as symptoms requiring suppression, and the first task is always to look for an unmet need. Pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, delirium, sensory impairment, boredom, fear and an over-stimulating environment account for a large share of behaviour that would otherwise be medicated. Pain is particularly easy to miss because the standard question cannot be answered, so assessment relies on observational tools and on the pattern of when the behaviour occurs, with resistance confined to handling being highly suggestive. Randomised evidence supports a stepwise protocol beginning with regular paracetamol, and antipsychotics carry a well-quantified increase in cerebrovascular events and mortality that makes them a last rather than a first resort.
key_points: Behaviour in dementia is communication; look for an unmet need before prescribing
Pain, constipation, retention, infection and delirium are the commonest reversible drivers
Behaviour confined to personal care or movement strongly suggests pain
A stepwise trial of regular paracetamol reduces agitation in randomised trials
Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality risk in older people with dementia
explanation.pearls: When an antipsychotic is unavoidable in dementia, risperidone is the only agent with an Australian indication for persistent aggression, at a starting dose of 0.25 mg twice daily, and the approved duration is up to 12 weeks with review for withdrawal at that point.

sources.label: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement

subtopic_detail: Baseline cardiovascular assessment required before starting stimulant treatment in an adult
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in the adult outpatient clinic having completed a diagnostic assessment of a 28-year-old man with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, combined presentation, with a documented history of symptoms from primary school and current impairment at work and at home.

He drinks alcohol twice a week within recommended limits and uses no other substances. He has no history of psychosis, mania or tics. His mother has a pacemaker for complete heart block diagnosed in her sixties and there is no family history of sudden death under 40. He is otherwise well and takes no regular medication. You plan to start a long acting methylphenidate preparation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, heart sounds dual with no murmur, chest clear, no tremor, no thyroid enlargement

lead_in: What baseline assessment is most important before the first prescription?

options.text: Record pulse, blood pressure, weight and a cardiovascular and family cardiac history
options.rationale: Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure modestly in most people, so a documented baseline is what makes subsequent monitoring interpretable, alongside a structured cardiac history to identify who needs further investigation. Australian guidance treats this clinical assessment rather than routine investigation as the required baseline. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Arrange formal neuropsychological testing to confirm the diagnosis before treatment starts
options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing cannot diagnose or exclude this condition, which remains a clinical diagnosis based on history, developmental course and corroborative information. It is useful for characterising a suspected specific learning disorder alongside it. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Arrange urine drug screening and repeat it at every review while treatment continues
options.rationale: Substance use history is an important part of the assessment and influences the choice of preparation, but universal repeated urine screening is not recommended and damages the therapeutic relationship. He reports alcohol within limits and no other substance use. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Arrange a twelve lead electrocardiogram for every adult before any stimulant is commenced
options.rationale: Routine electrocardiography for all patients is not recommended because the yield in people without cardiac symptoms or a concerning family history is very low. It is indicated when the history reveals structural disease, exertional syncope, palpitations or premature sudden death in a relative. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Arrange transthoracic echocardiography given the family history of conduction system disease
options.rationale: Acquired heart block in a woman in her sixties is age related and does not indicate an inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy in her son. Echocardiography is reserved for a murmur, symptoms or a family history of cardiomyopathy or premature sudden death. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Stimulant medication is the most effective treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults, with effect sizes that exceed most interventions in psychiatry, and the safety framework around it is built on simple repeated clinical measurement rather than on investigation. The relevant physiological effects are a small rise in heart rate and blood pressure, appetite suppression with weight loss, and sleep disruption if dosing runs late in the day. Baseline pulse, blood pressure and weight are recorded so that change can be detected, and the cardiac history is taken to identify the small group with structural or electrical disease in whom a cardiology opinion is needed first. In Australia stimulant prescribing is regulated at state and territory level with authority requirements, and driving must be discussed because untreated symptoms themselves raise crash risk while treatment reduces it.
key_points: Baseline pulse, blood pressure and weight make later monitoring interpretable
Routine electrocardiography is not required in the absence of cardiac symptoms or family red flags
Red flags include exertional syncope, palpitations, structural disease and sudden death under 40 in a relative
Neuropsychological testing cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis
Stimulant prescribing in Australia requires state or territory authority
explanation.pearls: Treating adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder reduces motor vehicle crash risk rather than increasing it, and long acting preparations are preferred for drivers because the wearing-off period of short acting formulations produces a rebound window of impaired attention in the late afternoon.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Choosing between psychological therapy and medication as initial treatment for uncomplicated adult PTSD
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old paramedic who attended a multi-fatality road crash seven months ago. Since then he has had nightly nightmares, intrusive images of the scene when he hears sirens, and he has changed his driving route to avoid the intersection.

He has become irritable with his partner, sleeps four to five hours a night and startles at unexpected noises. He has reduced his shifts and describes feeling permanently on edge. He drinks two standard drinks most evenings, which has not changed. He has no psychotic symptoms, no history of mania and no thoughts of suicide, and he has never had psychiatric treatment.

data_table.Examination: Anxious but engaged, no psychomotor agitation, affect reactive, cognition intact, no psychotic phenomena, insight preserved
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Advise a period of sick leave with sleep hygiene measures and review him in two months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is appropriate in the first month after trauma when many people recover spontaneously, but symptoms established at seven months will not remit with rest alone. Extended avoidance of work can reinforce the avoidance that maintains the disorder. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review his response in four weeks
options.rationale: Medication is recommended when trauma focused therapy is declined, unavailable or ineffective, or when there is significant comorbid depression, none of which applies. Starting with a drug when therapy is accessible inverts the recommended order. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange a single session psychological debriefing focused on the details of the incident
