A raised or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone with hypercalcaemia means a parathyroid-driven process
Malignancy, myeloma, sarcoidosis and vitamin D excess all suppress parathyroid hormone
Lithium raises the calcium set point of the calcium sensing receptor, mimicking primary hyperparathyroidism
Do not stop lithium reflexively; rebound mania and suicide risk must be weighed against mild hypercalcaemia
explanation.pearls: Lithium-associated hyperparathyroidism is frequently multiglandular rather than a single adenoma, so localisation imaging can be negative and the surgeon may need to explore all four glands.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management of irritability in a gene positive adult with a hyperkinetic movement disorder
stem: A 45-year-old man whose predictive testing showed a CAG repeat length of 43 attends with his wife. Over 9 months he has become quick-tempered, shouting over small frustrations, and now sits for long periods unless prompted. He denies sadness or anhedonia. He has intermittent fidgety finger movements and impersistent tongue protrusion.

data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 27 out of 30 with reduced verbal fluency

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for his irritability?

options.text: Diazepam as required for episodes of agitation
options.rationale: As-required benzodiazepines add sedation and fall risk to a progressive neurodegenerative illness and provide no sustained benefit for a symptom that is present most of the day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Sodium valproate with liver function monitoring
options.rationale: Valproate is used for irritability where mood instability is prominent or an antidepressant has failed, but it is not the first agent and adds sedation, weight gain and hepatic monitoring burden. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease

options.text: Olanzapine at night with metabolic monitoring
options.rationale: An antipsychotic is the next step if a serotonergic agent fails, and it has the advantage of also suppressing chorea, but it carries metabolic and extrapyramidal burden and his movements are not yet disabling. The distinguishing consideration is whether chorea needs treating at the same time. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease

options.text: Sertraline with review of irritability and initiation
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first line for irritability and apathy in Huntington disease and are effective even when the patient does not describe sadness, since irritability in this illness is a frontostriatal symptom rather than a marker of depression. Starting here also avoids the metabolic and movement burden that an antipsychotic would add. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease

options.text: Tetrabenazine with screening for depression and suicidality
options.rationale: Tetrabenazine is licensed for chorea, not for irritability, and it depletes presynaptic monoamines, which causes or worsens depression and carries a recognised association with suicidality in a population whose suicide rate is already several times that of the general population. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat disorder in which the psychiatric and cognitive features frequently precede the movement disorder by years and cause more day-to-day disability than the chorea itself. Irritability, apathy, depression and obsessionality are the commonest neuropsychiatric features, and apathy in particular is often mistaken by families for laziness or by clinicians for depression. Treatment of irritability begins with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, with an antipsychotic or valproate added or substituted when that fails, and the choice is influenced by whether chorea also needs suppression. Suicide risk is substantially elevated across the illness, peaking around the time of diagnosis and again when independence is lost, so it is asked about at every review. Care is multidisciplinary and includes genetic counselling for at-risk relatives, since predictive testing has implications for the whole family.
key_points: Psychiatric and cognitive symptoms often precede chorea and cause more functional impairment than the movements
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first line for irritability and apathy, regardless of whether sadness is reported
Antipsychotics treat both irritability and chorea but add metabolic and extrapyramidal burden
Tetrabenazine treats chorea but depletes monoamines and is associated with depression and suicidality
Suicide risk is elevated throughout, peaking at diagnosis and at loss of independence
explanation.pearls: A CAG repeat length of 40 or more is fully penetrant, 36 to 39 is reduced penetrance and 27 to 35 is an intermediate allele that does not cause disease but can expand on paternal transmission.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease

subtopic_detail: Excessive daytime sleepiness with laughter induced weakness in an adolescent treated for depression
stem: A 17-year-old girl's depression has not responded to 6 months of sertraline. She enjoys her friends and art and denies guilt. She sleeps 10 pm to 7 am easily, naps an hour after school and wakes refreshed. Twice this year her knees buckled and she sank to the ground while laughing, staying fully aware.

data_table.Investigations: Epworth Sleepiness Scale 18 of 24; body mass index 23

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the sertraline to the maximum tolerated dose
options.rationale: She retains interest, enjoyment and reactivity with no guilt or hopelessness, so the diagnosis rather than the dose is the problem; increasing it prolongs a 12-month diagnostic delay. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance)

options.text: Arrange polysomnography then a multiple sleep latency test
options.rationale: Sleepiness with refreshing naps and episodes of laughter-triggered weakness with preserved awareness describes cataplexy, and the diagnosis of narcolepsy requires overnight polysomnography to exclude other causes of sleep disruption followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day. That sequence must be performed in the correct order, since a daytime test alone cannot be interpreted without knowing the preceding night's sleep. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance)

options.text: Switch her from sertraline to venlafaxine and review
options.rationale: Venlafaxine does suppress cataplexy and is sometimes used for that purpose, but switching antidepressants without recognising the underlying disorder treats one symptom while leaving the sleepiness and the diagnosis unaddressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange overnight home oximetry for sleep apnoea
options.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnoea produces unrefreshing sleep and morning headache rather than refreshing naps, and her body mass index of 23 and absence of snoring make it improbable; oximetry alone is also a poor test in adolescents. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia
options.rationale: She has no difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep and sleeps 9 hours a night, so insomnia therapy targets a problem she does not have. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance)

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy typically begins in adolescence or early adult life and is frequently misattributed to depression, laziness or poor sleep habits, with reported diagnostic delays of many years. The cardinal symptom is excessive daytime sleepiness with naps that are short and refreshing, which distinguishes it from the unrefreshing sleepiness of sleep apnoea, depression and insufficient sleep. Cataplexy, a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, most often laughter, with consciousness fully preserved, is specific to narcolepsy type 1 and reflects loss of hypocretin-producing neurons in the hypothalamus. Sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations complete the classical tetrad but are neither sensitive nor specific on their own. Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test, and treatment combines scheduled naps with wake-promoting agents and specific therapy for cataplexy.
key_points: Short refreshing naps distinguish narcolepsy from the unrefreshing sleepiness of apnoea or depression
Cataplexy is emotion-triggered loss of tone with preserved consciousness and is specific to narcolepsy type 1
Diagnosis requires polysomnography first, then a multiple sleep latency test the following day
Retained interest, enjoyment and reactivity argue against major depression as the explanation
Treatment combines scheduled naps, wake-promoting agents and specific anticataplectic therapy
explanation.pearls: Antidepressants suppress rapid eye movement sleep and can mask the sleep onset rapid eye movement periods that the multiple sleep latency test relies on, so they usually need to be withdrawn about 2 weeks before the study under sleep physician supervision.

subtopic_detail: Parenteral sedation for acute behavioural disturbance after novel psychoactive substance use
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 23-year-old man is brought in by police at 2 am, pacing, shouting at staff and repeatedly trying to leave through the ambulance bay. His friend says he smoked a synthetic product bought online about 2 hours ago and has had nothing else.

Verbal de-escalation in a quiet room has been attempted for 20 minutes by two experienced nurses and he has refused oral medication twice. He is now pushing past staff towards the doors and there is a genuine risk of injury to him and others.

He is sweating, his pupils measure 5 mm and react, he is moving all four limbs vigorously and there is no focal neurological deficit. A blood glucose taken at triage was 5.8 mmol/L (4.0-7.8) and a 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded earlier in the evening at another hospital showed sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 420 ms. He has no known cardiac history, no allergies and no alcohol on his breath.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, pupils 5 mm and reactive, moving all four limbs vigorously, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 5.8 mmol/L (4.0-7.8), 12-lead electrocardiogram earlier this evening in sinus rhythm with corrected QT interval 420 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly is the first line parenteral sedative in Australian emergency practice for acute behavioural disturbance, supported by randomised trials showing faster and more reliable sedation than midazolam with less respiratory depression. Its recorded corrected QT interval of 420 ms is well within the range at which droperidol at this dose has been shown to be safe. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.text: Midazolam 10 mg intramuscularly with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Midazolam sedates effectively but causes significantly more respiratory depression and airway intervention than droperidol at equivalent effect, which is why Australian protocols moved it to second line. It remains the agent of choice where an antipsychotic is contraindicated. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.text: Haloperidol 10 mg intramuscularly with promethazine 50 mg in the same syringe
options.rationale: This combination is used in some international settings but is not the Australian first line, and haloperidol at this dose carries a higher burden of dystonia and akathisia than droperidol without better sedation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg intramuscularly with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Intramuscular olanzapine is a reasonable option but is slower in onset than droperidol and must not be combined with parenteral benzodiazepines because of cardiorespiratory depression, which limits its usefulness when escalation may be needed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Ketamine 300 mg intramuscularly with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Ketamine is a rescue agent for sedation failure after two agents, and using it first exposes the patient to emergence phenomena, hypersalivation and a higher rate of intubation than necessary. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance is a medical emergency in which the risk of harm to the patient and to staff has to be balanced against the risks of sedation itself. Australian practice follows a graded approach: environmental and verbal de-escalation first, then oral medication if accepted, then parenteral sedation, with physical restraint used only for the minimum time needed to give medication safely. Droperidol became the preferred parenteral agent in Australia after trials showed it achieved sedation faster than midazolam with fewer airway interventions, and concerns about QT prolongation at the doses used in this setting were not borne out. Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists and other novel psychoactive substances are not detected on routine urine drug screens, produce far more severe agitation, tachycardia and hyperthermia than plant cannabis, and are recognised causes of seizures and acute kidney injury. After sedation, the priorities are continuous monitoring, a temperature check for hyperthermia, creatine kinase for rhabdomyolysis, and reassessment for an organic cause.
key_points: De-escalate and offer oral medication before parenteral sedation, and restrain only for the minimum time needed
Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly is the Australian first line parenteral agent, with midazolam second line
Ketamine is a rescue agent after failure of two sedatives, not a first choice
Synthetic cannabinoids are not detected on routine urine drug screens and cause more severe toxicity than plant cannabis
After sedation check temperature, creatine kinase and glucose, and reassess for a medical cause of the disturbance
explanation.pearls: Hyperthermia above 38.5 °C in a stimulant or synthetic cannabinoid presentation demands active cooling and a creatine kinase level, because it is the single best predictor of rhabdomyolysis and death in this group.

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

subtopic_detail: Assessing new behaviour change in a minimally verbal adult before altering psychotropic medication
stem: A 28-year-old man with severe intellectual disability and no speech lives in a group home. For 6 weeks he has struck the right side of his face, refused half his meals and woken calling out at 3 am. Nothing in his routine has changed. He has taken risperidone 1 mg daily for 4 years.

data_table.Examination: Grimaces on right cheek palpation, not the left; will not open his mouth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase his risperidone to 2 mg daily
options.rationale: Increasing an antipsychotic in response to behaviour change without first excluding a physical cause is the anti-pattern known as diagnostic overshadowing, and it adds metabolic and extrapyramidal risk while leaving the source of pain untreated. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.text: Start citalopram for a depressive episode
options.rationale: Depression can indeed present as behaviour change and sleep disturbance in intellectual disability, but it is a diagnosis reached after physical causes are excluded, and nothing here explains the strictly unilateral facial signs. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.text: Arrange a dental examination under sedation
options.rationale: New self-injury directed repeatedly at one body site, with food refusal, night waking and unilateral tenderness on that side, points to localised pain, and dental disease is the commonest treatable cause in adults with severe intellectual disability who cannot report toothache. Examination under sedation is often the only way to obtain an adequate look and to treat in the same episode. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.text: Request an abdominal radiograph for faecal loading
options.rationale: Constipation is a leading cause of behaviour change in this population and is always worth considering, but his bowel chart documents a soft formed stool daily and his abdomen is soft and non-tender, which makes it an unlikely explanation here. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.text: Commission a functional behaviour assessment
options.rationale: Functional behaviour assessment is a core part of management for established behaviours of concern, but it starts from the premise that the behaviour is environmentally maintained, and here the history of abrupt onset with no environmental change and localised physical signs points elsewhere first. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

explanation.summary: Adults with severe intellectual disability who have little or no speech communicate physical distress through behaviour, and a new or escalating behaviour of concern should be treated as a symptom needing a differential diagnosis rather than as a reason to increase psychotropic medication. Diagnostic overshadowing, the attribution of new symptoms to the intellectual disability or to a known psychiatric diagnosis, is the central error to avoid. The physical causes worth systematically excluding are dental disease, constipation, gastro-oesophageal reflux, urinary retention or infection, otitis media, fracture, menstrual pain and medication adverse effects including akathisia. Useful discriminators are the abruptness of onset, whether anything in the environment changed, whether the behaviour targets a particular body region, and whether sleep and appetite changed at the same time. Psychotropic reduction rather than escalation is the direction of travel in Australian policy, given the long history of overprescribing in this population.
key_points: New behaviour change in a minimally verbal adult is a symptom requiring a differential diagnosis, not an automatic dose increase
Diagnostic overshadowing is the error of attributing new symptoms to the disability or existing diagnosis
Exclude dental disease, constipation, reflux, urinary and ear infection, fracture and akathisia
Behaviour targeting one body site with unilateral tenderness points to localised pain
Australian policy direction is psychotropic reduction with positive behaviour support, not escalation
explanation.pearls: Akathisia from an existing antipsychotic can itself present as agitation and self-injury, so a dose increase can worsen the very behaviour it is meant to treat; ask staff specifically whether the person can now sit still for a meal or a television program.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

subtopic_detail: Selecting a relapse prevention strategy when adherence and substance use have both been excluded
stem: A 22-year-old man has a second schizophrenia relapse in 10 months. Every paliperidone palmitate depot has been given on time and his trough level is therapeutic. Drug screens were negative at both admissions. His mother speaks for him throughout family sessions; his father calls him lazy. Both relapses followed days of escalating arguments at home.

data_table.Mental state: Settles by day 10 without a dose change

lead_in: What is most likely to prevent further relapse?

options.text: Increase the paliperidone depot to the next dose band
options.rationale: A therapeutic plasma level with symptom resolution in 10 days without any dose change argues that the dose was not the limiting factor, and escalating it adds extrapyramidal and prolactin burden without addressing what preceded both relapses. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Arrange behavioural family intervention for the household
options.rationale: Behavioural family intervention is the intervention with the strongest evidence for relapse reduction in schizophrenia, roughly halving relapse rates over the following 2 years when delivered over at least 10 sessions, and it is specifically indicated where criticism and over-involvement are prominent at home. With adherence confirmed by the depot register and plasma level and substance use excluded twice, the family environment is the modifiable factor that both relapses point to. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Add sodium valproate and review him in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Anticonvulsant augmentation has little evidence in schizophrenia without a mood component or aggression, and it adds hepatic, haematological and teratogenic monitoring burden for no expected relapse benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Switch him to clozapine with haematological monitoring
options.rationale: Clozapine is indicated after failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials, whereas his symptoms remitted on his current agent both times, so this is relapse in a responsive illness rather than treatment resistance. The distinguishing question is whether the drug failed to control symptoms or whether something outside the drug precipitated relapse. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Provide weekly supportive counselling after discharge
options.rationale: Individual supportive contact maintains engagement and is valuable, but it has not been shown to reduce relapse in the way structured family intervention has, and it leaves the household dynamic that preceded both relapses unaddressed. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

explanation.summary: When a person with schizophrenia relapses, the reflex explanations are non-adherence and substance use, and these account for the majority of cases, which is why a long-acting injectable register and a urine drug screen are checked first. Once both are excluded and plasma levels confirm adequate exposure, the differential moves to psychosocial precipitants, and the best studied of these is the emotional climate of the household. Research on expressed emotion has consistently shown that high levels of criticism, hostility or emotional over-involvement in relatives predict relapse, and that structured family intervention reduces it. Effective programs run for at least 10 sessions over 6 months or more and combine psychoeducation, communication training and structured problem solving with the whole family rather than the patient alone. Family intervention is recommended in Australian and international guidelines yet remains substantially underdelivered, in part because services default to individual work.
key_points: Exclude non-adherence and substance use first, using the depot register, plasma levels and urine screening
High expressed emotion at home, meaning criticism, hostility or over-involvement, predicts relapse
Behavioural family intervention of at least 10 sessions roughly halves relapse rates
Clozapine is for treatment resistance after two adequate trials, not for relapse in a drug-responsive illness
A therapeutic plasma level with rapid remission argues against the dose being the problem
explanation.pearls: Family intervention needs a minimum of 10 sessions over 6 months to show relapse benefit; single-session psychoeducation for relatives improves knowledge but has not been shown to change relapse rates.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Psychiatric opinion on repeated shoplifting in an older adult with behavioural change
stem: A 64-year-old woman faces a third shoplifting charge in 8 months, each time taking unneeded items in full view of staff. She has no financial hardship or convictions, and denies tension before or relief after. Her husband reports 18 months of craving sweets, laughing at bad news and social withdrawal.

data_table.Mental state: Unconcerned; no low mood or psychotic symptoms
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 of 30; verbal fluency and trail making impaired

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise the solicitor that no psychiatric diagnosis is present
options.rationale: Closing the assessment at this point misses a syndrome that is plainly emerging in the collateral history, and a fitness opinion given without completing the neuropsychiatric workup is not defensible. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia

options.text: Diagnose kleptomania and start naltrexone with follow-up
options.rationale: Kleptomania requires a build-up of tension before the theft and pleasure or relief at the time, both of which she explicitly denies, and it usually begins in adolescence or early adult life rather than in the seventh decade with new behavioural change. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia

options.text: Diagnose a depressive episode and start an antidepressant
options.rationale: Apathy and social withdrawal in frontotemporal dementia are frequently misread as depression, but neither she nor her husband reports low mood, and the disinhibition, dietary change and loss of empathy do not fit a depressive episode. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia

options.text: Arrange neuropsychological assessment and brain magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: New criminal behaviour committed openly without concealment, together with loss of empathy, dietary change towards sweet foods, and executive deficits on a preserved overall cognitive score, is the recognisable behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia picture, and neuropsychological testing with structural imaging is the appropriate workup. Bedside screening tools are insensitive to this syndrome because memory and orientation are preserved early, so a near-normal score cannot be used to exclude it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia
Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia clinical information

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting impulse control
options.rationale: Psychological treatment for impulse control presumes intact capacity to learn and apply strategies, which is undermined by the executive impairment demonstrated here, and it would proceed without a diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia

explanation.summary: New antisocial or criminal behaviour beginning in mid to later life with no prior history is a neuropsychiatric red flag, and behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is the diagnosis most often missed in this presentation. Its core features are early behavioural disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, perseverative or ritualistic behaviour, hyperorality with a shift towards sweet foods, and executive dysfunction with relative preservation of memory and visuospatial function. That preservation is exactly why brief bedside screening tools perform poorly and why formal neuropsychological assessment is needed. Structural imaging typically shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, and functional imaging can help where structural imaging is equivocal. Recognition matters legally as well as clinically, because it bears on fitness to plead, on criminal responsibility and on decisions about guardianship and driving, and it redirects the family from blame towards support and planning.
key_points: New offending in mid to later life without prior history should prompt a neuropsychiatric assessment
Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia features disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and a shift towards sweet foods
Memory and orientation are preserved early, so bedside screening scores are often near normal
Formal neuropsychological testing plus structural imaging is the appropriate workup
Diagnosis has direct forensic implications for fitness to plead and criminal responsibility
explanation.pearls: Offences in behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia are characteristically committed in the open with no attempt at concealment and no apparent concern about consequences, which is the behavioural signature that most reliably separates them from ordinary offending.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia
Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia clinical information

subtopic_detail: Legal pathway for urgent surgery refused by an objecting patient already on a community treatment order
stem: A 58-year-old woman with schizophrenia on a community treatment order for 6 years is admitted with a black right forefoot. Below knee amputation is advised within 48 hours. She refuses: a radio voice told her the blackness is healing. She cannot repeat back that she may die. Her husband supports surgery; she does not want anyone deciding for her.

data_table.Investigations: Afebrile, lactate 1.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Assess capacity and apply to the guardianship tribunal
options.rationale: Capacity is decision specific, so it must be assessed and documented for this operation rather than inferred from her psychiatric diagnosis or her treatment order. In New South Wales the person responsible may consent for someone who lacks capacity, but that authority falls away when the patient objects to the treatment, and consent must then be sought from the guardianship tribunal. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual)
source_refs: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual
RANZCP: Clinical practice resources on capacity and consent

options.text: Authorise the amputation under the Mental Health Act
options.rationale: Mental health legislation authorises treatment for mental illness only, and a community treatment order confers no authority over surgical or other physical health treatment. This is the most tempting wrong branch because the legal framework is already in place for a different purpose. (Source: NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual)
source_refs: NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual

options.text: Obtain consent from her husband as person responsible
options.rationale: The husband would ordinarily be the person responsible and could consent for someone lacking capacity, but the legislation expressly removes that authority once the patient objects to the treatment, which she has done clearly and repeatedly. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual)
source_refs: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual

options.text: Proceed under the common law emergency doctrine
options.rationale: Emergency provisions cover treatment needed urgently to save life or prevent serious damage when there is no time to obtain consent, and with a normal lactate, no fever and a 48-hour window there is time to follow the proper process. (Source: NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual)
source_refs: NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual

options.text: Accept her refusal and document that she declined
options.rationale: Accepting a refusal requires the person to be able to understand, retain, weigh and communicate the decision, and she cannot retain or weigh the central fact that she may die, because a delusional belief displaces it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources on capacity and consent

explanation.summary: This scenario turns on keeping three legal frameworks separate: mental health legislation, which authorises treatment for mental illness; guardianship legislation, which governs consent to medical treatment for adults who cannot consent for themselves; and the common law emergency doctrine. A community treatment order or involuntary status under mental health legislation gives no authority to treat a physical illness, a point frequently misunderstood on medical and surgical wards. Capacity is decision specific and time specific, and it is assessed against the ability to understand the information, retain it, weigh it in the balance and communicate a choice, not against whether the clinician agrees with the outcome. In New South Wales the person responsible hierarchy allows a spouse, carer or relative to consent for major medical treatment, but that pathway closes when the patient objects, at which point the guardianship tribunal must decide. A psychotic illness does not by itself remove capacity, but it does so where the delusional content directly displaces the relevant reasoning, as it does here.
key_points: Mental health legislation authorises treatment for mental illness only, never for physical illness
Capacity is decision specific and rests on understanding, retaining, weighing and communicating
The person responsible can consent for major medical treatment, but not when the patient objects
An objecting patient without capacity requires an application to the guardianship tribunal
A psychiatric diagnosis never removes capacity by itself; the delusional content must displace the relevant reasoning
explanation.pearls: Terminology and thresholds differ by jurisdiction: New South Wales uses the person responsible under the Guardianship Act, Victoria uses a medical treatment decision maker under its own legislation, so state the state before naming the substitute decision maker.

sources.label: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual
NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual
RANZCP: Clinical practice resources on capacity and consent

subtopic_detail: Treatment choice for severe luteal phase mood symptoms with a symptom-free follicular phase
stem:
You are the resident in a general practice clinic. A 28-year-old woman attends because for the past 2 years she has had a week each month of intense irritability, tearfulness and a sense of being overwhelmed that has twice led to shouting arguments at work.

She describes feeling completely well for the remainder of each month and has taken no time off work outside those weeks. She has no history of depressive or manic episodes, no self-harm and no substance use. She uses condoms for contraception and does not wish to become pregnant.

She has kept a daily symptom diary for the past three cycles at her general practitioner's request. It shows symptom scores rising sharply from around day 21, peaking in the 3 days before menstruation, and returning to baseline within 2 days of bleeding starting, with no symptoms recorded between day 4 and day 20 of any cycle. Thyroid function, full blood count and ferritin are within normal limits.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, full blood count and ferritin within normal limits
data_table.Symptom diary: Three cycles charted: scores rise from about day 21, peak in the 3 days before menstruation, return to baseline within 2 days of bleeding; no symptoms between day 4 and day 20 of any cycle

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: A tricyclic antidepressant taken continuously throughout each day of the cycle
options.rationale: Tricyclics have not demonstrated the rapid luteal phase efficacy that serotonergic agents show and carry greater anticholinergic burden and overdose toxicity. A tricyclic would be a later-line consideration in treatment-resistant major depression rather than in this cyclical presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken during the luteal phase of each cycle
options.rationale: Two years of a prospectively charted symptom pattern confined to the luteal phase with complete follicular resolution establishes premenstrual dysphoric disorder, for which serotonergic agents are first-line. Response occurs within days rather than the weeks required in major depression, which is what makes intermittent luteal phase dosing effective and well tolerated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: A low dose atypical antipsychotic taken during the luteal phase of each cycle
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have no established role in premenstrual dysphoric disorder and carry metabolic and movement disorder risks disproportionate to the indication. They would be appropriate as augmentation in psychotic or treatment-resistant mood disorder, which is not the picture here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist given by depot injection each month
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression is effective but induces a hypo-oestrogenic state with bone loss and is reserved for severe symptoms refractory to first and second-line therapy, usually with add-back oestrogen. It would be considered after serotonergic agents and hormonal contraception have failed. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: A progestogen-only oral contraceptive taken continuously throughout each day of the cycle
options.rationale: Progestogen-only preparations do not reliably suppress ovulation at conventional doses and progestogens themselves can provoke the mood symptoms being treated. A combined preparation containing drospirenone taken continuously is the hormonal option with supporting evidence. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is distinguished from the far more common premenstrual syndrome by the severity of the mood component and the functional impairment it causes, and from an underlying mood disorder by the complete absence of symptoms in the follicular phase. Prospective daily charting over at least two cycles is required for diagnosis because retrospective recall consistently overattributes symptoms to the premenstrual window, and a substantial proportion of women referred with this presentation turn out to have premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying condition instead. The pathophysiology appears to involve differential central sensitivity to normal luteal progesterone metabolites rather than abnormal hormone levels, which is why measuring hormones is unhelpful. Serotonergic antidepressants work unusually quickly here, allowing luteal phase only dosing that halves drug exposure. Second-line options include continuous combined hormonal contraception, with ovarian suppression and, rarely, oophorectomy reserved for severe refractory disease.
key_points: Diagnosis requires prospective daily symptom charting across at least two cycles
Complete symptom resolution in the follicular phase separates this from an underlying mood disorder
Serotonergic agents are first-line and act within days, permitting luteal phase only dosing
Hormone measurement is unhelpful because levels are normal and sensitivity is the abnormality
Ovarian suppression is reserved for refractory disease because of hypo-oestrogenic bone loss
explanation.pearls: Luteal phase dosing typically starts around day 14 or at symptom onset and stops at the onset of menstruation, which distinguishes this from every other antidepressant indication where abrupt cessation risks discontinuation symptoms.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

subtopic_detail: First-line management of repetitive hair pulling producing visible scalp loss in an adolescent
stem:
You are the resident in an adolescent mental health clinic. A 15-year-old girl is brought in by her mother, who has noticed thinning at the crown of her scalp over 8 months.

The girl says she pulls hair out while watching television and while doing homework, often without noticing until she sees the hairs on her lap. She describes a build-up of tension beforehand and relief afterward. She denies any belief that her hair is infested or that pulling prevents harm to anyone.

She is embarrassed and has started wearing a cap at school, and she has declined invitations to swim. Her mood is reactive and she denies suicidal ideation. She eats normally and sleeps well. On examination there is an irregular area of hair loss at the crown with hairs of varying lengths and no scaling, no erythema, no scarring and no broken hair shafts elsewhere. Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Irregular crown hair loss with hairs of varying lengths, no scaling, erythema or scarring, no involvement of eyebrows or eyelashes
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor titrated to a standard therapeutic dose
options.rationale: Serotonergic agents are effective in obsessive compulsive disorder but trials in hair pulling disorder have been largely negative, which is one reason the two conditions are now separated. An antidepressant would be indicated if a comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder were present alongside. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: A topical corticosteroid scalp preparation applied to the affected area daily
options.rationale: Topical steroid treats inflammatory alopecia such as alopecia areata, which produces smooth round patches without hairs of varying lengths. It would be correct if examination showed exclamation mark hairs and completely bare, non-irregular patches. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Habit reversal training delivered as a structured behavioural therapy program
options.rationale: Habit reversal training is the intervention with the strongest evidence in hair pulling disorder and works by building awareness of the behaviour and substituting a competing response at moments of urge. It is first-line ahead of medication because no drug has consistent trial support in this condition. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: A low dose antipsychotic prescribed with baseline metabolic and movement monitoring
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are sometimes used as augmentation in refractory cases but carry metabolic and extrapyramidal risks unjustified as an initial approach in an adolescent. They would be considered only after behavioural therapy and other options had failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: A scalp punch biopsy to establish the histological pattern before treatment is commenced
options.rationale: The history of pulling with tension and relief and the finding of hairs at varying lengths without scarring make this a clinical diagnosis requiring no biopsy. Biopsy would be justified if there were scarring, scaling or diagnostic uncertainty about a primary dermatological cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Hair pulling disorder sits within the body-focused repetitive behaviours alongside skin picking, and it is classified near but separately from obsessive compulsive disorder because its treatment response differs markedly. The pulling is often automatic rather than deliberate, occurring during sedentary absorbed activities, and the absence of an obsessional belief driving it distinguishes it from a compulsion performed to neutralise an intrusive thought. Examination findings are characteristic: an irregular patch containing hairs of many different lengths, because regrowth is continually interrupted, with no scarring, scaling or inflammation. Onset typically occurs around puberty and the condition is substantially more common in females presenting to services. Habit reversal training is the treatment of choice, and asking about trichophagia is important because swallowing pulled hair can produce a gastric trichobezoar requiring surgical removal.
key_points: Tension before pulling and relief afterward, without an obsessional belief, characterises the disorder
Hairs of varying lengths in an irregular non-scarring patch distinguish it from alopecia areata
Habit reversal training is first-line; serotonergic antidepressants have largely negative trial data
Pulling is frequently automatic and occurs during sedentary absorbed activities
Screen for comorbid depression and anxiety, which commonly accompany the disorder
explanation.pearls: Ask directly whether she swallows the hair she pulls: trichophagia can form a gastric trichobezoar with a tail extending into the small bowel, which presents with obstruction and needs surgical removal.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Parasomnia occurring in the first third of the night with no dream recall in a preschool child
stem:
You are the resident in a general paediatric clinic. A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents because three or four nights a week he sits up and screams inconsolably about 90 minutes after falling asleep.

During the episodes his eyes are open and he appears terrified, sweating and breathing fast. He does not recognise his parents and pushes them away when they try to comfort him. Each episode lasts about 5 minutes and he then settles back to sleep.

In the morning he is cheerful and has no memory of the events. His parents say there is no limb stiffening, no jerking, no tongue biting and no incontinence during the episodes, and the events never happen in the early morning hours. He started 4-year-old kindergarten 3 months ago and has been going to bed about an hour later than before. His father had similar episodes as a child. Development, growth and neurological examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Development, growth and neurological examination normal
data_table.Event description: Onset about 90 minutes after sleep onset, eyes open, unresponsive to parents, terror with sweating and tachypnoea, duration about 5 minutes, no stiffening, jerking, tongue biting or incontinence, complete amnesia in the morning

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram and start an antiseizure medicine if the recording is abnormal
options.rationale: Nocturnal frontal lobe seizures are the differential but they are brief, stereotyped, occur multiple times per night and often involve dystonic posturing, none of which is described. An electroencephalogram would be indicated for stereotyped clustered events, daytime seizures or abnormal neurological findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems)

options.text: Prescribe low dose clonazepam at bedtime and review the frequency of events in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines suppress slow wave sleep and are occasionally used for dangerous or very frequent parasomnias, but they are not appropriate for a self-limiting condition in a preschool child. Medication would be considered for episodes causing injury or persisting despite optimised sleep. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Advise waking him fully during each episode and providing reassurance until he settles
options.rationale: Attempting to rouse a child from a slow wave sleep arousal typically prolongs the episode and increases agitation, because he is not awake and cannot be consoled. Gentle guidance back to bed without full waking is the correct approach during an event. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems)

options.text: Explain the benign nature, advise a regular earlier bedtime and safety-proof the bedroom
options.rationale: Events arising 90 minutes after sleep onset with unresponsiveness, autonomic arousal and complete amnesia are night terrors from slow wave sleep, and insufficient sleep is the main precipitant given the recent later bedtime. Management is reassurance, restoring adequate sleep duration and making the environment safe, since the child may get out of bed during an event. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems)

options.text: Refer for trauma-focused psychological assessment and review the frequency of events in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Night terrors are not caused by psychological trauma and the child is well, developing normally and has no daytime distress. Trauma assessment would be warranted if there were nightmares with recall, behavioural regression, or disclosure or suspicion of adverse experiences. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems)

explanation.summary: Night terrors are disorders of arousal from slow wave sleep, which is concentrated in the first third of the night, and this timing is the most useful single discriminator from nightmares. A child having a nightmare wakes in the second half of the night, can be consoled, and recalls the dream, whereas a child having a night terror appears awake but is not, cannot be consoled, and has no memory of it. Parents often find the amnesia hardest to believe and are reassured to learn that the child is not suffering in the way the screaming suggests. Precipitants are anything that increases slow wave sleep pressure or fragments sleep: insufficient sleep, irregular schedules, febrile illness, a full bladder and obstructive sleep apnoea. There is a strong familial tendency, and the great majority of children outgrow the episodes by adolescence without any specific treatment.
key_points: Slow wave sleep arousals occur in the first third of the night; nightmares occur in the later half
Unresponsiveness during the event and complete morning amnesia are characteristic
Sleep deprivation and irregular schedules are the commonest precipitants
Attempting to fully wake the child prolongs and worsens the episode
Screen for obstructive sleep apnoea, since sleep fragmentation triggers arousals
explanation.pearls: Scheduled awakening, gently rousing the child about 15 to 30 minutes before the usual event time for a couple of weeks, interrupts the slow wave cycle and is the behavioural option when events are frequent and predictable.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing bowel disimpaction and behavioural work in a school-aged child soiling daily
stem: A 7-year-old boy soils his underwear most days. His mother says he does it deliberately and hides the soiled underwear; a reward chart has not helped. He passes a very large painful stool about every 8 days and leaks small amounts of loose brown material between these.

data_table.Examination: Firm, indentable mass from the left iliac fossa to the umbilicus; normal anus and lower limb neurology

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for family behavioural therapy with a reward program
options.rationale: Behavioural work is a valuable adjunct but achieves little while a rectal faecal mass continues to cause involuntary leakage, and framing the problem behaviourally sustains the blame the child is already receiving. It becomes useful once disimpaction has occurred and toileting routines are being established. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Request an abdominal radiograph to quantify faecal loading
options.rationale: Faecal loading is already evident on palpation and radiography adds radiation without changing management or correlating reliably with symptoms. Imaging would be considered where examination is unreliable or an alternative diagnosis is suspected. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Arrange anorectal manometry and rectal biopsy
options.rationale: These investigate Hirschsprung disease, which typically presents with delayed meconium passage in the newborn period and an empty rectum rather than with overflow soiling after years of normal continence. They would be indicated for constipation from birth with failure to thrive or an empty rectum on examination. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Prescribe a maintenance stimulant laxative and fibre advice
options.rationale: A stimulant alone will not clear an established impaction and can cause severe cramping when driving peristalsis against a hard retained mass. Stimulants are used as adjuncts to osmotic laxatives when maintenance with macrogol alone proves insufficient. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

options.text: Commence macrogol disimpaction, then maintenance laxative
options.rationale: Daily leakage around a palpable faecal mass is overflow incontinence from chronic retention rather than voluntary soiling, and it cannot improve until the impaction is cleared. Maintenance laxative and scheduled post-meal toileting then continue for months, because relapse is common if treatment stops as soon as soiling resolves. (Source: RCH CPG: Constipation)

explanation.summary: Faecal soiling in a school-aged child who was previously continent is overflow incontinence from chronic constipation in the great majority of cases, and the history of infrequent enormous stools with daily leakage between them is close to diagnostic. The mechanism explains why punishment and reward systems fail: the rectum becomes chronically distended, stretch receptors adapt so the child stops sensing fullness, and softer stool tracks passively around the impacted mass without any voluntary control. Hiding soiled underwear reflects shame rather than defiance, and reframing this for the family is a therapeutic act in itself. Treatment has two distinct phases that must happen in order, disimpaction followed by maintenance, and the most common reason for failure is stopping maintenance laxatives too early, before the stretched rectum has regained normal tone and sensation. Red flags warranting further investigation include constipation from birth, delayed meconium, failure to thrive, an empty rectum, abnormal anal position or sacral and neurological signs.
key_points: Daily leakage with infrequent large stools indicates overflow incontinence, not voluntary soiling
Disimpaction must precede maintenance therapy and behavioural work
Rectal distension blunts sensation, so the child genuinely cannot feel the leakage
Maintenance laxatives continue for months after soiling resolves to allow rectal tone to recover
Red flags include constipation from birth, delayed meconium, failure to thrive and sacral or neurological signs
explanation.pearls: Warn families that soiling often worsens for the first few days of a macrogol disimpaction regimen as the retained mass mobilises, because parents who are not warned commonly stop the treatment at exactly that point.

sources.label: NICE: Constipation in children and young people

subtopic_detail: Separating drug-induced inner restlessness from an urge to move relieved by walking at night
stem: A 47-year-old man with schizophrenia started risperidone 3 mg daily 5 weeks ago. He describes a crawling urge to move his legs, worst when sitting in the evening and worse in bed, relieved by walking. His partner says he kicks in his sleep. He denies daytime mental restlessness.

data_table.Examination: Sits still through a 30 minute consultation; no tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 22 micrograms/L (30-500), transferrin saturation 14 per cent, haemoglobin 128 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral iron replacement
options.rationale: A circadian urge to move confined to rest and the evening, relieved by walking and associated with sleep kicking, is restless legs syndrome rather than akathisia, and low ferritin with reduced transferrin saturation identifies a reversible cause. Iron replacement is first-line when ferritin is below 75 micrograms/L, and correcting it frequently resolves symptoms without any change to antipsychotic therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Reduce the risperidone dose
options.rationale: Dose reduction is the correct response to akathisia, but akathisia produces continuous subjective inner restlessness with observable fidgeting that does not follow a circadian pattern or resolve with walking. Reducing the dose here risks psychotic relapse without addressing the actual cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence low dose propranolol
options.rationale: Propranolol is a recognised treatment for akathisia but has no established role in restless legs syndrome. It would be appropriate if the patient described generalised inner restlessness present throughout the day with visible motor manifestations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence low dose benzatropine
options.rationale: Anticholinergics treat drug-induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia, and examination shows no tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia to support either. Benzatropine is notably ineffective for akathisia as well, so it does not fit any of the plausible drug-induced alternatives here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a dopamine agonist
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists are effective in restless legs syndrome but carry a substantial risk of augmentation with long-term use and would also antagonise the antipsychotic effect being relied on. They are reserved for persistent symptoms after iron has been replaced and non-dopaminergic options considered. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Akathisia and restless legs syndrome are confused constantly in psychiatric practice because both produce an urge to move in someone taking a dopamine antagonist, and getting the distinction right determines whether an effective antipsychotic is unnecessarily reduced. Restless legs syndrome follows a circadian pattern that worsens in the evening and at rest, is relieved by movement, and is focused on the legs, whereas akathisia is present throughout the day, is experienced as generalised mental restlessness as much as physical, and is not relieved by walking. Periodic limb movements during sleep accompany restless legs syndrome in the majority of cases and are a useful collateral clue from a bed partner. Iron deficiency is the most important reversible contributor, and the treatment threshold uses a ferritin considerably higher than that used for anaemia because brain iron status is the relevant variable. Dopamine antagonists can certainly unmask or worsen restless legs syndrome, so the two conditions can coexist with the same precipitant.
key_points: Circadian worsening at rest and in the evening with relief on movement indicates restless legs syndrome
Akathisia is continuous, generalised and subjectively mental as well as motor, and is not relieved by walking
Periodic limb movements reported by a bed partner support restless legs syndrome
Replace iron when ferritin is below 75 micrograms/L or transferrin saturation below 20 per cent
Dopamine agonists risk augmentation and are not first-line despite their efficacy
explanation.pearls: The ferritin threshold for treating restless legs syndrome is below 75 micrograms/L, far above the threshold used to diagnose iron deficiency anaemia, because central nervous system iron availability rather than red cell production is the target.

subtopic_detail: Hyponatraemia developing weeks after starting an antidepressant in an older adult on a thiazide
stem: A 76-year-old woman has a low sodium on routine bloods. She started sertraline 50 mg daily 4 weeks ago and has taken hydrochlorothiazide for 6 years. She feels unsteady, without seizures or confusion.

data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic, no oedema, postural drop 6 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 124 mmol/L (138 mmol/L 3 months ago), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the hydrochlorothiazide, restrict fluid and recheck the sodium
options.rationale: Thiazides are a classic cause of hyponatraemia and would be the answer if the timing fitted, but she has taken it for 6 years with a normal sodium 3 months ago. It would be the correct target if the antidepressant were long-established and the diuretic recently started. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Cease the sertraline, restrict fluid and recheck the sodium
options.rationale: Euvolaemic hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L is the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, and the temporal link to a drug started 4 weeks ago in a normonatraemic patient identifies the culprit. Serotonergic antidepressants characteristically cause this within the first few weeks, most commonly in older women, and stopping the drug with fluid restriction corrects it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Give hypertonic saline, restrict fluid and recheck the sodium urgently
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptoms such as seizures, coma or marked confusion, and rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia risks osmotic demyelination. It would be indicated if she presented with a seizure or a depressed level of consciousness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give isotonic saline, continue current medicines and recheck the sodium
options.rationale: Isotonic saline treats hypovolaemic hyponatraemia but can worsen sodium in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, because the salt is excreted while the water is retained. It would be correct if she were clinically volume deplete with a low urine sodium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Switch sertraline to a tricyclic, restrict fluid and recheck the sodium
options.rationale: Tricyclics also cause the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis and add anticholinergic and cardiac conduction risks that are poorly tolerated in this age group. A switch would be considered later, to an agent such as mirtazapine or agomelatine, after the sodium has normalised. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Drug-induced hyponatraemia in older adults is common, underdiagnosed and frequently attributed to the wrong agent because patients typically take several implicated drugs at once. The diagnostic framework is unchanged regardless of the culprit: confirm true hypo-osmolality, assess volume status clinically, and use paired serum and urine osmolality with urine sodium to separate the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis from hypovolaemia and from renal salt wasting. Thyroid and adrenal insufficiency must be excluded because both mimic it exactly. Attribution then rests on timing, and a documented normal sodium before the new drug is the single most valuable piece of evidence, which is why baseline electrolytes before starting an antidepressant in an older patient are worth the trouble. Serotonergic agents typically cause hyponatraemia within the first 2 to 4 weeks, and risk is substantially higher with advanced age, female sex, low body weight and concurrent diuretic use, all of which compound here.
key_points: Confirm hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia and assess volume status before attributing a cause
Urine osmolality above 100 mmol/kg with urine sodium above 30 mmol/L in a euvolaemic patient indicates inappropriate antidiuresis
Exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, which mimic the syndrome
Serotonergic antidepressants typically cause hyponatraemia within the first 2 to 4 weeks
Correct chronic hyponatraemia slowly; hypertonic saline is only for severe neurological symptoms
explanation.pearls: Check electrolytes at baseline and again about 2 weeks after starting a serotonergic antidepressant in anyone over 65, particularly if they also take a thiazide, because the fall is usually asymptomatic until sodium drops below about 125 mmol/L.

subtopic_detail: Selecting a replacement antipsychotic after a markedly prolonged corrected QT interval
stem:
You are the registrar in an inpatient psychiatric unit. A 52-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder has been taking haloperidol 10 mg daily for 3 weeks with good symptomatic response after a relapse with command hallucinations.

A routine electrocardiogram taken this morning shows sinus rhythm at 68 beats per minute with a corrected QT interval of 512 ms, repeated and confirmed on a second recording. His admission electrocardiogram 3 weeks ago showed a corrected QT interval of 432 ms.

He has had no syncope, no palpitations and no chest pain. He takes no other medicines and denies illicit substance use, and a urine drug screen is negative. Potassium is 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.88 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), thyroid function normal and renal and liver function within normal limits. There is no family history of sudden death or of unexplained drowning. Echocardiography shows structurally normal heart with normal systolic function.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 126/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram: sinus rhythm 68/min, corrected QT interval 512 ms confirmed on repeat, versus 432 ms on admission. Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.88 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), thyroid, renal and liver function within normal limits. Urine drug screen negative. Echocardiogram structurally normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reduce the haloperidol dose to 5 mg daily, repeating the electrocardiogram after the reduction
options.rationale: Although the effect is dose-related, continuing the same agent above a corrected QT interval of 500 ms leaves the patient exposed to arrhythmia for the sake of convenience. Dose reduction would be a reasonable response to a modest prolongation in the 460 to 500 ms range with close monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease haloperidol and commence ziprasidone, repeating the electrocardiogram after the switch
options.rationale: Ziprasidone produces greater corrected QT prolongation than most other antipsychotics, so substituting it exchanges one repolarisation risk for a similar or larger one. The near-pair point is that both are effective antipsychotics but they sit at opposite ends of the repolarisation risk spectrum. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease haloperidol and commence aripiprazole, repeating the electrocardiogram after the switch
options.rationale: A corrected QT interval above 500 ms carries a materially increased risk of torsades de pointes and requires the offending agent to be stopped rather than continued at a lower dose. Aripiprazole has among the least effect on cardiac repolarisation of the available antipsychotics, making it the rational replacement when antipsychotic cover must continue. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease haloperidol and commence citalopram, repeating the electrocardiogram after the switch
options.rationale: Citalopram is an antidepressant with its own dose-dependent corrected QT prolongation and would leave the psychotic symptoms untreated. An antidepressant might be added later for the affective component once an antipsychotic with a favourable cardiac profile is established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue haloperidol and give intravenous magnesium sulfate, repeating the electrocardiogram afterward
options.rationale: Magnesium is the treatment for established torsades de pointes and for correcting hypomagnesaemia, and this patient's magnesium is already normal with no arrhythmia. It would be given immediately if he developed polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-associated corrected QT prolongation is a genuine but often mismanaged risk, and the practical decisions turn on two numbers: an absolute corrected QT interval above 500 ms, or an increase of more than 60 ms from baseline, both of which mark a materially elevated arrhythmia risk. This patient meets both. Before attributing the change to the drug, reversible contributors must be corrected, since hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, bradycardia and hypothyroidism all prolong repolarisation and are far easier to fix than a psychotropic regimen. Antipsychotics differ substantially in this effect, with haloperidol, particularly intravenously, and ziprasidone among the higher risk agents, while aripiprazole, lurasidone and brexpiprazole have minimal effect. Because untreated psychosis carries its own substantial mortality, the answer is almost never to stop antipsychotic treatment altogether but to move to an agent with a better repolarisation profile and repeat the electrocardiogram once the new drug is at steady state.
key_points: A corrected QT interval above 500 ms or a rise of more than 60 ms from baseline requires action
Correct potassium, magnesium, calcium and thyroid abnormalities before attributing prolongation to a drug
Haloperidol and ziprasidone are higher risk; aripiprazole and lurasidone have minimal effect
Stopping all antipsychotic treatment is rarely correct given the mortality of untreated psychosis
Repeat the electrocardiogram once the replacement agent reaches steady state
explanation.pearls: Intravenous haloperidol prolongs the corrected QT interval considerably more than the oral route at equivalent doses, which is why continuous cardiac monitoring is advised whenever it is given intravenously for acute behavioural disturbance.

subtopic_detail: New onset misidentification delusion with fluctuating attention in an older adult
stem: A 74-year-old man admitted 3 days ago with cellulitis, now improving, insists his wife is an impostor. His daughter reports 8 months of visual hallucinations of small animals and increasing slowness, and over a year of shouting and thrashing during dreams.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity, fluctuating attention
data_table.Investigations: Screening bloods normal; brain CT shows atrophy only

lead_in: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

options.text: An acute confusional state precipitated by the current infection
options.rationale: Delirium is a genuine contributor to the acute deterioration, but it does not explain 8 months of progressive parkinsonism, visual hallucinations and over a year of dream enactment reported by the family. A purely delirious picture would be correct if collateral history described normal baseline cognition and function. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.text: A primary psychotic disorder presenting for the first time in later life
options.rationale: Very late onset schizophrenia-like psychosis typically features persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations without parkinsonism, fluctuating attention or dream enactment. It would be the diagnosis if motor signs and cognitive fluctuation were absent and cognition were otherwise preserved. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.text: A neurodegenerative disorder with cortical tau and amyloid deposition
options.rationale: Alzheimer disease presents with prominent early episodic memory loss and does not typically produce early parkinsonism, marked cognitive fluctuation or dream enactment behaviour. The near-pair distinction is that both cause dementia with psychotic features, but visual hallucinations and parkinsonism arise early in synucleinopathy and late in Alzheimer disease. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.text: A neurodegenerative disorder with cortical synuclein deposition
options.rationale: Fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism and a long history of dream enactment together identify dementia with Lewy bodies, of which delusional misidentification is a recognised feature. The dream enactment behaviour is particularly telling, since it frequently precedes cognitive symptoms by years and is strongly predictive of an underlying synucleinopathy. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.text: A cerebrovascular disorder producing stepwise small vessel decline
options.rationale: Vascular cognitive impairment produces stepwise deterioration with focal neurological signs and imaging evidence of infarction or extensive white matter disease, and this scan shows atrophy only. It would be the diagnosis with a stepwise history and corresponding vascular lesions on imaging. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

explanation.summary: Delusional misidentification, in which a familiar person is believed to have been replaced by an identical impostor, is far more often a sign of organic brain disease than of a primary psychiatric disorder, particularly when it appears for the first time in later life. The task is to identify what underlies it, and the collateral history usually carries the diagnosis where the mental state examination alone cannot. Here the combination of fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism and rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder gives the core clinical features of dementia with Lewy bodies. Recognising it has immediate and serious practical consequences because severe sensitivity to antipsychotics occurs in a substantial proportion of patients and can produce irreversible parkinsonism, sedation, autonomic instability and death. Cholinesterase inhibitors, by contrast, are often strikingly effective for the hallucinations and cognitive fluctuation, so the correct diagnosis changes treatment in the opposite direction to instinct.
key_points: New misidentification delusions in later life suggest organic disease rather than primary psychiatric illness
Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and dream enactment define the core clinical picture
Dream enactment behaviour often precedes cognitive symptoms by years and predicts synucleinopathy
Severe antipsychotic sensitivity can cause irreversible deterioration and death
Cholinesterase inhibitors frequently improve hallucinations and cognitive fluctuation
explanation.pearls: If an antipsychotic is unavoidable in suspected Lewy body disease, quetiapine at the lowest possible dose is the conventional choice, and typical agents such as haloperidol are avoided entirely because of the risk of irreversible parkinsonism and death.

sources.label: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with dementia

subtopic_detail: Engaging a patient presenting to dermatology with fixed belief of skin infestation and specimen collection
stem: A 58-year-old woman attends dermatology for a fourth referral in 8 months, convinced tiny parasites live under her skin. She brings a container of lint and fibres she calls the organisms, and has applied bleach and kerosene to her forearms. She functions independently. Her skin infection is being treated.

data_table.Examination: Excoriations and secondary infection on both forearms
data_table.Investigations: Microscopy of her specimen shows fibres and keratin only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the specimen has no parasites, then discharge
options.rationale: Direct contradiction of a fixed delusion does not alter the belief and typically leads the patient to seek another clinician, continuing the cycle of presentations and self-treatment. Explaining negative results works where the belief is an overvalued idea held with doubt rather than a fixed delusion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe topical permethrin and review in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Prescribing an antiparasitic reinforces the delusional belief and exposes her to further unnecessary treatment while the underlying disorder progresses. Permethrin would be correct for genuine scabies, which produces burrows and webspace involvement and typically affects household contacts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Arrange involuntary assessment under the Mental Health Act
