options.rationale: Involuntary assessment requires risk to the person or others that cannot be managed voluntarily, and she is functioning independently and engaging with services. It would become appropriate if self-treatment escalated to serious harm or if she refused all care while deteriorating markedly. (Source: RANZCP: Mental health legislation)

options.text: Start a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants have a role in body dysmorphic disorder and in obsessional preoccupations held with insight, but not in a fixed delusion of infestation. An antidepressant would be added if a comorbid depressive disorder emerged alongside antipsychotic treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Build rapport over visits, then offer an antipsychotic
options.rationale: A single fixed delusion with preserved functioning in every other domain is delusional disorder of the somatic type, which responds to antipsychotic treatment but only if the patient accepts it. Treating the visible skin damage first and framing medication around distress and skin healing rather than around belief is what makes acceptance possible, since direct confrontation reliably ends the therapeutic relationship. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Delusional infestation is the most common somatic delusional disorder and presents almost exclusively to dermatology and general practice rather than to mental health services, because the patient's explanatory model is dermatological. The defining feature is that the delusion is encapsulated: outside this single belief, thought form, mood, perception and social and occupational functioning are entirely intact, which is why involuntary treatment is rarely justified and why the person seems so credible. Secondary causes must be excluded first, including substance use, particularly stimulants, thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, diabetes, human immunodeficiency virus infection and dementia, since any of these can produce an identical picture with a different treatment. The specimen sign, in which the patient brings collected material as proof, is characteristic and should be examined seriously and microscopically rather than dismissed, because taking the complaint seriously is the foundation of any therapeutic relationship. Antipsychotics achieve substantial improvement in most patients, but only a minority of the therapeutic effort is pharmacological and the rest is engagement.
key_points: An encapsulated delusion with otherwise preserved functioning defines delusional disorder
Exclude stimulant use, thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, diabetes, human immunodeficiency virus infection and dementia
Examine patient-collected specimens microscopically rather than dismissing them
Direct confrontation of the belief ends the therapeutic relationship without changing it
Antipsychotics are effective, but acceptance depends on framing treatment around distress and skin healing
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about methamphetamine and prescribed stimulants before diagnosing primary delusional infestation, because stimulant-induced formication with secondary delusional elaboration resolves with abstinence and needs no long-term antipsychotic.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing corticosteroid-induced mood elevation from a first manic episode during an asthma admission
stem: A 34-year-old man admitted 5 days ago with severe asthma is on prednisolone 50 mg daily. For 3 days he has slept about 2 hours a night, talks rapidly, describes a business plan that will make him wealthy and telephoned colleagues after midnight. He has no personal or family psychiatric history.

data_table.Examination: Pressured speech, elevated mood, oriented with sustained attention
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, glucose and thyroid function normal; drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discuss corticosteroid reduction and start an antipsychotic
options.rationale: Manic symptoms emerging within days of high dose corticosteroid in someone with no psychiatric history are a substance-induced mood disturbance, and the primary treatment is to reduce or withdraw the causative agent as the respiratory condition allows. An antipsychotic provides symptom control during the taper, since symptoms persist for days to weeks after the steroid is reduced and the behaviour carries real financial and interpersonal risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue the corticosteroid unchanged and start lithium
options.rationale: Committing to long-term mood stabilisation treats this as a primary bipolar disorder when the temporal relationship to a known precipitant has not yet been tested by withdrawing it. Lithium would be appropriate if manic episodes recurred independently of corticosteroid exposure. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Continue the corticosteroid and start an antidepressant
options.rationale: Antidepressants can precipitate or worsen manic symptoms and have no role in an elevated mood state. They would be considered for the depressive phase that sometimes follows corticosteroid withdrawal, not for the manic phase. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Order brain MRI and defer treatment meanwhile
options.rationale: Structural imaging is warranted for first-episode mania with focal neurological signs, atypical age of onset or altered consciousness, none of which is present alongside an obvious pharmacological precipitant. Deferring treatment also leaves the disinhibited spending and calling unaddressed. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Treat as hyperactive delirium with reorientation measures
options.rationale: Hyperactive delirium features impaired attention, disorientation and a fluctuating course, and this man is oriented with sustained attention and a sustained elevation of mood. Delirium management would be correct if attention were impaired and the picture waxed and waned across the day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Corticosteroid-induced psychiatric disturbance is common, dose-related and frequently missed because the patient is on a medical ward being treated for something else. Risk rises substantially above prednisolone 40 mg daily, symptoms typically appear within the first week, and elevated mood, irritability and insomnia predominate on initiation, whereas depressive symptoms are more characteristic of prolonged therapy or withdrawal. The absence of any prior psychiatric history, of family history and of previous reaction to lower-dose courses does not exclude the diagnosis, since the reaction is dose-dependent rather than idiosyncratic. Management is a negotiation with the treating team, because the corticosteroid is often genuinely needed, and symptom control with an antipsychotic buys time while the dose is reduced. Documenting the reaction matters for the future, since recurrence on re-exposure at similar doses is likely and prophylaxis can be planned.
key_points: Risk rises markedly above prednisolone 40 mg daily, with onset usually in the first week
Mania and irritability predominate on initiation; depression is more typical of prolonged use or withdrawal
Reducing or withdrawing the corticosteroid is the primary treatment where the medical condition allows
Antipsychotics give symptom control during the taper; antidepressants can worsen the elevated phase
Sustained attention and orientation distinguish this from hyperactive delirium
explanation.pearls: Symptoms usually resolve within about 6 weeks of stopping the corticosteroid, so document the reaction clearly in the record, since re-exposure at a similar dose carries a high risk of recurrence and may warrant prophylactic cover.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological choice for persistent aggression months after a moderate traumatic brain injury
stem: A 29-year-old man is 5 months after a moderate traumatic brain injury with bifrontal contusions. Several times a week he shouts, throws objects and has twice pushed staff during personal care, settling within minutes and expressing regret. A behavioural support plan has run 6 weeks with partial benefit.

data_table.Examination: No pain, constipation or retention; euthymic with no psychosis
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function and electroencephalogram normal

lead_in: What medication is most appropriate to add?

options.text: Risperidone, with metabolic and movement side effect monitoring
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are widely used but animal and clinical data suggest dopamine blockade may impair motor and cognitive recovery after brain injury, and sedation compromises rehabilitation participation. Risperidone would be reserved for aggression driven by psychotic symptoms, which are absent here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Propranolol, with pulse rate and blood pressure monitoring
options.rationale: Beta blockade has the strongest evidence base of any drug class for aggression following traumatic brain injury, and it is added here because a properly implemented behavioural plan has given only partial benefit. It is preferred over sedating alternatives because it does not impair the arousal and attention on which ongoing rehabilitation depends. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Diazepam, with sedation and respiratory rate monitoring
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines can cause paradoxical disinhibition in frontal lobe injury and impair the memory consolidation needed for new learning in rehabilitation. They have a role in brief acute sedation for immediate safety, not in ongoing management of recurrent outbursts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Sodium valproate, with liver function and platelet monitoring
options.rationale: Anticonvulsant mood stabilisers are sometimes used for post-injury agitation but the supporting evidence is weaker than for beta blockade, and the electroencephalogram shows no epileptiform activity to justify it on seizure grounds. Valproate would be more attractive if post-traumatic seizures coexisted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Sertraline, with mood, sleep and gastrointestinal monitoring
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants help where irritability arises from post-injury depression or emotional lability, and he is euthymic between episodes with no depressive symptoms. Sertraline would be appropriate if a depressive disorder were driving the irritability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Aggression after traumatic brain injury is one of the strongest predictors of poor community reintegration and of carer breakdown, and it is usually the behaviour that determines whether someone can return home. Frontal injury impairs inhibition of responses to frustration, which is why outbursts are typically triggered, brief, followed by remorse, and clustered around specific care activities. Two steps precede any prescription: excluding treatable medical contributors such as pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, sleep disruption and post-traumatic seizures, and implementing a structured behavioural plan, since environmental antecedents are modifiable and drugs cannot substitute for consistent handling. Where medication is needed, beta blockade is best supported, though often at doses higher than those used in cardiology and requiring several weeks for full effect. The overarching principle is to avoid agents that dull arousal, because rehabilitation gains depend on the patient being alert enough to participate.
key_points: Exclude pain, constipation, retention, infection, sleep disruption and seizures before prescribing
Implement a structured behavioural plan first, since triggers are identifiable and modifiable
Beta blockade has the strongest evidence for aggression after traumatic brain injury
Antipsychotics may impair motor and cognitive recovery and are reserved for psychotic drivers
Benzodiazepines risk paradoxical disinhibition and impair new learning
explanation.pearls: Propranolol for post-injury aggression often requires doses well above cardiac dosing and takes several weeks to show full benefit, so review pulse and blood pressure at each increment rather than abandoning it as ineffective at low dose.

sources.label: RANZCP: Neuropsychiatry of acquired brain injury
BMJ Best Practice: Traumatic brain injury

subtopic_detail: Recognising an immune cause of first-episode psychosis when catatonia and seizures follow a viral prodrome
stem: A 23-year-old woman has 3 weeks of disorganised behaviour and believes her thoughts are broadcast. She had a flu-like illness a month ago and this week has held odd postures. She then has a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds, followed by repetitive lip-smacking and choreiform hand movements.

data_table.Examination: Intermittent mutism, resists passive movement
data_table.Investigations: CT brain, electrolytes, glucose and thyroid function normal; drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Electroencephalogram before antiseizure treatment
options.rationale: An electroencephalogram is a reasonable adjunct and may show the extreme delta brush pattern, but it will not establish the cause and antiseizure treatment alone leaves the underlying process untreated. It would be the priority if the question were whether ongoing non-convulsive status was present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Serum creatine kinase for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requires exposure to a dopamine antagonist, and she has taken no antipsychotic medication, nor does she have the lead-pipe rigidity and marked hyperthermia typical of it. Creatine kinase would be central if she had received antipsychotics and developed rigidity with high fever. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Lumbar puncture with neuronal surface antibody testing
options.rationale: Subacute psychosis with a viral prodrome, new seizures, orofacial dyskinesia, catatonia and autonomic instability in a young woman is the recognised presentation of anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis, and cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing is the definitive investigation. Cerebrospinal fluid testing is specifically required because serum testing alone misses a meaningful proportion of cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Transvaginal ultrasound for an ovarian teratoma
options.rationale: Tumour screening is an essential part of management once the diagnosis is established, since an ovarian teratoma is found in a substantial minority of affected young women, but it follows rather than precedes antibody confirmation. It becomes the next step once cerebrospinal fluid antibodies return positive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Serum caeruloplasmin for a copper metabolism disorder
options.rationale: Wilson disease can present with psychiatric symptoms and movement abnormalities in this age group but evolves over months to years with hepatic involvement and Kayser-Fleischer rings, not over 3 weeks with seizures and fever. It would be worth testing in a subacute psychiatric presentation with tremor, dysarthria and deranged liver function. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor encephalitis characteristically begins with a viral-like prodrome and then produces psychiatric symptoms that are indistinguishable from a primary psychotic illness for days to weeks, which is why many patients are admitted to mental health units before the diagnosis is made. The features that should redirect thinking are neurological and autonomic rather than psychiatric: new seizures, orofacial dyskinesia, catatonia, autonomic instability and a decreased level of consciousness, particularly in a young woman with no psychiatric history. Standard investigations are frequently unremarkable, since computed tomography is typically normal, magnetic resonance imaging is normal in around half of cases, and inflammatory markers may be only mildly raised, so a normal first-line workup does not exclude it. Cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing is essential because serum testing alone has lower sensitivity and can be falsely negative. Treatment with corticosteroids, immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, plus removal of any associated teratoma, produces good recovery in the majority, and delay in immunotherapy is the strongest modifiable predictor of a poor outcome.
key_points: A viral prodrome followed by subacute psychosis, seizures, dyskinesia and catatonia is the characteristic sequence
Computed tomography is normal and magnetic resonance imaging is normal in roughly half of cases
Cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing is required, since serum testing alone misses cases
Ovarian teratoma is present in a substantial minority of affected young women and must be sought
Time to immunotherapy is the strongest modifiable determinant of outcome
explanation.pearls: Orofacial dyskinesia persisting while the patient is otherwise still is the single most discriminating bedside sign, because it does not occur in primary psychotic illness in an antipsychotic-naive patient.

subtopic_detail: First-line treatment for difficulty discarding possessions without obsessions or compulsive rituals
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 62-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner after a home visit. The practitioner's letter says the hallway and both bedrooms are filled chest-high with newspapers, plastic containers and unopened mail, and that the kitchen bench and the stove cannot be reached.

She tells you the items are 'all things I will need one day' and that the thought of putting any of them out makes her feel physically sick. She collects free newspapers and takes containers from recycling bins because she cannot bear to see them wasted. She has stopped inviting her sister in and eats takeaway because she cannot cook.

She describes no intrusive thoughts about contamination, harm or symmetry, and performs no checking, washing or counting rituals. Her mood is reactive, her appetite and sleep are unchanged, and she scores 28 out of 30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. She holds no beliefs that the items have special powers.

data_table.Mental state: Reactive mood, no psychomotor change, no perceptual disturbance, insight that the accumulation is a problem
data_table.Obsessive compulsive features: No contamination, harm or symmetry obsessions; no checking, washing or counting rituals
data_table.Functional impact: Kitchen bench and stove unreachable; hallway and both bedrooms filled chest-high; social withdrawal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Start high dose fluoxetine and review her response again in twelve weeks
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors at high dose are first line for obsessive compulsive disorder, where they act on the obsessions that drive the compulsions, and the evidence for them in hoarding disorder as a standalone condition is much weaker. Medication is added when a comorbid depressive or obsessive compulsive disorder is present or when therapy alone has not worked. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Arrange a council clean-out of the property and review her again afterwards
options.rationale: Forced clearance without the person's participation reliably produces acute distress and rapid reaccumulation, because it removes the objects without changing the beliefs and decision-making difficulties that generated them. Enforced clearance is reserved for genuine public health or fire risk and is done alongside therapy, not instead of it. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Start low dose risperidone and review her response again in twelve weeks
options.rationale: An antipsychotic would be considered if the beliefs about the possessions were held with delusional intensity, for instance that the objects were sentient or had special powers. She retains insight that the accumulation is a problem, which places this outside the psychotic spectrum. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer her for cognitive behavioural therapy specifically adapted for hoarding
options.rationale: Difficulty discarding possessions with distress on parting from them and excessive acquisition, in the absence of obsessions and compulsive rituals, is hoarding disorder, and the treatment with the best evidence is a specifically adapted cognitive behavioural therapy. It targets the decision-making and categorisation difficulties, the beliefs about the objects, and the acquisition behaviour, typically with in-home sorting practice alongside clinic sessions. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer her for neuropsychological testing and defer treatment until it is completed
options.rationale: Cognitive assessment matters when hoarding emerges for the first time in later life with other features of frontal or degenerative disease, and a Montreal Cognitive Assessment of 28 out of 30 argues against that. Deferring treatment for testing that is unlikely to change management wastes the therapeutic window. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Hoarding disorder was separated from obsessive compulsive disorder in DSM-5 because its phenomenology, course and treatment response differ. The defining features are persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of their value, distress associated with discarding, and consequent accumulation that congests living areas, with excessive acquisition present in most cases and specified when it occurs. The differential includes obsessive compulsive disorder where hoarding is driven by contamination or harm obsessions, a depressive episode with amotivation, psychosis with delusional beliefs about the objects, autism spectrum collecting, and frontotemporal dementia when onset is late and accompanied by other behavioural change. Insight is specified as good, poor or absent, and poor insight is common and does not exclude the diagnosis. Response to treatment is slower and less complete than in obsessive compulsive disorder, and the safety issues of fire risk, falls, vermin and structural load often need parallel attention from fire services and council.
key_points: Hoarding disorder requires difficulty discarding plus distress plus congestion of living areas
The absence of obsessions and rituals distinguishes it from obsessive compulsive disorder
Adapted cognitive behavioural therapy is first line; serotonergic medication has weaker evidence
Forced clearance without participation causes distress and rapid reaccumulation
New onset hoarding in later life warrants consideration of frontotemporal dementia
explanation.pearls: Animal hoarding is a distinct and more severe presentation, almost always accompanied by absent insight and squalor, and it carries much higher recidivism after intervention than object hoarding, so it warrants involvement of animal welfare services from the outset.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Investigating excessive daytime sleepiness with episodic loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter
stem: A 19-year-old student is referred for depression. For eight months she has fallen asleep in lectures and once at the wheel. She sleeps 11 pm to 8 am and a fifteen minute nap refreshes her. When she laughs hard her knees buckle and jaw sags for seconds, with preserved awareness.

data_table.Episodic features: Sleep paralysis two to three mornings weekly
data_table.Mental state: Bright reactive mood, body mass index 22

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review
options.rationale: The hypersomnia of a depressive episode is unrefreshing, is accompanied by low mood, anhedonia and diurnal variation, and does not produce brief episodes of muscle weakness triggered by emotion. A Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score of 3 with a bright reactive mood makes depression an implausible explanation. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Start modafinil and arrange sleep studies if needed
options.rationale: Treating first and investigating later removes the ability to interpret the sleep studies, because stimulants alter sleep latency and suppress rapid eye movement sleep. Formal diagnosis is also required in Australia for subsidised access and for the driving and occupational advice that follows. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Refer for polysomnography then multiple sleep latency testing
options.rationale: Brief bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter with preserved consciousness is cataplexy, and combined with daytime sleepiness, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations this is narcolepsy type 1. Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography to exclude another cause of disrupted sleep followed immediately by a multiple sleep latency test, which shows a mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Advise sleep hygiene and review her sleep diary
options.rationale: Insufficient sleep syndrome is the commonest cause of sleepiness in this age group and responds to extending sleep opportunity, but her diary already shows nine hours of consolidated sleep. Sleep hygiene advice is a useful adjunct in narcolepsy alongside scheduled naps, not a substitute for diagnosis. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Arrange oximetry and continuous positive airway pressure
options.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnoea produces unrefreshing sleep with snoring and witnessed apnoeas, typically in an older or higher weight patient, and naps are not restorative. A body mass index of 22 kg/m2 with refreshing short naps and cataplexy points elsewhere. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurons, probably through an autoimmune mechanism in genetically susceptible people, and it is defined by excessive daytime sleepiness plus cataplexy or a low cerebrospinal fluid orexin concentration. The classic tetrad of sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations represents intrusion of rapid eye movement sleep phenomena into wakefulness, although fewer than a third of patients have all four. Cataplexy is the one feature that is close to pathognomonic and is distinguished from syncope and seizure by the emotional trigger, the preserved consciousness and the rapid complete recovery. Naps that are short and refreshing help separate it from the unrefreshing sleepiness of depression, sleep apnoea and insufficient sleep. Treatment combines scheduled naps and sleep hygiene with modafinil or another wake promoting agent for sleepiness, and venlafaxine or sodium oxybate for cataplexy, alongside mandatory discussion of driving and notification requirements.
key_points: Cataplexy is brief bilateral weakness triggered by emotion with consciousness fully preserved
Short refreshing naps separate narcolepsy from depressive and apnoeic hypersomnia
Diagnosis needs overnight polysomnography then a multiple sleep latency test
Diagnostic criteria are mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods
Do not start a stimulant before the sleep studies, as it invalidates the result
explanation.pearls: Untreated narcolepsy with cataplexy makes a person unfit to drive in Australia; a conditional licence can be granted once treatment has produced satisfactory control, documented by a sleep physician, and the patient carries a legal obligation to notify the driver licensing authority.

subtopic_detail: Declaring serotonergic treatment failure in body dysmorphic disorder before the dose has been optimised
stem: A 23-year-old man spends three to four hours daily checking his nose in mirrors, believing it crooked and bulbous. A rhinoplasty eighteen months ago left him feeling worse. He has taken sertraline 50 mg daily for twelve months without missing doses, with no change and no adverse effects.

data_table.Examination: Nose of normal contour with a well healed scar; insight poor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer him to a plastic surgeon for another opinion
options.rationale: Cosmetic procedures in body dysmorphic disorder leave the preoccupation unchanged or worse in the great majority of cases, and his own experience after rhinoplasty demonstrates exactly that. Surgery would be appropriate only if there were an objective deformity, and his nose has a normal contour. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Switch to low dose olanzapine and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: An antipsychotic is used as augmentation when beliefs are held with delusional conviction and a properly dosed serotonergic trial has failed, not as a substitute for optimising that trial. His insight is poor rather than absent, which does not by itself change first-line treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase the sertraline towards 200 mg daily for twelve weeks
options.rationale: Body dysmorphic disorder characteristically requires serotonergic doses at the upper end of the range, comparable to those used in obsessive compulsive disorder, and 50 mg of sertraline is a starting dose rather than an adequate trial. An adequate trial is defined as 12 weeks at the maximum tolerated dose, so treatment failure cannot be declared until the dose has been pushed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop the sertraline and start a tricyclic antidepressant
options.rationale: Clomipramine is the one tricyclic with evidence in this disorder because of its potent serotonin reuptake inhibition, and other tricyclics have none. Switching agents before optimising the current one also loses whatever partial response has accrued. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop the sertraline and arrange supportive counselling
options.rationale: Generic supportive counselling has no evidence in body dysmorphic disorder, which responds to a specifically structured cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention and perceptual retraining. Withdrawing medication at the same time removes the one active treatment he is receiving. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder is a preoccupation with one or more perceived defects in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking or comparing. It is under-recognised because sufferers present to dermatologists and cosmetic surgeons rather than to mental health services, and insight is frequently poor, with a substantial minority holding their beliefs with delusional conviction. Suicidality is high, exceeding that seen in obsessive compulsive disorder and major depression, so risk is assessed at every review. Treatment combines a specifically adapted cognitive behavioural therapy with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor, and the doses required are consistently higher and the time to response longer than in depression, which is why premature dose-limited trials are the commonest reason for apparent treatment resistance. Cosmetic intervention rarely satisfies the concern and often shifts it to another body area.
key_points: The perceived defect is absent or slight to an observer, while the distress and time cost are large
Serotonergic doses must reach the upper end of the range, as in obsessive compulsive disorder
An adequate trial is 12 weeks at the maximum tolerated dose before declaring failure
Suicide risk is higher than in obsessive compulsive disorder or major depression
Cosmetic procedures usually leave the preoccupation unchanged or displaced elsewhere
explanation.pearls: Muscle dysmorphia, the belief that the body is insufficiently muscular, is a specifier of body dysmorphic disorder that occurs almost entirely in men and carries a high rate of anabolic androgenic steroid use, so ask directly about supplement and injectable use.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders
BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder

subtopic_detail: First-line intervention for electronic gaming machine losses disclosed during a consultation for insomnia
stem: A 41-year-old man asks for help sleeping, lying awake until 3 am for months. He discloses losing about 60,000 dollars on electronic gaming machines over two years, chasing the losses, concealing them and taking a mortgage redraw. Ten attempts to stop have each lasted a week.

data_table.Mental state: Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score of 8, no suicidal ideation

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Start naltrexone 50 mg daily and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists have modest evidence in gambling disorder and are considered when structured psychological therapy has failed or when there is a strong family history of alcohol use disorder. Starting a drug before any psychological or financial intervention inverts the treatment hierarchy. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

options.text: Refer for gambling specific therapy with financial counselling
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy addressing the erroneous beliefs about randomness and near misses, combined with financial counselling to restructure access to money, is first line and is available free through Gambling Help services in every Australian state. Addressing the debt is part of treatment rather than separate from it, because unmanaged financial pressure is itself a driver of chasing behaviour and of suicide risk. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants treat a comorbid depressive disorder but do not reduce gambling behaviour in their own right, and his low mood is described as entirely reactive to the financial situation. Treating the mood alone would leave the behaviour and the debt untouched. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

options.text: Advise venue self-exclusion alone and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Self-exclusion is a useful adjunct that reduces access to particular venues, but it is readily circumvented, does not cover online platforms, and does nothing about the cognitions that sustain the behaviour. It belongs within a treatment plan rather than as the whole of it. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

options.text: Refer to a residential withdrawal unit for admission this week
options.rationale: Residential withdrawal exists to manage the physiological withdrawal syndromes of alcohol, opioids and benzodiazepines, and gambling has no such syndrome requiring medical supervision. He drinks two standard drinks weekly and uses no other substances. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is classified among the substance related and addictive disorders because it shares the reward pathway, tolerance and withdrawal-like features of substance dependence, and in Australia electronic gaming machines account for the majority of harm. It is almost never the presenting complaint, surfacing instead through insomnia, anxiety, depression, relationship breakdown or financial crisis, so asking about gambling directly is what makes the diagnosis. The diagnostic features to elicit are preoccupation, escalating stakes to achieve the same excitement, repeated failed attempts to cut down, chasing losses, lying to conceal involvement, and jeopardising relationships or employment. Suicide risk is substantially elevated and rises sharply at moments of financial disclosure or crisis, so it is asked about at every contact. First-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy targeting erroneous cognitions about randomness, combined with financial counselling and practical restriction of access to funds, with pharmacotherapy reserved for non-response.
key_points: Gambling presents through insomnia, mood, relationship or financial problems rather than directly
Ask about preoccupation, escalation, chasing losses, concealment and failed attempts to stop
Cognitive behavioural therapy plus financial counselling is first line
Free state-based Gambling Help services provide both components
Suicide risk is elevated and peaks around financial disclosure and crisis
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about dopamine agonists in any patient with new onset gambling: pramipexole and ropinirole prescribed for Parkinson disease or restless legs cause impulse control disorders in up to 17 per cent of users, and the behaviour resolves when the drug is withdrawn.

subtopic_detail: Consistent failure to speak at school with fluent speech at home for more than a year
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a child and adolescent clinic seeing a 6-year-old girl referred by her school. The teacher's report says she has not spoken a single word in the classroom or playground in the fourteen months since she started school, and communicates by nodding, pointing and writing.

Her mother says she 'never stops talking' at home, tells long stories, argues with her older brother and sings loudly. A recording made at home and played in the clinic confirms fluent, well structured speech with age appropriate vocabulary and articulation.

At her school entry health check her hearing was normal on audiometry. She makes eye contact with you, smiles at her mother, shares a drawing spontaneously and plays imaginatively with the clinic dolls, and her teacher reports she has two friends she plays with silently at lunchtime. She freezes and looks at the floor when the teacher addresses her directly in front of the class.

data_table.School report: No speech in class or playground for 14 months; communicates by nodding, pointing and writing; freezes when addressed in front of the class
data_table.Home observation: Fluent, well structured, age appropriate speech confirmed on a home recording
data_table.Social development: Eye contact maintained, shared enjoyment with mother, spontaneous showing behaviour, imaginative doll play, two reciprocal friendships
data_table.Investigations: Audiometry at school entry within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange audiological assessment before any other referral is considered
options.rationale: Hearing assessment is essential in any child with reduced speech output and has already been done with a normal result at school entry. Repeating it delays treatment and cannot explain speech that is fluent at home and absent at school. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Start fluoxetine and review her speech at school again in twelve weeks
options.rationale: A serotonin reuptake inhibitor is added when a structured behavioural program has been properly delivered and has not produced progress, or when the impairment is severe and entrenched. Medication as the opening move skips the intervention with the strongest evidence in this age group. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Refer for an autism spectrum diagnostic assessment before any treatment
options.rationale: Reduced speech at school would raise this question, but she maintains eye contact, shows spontaneous sharing, plays imaginatively and sustains reciprocal friendships, all of which argue against a pervasive social communication difficulty. The selectivity of the mutism by setting is itself the discriminating feature. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Refer for graded exposure behavioural therapy delivered with the school
options.rationale: Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations despite speaking fluently elsewhere, persisting beyond a month of school and interfering with education, is selective mutism, an anxiety disorder rather than a language or oppositional problem. Behavioural treatment using stimulus fading and graded exposure delivered jointly by clinician, family and school is first line, and early intervention prevents the pattern becoming entrenched. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Advise the school to wait and review her speech again in twelve months
options.rationale: A brief settling-in period of up to a month after starting school is expected and does not warrant diagnosis, which is why the criteria require a duration beyond one month. Fourteen months of complete mutism is well past that point, and delay is associated with poorer outcomes. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is classified as an anxiety disorder and is defined by consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where speaking is expected, despite speaking normally in others, for at least one month beyond the first month of school. It is commonly misread as shyness, wilful refusal, a language disorder or autism, and the delay to referral averages several years, which matters because outcomes are better with earlier intervention. The diagnostic work is largely exclusionary: confirm normal hearing, confirm fluent age appropriate speech in at least one setting, and confirm that social reciprocity is intact outside the feared situations. Comorbid social anxiety disorder is present in the majority, and a smaller group has a coexisting speech or language difficulty that warrants its own assessment. Treatment is behavioural, using stimulus fading, shaping and graded exposure delivered collaboratively across home, clinic and classroom, with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor reserved for severe or treatment resistant cases.
key_points: Speech is fluent in at least one setting, which distinguishes this from a language disorder
Duration must exceed one month beyond the first month of schooling
Preserved eye contact, shared enjoyment and imaginative play argue against autism spectrum disorder
Behavioural therapy with school involvement is first line; medication is second line
Most children have comorbid social anxiety disorder, which is treated at the same time
explanation.pearls: Pressing a mute child to speak, or rewarding a single word in front of the class, reliably worsens the avoidance; the effective technique is stimulus fading, in which a new person is gradually introduced into a setting where the child is already speaking comfortably.

sources.label: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

subtopic_detail: Choosing ADHD pharmacotherapy in an adult with concurrent methamphetamine use
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 30-year-old man referred for assessment of attention difficulties. He says he 'cannot hold a thought long enough to finish anything' and has been dismissed from three jobs in two years for missed deadlines and lateness.

His primary school reports, which he brings with him, document inattention, fidgeting and disrupted classwork from Year 2 onwards, well before the age of 12. His partner confirms current difficulties with organisation, losing possessions and interrupting, present across work, home and social settings.

He uses methamphetamine by smoking it two to three times a week and has done so for about four years, describing it as 'the only thing that gets me through a shift'. He has no psychotic symptoms now and has never had any. He drinks alcohol rarely, has a normal physical examination, a blood pressure of 124/78 mmHg and a normal electrocardiogram.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Developmental history: Primary school reports documenting inattention and hyperactivity from Year 2, before age 12
data_table.Current impairment: Organisation, losing possessions and interrupting across work, home and social settings; three job losses in two years
data_table.Substance use: Methamphetamine smoked two to three times weekly for four years; alcohol rarely; no psychotic symptoms ever
data_table.Investigations: Physical examination and electrocardiogram within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start atomoxetine and refer him concurrently to a drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Australian guidance is explicit that ADHD treatment should not be withheld while a substance use disorder is addressed, because untreated ADHD worsens substance use outcomes, and the two are treated concurrently. A non-stimulant such as atomoxetine has no misuse or diversion liability and is preferred while methamphetamine use is active, with a long-acting stimulant considered once use is stable. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Start immediate release dexamfetamine and refer him to a drug service
options.rationale: Immediate release stimulants have the highest misuse and diversion potential of the available options and share a pharmacological class with the drug he is already using. If a stimulant is used at all in this setting it is a long-acting preparation, and only once the substance use is stable. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Withhold all ADHD treatment until he has been abstinent for six months
options.rationale: Requiring abstinence before treatment is an outdated position that the Australian guideline specifically rejects, since untreated ADHD is itself a driver of continued substance use and of attrition from drug and alcohol services. Abstinence is a goal of the concurrent treatment, not a precondition for it. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Refer him to a drug and alcohol service and defer the ADHD diagnosis
options.rationale: Deferring the diagnosis would be defensible if the only evidence of inattention came from the period of substance use, since stimulant use can mimic the symptom profile. Contemporaneous school reports documenting symptoms from Year 2 establish onset well before age 12 and before any drug exposure. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Start a sedating antipsychotic and refer him to a drug and alcohol service
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have a role in methamphetamine induced psychosis and in acute behavioural disturbance, and he has never had psychotic symptoms. They do not treat inattention and carry metabolic and extrapyramidal burden without benefit here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD requires several symptoms to have been present before the age of 12, impairment in two or more settings, and symptoms not better explained by another disorder, and the childhood onset criterion is the one that substance use most often obscures. Collateral evidence from school reports, parents or a long-term partner is therefore central to the assessment rather than optional. Substance use disorders are two to three times more common in adults with ADHD than in the general population, and the relationship runs both ways, with untreated ADHD predicting earlier onset and poorer treatment retention. The Australian guideline recommends treating both conditions concurrently rather than sequentially, favouring non-stimulants or long-acting stimulant formulations where diversion or misuse is a concern. Stimulant prescribing for adults in Australia additionally requires a state or territory authority and is generally initiated by a psychiatrist, and driving and occupational implications are discussed at initiation.
key_points: Childhood onset before age 12 must be established, ideally with contemporaneous collateral evidence
Treat ADHD and substance use disorder concurrently; abstinence is not a precondition
Non-stimulants and long-acting stimulants are preferred where misuse or diversion is a concern
Immediate release stimulants carry the highest diversion potential
Adult stimulant prescribing in Australia requires a state authority and usually psychiatrist initiation
explanation.pearls: Atomoxetine takes 4 to 6 weeks to reach full effect, unlike stimulants which work within hours, so patients must be warned in advance or they will discontinue it in the second week believing it has failed.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Consent for continuing maintenance electroconvulsive therapy when a family member objects
stem: A 74-year-old woman has had four episodes of psychotic depression over 11 years, each remitting with electroconvulsive therapy after failed antidepressant trials. Nine months of four-weekly maintenance has kept her well and she wants it continued. Her son telephones asking that it stop.

data_table.Capacity: Understands and weighs the memory effects, anaesthetic risk and alternatives
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic; Montreal Cognitive Assessment 27 out of 30

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Defer the treatment until her son agrees to it
options.rationale: A relative has no legal authority to veto treatment for an adult with decision-making capacity, and deferring on that basis would expose her to relapse of an illness that has previously involved food and fluid refusal. Family concerns are addressed by discussion with her consent, not by suspending her treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

options.text: Apply to the guardianship tribunal for a decision maker
options.rationale: Substitute decision making processes are engaged only when a person lacks capacity for the decision in question. Invoking a tribunal for a woman who demonstrably retains capacity removes her rights rather than protecting them. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

options.text: Stop maintenance treatment and continue nortriptyline
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy has already failed to prevent four episodes, and relapse rates after a successful acute course are substantially higher without maintenance electroconvulsive therapy in this group. Stopping would also be a unilateral decision against the expressed wish of a capacitous patient. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

options.text: Ask her son to sign the consent form for her
options.rationale: Consent signed by another person is valid only where that person holds a formal substitute decision making role and the patient lacks capacity. Obtaining a relative's signature for a capacitous adult is legally ineffective and would invalidate the consent. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

options.text: Proceed on her own consent and document capacity
options.rationale: She retains, understands, weighs and communicates the relevant information, which satisfies the test for decision-making capacity, and consent for electroconvulsive therapy in Australia rests with the patient whenever capacity is present. The right response to the son's concern is to offer, with her permission, a discussion of the actual evidence on cognitive effects, while documenting the capacity assessment and re-confirming consent before each treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

explanation.summary: Electroconvulsive therapy is the most effective acute treatment for severe depression with psychotic features, with remission rates well above those of antidepressant pharmacotherapy, and relapse after a successful acute course is high enough that maintenance treatment is offered to patients with a recurrent pattern. Consent is specific to the procedure, must be informed and voluntary, and is reconfirmed before each treatment rather than obtained once for an open-ended course. Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific, and is assessed against whether the person can understand and retain the relevant information, weigh it in arriving at a decision, and communicate that decision. Where capacity is absent, each Australian state and territory has its own statutory pathway, typically involving a mental health tribunal or guardianship body rather than family consent, and these differ enough that local legislation must be checked. The documented cognitive effect is anterograde and retrograde amnesia around the treatment period, which improves over weeks to months and is reduced by right unilateral ultrabrief pulse electrode placement.
key_points: Capacity is decision-specific: understanding, retaining, weighing and communicating
A relative cannot consent for, or veto treatment for, a capacitous adult
Consent for electroconvulsive therapy is reconfirmed before each treatment in a course
Maintenance treatment substantially reduces relapse after a successful acute course
Where capacity is absent, a statutory tribunal pathway applies, and it varies between states
explanation.pearls: Right unilateral ultrabrief pulse placement produces markedly less retrograde amnesia than bitemporal placement but needs stimulation at around six times seizure threshold to match its efficacy, which is why an inadequately dosed unilateral course is a common reason for apparent non-response.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Depression in adults

subtopic_detail: Arranging trauma focused therapy for a patient with limited English after a partial response to medication
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 35-year-old woman who arrived in Australia four years ago as a refugee and was granted a permanent visa eighteen months ago. Speaking through a professional interpreter, she describes nightmares almost every night, sudden intrusive images of events in a detention setting, and avoiding the supermarket because the lighting brings the images back.

She lives in stable public housing with her adult daughter, uses no alcohol or other substances, and has no current thoughts of self harm. She is not in contact with anyone who threatens her and has no outstanding legal or immigration matters.

She has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for eight months with good adherence, and reports her sleep has improved a little and the daytime irritability has settled, but the nightmares and intrusive images are unchanged. Her conversational English is limited to short exchanges and she asks her daughter to translate when she attends her general practitioner.

data_table.Mental state: Nightmares, intrusive imagery, avoidance of supermarket lighting, hyperarousal partially improved; no suicidal ideation
data_table.Current treatment: Sertraline 100 mg orally daily for eight months with good adherence and partial response
data_table.Psychosocial: Stable public housing, permanent visa granted, no ongoing threat, no legal or immigration matters outstanding
data_table.Substance use: No alcohol or other substance use
data_table.Language: Limited conversational English; attends with her adult daughter translating at the general practice

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her treatment?

options.text: Increase the sertraline to 200 mg daily and review her again in eight weeks
options.rationale: Dose escalation is reasonable when psychological therapy is unavailable or declined, and medication is a second-line option in post-traumatic stress disorder rather than the treatment with the best effect size. Escalating without offering the more effective intervention accepts a partial response unnecessarily. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for trauma focused psychological therapy with her daughter interpreting
options.rationale: Using a family member as interpreter is not acceptable practice in any clinical setting and is particularly damaging in trauma work, where the patient will censor disclosure to protect the relative and the relative may be re-traumatised or may filter the content. Professional interpreters are engaged even when the family offers to help. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Add low dose quetiapine at night for the nightmares and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation has limited evidence in post-traumatic stress disorder and carries metabolic and sedative burden, so it sits well down the list of options. Prazosin has better evidence specifically for nightmares if a pharmacological adjunct is needed after trauma focused therapy has been offered. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for generic supportive counselling delivered in English at the practice
options.rationale: Non-directive supportive counselling performs no better than waiting list in post-traumatic stress disorder and is specifically not recommended as a substitute for trauma focused therapy. Delivering it in a language she cannot follow compounds the problem. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for trauma focused psychological therapy with a professional interpreter
options.rationale: Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing are the first-line treatments with the largest effect sizes, and she has the stability in housing, immigration status and substance use that makes trauma processing appropriate now. A professional interpreter, ideally the same one across sessions and briefed about the content, is essential so that she can disclose freely and the therapy retains its fidelity. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian guidelines place trauma focused psychological therapies, principally trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing, ahead of pharmacotherapy for post-traumatic stress disorder on the strength of their effect sizes. Medication is offered when psychological therapy is unavailable, declined or insufficient, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are the usual first choice. Trauma processing requires a baseline of safety and stability, meaning the person is not living under continuing threat, has somewhere to live, and is not in uncontrolled substance withdrawal; where those conditions are absent, practical and stabilisation work comes first. For people from refugee backgrounds the assessment must also consider the effects of the settlement process itself, including visa insecurity, family separation and the loss of occupational identity, all of which can maintain symptoms independently of the original trauma. Engaging a professional interpreter, rather than a family member, is a requirement of safe and effective care and is arranged as a matter of course rather than on request.
key_points: Trauma focused psychological therapy is first line and outperforms medication
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are second line; supportive counselling is not recommended
Trauma processing requires baseline safety and stability in housing, threat and substance use
Never use a family member as interpreter, particularly in trauma work
Settlement stressors such as visa insecurity and family separation maintain symptoms independently
explanation.pearls: Prazosin, titrated from 1 mg at night, has the best evidence of any drug specifically for trauma related nightmares, and the dose-limiting problem is first dose postural hypotension rather than any central effect.

sources.label: Foundation House: Working with interpreters in mental health

subtopic_detail: Acute toxicity from an unregulated smoking product with a negative routine urine drug immunoassay
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar receiving a 22-year-old man brought in by ambulance from a share house. His flatmate says he smoked 'a herbal blend he bought off a website' about ninety minutes ago and then became terrified, shouting that the walls were closing in.

En route he vomited repeatedly and had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting about forty seconds that terminated without treatment. He is now agitated, pacing and pulling at the monitoring leads, and will not sit for examination.

His pupils are 6 mm and reactive, he is diaphoretic and his skin is flushed. A urine drug immunoassay is negative for amphetamines, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, cocaine metabolites, opioids and benzodiazepines. Point of care glucose is 6.1 mmol/L and the electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with a corrected QT interval of 430 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 146/min, blood pressure 168/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4°C
data_table.Examination: Agitated and pacing, pupils 6 mm and reactive, diaphoretic, flushed skin
data_table.Investigations: Urine immunoassay negative for amphetamines, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, cocaine metabolites, opioids and benzodiazepines; glucose 6.1 mmol/L
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia, corrected QT interval 430 ms
data_table.Event: One generalised tonic-clonic seizure of about 40 seconds, self-terminating, 90 minutes after smoking an online herbal product

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg and repeat the dose after thirty minutes
options.rationale: Butyrophenones lower the seizure threshold, impair thermoregulation and prolong the corrected QT interval, all of which are active hazards in a patient who has already seized and is hyperthermic. Antipsychotics are second line in stimulant-type toxicity and only after adequate benzodiazepine loading. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous naloxone 400 micrograms and repeat the dose after two minutes
options.rationale: Opioid toxicity presents with pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and reduced conscious state, which is the opposite of this hyperadrenergic picture with 6 mm pupils and tachypnoea. Naloxone would achieve nothing and would precipitate withdrawal if opioids were also on board. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give oral activated charcoal 50 g and observe him in the short stay unit
options.rationale: Charcoal has no role after an inhaled exposure, since the drug has bypassed the gut entirely, and administering it to an agitated patient risks aspiration. Decontamination is relevant to recent large oral ingestions with a protected airway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Titrate intravenous diazepam to sedation with supportive cooling measures
options.rationale: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists are full agonists at the cannabinoid receptor, far more potent than delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, and are not detected by the routine immunoassay, which is why a negative screen in a classic presentation does not exclude them. Treatment is supportive with titrated benzodiazepine sedation, which simultaneously controls agitation, raises the seizure threshold, reduces the adrenergic drive and lowers heat generation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg and repeat the dose after thirty minutes
options.rationale: Olanzapine is a reasonable adjunct once benzodiazepines have been loaded and agitation persists, and it is not the first agent when seizures and hyperthermia are present. Its anticholinergic burden also impairs sweating in a patient who is already at 38.4 degrees. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists are sprayed onto plant material and sold as herbal smoking blends, and their toxicity differs sharply from that of cannabis because they are full rather than partial agonists at the cannabinoid receptor and carry no cannabidiol to moderate the effect. The clinical picture includes severe agitation, psychosis, vomiting, seizures, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, and occasionally acute kidney injury or myocardial ischaemia, which are essentially unseen with cannabis itself. Routine urine immunoassays target delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol metabolites and do not cross-react with these compounds, so a negative cannabis screen is expected and must not be used to exclude the exposure. The chemical structures are altered continually to stay ahead of scheduling, which means potency and effect vary unpredictably between batches sold under the same brand name. Management is supportive, centred on titrated benzodiazepine sedation, active cooling, fluids, and monitoring for rhabdomyolysis and renal impairment.
key_points: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists are full agonists and far more potent than cannabis
Routine urine immunoassay does not detect them, so a negative screen is uninformative
Seizures, hyperthermia and severe agitation distinguish them from cannabis intoxication
Titrated benzodiazepine sedation is the first-line treatment, not an antipsychotic
Monitor for rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury after significant agitation or hyperthermia
explanation.pearls: Check a creatine kinase and renal function in anyone sedated after synthetic cannabinoid toxicity: acute kidney injury has been reported in clusters with these products even without prolonged struggling or marked hyperthermia.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Synthetic cannabinoid toxicity

subtopic_detail: New onset shoplifting in middle age with preserved memory and a near normal cognitive screen
stem: A 58-year-old accountant has had a third shoplifting charge in six months, taking items he could afford. His wife says that over two years he has become socially disinhibited, laughed when their dog died, eats sweet pastries daily with 11 kg weight gain, and no longer starts conversation.

data_table.Montreal Cognitive Assessment: 26 of 30, losing points only on fluency and abstraction
data_table.Magnetic resonance imaging: Bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a specialist cognitive and neurology service
options.rationale: Progressive disinhibition, loss of empathy, apathy, compulsive repetitive behaviour and hyperorality with carbohydrate craving are the core diagnostic features of behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, and the imaging corroborates them. Memory is characteristically preserved early, so a near normal cognitive screen argues for the diagnosis rather than against it, and specialist assessment is needed for neuropsychology, genetic counselling and medicolegal input into the charges. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

options.text: Diagnose kleptomania and refer for therapy
options.rationale: Kleptomania requires rising tension before the theft and relief or gratification afterwards, with the person recognising the act as wrong, and it typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood. He shows puzzlement rather than tension or remorse, and the onset in middle age alongside other behavioural change points to an acquired cause. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

options.text: Start naltrexone for the impulsive behaviour
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists are used for impulse control disorders such as gambling and are not a treatment for behaviour arising from frontal degeneration. Treating the symptom pharmacologically without establishing the cause would also leave the driving, financial and medicolegal consequences unaddressed. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

options.text: Start an antidepressant and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Apathy in frontotemporal dementia is frequently misread as depression, and this is the commonest initial misdiagnosis, but he reports no low mood, no sleep disturbance and no anhedonia, and apathy without subjective sadness is the distinguishing pattern. Serotonergic agents can help the compulsive and disinhibited behaviours later but do not substitute for making the diagnosis. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

options.text: Refer to forensic psychiatry for possible feigning
options.rationale: Feigning would be a consideration if the presentation had begun after the charges and served an obvious external incentive, whereas his wife dates the change to two years before any legal involvement. Structural imaging showing focal atrophy also provides objective corroboration that exaggeration cannot produce. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

explanation.summary: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is the commonest cause of dementia with onset before 60 years and is defined by progressive change in personality and social conduct rather than by amnesia. The diagnostic criteria require three of six features: behavioural disinhibition, apathy or inertia, loss of sympathy or empathy, perseverative or compulsive behaviour, hyperorality or dietary change, and a dysexecutive neuropsychological profile with relative sparing of memory and visuospatial function. That sparing is precisely why bedside screening tools perform poorly, since instruments weighted towards memory and orientation can return a near normal score in a person whose social functioning has collapsed, and the commonest misdiagnoses are depression, bipolar disorder and a primary personality disorder. New onset criminal behaviour in middle age, particularly theft, trespass and sexually inappropriate conduct, is a recognised presentation and carries obvious medicolegal implications for culpability and for driving. Around 40 per cent of cases have a family history and a significant proportion carry mutations in the C9orf72, MAPT or GRN genes, so genetic counselling is part of specialist assessment.
key_points: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia presents with conduct change, not memory loss
Diagnosis needs three of six features including disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and hyperorality
A near normal Montreal Cognitive Assessment does not exclude it, as memory is spared early
New onset criminal behaviour in middle age is a recognised presentation
A family history is present in around 40 per cent, so genetic counselling forms part of assessment
explanation.pearls: Cholinesterase inhibitors are not indicated in frontotemporal dementia and can worsen disinhibition and agitation, which is the opposite of their effect in Alzheimer disease, so an empirical trial while awaiting the specialist opinion is actively unhelpful.

subtopic_detail: first line treatment for repetitive hair pulling causing visible loss and concealment
stem: A 22 year old student has pulled out her own hair since she was fourteen and has a bare patch at her crown she keeps covered. Tension rises before pulling and is relieved afterwards. She has no obsessions or rituals.

data_table.Examination: Incomplete alopecia at the vertex, hairs of varying lengths, no scarring
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and iron studies normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Low dose olanzapine at night, reviewed in six weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have some evidence as augmentation in refractory cases but carry metabolic burden that is hard to justify as an initial step in a young woman. They sit well behind behavioural therapy in the treatment sequence. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Advise that this is a habit that will settle with time
options.rationale: Trichotillomania is a chronic condition with a waxing and waning course that rarely remits without treatment, and this advice offers a fragment of a therapeutic technique without the structure that makes it work. It also risks her hearing her distress as trivial. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Habit reversal training with a competing response
options.rationale: Hair pulling with premonitory tension and subsequent relief, without obsessions or appearance related beliefs, is trichotillomania, for which habit reversal training within a behavioural package has the strongest evidence and outperforms any medication. Awareness training addresses the automatic pulling that occurs during sedentary activities. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: A serotonin reuptake inhibitor at the higher dose range
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are effective in obsessive compulsive disorder but trials in trichotillomania have been largely negative, which is one of the clearest pharmacological differences between these related conditions. They remain useful for a comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Dermatology referral for biopsy and a topical corticosteroid
options.rationale: The clinical picture of irregular alopecia with hairs of differing lengths and intact skin is characteristic of pulling, whereas alopecia areata gives smooth round patches with exclamation mark hairs and tinea capitis gives scaling with broken hairs. Biopsy and topical steroid treat neither the behaviour nor its cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Trichotillomania sits within the obsessive compulsive and related disorders but differs from obsessive compulsive disorder in both phenomenology and treatment response. Pulling is preceded by mounting tension or an urge and followed by relief or gratification, and it occurs in both a focused mode, where the person is aware and often distressed, and an automatic mode during sedentary activities such as reading, studying or screen time. There are no obsessions, and the absence of appearance related preoccupation distinguishes it from body dysmorphic disorder, in which hair removal is driven by a belief that the hair itself is defective. The dermatological differential matters because irregular patches with hairs of varying length and normal underlying skin point to pulling, whereas smooth patches with exclamation mark hairs suggest alopecia areata and scaling with broken hairs suggests tinea capitis. Habit reversal training, usually delivered within a broader behavioural package, is first line, and unlike obsessive compulsive disorder the condition responds poorly to serotonin reuptake inhibitors, with N-acetylcysteine having modest supporting evidence as an adjunct.
key_points: Premonitory tension with relief after pulling is the defining phenomenology
Automatic pulling during sedentary activity requires awareness training to address
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors work in obsessive compulsive disorder but not in trichotillomania
Irregular patches with varying hair lengths and normal skin distinguish it dermatologically
Habit reversal training within a behavioural package is first line treatment
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about trichophagia, because swallowing pulled hair can form a trichobezoar that extends into the small bowel as Rapunzel syndrome and presents with obstruction, and it requires surgical rather than psychiatric management.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: identifying a stimulant beverage load before diagnosing a primary anxiety disorder in a young adult
stem: A 21-year-old man has four months of palpitations, tremor and restlessness, and twice left a worksite convinced he was about to collapse. Since moving to night shifts five months ago he drinks four to six energy drinks, a pre-workout powder and two to three coffees daily. He has no low mood or persistent worry.

data_table.Examination: Pulse 98 /min, fine postural tremor, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, electrolytes and electrocardiogram normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Commence a low dose serotonin reuptake inhibitor
options.rationale: Serotonergic therapy is first line for a primary anxiety disorder, but he lacks the pervasive worry, avoidance or unexpected attacks outside the stimulant context that would define one. Treating before removing the pharmacological driver means an antidepressant is credited with a response that dietary change would have produced. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders)

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines have a narrow role in short term crisis management and carry dependence risk in a young man with an ongoing stimulant exposure. Sedating the effects of a stimulant he continues to consume treats neither the symptom nor its cause. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for panic
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy is effective for panic disorder, and interoceptive exposure deliberately provokes the bodily sensations that are feared. Delivering it while a pharmacological agent is generating those same sensations undermines the therapy and the formulation. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders)

options.text: Arrange ambulatory electrocardiographic monitoring
options.rationale: Cardiac investigation is warranted for palpitations with syncope, exertional onset, structural signs or an abnormal resting electrocardiogram, and none of these are present. Repeated negative testing tends to entrench health anxiety rather than resolve it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
